title: Staying active and engaged at home after surgery or rehab in NJ
dek: How Medicare covers therapy at home and at the clinic, how to stick with the therapist's plan, prevent a fall and keep the mind busy during recovery, and who in New Jersey can help.
keyFacts: Medicare home health is $0 for covered services if your parent is homebound and needs part-time skilled care.
Outpatient physical therapy: after the Part B deductible you pay 20%, with no yearly limit on medically necessary therapy.
The CDC says more than one in four people 65+ falls each year, and one fall doubles the chance of another.
Medicare does not pay for home meal delivery. County meal programs can help.
body:
Coming home after surgery, a hospital stay or a few weeks in rehab is a relief. It can also be the moment things quietly go wrong. The days get long, the walker sits in the corner, and a person who was busy a month ago spends most of the day in one chair.

In our October 2026 conversations with North Jersey instructors, families and care professionals, coming home after surgery or rehab came up as a turning point. Families told us what they wanted most: for their mom or dad to stay safe at home, avoid a fall, stay sharp and have something to look forward to every week. This guide covers how to get there, from Medicare therapy rules to small daily routines.

If your parent has not left the hospital yet, start with our hospital discharge guide for New Jersey families. It covers the discharge plan and the questions to ask before anyone signs papers.

What does Medicare cover for therapy at home or nearby?

There are two main paths. Which one fits depends on whether your parent can get out of the house.

Home health care (therapy comes to you)

Medicare covers home health services under Part A and Part B when a person needs part-time or intermittent skilled care and is "homebound." Medicare.gov says that means leaving home is not recommended because of the condition, or leaving takes help, like a walker, a wheelchair, special transportation or another person, and leaving normally takes a lot of effort.

Being homebound does not mean never leaving. Medicare.gov says a person can still leave for medical care and for short, infrequent outings, like religious services, and can still attend adult day care.

Home health can include skilled nursing, physical therapy, occupational therapy, speech therapy, medical social services and part-time home health aide help with things like bathing and walking. The aide help is only covered while your parent also gets skilled nursing or therapy.

  • Cost: you pay nothing for covered home health services. After the Part B deductible, you pay 20% of the Medicare-approved amount for covered medical equipment, like a walker.
  • How it starts: a doctor or other provider, such as a nurse practitioner, must see your parent in person, confirm the need and order the care. A Medicare-certified home health agency provides it.
  • Choosing an agency: the provider should give you a list of agencies that serve your area and tell you if their organization has a financial interest in any of them.
  • What it does not cover: 24-hour care, home meal delivery, housekeeping unrelated to the care plan, or personal care when that is the only help needed.

Outpatient physical therapy (you go to the clinic)

Once your parent can get out more easily, therapy usually moves to an outpatient clinic. Medicare Part B helps pay for medically necessary outpatient physical therapy when a doctor or other provider certifies the need. After the Part B deductible, you pay 20% of the Medicare-approved amount. Medicare.gov says there is no limit on how much Medicare pays for medically necessary outpatient therapy in a calendar year.

If your parent has a Medicare Advantage plan, the plan sets its own rules, networks and copays. Call the number on the card before the first visit. For free, unbiased help with Medicare questions, call New Jersey's State Health Insurance Assistance Program (SHIP) at 1-800-792-8820.

Getting to outpatient therapy

Three visits a week is hard when your parent cannot drive yet. Ask the clinic about early or late slots that fit a family member's schedule, and call your county paratransit service early. Many need several days' notice. Our guide to getting around when a parent stops driving lists the numbers.

How do you follow the therapist's plan without overdoing it?

The therapist's home exercise plan is the most important piece of paper in the house. The visits matter, but most of the progress happens between them.

  1. Ask for the plan in writing. Large print, with pictures if possible. Tape it where your parent sits most.
  2. Pick set times. Exercises after breakfast and after lunch are easier to remember than "twice a day."
  3. Write down what was done. A simple sheet with the date, the exercise and how it felt helps the therapist adjust the plan.
  4. Ask about limits. After hip, knee, back or heart surgery there are often rules about bending, lifting or reaching. Ask what is off limits and for how long.
  5. Know the warning signs. Ask the surgeon's office which symptoms mean "call us today" and which mean "call 911." Keep that list by the phone.

Family members can help most by showing up. A daughter who calls at 10 a.m. and says "let's do your leg lifts together" often gets more done than a reminder note. A spouse can walk the hallway alongside, if the therapist says that is safe.

Do not add new exercise on your own. If your parent wants more, ask the therapist what is safe to add. Once therapy ends, our guides to exercise at home and chair yoga are good next steps, with the doctor's OK.

How do you prevent a fall in the first weeks home?

The weeks after a hospital stay are a risky time. Strength is down, new medicines may cause dizziness, and the house was set up for the person your parent was before surgery.

The CDC says more than one in four people 65 and older falls each year, and falling once doubles the chance of falling again. It also notes that fear of falling can make people cut back on activity, which makes them weaker and more likely to fall. Staying gently active is part of staying safe.

  • Clear a wide path from the bed to the bathroom and from the chair to the kitchen. Remove throw rugs and cords.
  • Add night lights between the bedroom and bathroom.
  • Put everyday items between waist and shoulder height.
  • Ask the home health occupational therapist about grab bars, a shower chair or a raised toilet seat.
  • Ask the doctor or pharmacist to review every medicine, including over-the-counter sleep aids.
  • Wear sturdy shoes with backs, even inside. No loose slippers.
  • Get up slowly. Sit on the edge of the bed for a moment before standing.

Our full fall prevention guide covers a room-by-room home check and where to find help in New Jersey.

How do you keep the mind busy while the body heals?

Recovery is boring. That sounds small, but it matters. Long days with only television can lead to poor sleep, low mood and less interest in the exercises that speed healing.

Try to give each day a shape: exercises in the morning, something engaging in the afternoon, a phone call or visit before dinner. Even 30 minutes of real focus helps.

  • Puzzles and games: crosswords, jigsaw puzzles on a lap tray, cards, a weekly online game with a grandchild.
  • Music: a playlist of songs from their twenties, a radio station they love, or picking up an old instrument.
  • Hands-on projects: knitting, sketching, sorting family photos, a small herb garden on the windowsill.
  • Learning: audiobooks from the public library, free online classes, or a language app. See learning something new.
  • Telling their story: recovery can be a good time to record family memories. See our guide to writing a parent's life story.
  • People: a standing coffee visit, a video call with family, a call from a friend from church or the senior center.
Give each day three anchors: the exercises, one thing to enjoy and one person to talk to.

Watch for signs of depression, like losing interest in everything, sleeping much more or less, or saying things like "what's the point." Mention them to the doctor. Depression is treatable, and the doctor would rather hear about it early.

Can you bring activities to the house?

Yes. Many older adults stop doing what they love only because they can no longer get there. Recovery makes that worse for a while. Bringing the activity home bridges the gap.

Some ideas:

  • Ask the senior center or library whether a class is offered by phone or video. Some library programs, like Plainfield Public Library's monthly memoir club, meet on Zoom.
  • Invite the regular card group or book club to meet at your parent's home for a few weeks.
  • Look into a private instructor who comes to the house for art, music, cards or gentle movement. In our October 2026 conversations, private instructors in North Jersey said they generally charge about $60 to $150 an hour, depending on the activity. Many travel about 15 to 25 minutes and may charge more for longer trips.
  • Choose a regular day and time. Families told us they want their parent to have something to look forward to every week.

Our guide to activities for homebound older adults has more options, and our free and discounted list covers low-cost ideas.

Safety first when someone new comes to the door

Trust came up in almost every conversation we had. Before anyone works with your parent at home, check a few things:

  • Ask about background checks and whether they carry their own liability insurance.
  • Get two references and call them.
  • Be home for the first visit, or arrange a video call during it.
  • Pay by check or card to the business, never cash in advance, and never let anyone handle your parent's checkbook or bank cards.

Our guide to vetting in-home help walks through the full checklist.

Who in New Jersey can help during recovery?

Medicare does not pay for home meal delivery or for help with chores when that is the only need. New Jersey has public programs that fill some of those gaps.

NeedWhere to start
Local services, home help programs, caregiver supportNJ Aging and Disability Resource Connection (ADRC), 1-877-222-3737. It connects you with your county office on aging.
Meals at homeYour county's home-delivered meals program. See Meals on Wheels in NJ.
Rides to therapy and appointmentsCounty paratransit. Call your county office on aging or see our county pages.
Medicare questions and appealsSHIP, 1-800-792-8820.
Food, utilities and other helpNJ 211: dial 2-1-1 or 1-877-652-1148.

If your parent needs more help than family can give, a care manager can build a plan and coordinate services. See Find care help and our guide to geriatric care managers. If you are the one doing most of the helping, read caregiver burnout and respite care in NJ early, before you need them.

Recovery takes longer than most people expect. Small steps count. A walk to the mailbox, a finished puzzle, a good phone call. Those add up to a person who feels like themselves again.

faq.q: My mom just got home from rehab. How do I keep her from sitting in a chair all day?
faq.a: Give each day a shape: the therapist's exercises at set times, one thing she enjoys, and one person to talk to. A weekly activity on the calendar, at home or out, gives her something to look forward to. Ask her therapist what activity is safe right now.

faq.q: Does Medicare pay for physical therapy at home after surgery?
faq.a: Yes, through home health care, if a doctor or other provider sees your parent in person, orders the care and confirms they are homebound and need part-time skilled care. A Medicare-certified agency provides it, and you pay nothing for covered services. Equipment like a walker is 20% after the Part B deductible.

faq.q: What does homebound mean for Medicare?
faq.a: Leaving home is not recommended because of the condition, or it takes help like a walker, a wheelchair, special transportation or another person, and leaving normally takes a lot of effort. Short, infrequent outings, like religious services or adult day care, are allowed.

faq.q: Is there a limit on outpatient physical therapy under Medicare?
faq.a: Medicare.gov says there is no limit on how much Medicare pays for medically necessary outpatient therapy in a calendar year. After the Part B deductible, you pay 20% of the Medicare-approved amount. Medicare Advantage plans set their own copays and networks.

faq.q: Who can help with meals and rides during recovery in New Jersey?
faq.a: Call the NJ Aging and Disability Resource Connection at 1-877-222-3737. It connects you with your county office on aging, which runs or refers to home-delivered meals, paratransit and other help. You can also dial 2-1-1.

sources: CDC: Facts about older adult falls
NJ Division of Disability Services: Transportation
seoDesc: Helping a parent stay active at home after surgery or rehab in NJ: Medicare home health and PT, fall prevention, keeping busy and local help.

title: POLST in New Jersey: what it is and how to get one
dek: The green medical order form that tells EMS and hospitals what treatment a seriously ill person wants. Who it is for, who signs it, where to keep it and how to change it.
keyFacts: POLST stands for Practitioner Orders for Life-Sustaining Treatment.
In New Jersey it must be signed by a physician, advanced practice nurse or physician assistant, plus the patient or their representative.
EMS, hospitals and nursing homes in New Jersey must follow a completed POLST.
Any section left blank means full treatment for that section.
The free state form is on the NJ Department of Health site in six languages.
body:
A POLST is a one-page medical order that tells ambulance crews, hospitals and nursing homes what treatment a seriously ill person wants in an emergency. In New Jersey it stands for Practitioner Orders for Life-Sustaining Treatment. It covers CPR, breathing tubes, hospital transfers and feeding tubes, and it is signed by both the patient and a physician, advanced practice nurse or physician assistant.

It is meant for people with a serious, advancing illness or frailty, not for healthy adults planning ahead. Under New Jersey law, everyone from the EMTs in your parent's living room to the staff at a hospital must follow a completed POLST. If your mom or dad is getting sicker and has strong feelings about what should happen in a crisis, this is the form that makes those wishes work at 2 a.m.

This guide explains what the form does. It is not legal or medical advice. Your parent's doctor or nurse practitioner is the right person to talk through the choices, and an elder law attorney can help with the legal documents that go alongside it.

What is a POLST form in New Jersey?

A POLST turns a person's wishes about life-sustaining treatment into signed medical orders that travel with them. New Jersey created it by law in 2011, and a 2019 law renamed it and let physician assistants sign it.

The state form is a standard two-sided sheet, often printed on bright green paper so it is easy to spot, though a signed copy on any color is valid. The current version from the New Jersey Department of Health has six parts:

  • A. Goals of care. What matters most right now, such as more time, comfort, staying out of the hospital or reaching a family milestone. This part is not a medical order. It explains the choices that follow.
  • B. Medical interventions. For when the person is breathing or has a pulse. The choices are Full Treatment, Limited Treatment (things like antibiotics and IV fluids, generally avoiding intensive care) or Symptom Treatment Only, which focuses on comfort.
  • C. Artificially given fluids and nutrition. No artificial nutrition, a defined trial period, or long-term artificial nutrition. Food and drink by mouth are always offered if possible.
  • D. CPR and airway. Attempt resuscitation, or Do Not Attempt Resuscitation (Allow Natural Death). A separate choice covers whether to put in a breathing tube if the person is struggling to breathe but still has a pulse.
  • E. Surrogate authority. Whether a named family member or other decision maker may change the form later if the person can no longer decide.
  • F. Signatures. The practitioner's signature is mandatory. The patient, or their representative, signs too.
Blank sections mean full treatment

The form says any section left blank means full treatment for that section. If your dad does not want a breathing tube, that box has to be checked. Do not leave it to memory.

Who should have a POLST?

A POLST is for people with a serious, life-limiting illness, advanced frailty or strong wishes about end-of-life care. It is voluntary. No one is required to have one.

The state's consumer brochure says you should consider one if you are seriously ill with an advanced illness, frail and having trouble with daily activities, worried about losing the ability to make your own decisions soon, or living in a nursing home or hospice. New Jersey's law describes it as recommended for people with advanced chronic progressive illness or a life expectancy of less than five years.

Guidance for New Jersey clinicians suggests a simple test: would the doctor be surprised if this person died in the next three to five years? If not, a POLST conversation probably makes sense. The same guidance says using a POLST to limit treatment is generally not appropriate for someone who is medically stable with many years ahead, unless that is their own clear preference.

Say your mother is 84, has heart failure and has been in the hospital twice since spring. She has told you she never wants to be on a ventilator again. A POLST is exactly the tool for her. Your healthy 66-year-old uncle who just retired probably needs an advance directive instead.

An advance directive speaks for you later. A POLST is a doctor's order that works right now.

How is a POLST different from a living will, advance directive or DNR?

An advance directive is a legal document you can fill out on your own. A POLST is a medical order signed by a practitioner. Most people who need a POLST should also have an advance directive, because the two do different jobs.

DocumentWhat it does
Proxy directive (health care power of attorney)Names a health care representative to make decisions if you cannot. The state recommends every adult have an advance directive.
Instruction directive (living will)Describes the treatment you would or would not want in different situations. Takes effect only after a doctor finds you cannot make your own decisions.
POLSTSigned medical orders for current treatment choices. Must be followed right away by EMS and all health care settings.
Out-of-hospital DNRAn older New Jersey form that covers only CPR. It is still valid, but a POLST covers CPR plus other treatment. New Jersey Hospital Association guidance says a signed POLST replaces it.

The difference matters most in an emergency. When someone calls 911, the crew has no time to read a living will and decide whether it applies. Without a POLST or another valid medical order, your parent will get routine emergency care, which can include CPR and a breathing tube. A POLST gives the crew orders they can follow on the spot.

A POLST does not cancel an advance directive. The Department of Health's brochure says it complements one, and you may still need an advance directive to name a health care representative. Signing a new POLST does void any earlier POLST. If the documents seem to conflict, talk with the practitioner soon and update whichever is out of date. Our estate planning guide covers advance directives and powers of attorney.

Who can sign a POLST in New Jersey, and how do you get one?

In New Jersey, a POLST must be signed by the patient's attending physician, advanced practice nurse (APN) or physician assistant (PA). The patient signs too, or their representative if they cannot.

You cannot complete a valid POLST alone at the kitchen table. It starts with a conversation.

  1. Ask for the conversation. Tell your parent's doctor, nurse practitioner or PA that you would like to talk about a POLST. Hospital palliative care teams, hospices and nursing homes do these conversations often.
  2. Bring what you have. Bring any advance directive, the name of the health care representative and a current list of diagnoses and medicines.
  3. Talk about goals first. State guidance encourages clinicians to start with what matters to the person and their prognosis, then talk about specific treatments. Ask plain questions: What would CPR likely mean for Dad? What does "limited treatment" look like at home?
  4. Fill in every section. The practitioner completes the form with your parent. Check that every box reflects what was decided, since blank sections mean full treatment.
  5. Decide on Section E. If your parent wants a family member to be able to change the orders later, they must check yes and name that person while they still can.
  6. Sign and make copies. The original goes home with your parent. Photocopies and faxes of a signed form are valid too.

The blank form is free on the New Jersey Department of Health POLST page, in English, Spanish, Hindi, Korean, Russian and Vietnamese. A printed form on its own is not valid without the practitioner's signature.

If your parent no longer has the capacity to decide, their health care representative or other legal decision maker can complete a POLST with the practitioner, based on what your parent wanted or, if that is unknown, their best interests. Our guide to guardianship in New Jersey explains what happens when no one has legal authority.

Where should you keep a POLST at home?

Keep the original where EMS will see it fast. New Jersey hospital association guidance suggests the refrigerator, by the phone, by the bed or on the inside of the front door.

  • Pick one spot and tell everyone, including aides, neighbors with a key and out-of-town siblings.
  • Do not lock it in a safe, a file cabinet or a sealed envelope. Responders need to read it.
  • Send the original with your parent to the hospital, rehab or a nursing home. The form itself says to send the original whenever the person is transferred.
  • Keep a copy in your own records and ask the doctor's office to put one in the chart.

Our printable emergency information sheet has a line for where the POLST and advance directive are kept, so whoever opens the fridge knows where to look.

Moving or visiting another state?

New Jersey law treats a POLST-type form signed in another state as valid here if it meets New Jersey's requirements. If your parent spends winters elsewhere, ask that state's doctors whether they honor New Jersey's form.

Will EMS and hospitals follow a POLST?

Yes. New Jersey law says a health care professional, health care institution or emergency care provider must treat a patient with a completed POLST according to the form.

A completed form has the patient's preferences, the patient's or representative's signature, and the practitioner's signature and date. EMS crews must follow those orders, and the original form should go with your parent to the hospital.

Disagreements do happen, often when a frightened relative asks for something different in the moment. State guidance says the POLST still controls and only the patient, or a surrogate authorized in Section E, can change it. If the family and the care team disagree about what the form means, the law points to the facility's own process, such as an ethics committee, or a court.

A POLST also never means "no care." The form itself says comfort measures will always be provided. Our guides on leaving the hospital and hospice and palliative care cover what comes next for many families.

How do you change or cancel a POLST?

A person who can make their own decisions can change or cancel their POLST at any time. To void the paper form, draw a line through all sections, write VOID in large letters, then sign and date it.

A new or changed order takes effect once the practitioner signs it. The form recommends a review whenever your parent moves to a new care setting, has a major change in health or changes their mind about treatment. A new primary doctor is a good moment to review it too.

If your parent has lost capacity, a surrogate can change the form only if your parent checked yes in Section E. If they checked no, no one else can change it. That is why this one box deserves a real conversation while your parent can still have it. Our guide on talking with a parent about care has ideas for starting hard conversations gently.

More guides that may help: advance directives in New Jersey.

faq.q: How do I get a POLST form for my mom in New Jersey?
faq.a: Ask her doctor, nurse practitioner or physician assistant for a POLST conversation. They complete the form with her and sign it. The blank form is free on the New Jersey Department of Health website, but it is not valid until a practitioner signs it.

faq.q: Is a POLST the same as a DNR in New Jersey?
faq.a: No. A POLST can include a Do Not Attempt Resuscitation order, but it also covers breathing tubes, hospital transfers and artificial nutrition. The older out-of-hospital DNR form is still valid, but New Jersey Hospital Association guidance says a signed POLST replaces it.

faq.q: Does my dad need a POLST if he already has a living will?
faq.a: If he is seriously ill or frail, probably yes. A living will only takes effect after a doctor finds he cannot decide for himself, and EMS cannot use it in an emergency. A POLST is a medical order crews can follow right away. He should keep both.

faq.q: Can a family member change a parent's POLST?
faq.a: Only if the parent checked yes in Section E and named that person while they still had capacity. Otherwise only the patient can change it. Any change takes effect once the practitioner signs.

faq.q: Where should a POLST be kept at home?
faq.a: Somewhere EMS will see it quickly, such as on the refrigerator, by the bed or inside the front door. Keep the original with the person and send it along whenever they go to a hospital or facility.

faq.q: Is a POLST from another state valid in New Jersey?
faq.a: New Jersey law treats a form signed in another state as valid if it meets New Jersey's requirements for a completed POLST.

title: Hospice vs. palliative care in NJ: what Medicare covers
dek: How hospice and palliative care differ, who qualifies for Medicare's hospice benefit, what families pay, and how to check and choose a hospice in New Jersey.
keyFacts: Palliative care can be given alongside treatment aimed at a cure. Hospice is for a life expectancy of 6 months or less.
Medicare Part A covers hospice from a Medicare-approved hospice, with no deductible.
Hospice drug copays are up to $5 per prescription. Inpatient respite costs 5% of the Medicare-approved amount.
Hospice does not cover room and board in a home, assisted living or nursing home.
NJ Department of Health complaint hotline for health care facilities: 1-800-792-9770.
body:
Palliative care is extra support for anyone with a serious illness, at any stage, and you can keep getting treatment aimed at a cure. Hospice is a kind of palliative care for people who are expected to live six months or less and who have decided to stop treatment meant to cure the illness. Both focus on comfort, symptoms and the whole family.

The money works differently too. Medicare Part A covers hospice with almost no out-of-pocket cost, from a Medicare-approved hospice. Palliative care is usually billed like regular doctor visits under Part B, with the usual coinsurance. If your mom or dad is getting sicker, it is fair to raise both with their doctor now.

This guide explains the rules. It is not medical or financial advice, and for coverage questions about a specific plan, the free SHIP counselors at 1-800-792-8820 can help.

What is the difference between hospice and palliative care?

The main difference is curative treatment. With palliative care, your parent can keep chemotherapy, dialysis or any other treatment. With hospice, treatment aimed at curing the terminal illness stops, and care shifts fully to comfort.

Palliative careHospice
WhoAnyone with a serious illnessPeople with a life expectancy of 6 months or less if the illness runs its normal course
Curative treatmentCan continueStops for the terminal illness
WhereHospital, clinic, nursing home or homeMostly at home, also in assisted living, nursing homes and inpatient hospice units
MedicareUsually Part B, 20% coinsurance after the deductiblePart A hospice benefit, little or no cost for covered care

Palliative care teams include specialist doctors and nurses, social workers and often chaplains. They treat pain, breathlessness, nausea, anxiety and fatigue, and they help families understand choices. People with heart failure, COPD, cancer, dementia, Parkinson's and kidney disease all use palliative care.

Hospice brings a similar team home. A nurse visits regularly, an aide helps with bathing, and a social worker and chaplain are available. A hospice nurse and doctor are on call 24 hours a day, 7 days a week. Hospice is not only for cancer, and choosing it does not mean giving up on care. Your parent still gets treatment for other conditions, like blood pressure medicine.

Palliative care can start the day of a diagnosis. Hospice is for the last months, and it works best when it is not left to the last days.

Who qualifies for the Medicare hospice benefit?

Your parent qualifies if they have Medicare Part A, a doctor certifies that they are terminally ill with a life expectancy of six months or less, and they choose comfort care instead of treatment to cure the illness.

  • Two certifications. The hospice doctor and your parent's regular doctor, if they have one, both certify the terminal illness at the start.
  • An election statement. Your parent, or their representative, signs a Hospice Election Statement naming the hospice, the start date and the attending doctor they want.
  • Benefit periods. Hospice comes in two 90-day periods, then an unlimited number of 60-day periods. Living past six months is fine. The hospice doctor recertifies at the start of each new period, after a face-to-face visit once the first six months have passed.
  • A one-time consultation. Before choosing hospice, your parent can meet once with a hospice medical director or hospice doctor to talk through options, even if they decide not to enroll.

Your parent can stop hospice at any time and go back to treatment aimed at a cure. If they qualify again later, they can return to hospice. Medicare warns that no one should ask your parent to sign forms to stop hospice unless they asked to stop.

If your parent is in a Medicare Advantage plan, Original Medicare pays for the hospice care. They can keep the plan for extra benefits and for health problems unrelated to the terminal illness, as long as they keep paying its premium.

What does Medicare cover in hospice, and what will you pay?

Medicare covers nearly everything related to the terminal illness: the team's visits, medicines for pain and symptoms, equipment, supplies, therapy, counseling and short inpatient stays. There is no deductible. The two main costs are small copays and room and board.

ItemWhat your parent pays
Hospice team visits, nursing, aide and social workNothing
Medical equipment and supplies, like a hospital bed, wheelchair or cathetersNothing
Outpatient drugs for pain and symptom controlUp to $5 per prescription
Inpatient respite care (up to 5 days at a time)5% of the Medicare-approved amount
Room and board at home, in assisted living or in a nursing homeNot covered

Respite care gives a worn-out family caregiver a break. The hospice arranges a short stay in a hospice unit, hospital or nursing home, up to five days each time, on an occasional basis. Short inpatient stays for pain and symptoms that the hospice arranges are covered too.

Room and board is the cost families most often miss. If your dad lives in a nursing home or assisted living, hospice covers his hospice care there, but the monthly facility bill continues. If he has NJ FamilyCare (Medicaid), ask the facility and the plan how the bill is handled. Our guide to NJ FamilyCare and MLTSS explains long-term care coverage.

Call the hospice first

Once hospice starts, call the hospice team before going to the emergency room, calling an ambulance or seeing another provider for the terminal illness. If the hospice did not arrange the care, Medicare says you could owe the full cost.

A Medigap policy covers the hospice drug copays and respite coinsurance. Our guide to Medicare Advantage and Medigap explains those plans.

Does Medicare pay for palliative care?

Often, yes, but there is no separate palliative care benefit. Visits from palliative care doctors, nurse practitioners and physician assistants are generally covered like other Part B doctor services, so your parent usually pays 20% of the Medicare-approved amount after the Part B deductible, which is $283 in 2026.

Where your parent gets it changes how it is billed.

  • In the hospital. Many New Jersey hospitals have palliative care teams that see patients during a stay. Ask the attending doctor or nurse for a palliative care consult.
  • In a clinic. Some health systems run outpatient palliative clinics, often near their cancer or heart centers.
  • At home. Some home health agencies and hospices run home palliative programs. Coverage depends on the program and your parent's insurance, so ask exactly what is billed and to whom.

Medicare Advantage plans, NJ FamilyCare and private insurers each set their own rules. Call the number on the card and ask whether a specific palliative program is in network. The New Jersey Department of Health's end-of-life resources page lists palliative care programs at many New Jersey health systems.

How do I choose a hospice in New Jersey?

Make sure the hospice is Medicare-approved and licensed by the New Jersey Department of Health, check its ratings on Medicare's Care Compare, and then call two or three to compare.

  1. Get names. Ask your parent's doctor, the hospital social worker or a geriatric care manager. If your parent is in a Medicare Advantage plan, the plan must help find a Medicare-approved hospice nearby.
  2. Check Care Compare. Search Medicare Care Compare for hospices by ZIP code. Hospices with at least 75 completed family surveys get a Family Caregiver Survey Rating from 1 to 5 stars, based on what families said about their care. Smaller hospices may show survey results without stars.
  3. Confirm the state license. The Department of Health licenses hospices in New Jersey, and the license must be posted at the hospice. Use the state's health facility search (choose the acute care search, which includes hospices) or ask the hospice for its license.
  4. Interview. Use the questions below. Pay attention to how quickly they call back and how clearly they explain things.

Your parent can change hospice providers once in each benefit period, so the first choice is not permanent.

Be wary of anyone who offers gifts, free housekeeping or other perks for signing up, or who pushes hospice when no doctor has raised it. Medicare says only a doctor can certify that someone is terminally ill. Report suspected fraud to 1-800-633-4227, and see our guide to scams aimed at older adults in New Jersey.

What questions should we ask a hospice before choosing?

Ask how fast they can start, who answers the phone at night and how often a nurse will visit. The answers tell you more than any brochure.

  • How soon can you do the first visit after a referral?
  • Who answers after hours, and how fast will a nurse come to the house at night or on a weekend?
  • How often will the nurse and aide visit at first? Who decides when visits increase?
  • Which medicines and supplies will you cover, and which will you not? Can we get that list in writing?
  • Do you have your own inpatient unit, or which facilities do you use for symptom care and respite?
  • Do you work with my parent's nursing home or assisted living? How often do you visit there?
  • Do you have staff experienced with dementia, heart failure or the illness my parent has?
  • Can my parent keep their regular doctor as the attending doctor?
  • What volunteer, chaplain and music or companion support do you offer?
  • What grief support do you offer the family afterward?

Federal rules require every Medicare hospice to make bereavement services available to the family for up to a year after a death. Ask what that looks like in practice, from phone calls to support groups. Our guide to grief support in New Jersey has more.

What should families do if hospice care is not going well?

Start with the hospice's nurse manager or director. If that does not fix it, you can complain to the state or to Medicare's quality review organization.

  • New Jersey Department of Health. Its 24-hour complaint hotline for health care facilities is 1-800-792-9770.
  • Medicare. You can file a quality of care complaint with Medicare's Beneficiary and Family Centered Care Quality Improvement Organization (BFCC-QIO), or call 1-800-633-4227 for help.
  • Discharge from hospice. If the hospice says your parent no longer qualifies and you disagree, you have the right to a fast review by the BFCC-QIO. The hospice should give you a notice explaining how. If it does not, ask for it.

Hospice works best alongside clear paperwork. A POLST makes sure an ambulance crew follows your parent's wishes, and our caregiver respite guide covers more ways to get a break.

Ready to pick a hospice? Our guide to finding and paying for hospice care in New Jersey walks through Care Compare and the questions to ask, and our Essex County hospice guide lists the hospices that serve Essex towns.

To find a palliative care team, including the NJ FamilyCare benefit that started in April 2026, see our palliative care guide.

faq.q: How do I know if my mom is ready for hospice?
faq.a: Ask her doctor directly whether she would qualify, meaning a life expectancy of six months or less if the illness runs its normal course. Medicare also covers a one-time consultation with a hospice doctor to talk through options, even if she decides not to enroll.

faq.q: Can my dad get palliative care and still have chemotherapy?
faq.a: Yes. Palliative care can be given alongside treatment meant to cure or control the illness. Hospice is different. It stops treatment aimed at curing the terminal illness.

faq.q: Does Medicare pay for hospice in a nursing home in New Jersey?
faq.a: Medicare covers the hospice care itself in a nursing home or assisted living. It does not cover room and board, so the facility's regular bill continues unless another source, such as NJ FamilyCare, pays it.

faq.q: What happens if my parent lives longer than six months on hospice?
faq.a: They can keep getting hospice. After two 90-day periods there are unlimited 60-day periods, as long as the hospice doctor recertifies that they are still terminally ill.

faq.q: Can you leave hospice once you start?
faq.a: Yes. Your parent can stop hospice at any time and return to regular Medicare coverage and treatment. If they qualify later, they can go back to hospice.

faq.q: How do I check a hospice in New Jersey?
faq.a: Look it up on Medicare Care Compare for star ratings and family survey results, confirm its New Jersey Department of Health license, and ask about after-hours response, visit frequency and what they will not cover.

title: Free memory screening in NJ: where to go and what comes next
dek: Where older adults in New Jersey can get a free memory screening, what Medicare covers, what a screening can and cannot tell you, what happens after a worrying result and how to bring it up with a parent.
keyFacts: Medicare's yearly Wellness visit includes a cognitive assessment. You pay nothing if the provider accepts assignment.
If problems are found, Medicare Part B covers a separate cognitive assessment and care plan visit (20% coinsurance after the deductible).
The Alzheimer's Foundation of America offers free virtual memory screenings: 866-232-8484.
A screening is not a diagnosis. Medicines, thyroid problems, low B12, poor sleep and depression can all affect memory and may be treatable.
Alzheimer's New Jersey helpline: 1-888-280-6055. Alzheimer's Association 24/7 Helpline: 1-800-272-3900.
body:
A memory screening is a short set of questions, usually 10 to 15 minutes, that checks memory, language and thinking. In New Jersey you can get one free in two main ways. Medicare's yearly Wellness visit includes a cognitive assessment at no cost when the doctor accepts Medicare. The Alzheimer's Foundation of America also offers free screenings by video call to anyone, at 866-232-8484.

A screening cannot diagnose dementia. It tells you whether a fuller evaluation makes sense. Many things that cause memory trouble, like medication side effects, thyroid problems, low vitamin B12, poor sleep or depression, can be treated. So a worrying result means see a doctor soon. It does not mean the worst. This guide is general information and not medical advice.

What is a memory screening?

It is a brief check of memory and thinking, similar to a blood pressure or cholesterol screening. The person answers questions or does simple tasks, and the screener looks for signs that a closer look is needed.

A screener might ask your mom to remember a few words and repeat them later, draw a clock, name some objects or answer questions about the date. The Alzheimer's Foundation of America describes its screenings as simple, quick and noninvasive, and says they are confidential.

What a screening can do:

  • Give a starting point to compare against next year.
  • Flag changes that need a full medical evaluation.
  • Open a conversation with the doctor that might not happen otherwise.

What it cannot do:

  • Diagnose Alzheimer's disease or any other kind of dementia.
  • Find the cause of memory problems.
  • Rule out a problem completely. If you are still worried, see a doctor.

Help your parent do their best. Make sure they bring their glasses and wear their hearing aids. You want the questions heard and read clearly. Our guide to hearing aids in New Jersey explains how to get hearing checked.

Does Medicare cover a memory screening?

Yes. Medicare's yearly Wellness visit includes a cognitive assessment, and you pay nothing for the visit if the provider accepts assignment. If the doctor sees signs of trouble, Medicare covers a separate, more thorough cognitive assessment visit.

Medicare visitWhat it includesCost
Yearly Wellness visitA cognitive assessment to look for signs of dementia, plus a review of medicines and a prevention plan$0 if the provider accepts assignment. The Part B deductible does not apply.
Cognitive assessment and care plan visitA full review of thinking and memory, a diagnosis if one is found, a care plan and referrals20% of the Medicare-approved amount after the Part B deductible

A few details trip families up. The first Wellness visit cannot happen within 12 months of starting Part B or of the "Welcome to Medicare" visit. After that, it is covered once every 12 months. It is a conversation-based visit, not a physical. If the doctor adds tests or treats other problems at the same visit, you may owe a copay or coinsurance for those.

When you book, say clearly that you want the Annual Wellness Visit and that you would like the memory part done. If you already have specific worries, Medicare suggests booking a separate appointment to talk them through, so the Wellness visit can stay focused on prevention. For a cognitive assessment, Medicare says your parent can bring someone, like a spouse, friend or caregiver, to help listen and answer questions. That is a good job for you.

If your parent has a Medicare Advantage plan, call the number on the plan card to ask how the Wellness visit works and which doctors are in network. For help comparing coverage, call New Jersey's free SHIP Medicare counseling line at 1-800-792-8820, or see Medicare 101 for New Jerseyans.

Where can I get a free memory screening in New Jersey?

The two most reliable options are your parent's own doctor through the Medicare Wellness visit and the Alzheimer's Foundation of America's free virtual screenings. Community screenings also turn up at senior centers, libraries and health fairs.

  • Your parent's primary care doctor. This is usually the best place. The doctor knows your parent's history and medicines and can order follow-up tests right away.
  • Alzheimer's Foundation of America virtual screenings. Free, one-on-one screenings by secure video on a computer, tablet or smartphone. AFA says there is no minimum age and no insurance is needed. It also offers a short online self-test, though a screening with a trained screener tells you more. Call 866-232-8484 to schedule or visit alzfdn.org. The same number reaches AFA's helpline, staffed by licensed social workers from 9 a.m. to 9 p.m. Eastern, seven days a week.
  • Community events. Senior centers, public libraries, hospitals and county offices on aging sometimes host free screening days. Ask your county office on aging through the ADRC at 1-877-222-3737, or check the senior center calendar in your county. Our county pages list local offices.
  • The helplines. Alzheimer's New Jersey (1-888-280-6055) and the Alzheimer's Association's 24/7 Helpline (1-800-272-3900) can talk through your worries and point you to local help.

Be wary of anyone selling a screening, a supplement or a "brain test" by phone or at the door. Free means free. Our scams guide covers common pitches aimed at older adults.

What else can cause memory problems?

Plenty, and some of it is fixable. The National Institute on Aging lists medication side effects, depression and anxiety, thyroid, kidney or liver problems, low vitamin B12, sleep problems, infections, alcohol and head injuries among the causes.

Big life changes count too. The NIA notes that someone coping with the death of a spouse or a recent retirement may feel sad, lonely or worried enough to become forgetful for a while. Those problems often improve as life settles. If they last more than a few weeks, see the doctor.

Normal aging and dementia also look different. The NIA puts it this way.

Normal agingPossible dementia
Making a bad decision once in a whileMaking poor judgments a lot of the time
Missing a monthly paymentProblems taking care of monthly bills
Forgetting which day it is and remembering laterLosing track of the date or time of year
Sometimes forgetting which word to useTrouble having a conversation
Losing things from time to timeMisplacing things often and being unable to find them

Other signs that it is time to talk with a doctor include asking the same questions over and over, getting lost in familiar places and trouble following a recipe or directions.

What happens if the screening shows a problem?

The next step is a full evaluation with your parent's doctor, who may then refer them to a specialist or memory center. Getting a diagnosis often takes more than one visit.

  1. See the primary care doctor. Bring the screening results, a full list of medicines and supplements, and your own written notes about what you have noticed and when it started.
  2. Tests to look for other causes. According to the NIA, doctors may ask about health and daily life, test memory and problem solving, order blood and urine tests, check for depression, and order brain scans such as a CT or MRI.
  3. A specialist if needed. This might be a geriatrician, neurologist, geriatric psychiatrist or neuropsychologist. Memory clinics at large hospitals bring these specialists together.
  4. A care plan. If dementia or mild cognitive impairment is found, ask for Medicare's cognitive assessment and care plan visit. Ask too whether the practice takes part in Medicare's GUIDE Model, a program that offers extra dementia support for people living with dementia and their unpaid caregivers.
  5. Follow-up. The NIA says people with memory problems should go back to the doctor every six to 12 months.

An early answer gives your family time. The NIA notes that an early diagnosis can help people plan for the future, handle legal and money matters, address safety and look at treatments while they work best. It can also open the door to clinical trials. Alzheimer's New Jersey runs a Clinical Trial Connections program that helps families find studies nearby.

If the diagnosis is dementia, our guide on where New Jersey families can turn after a diagnosis covers helplines, memory cafes, adult day programs and respite. It is also a good time to get legal papers in order while your parent can take part. See estate planning basics.

How do I bring up a memory screening with my mom or dad?

Keep it calm, private and low key. Frame it as routine, or as something that would ease your own mind, and avoid arguing about whether there is a problem.

Alzheimer's New Jersey hears from many families whose parent refuses to see a doctor. It points out that some people with brain changes truly cannot recognize their own symptoms, a condition called anosognosia. That is different from stubbornness. These ideas, drawn from its advice to families, often help.

  • Make it routine. "Let's get our yearly checkups done together." Alzheimer's New Jersey suggests pointing to Medicare's Annual Wellness Visit as something everyone does once a year.
  • Make it about you. "I know you feel fine, but I'd feel so much better if we checked."
  • Point to fixable causes. "Let's ask whether your blood pressure pills could be making you tired and foggy."
  • Get help from the doctor's office. Ask the office to call your parent to schedule a checkup or a medication review. You can also call ahead and share your concerns privately with the doctor.
  • Plan something nice after. Lunch at a favorite spot or a visit with the grandkids gives the day a better shape.
  • Don't announce it days ahead if your parent tends to get anxious. Telling them the morning of may go more smoothly.

For a wider talk about getting help, see how to talk with a parent about getting help at home. And if you are the one worried about your own memory, the same advice holds. Book the Wellness visit, bring someone you trust and write your questions down before you go.

A screening only tells you whether to look closer. Finding out early gives your family time to act.

Whatever the result, staying active and connected is good for the brain. The NIA suggests learning a new skill, exercise, seven to eight hours of sleep, keeping blood pressure in check and time with friends and family. Our guide to staying well in New Jersey has ideas close to home.

More guides that may help: getting a dementia diagnosis and the new Alzheimer's drugs.

faq.q: How do I get my mom a free memory screening in New Jersey?
faq.a: The simplest route is to book her Medicare Annual Wellness Visit with her primary care doctor, which includes a cognitive assessment at no cost if the doctor accepts assignment. You can also schedule a free video screening with the Alzheimer's Foundation of America at 866-232-8484, or ask your county office on aging (via the ADRC at 1-877-222-3737) about local screening days.

faq.q: Is a memory screening the same as a dementia diagnosis?
faq.a: No. A screening is a 10 to 15 minute check that shows whether a fuller evaluation is needed. Only a doctor can diagnose dementia, usually after an exam, lab tests, memory testing and sometimes brain scans.

faq.q: Does Medicare pay for memory testing?
faq.a: Yes. The yearly Wellness visit includes a cognitive assessment at no cost when the provider accepts assignment. If the doctor finds signs of a problem, Part B covers a separate cognitive assessment and care plan visit, where you pay 20% of the Medicare-approved amount after the Part B deductible.

faq.q: What if my dad refuses to get his memory checked?
faq.a: Don't argue. Alzheimer's New Jersey suggests framing the visit as routine or as something that would ease your own mind, asking the doctor's office to call him to schedule a checkup, and planning something enjoyable afterward. Some people truly cannot see their own symptoms. The Alzheimer's New Jersey helpline at 1-888-280-6055 can talk through your situation.

faq.q: How often should an older adult get a memory screening?
faq.a: Medicare covers the Wellness visit, with its cognitive assessment, once every 12 months. The National Institute on Aging says people who already have memory problems should see their doctor every six to 12 months.

faq.q: Can memory problems be reversed?
faq.a: Sometimes. The National Institute on Aging lists causes such as medication side effects, depression, thyroid or kidney problems, low vitamin B12, sleep problems and infections. These often improve once treated, which is one reason to get checked early.

title: Does Medicare cover home health care? A New Jersey guide
dek: Medicare pays in full for part-time skilled care at home when your parent is homebound and a doctor orders it. Here is who qualifies, what is not covered, how to choose a New Jersey agency and how to get visits started.
keyFacts: Covered home health visits cost $0 under Original Medicare.
Your parent must be homebound and need part-time skilled nursing or therapy ordered by a doctor.
A face-to-face visit must happen within 90 days before or 30 days after care starts.
Medicare does not pay for 24-hour care, homemaker help or personal care when that is the only need.
Free Medicare counseling (SHIP): 1-800-792-8820.
body:
Yes, Medicare covers home health care, and for covered services your parent pays nothing. The catch is that the benefit is narrower than most families expect. Medicare pays for part-time skilled care at home, such as a nurse changing a surgical dressing or a physical therapist helping your dad walk again, when he is homebound and a doctor orders it.

Medicare does not pay for an aide who comes every day just to help with bathing, meals and errands. It does not pay for round-the-clock care. This guide explains who qualifies, what you get, what you pay, how to pick an agency in New Jersey and how to get visits started after a hospital stay.

Does Medicare pay for home health care?

Yes, if your parent meets the rules. Original Medicare Part A and Part B both cover home health, and your parent pays nothing for covered home health services.

Covered services, according to Medicare.gov, include:

  • Skilled nursing, part-time or intermittent. Wound care for a pressure sore or surgical wound, injections, IV or nutrition therapy, monitoring a serious illness, and teaching your parent and the family how to manage care.
  • Therapy. Physical therapy, occupational therapy and speech-language pathology.
  • Medical social services. Help with emotional and practical problems that get in the way of recovery, such as finding community resources.
  • A home health aide, part-time. Help with walking, bathing, grooming and feeding, but only while your parent is also getting skilled nursing or therapy.
  • Medical supplies and equipment. Dressings and other supplies ordered as part of care, plus durable medical equipment such as a walker or wheelchair.

Home health is not only for people who will get better. Medicare.gov says it can help a person recover, keep their current level of function or slow a decline. If an agency tells you visits must end because your mom "stopped improving," ask them to show you the rule they are using.

The aide comes with the nurse or therapist. When the skilled care ends, Medicare's aide visits end too.

Who counts as homebound?

Your parent is homebound if leaving home takes a major effort and they normally can't leave without help. Going out for medical care, church or adult day care does not disqualify them.

Medicare uses two tests, and your parent must meet both:

  • Because of an illness or injury, leaving home isn't recommended, or they need help to leave, such as a cane, walker, wheelchair, crutches, special transportation or another person.
  • They are normally unable to leave home, and leaving takes a considerable and taxing effort.

Homebound does not mean bedbound. Medicare's home health booklet says your parent may still leave for medical treatment and for short, infrequent outings such as a trip to the barber, a walk around the block, or a family reunion, funeral or graduation. Attending adult day care or religious services does not end eligibility either.

Say your mom had a hip replacement and uses a walker. She needs you to drive her and help her down the porch steps, and a trip to the store wipes her out for the day. She would likely meet the test. If she still drives herself to the mall twice a week, she probably would not.

What has to happen before visits start?

A doctor or another allowed provider must see your parent in person, confirm they need home health care and order it. A Medicare-certified home health agency then provides the care.

  1. The face-to-face visit. CMS requires a face-to-face encounter related to the main reason for home health care. It must happen no more than 90 days before care starts or within 30 days after. It can be a regular appointment with the primary care doctor, a visit in the hospital or rehab, and in some cases a telehealth visit. Nurse practitioners, clinical nurse specialists and physician assistants can also do it under Medicare's rules.
  2. The certification. The doctor certifies that your parent is homebound and needs intermittent skilled nursing, physical therapy or speech therapy. Occupational therapy can continue on its own once it has started alongside one of those.
  3. The agency list. The provider should give you a list of agencies that serve your parent's area and tell you if their organization has a financial interest in any of them.
  4. The first home visit. The agency comes to assess your parent's needs and health.
  5. The plan of care. The agency and the doctor write a plan listing which services, from whom, how often and what results to expect. The doctor reviews it at least once every 60 days.

A hospital stay is not required. Medicare's booklet gives a regular appointment with the primary care doctor as an example of the face-to-face visit, so a doctor can order home health for a parent who has been slowly losing strength at home.

What doesn't Medicare cover at home?

Medicare does not pay for 24-hour care, meal delivery, homemaker help such as shopping, cleaning and laundry, or personal care when that is the only help your parent needs.

Many families don't expect this. If your dad mainly needs someone to help him shower, dress and get lunch, that is custodial care. Medicare treats it as long-term care and does not pay for it, at home or in a nursing home.

The hours are limited too. In most cases, "part-time or intermittent" means skilled nursing and aide services together for fewer than 8 hours a day and no more than 28 hours a week. A doctor can approve up to 35 hours a week for a short time if it is necessary. The plan of care sets how often each nurse, therapist or aide visits.

So plan for the gaps. Our guides to choosing a home care agency in New Jersey and what senior care costs in New Jersey cover private aides, and our guide to vetting someone coming into the home covers the safety checks.

How much does Medicare home health cost?

Your parent pays $0 for covered home health visits. For durable medical equipment, such as a walker, wheelchair or oxygen equipment, they pay 20% of the Medicare-approved amount after the Part B deductible.

ItemWhat your parent pays (Original Medicare)
Covered nursing, therapy, aide and social work visits$0
Medical supplies ordered as part of care$0
Durable medical equipment20% of the Medicare-approved amount after the Part B deductible ($283 in 2026)
Care Medicare won't coverFull cost, after written notice from the agency

Before care starts, the agency should tell you, out loud and in writing, what Medicare will pay and what your parent would owe. If the agency thinks Medicare probably won't pay for a service, it must give you a written Advance Beneficiary Notice of Noncoverage (ABN) first. You can ask the agency to bill Medicare anyway so Medicare makes the decision.

A Medigap policy may cover the 20% for equipment. Medicare Advantage plans must cover home health, but they can require you to use agencies in their network and may have their own rules for approval. Call the plan before you choose an agency. Our guide to Medicare Advantage and Medigap in New Jersey explains the difference.

How do I find a good home health agency in New Jersey?

Use Medicare's Care Compare tool to see Medicare-certified agencies that serve your parent's ZIP code, then call two or three. Your parent has the right to choose, and the doctor or hospital should honor that choice.

In New Jersey, home health agencies are licensed by the Department of Health under the state's home health agency rules (N.J.A.C. 8:42). Medicare certification is a separate step that lets the agency bill Medicare. For Medicare to pay, the agency must be Medicare-certified. You can search Care Compare on Medicare.gov by ZIP code and compare agencies on quality measures and patient survey results.

Questions to ask on the phone, drawn from Medicare's own checklist:

  • Are you Medicare-certified? Medicaid-certified too, if my parent has both?
  • Can you start on the date the doctor ordered, at the hours and frequency in the order?
  • Do you offer the specific care she needs, such as wound care or physical therapy?
  • Is someone available at night and on weekends if there's a problem?
  • Do you have staff who speak my parent's language?
  • Have you explained in writing what Medicare covers and what we would pay?

Medicare pays only one home health agency at a time. If the agency isn't working out, your parent can switch. Ask the doctor for a referral to the new agency and tell both agencies about the change.

Watch for home health fraud

Medicare warns families about visits nobody ordered, bills for services your parent never got, pressure to accept equipment you don't need, and anyone offering free goods in exchange for a Medicare number. Check each Medicare Summary Notice. Report concerns to 1-800-MEDICARE or the HHS Inspector General at 1-800-447-8477.

How do we get home health started after a hospital stay?

Ask the hospital or rehab discharge planner to arrange it before your parent leaves. The hospital doctor can usually handle the face-to-face visit and order, and the planner will send the referral to the agency you choose.

  1. Raise it early. Ask on day one or two of the stay whether home health is being planned. Starting early gives the agency time to schedule the first visit.
  2. Pick the agency yourself. Look at the list you are given, check Care Compare and say which agency you want.
  3. Get the details in writing. The agency name, phone number and the date of the first visit. Ask what equipment is coming and who delivers it.
  4. Plan the first week. A nurse visit is not the same as having someone there. Line up family, friends or private help for the hours in between. Our hospital discharge guide walks through the first days home.
  5. Be at the first visit if you can. Join by phone or video if you live far away. Ask about fall risks, grab bars and how to reach the agency after hours.

If the agency gives your parent a Notice of Medicare Non-Coverage and you think visits are ending too soon, your parent can ask for a fast appeal. The notice should arrive at least 2 days before services end. In New Jersey, the reviewer is the Medicare quality improvement organization Commence Health (formerly Livanta), at 1-866-815-5440. Call the number on the notice and follow its deadline.

To complain about the quality of care from a licensed New Jersey home health agency, call the Department of Health's 24-hour complaint hotline at 1-800-792-9770.

When your parent needs more help than Medicare gives

If your parent needs ongoing help with daily care, Medicaid's Managed Long Term Services and Supports (MLTSS) can pay for the custodial help Medicare won't. JACC and the Statewide Respite Care Program help some families who don't qualify for Medicaid.

  • MLTSS. For people who need nursing-home-level care and meet NJ FamilyCare's income and asset rules. In 2026 the income limit is $2,982 a month for the applicant. Services can include a personal care assistant, home-based supportive care, adult day, home-delivered meals, respite and home modifications. See our MLTSS guide.
  • JACC. A state program for people 60 and older who need nursing-home-level care but are not on Medicaid, with services capped at $1,156 a month plus care management. See our JACC guide.
  • Respite. The Statewide Respite Care Program gives unpaid family caregivers a break. See help for family caregivers in NJ.

Start all three with your county's Aging and Disability Resource Connection at 1-877-222-3737. For free, unbiased Medicare counseling, call New Jersey's State Health Insurance Assistance Program (SHIP) at 1-800-792-8820.

faq.q: How do I get Medicare home health care for my mom?
faq.a: Ask her doctor whether she qualifies. The doctor or another allowed provider must see her in person within 90 days before or 30 days after care starts, confirm she is homebound and needs part-time skilled nursing or therapy, and order it. Then choose a Medicare-certified agency, which you can compare on Care Compare at Medicare.gov.

faq.q: Will Medicare pay for an aide to help my dad bathe and dress every day?
faq.a: Only while he is also getting skilled nursing or therapy through Medicare home health, and only part-time. If personal care is the only help he needs, Medicare does not pay. NJ FamilyCare MLTSS, JACC or private pay may cover it.

faq.q: Can my parent still leave the house and get home health care?
faq.a: Yes. Medicare allows trips for medical care, adult day care and religious services, plus short, infrequent outings such as a trip to the barber or a family event. What matters is that leaving home normally takes a major effort and help.

faq.q: Does my parent need a hospital stay first?
faq.a: No. Medicare's home health booklet gives a regular appointment with the primary care doctor as an example of the required face-to-face visit, so a doctor can order home health without a hospital stay.

faq.q: How long does Medicare home health last?
faq.a: There is no set number of visits. Care continues as long as your parent qualifies and the doctor renews the plan of care, which must be reviewed at least every 60 days. If visits are ending and you disagree, ask for a fast appeal using the notice the agency gives you.

faq.q: What does Medicare home health cost in New Jersey?
faq.a: Nothing for covered visits. Your parent pays 20% of the Medicare-approved amount for durable medical equipment after the Part B deductible, which is $283 in 2026. Medicare Advantage plans may have different rules and networks, so call the plan.

title: Free and low-cost eye exams and glasses for seniors in NJ
dek: What Medicare covers for eyes, how Medicare Advantage and NJ FamilyCare help, and where to find a no-cost eye exam, free glasses and low vision services in New Jersey.
keyFacts: Original Medicare does not cover routine eye exams for glasses or contacts.
Part B covers a yearly diabetic eye exam and glaucoma screening every 12 months for people at high risk.
After each cataract surgery with a lens implant, Part B covers one pair of glasses with standard frames.
EyeCare America offers a one-time medical eye exam at no out-of-pocket cost to people who qualify: 877-887-6327.
NJ Commission for the Blind and Visually Impaired offers in-home training and low vision help: 1-877-685-8878.
body:
Original Medicare does not pay for a routine eye exam or for everyday glasses. It does help pay for eye care tied to a medical problem, such as a yearly diabetic eye exam, glaucoma screening for people at high risk, macular degeneration care, cataract surgery, and one pair of glasses after each cataract surgery with a lens implant.

For the rest, New Jersey families have real options. Many Medicare Advantage plans add vision benefits. NJ FamilyCare covers vision care. EyeCare America offers a no-cost medical eye exam to people who qualify, and a Short Hills charity called New Eyes buys new glasses for people who cannot afford them. Here is how each one works, and how to set your mom or dad up with care they can keep up with.

Does Medicare pay for eye exams and glasses?

Only for certain medical eye care. Medicare says plainly that it does not cover routine eye exams, sometimes called refractions, for glasses or contact lenses.

Eye careWhat Original Medicare Part B does
Routine exam for glassesNot covered. You pay all costs.
Diabetic eye examCovered once a year for people with diabetes, to check for diabetic retinopathy.
Glaucoma screeningCovered once every 12 months for people at high risk: diabetes, a family history of glaucoma, African Americans 50 and older, or Hispanic adults 65 and older.
Macular degenerationCertain tests and treatments, including some injected drugs, may be covered.
Cataract surgeryCovered by Part B when a standard (conventional) lens is implanted.
Glasses after cataract surgeryOne pair with standard frames, or one set of contact lenses, after each surgery with a lens implant. Upgraded frames cost extra.

For the covered items, your parent pays 20% of the Medicare-approved amount after the Part B deductible ($283 in 2026). A hospital outpatient visit can add a copayment. Medicare pays for the post-cataract glasses only if they come from a supplier that participates in Medicare, so ask before you order.

Medigap plans generally do not cover vision care or glasses. Most do help pay the 20% for Medicare-covered eye care. If your parent is new to all this, our Medicare 101 guide explains the parts.

Medicare pays for eye disease. The everyday checkup for new glasses is on you, unless another program steps in.

Does Medicare Advantage cover vision?

Often, yes, but it varies by plan. Medicare says some Medicare Advantage plans offer extra benefits that Original Medicare does not, such as vision, hearing and dental. The details are set by each plan.

Call the number on your parent's plan card and ask:

  • Is a routine eye exam covered, and how often?
  • Is there an allowance for glasses or contacts? How much, and how often?
  • Do we have to use certain eye doctors or optical stores?
  • Is there a copay for the exam?

Open enrollment runs October 15 to December 7. If your parent needs glasses every year or two, compare vision benefits on the Medicare Plan Finder before the deadline. Our guide to open enrollment for 2027 walks through what to compare. Free, unbiased help comes from SHIP Medicare counselors at 1-800-792-8820.

Does NJ FamilyCare cover eye exams and glasses?

Yes. NJ FamilyCare, New Jersey's Medicaid program, lists vision among its covered services. The state's own help page says it covers medically necessary eye exams and prescription glasses.

Most members get care through a health plan, and each plan's member handbook spells out how often your parent can get an exam and new glasses. Look it up or call the member services number on the card. To ask about coverage or applying, call NJ FamilyCare at 1-800-701-0710. Our guide to NJ FamilyCare for older adults covers the income and asset rules.

If your parent's income is a bit too high for full Medicaid, check the Medicare Savings Programs. Under the QMB program, Medicare providers are not allowed to bill for deductibles, coinsurance and copayments on services Medicare covers. For someone with glaucoma or macular degeneration, that 20% adds up fast. See our guide to Medicare Savings Programs in NJ.

How can my mom or dad get a free eye exam?

The best-known option is EyeCare America, a public service program of the American Academy of Ophthalmology. It matches people who qualify with a volunteer ophthalmologist for a medical eye exam at no out-of-pocket cost.

To qualify, a person must:

  • Be a U.S. citizen or legal resident, 18 or older.
  • Not belong to an HMO or PPO, and not have private insurance or benefits through the Department of Veterans Affairs.
  • Not have seen an ophthalmologist in three or more years.
  • Never have used EyeCare America before. It is a one-time program.

If your parent qualifies, the program covers the medical eye exam and up to one year of follow-up visits for anything found at that first exam, at no out-of-pocket cost. It does not cover a refraction for glasses, the glasses themselves, surgery, medications or extra tests. You can fill out the referral questionnaire for your parent online at aao.org/eyecare-america, or call 877-887-6327.

Because of the HMO and PPO rule, a parent in a Medicare Advantage HMO or PPO plan will not qualify. If that is your parent, start with the plan's own vision benefit. EyeCare America also says that if you only need glasses or contacts, you should not apply, and points people to other resources instead.

Other places to look:

  • The VA. Veterans who get VA health care can have routine eye exams and preventive vision testing covered, and may get glasses too. Our veterans benefits guide explains how to enroll.
  • Community health centers. The National Eye Institute notes some have eye clinics with free or low-cost care.
  • Your parent's regular doctor or eye doctor. Ask directly about payment plans or programs they know.
  • Local help lines. Dial 2-1-1, or call the Aging and Disability Resource Connection at 1-877-222-3737 to reach your county's office on aging.

The American Academy of Ophthalmology advises a complete eye exam every year or two after 65. Glaucoma can steal vision without symptoms, and an exam can catch it early.

Where can we get free or low-cost glasses in New Jersey?

New Eyes (New Eyes for the Needy) is a Short Hills nonprofit founded in 1932. It buys new prescription glasses for people in financial need anywhere in the U.S. through an e-voucher.

  • The household's net monthly income must be below 250% of the federal poverty guidelines.
  • Your parent needs a glasses prescription dated within the last 24 months, with the pupillary distance measurement. New Eyes does not pay for the exam.
  • The voucher covers a basic pair with single vision or lined bifocal lenses. Upgrades such as progressives are offered at a discounted out-of-pocket price.
  • A social worker, care manager or health advocate can apply for your parent, which New Eyes says works best. Individuals can apply directly with proof of eligibility. Each application has a non-refundable fee.

Apply at new-eyes.org. The glasses are ordered from New Eyes' own online store once the voucher is approved.

Whatever route you take, keep a copy of the written prescription. It lets you compare prices between stores, use a plan allowance where it is accepted, or apply for a voucher later.

Lions Clubs. Local Lions Clubs may help pay for eye care, and some provide glasses. Use the club locator at lionsclubs.org to find the club in your parent's town and call to ask what it offers.

Cataract surgery. For people who cannot pay, the National Eye Institute lists Mission Cataract USA and Operation Sight, which offer free or low-cost cataract surgery.

What help is there for low vision in New Jersey?

When glasses or surgery cannot fix the problem, the New Jersey Commission for the Blind and Visually Impaired (CBVI) can help your parent keep living safely at home.

CBVI serves people whose vision problem affects daily life and who have best corrected vision of 20/70 or worse in the better eye, or a visual field of 40 degrees or less in the better eye. Instructors can come to the home to teach daily living skills, home management and safe travel. Community low vision doctors can provide devices such as special glasses and magnifiers. Many services are free, though people above an income standard may share some costs.

CBVI also runs Project BEST, which holds eye screenings around the state, including screenings for diabetic eye disease. Call 973-648-7400 to find one nearby. To apply or refer your parent for services, call CBVI at 1-877-685-8878 or 973-648-3333.

How do I help my parent keep up with eye care?

A little planning keeps exams from slipping. The AAO says lower contrast sensitivity, a subtle change with age, raises the risk of falls and car accidents. That is a good reason to keep exams on the calendar.

  1. Find out what is covered. Pull out the Medicare, Advantage plan or NJ FamilyCare card and call before booking.
  2. Book the right kind of visit. Tell the office if your parent has diabetes, glaucoma risk or a cataract, since those visits may be covered by Medicare.
  3. Ask about dilation. If the eyes will be dilated, plan for a ride home. Our guide to rides to medical appointments lists options by county.
  4. Bring a list. Medications, current glasses and any changes your parent has noticed, like glare at night or trouble reading.
  5. Get the prescription in writing. Include the pupillary distance. You will need it for New Eyes or for shopping around.

If your parent also needs help with hearing or teeth, our guides to hearing aids and affordable dental care cover the help available in New Jersey.

faq.q: Does Medicare cover eye exams for seniors?
faq.a: Original Medicare does not cover routine eye exams for glasses. Part B does cover a yearly eye exam for people with diabetes, glaucoma screening every 12 months for people at high risk, and certain tests and treatment for macular degeneration, with 20% coinsurance after the deductible.

faq.q: Does Medicare pay for glasses after cataract surgery?
faq.a: Yes. Part B covers one pair of glasses with standard frames, or one set of contact lenses, after each cataract surgery that implants a lens. Your parent pays 20% after the deductible, plus any cost for upgraded frames, and the supplier must participate in Medicare.

faq.q: How do I get my mom a free eye exam in NJ?
faq.a: Check whether she qualifies for EyeCare America (877-887-6327). She must not have seen an ophthalmologist in three or more years and must not be in an HMO or PPO or have VA health benefits. Also check her Medicare Advantage plan or NJ FamilyCare, and ask about community health centers.

faq.q: How can I get free glasses for my dad in New Jersey?
faq.a: New Eyes in Short Hills buys basic prescription glasses for people with household income below 250% of the poverty guidelines. He needs a prescription from the last 24 months with the pupillary distance. A social worker can apply for him, or he can apply at new-eyes.org.

faq.q: Does NJ FamilyCare cover glasses for older adults?
faq.a: Yes. NJ FamilyCare covers medically necessary eye exams and prescription glasses. How often your parent can get new ones depends on the health plan, so check the member handbook or call NJ FamilyCare at 1-800-701-0710.

faq.q: Who helps with low vision in New Jersey?
faq.a: The NJ Commission for the Blind and Visually Impaired serves residents with 20/70 vision or worse in the better eye, or a visual field of 40 degrees or less, with in-home independent living training and low vision services. Call 1-877-685-8878.
