title: Hospice care in New Jersey: how to find it and pay for it
dek: How to find and check a hospice anywhere in NJ, what the Care Compare scores mean, who pays, the four levels of care, and how to switch or complain.
keyFacts: Search Medicare Care Compare by ZIP code to find Medicare-approved hospices serving your parent's town.
Hospice has four levels of care: routine home care, continuous home care, general inpatient care and inpatient respite.
A hospice nurse must do an initial assessment within 48 hours after hospice is chosen.
Your parent can change hospices once in each benefit period and stop hospice at any time.
NJ Department of Health complaint hotline, 24 hours: 1-800-792-9770.
body:
To find a hospice anywhere in New Jersey, search Medicare's Care Compare tool by your parent's ZIP code, check each hospice's state license, and call two or three. Every hospice that Medicare pays for must be Medicare-approved, and New Jersey hospices must also be licensed by the state Department of Health.

For most older adults, Medicare Part A pays for hospice with almost no out-of-pocket cost. NJ FamilyCare (Medicaid) covers hospice too, and for people in a nursing home it can also cover room and board. Veterans enrolled in VA health care pay no copays for hospice. This guide is general information, not medical, legal or financial advice.

How do I find a hospice in New Jersey?

Start with names from your parent's doctor or the hospital social worker, then look each one up on Care Compare and the state's license search.

  1. Search Care Compare. Go to Medicare Care Compare, choose hospice care, and enter your parent's ZIP code.
  2. Compare a few side by side. Look at the family survey results and the quality measures explained below.
  3. Confirm the state license. New Jersey licenses hospices through the Department of Health. Use the state's health facility search and choose the acute care search, which includes hospices.
  4. Call. Ask whether they serve your parent's town, how soon they can do a first visit, and whether they take your parent's insurance.

If your parent is in a Medicare Advantage plan, the plan must help find a Medicare-approved hospice nearby. Medicare also suggests calling your state hospice organization; 1-800-MEDICARE (1-800-633-4227) can give you the number. For hospices serving Newark, Montclair and the rest of the county, see our Essex County hospice guide.

If you are still deciding whether hospice is right, our guide to hospice vs. palliative care explains who qualifies and what Medicare covers.

What do the Care Compare hospice ratings mean?

Care Compare shows two kinds of information. One is what families said in a survey after their loved one died. The other is a set of measures Medicare calculates from the hospice's own records and bills.

What families said. The CAHPS Hospice Survey asks family caregivers about communication, getting timely help (including evenings, weekends and holidays), treating the patient with respect, emotional and spiritual support, help for pain and symptoms, and training to care for their family member at home. A newer measure, added for deaths from April 2025 on, asks whether care respected the patient's wishes. Two overall questions ask how families rated the hospice from 0 to 10 and whether they would recommend it.

Hospice Care Index. This single score runs from 0 to 10. A hospice earns a point for each of ten indicators it meets, drawn from Medicare claims. They include:

  • Whether it ever provides the two higher levels of care (continuous home care or general inpatient care)
  • Gaps between nursing visits
  • Nursing minutes per day at home, and nursing minutes on weekends
  • Visits near death
  • Patients discharged alive very early or very late in their stay
  • Patients discharged and then hospitalized, which Medicare calls burdensome transitions

Visits in the last days of life. This shows how often a registered nurse or social worker visited in person on at least two of the last three days of a patient's life. For a family at home, those days are usually the hardest.

Comprehensive assessment at admission. This shows how often the hospice checked for pain and shortness of breath, asked about treatment preferences and beliefs, and started a bowel plan for patients on opioids.

Small hospices may not have enough data for every score. A missing score is not a bad sign by itself. Use it as a reason to ask the hospice directly.

Ask every hospice who answers the phone at 2 a.m. on a Sunday, and how long it takes a nurse to get to the house.

Who pays for hospice in New Jersey?

Medicare pays for most hospice care for older adults. NJ FamilyCare, the VA and private insurance can also pay, and the rules on room and board differ.

  • Medicare. Part A covers hospice from a Medicare-approved hospice with no deductible. Your parent pays up to $5 per prescription for pain and symptom drugs and 5% of the Medicare-approved amount for inpatient respite. Medicare does not pay room and board at home, in assisted living or in a nursing home. A Medigap policy covers the drug copays and respite coinsurance.
  • NJ FamilyCare (Medicaid). New Jersey's Medicaid hospice rules cover hospice for people who qualify. Someone who has both Medicare and Medicaid must choose Medicare's hospice benefit. For a fee-for-service member living in a nursing home, Medicaid also covers room and board through the hospice. If your parent is in a NJ FamilyCare managed care plan, including MLTSS, the hospice must follow that plan's rules, such as prior approval. Call the member services number on the plan card. Our guide to NJ FamilyCare and MLTSS explains long-term care coverage, and NJ FamilyCare answers questions at 1-800-701-0710.
  • The VA. Hospice is part of the standard medical benefits package, so any veteran enrolled in VA health care can get it if they meet the clinical need. The VA says there are no copays for hospice, whether the VA provides it or a contracted community hospice does. Ask your parent's VA social worker.
  • Private insurance. Employer and retiree plans set their own hospice rules. Call the number on the card and ask which hospices are in network and what you will owe.

The free State Health Insurance Assistance Program counselors at 1-800-792-8820 can walk you through how Medicare, Medigap and Medicaid fit together for your parent.

What are the four levels of hospice care?

Medicare and New Jersey's Medicaid rules both recognize four levels of hospice care. The hospice team decides which one your parent needs, and it can change as needs change.

LevelWhen it is used
Routine home careMost days. Scheduled visits wherever your parent lives.
Continuous home careA crisis at home. Mostly nursing care for 8 to 24 hours a day.
General inpatient carePain or symptoms that cannot be managed at home.
Inpatient respite careA break for the caregiver, up to 5 days at a time.

Under New Jersey's Medicaid rules, continuous home care requires at least eight hours of nursing care in a 24-hour period, given mainly by a registered nurse or a licensed practical nurse working under one. It is meant to keep your parent at home through a short period of crisis.

General inpatient care can happen in a hospital, a nursing facility or a hospice's own inpatient unit. The hospice must arrange it. If your parent goes to the hospital for the terminal illness without the hospice setting it up, Medicare warns you could owe the full cost. That is why Medicare tells hospice families to call the hospice team first.

When you interview hospices, ask whether they actually provide continuous home care, and where they send patients for inpatient care. A hospice that says it rarely or never offers those levels is telling you something useful. A POLST form helps make sure emergency crews follow your parent's wishes too.

Can my parent get hospice in a nursing home or assisted living?

Yes. Hospice comes to wherever your parent lives, including a nursing home or assisted living. The hospice team adds visits, medicines, equipment and support on top of the care the facility already gives.

Federal rules require a written agreement between the hospice and any nursing facility where it cares for residents. Under that agreement the facility keeps providing 24-hour room and board and the personal care your parent got before. The hospice must provide services at the same level it would at home, takes charge of the hospice plan of care, and gives the facility a way to reach its 24-hour on-call nurse.

Before you choose, ask the facility which hospices it already works with. Then ask the hospice how often it visits that facility, and who to call when something changes. If you are still comparing facilities, our guide to nursing home ratings in New Jersey explains the inspection reports.

Some hospices also run inpatient units or residences. Medicare does not cover room and board in a hospice inpatient facility, except during short-term inpatient or respite care that the hospice arranges. If your parent stays on after that, ask in writing what the daily cost would be and when it would start.

How fast can hospice start?

Timing depends on the hospice and the day of the week, so ask each one how soon it can do a first visit. Once the paperwork is signed, federal rules set the pace.

  • The election statement comes first. Your parent, or their representative, signs a Hospice Election Statement naming the hospice, the start date and the attending doctor. No hospice services can start before it is complete.
  • A nurse visits within 48 hours. A hospice registered nurse must complete an initial assessment within 48 hours after the election, sooner if the doctor, patient or family asks.
  • A full plan within 5 days. The hospice team must finish a comprehensive assessment, including the family's grief needs, within 5 calendar days.

If your parent is in the hospital, ask the case manager to start the hospice referral before discharge, so equipment like a hospital bed reaches the house first. Our guide to leaving the hospital has a checklist. Ask the hospice for its list of items, services and drugs it considers unrelated to the terminal illness. Medicare says the hospice must give it to you within 3 to 5 days of asking.

How do we switch hospices or stop hospice?

Your parent can change hospices once in each benefit period, and can stop hospice at any time. Changing hospices does not end the hospice benefit.

To switch, your parent signs a statement naming the old hospice, the new one and the date of the change, and files it with both. Under New Jersey Medicaid this is the Change of Hospice form, FD-384. Call the new hospice first so there is no gap in care.

To stop, your parent signs a form with the date hospice will end, and goes back to regular Medicare coverage. If they qualify later, they can return. Medicare warns that no one should ask your parent to sign forms to stop hospice unless your parent asked to stop.

If something goes wrong

Start with the hospice's director of nursing. If that does not fix it, call the New Jersey Department of Health's 24-hour complaint hotline at 1-800-792-9770. For a Medicare quality of care complaint, or to appeal if the hospice says your parent no longer qualifies, call the BFCC-QIO for New Jersey, Commence Health (formerly Livanta), at 1-866-815-5440.

Medicare's hospice benefit includes grief and loss counseling for the family. Our guide to grief support in New Jersey lists more places to turn, and our caregiver respite guide may help while you are still caring for your parent.

faq.q: How do I find a hospice for my mom in New Jersey?
faq.a: Ask her doctor or the hospital social worker for names, then search Medicare Care Compare by her ZIP code. Confirm the state license on the NJ Department of Health facility search, and call two or three hospices to ask about first visits, night coverage and her insurance.

faq.q: Does NJ Medicaid pay for hospice in a nursing home?
faq.a: Yes. NJ FamilyCare covers hospice, and for a fee-for-service member living in a nursing home it also covers room and board through the hospice. If your parent is in a managed care plan such as MLTSS, call the plan, because the hospice must follow its rules.

faq.q: What is continuous home care in hospice?
faq.a: It is a higher level of hospice care for a short crisis at home, such as pain that is out of control. Under New Jersey Medicaid rules it means at least eight hours of mostly nursing care in a 24-hour period, so your parent can stay home instead of going to the hospital.

faq.q: How do I switch my dad to a different hospice?
faq.a: He can change hospices once in each benefit period. He signs a statement naming the old hospice, the new one and the date, and files it with both. Call the new hospice first so care does not stop.

faq.q: Do veterans pay for hospice?
faq.a: Not through the VA. Hospice is part of the VA's standard medical benefits package for enrolled veterans who need it, and the VA says there are no copays, whether the VA or a contracted community hospice provides the care.

faq.q: Who do I call with a complaint about a hospice in New Jersey?
faq.a: Talk to the hospice's director of nursing first. Then call the NJ Department of Health complaint hotline at 1-800-792-9770, any time. For Medicare quality complaints or a discharge you disagree with, call Commence Health, New Jersey's BFCC-QIO, at 1-866-815-5440.

title: Hospice care in Essex County, NJ: who serves your town
dek: The Medicare-certified hospices that serve Newark, Montclair, Livingston, the Oranges and the rest of Essex County, where inpatient hospice is close by, and how to get started from a hospital bed.
keyFacts: Search Medicare Care Compare by your parent's ZIP code to see which hospices serve that town.
Your parent has the right to choose the hospice, even when a hospital suggests one.
Hospice of New Jersey provides inpatient hospice care at Mountainside Medical Center in Montclair.
NJ Department of Health complaint hotline: 1-800-792-9770.
body:
Most hospice care in Essex County happens at home, delivered by hospice agencies whose nurses and aides drive in from offices in Bloomfield, Livingston, West Orange and nearby counties. In Medicare's own data, at least ten Medicare-certified hospices report serving towns across Essex, from Newark and the Oranges to Montclair, Livingston and West Orange. Families can choose any of them, and the choice belongs to your mom or dad, not the hospital.

This page lists the hospices we confirmed in Medicare's data and on each hospice's own website, notes which ones have an inpatient option in or near Essex, and explains how to get hospice started, especially from a hospital bed. For how the Medicare benefit works and what it costs, see our statewide guide to hospice care in New Jersey.

Which hospices serve Essex County?

The hospices below reported serving Essex ZIP codes to Medicare and list Essex County, or New Jersey statewide, on their own websites. They are in alphabetical order. This is not an endorsement or a ranking.

To build the list, we checked Medicare's hospice ZIP code data (released August 2026) for four sample ZIP codes: 07042 (Montclair), 07102 (downtown Newark), 07039 (Livingston) and 07052 (West Orange). Every hospice here served all four, except Life Hospice, which did not list 07102. We left out hospices whose own websites did not name Essex County as part of their area. We checked these listings in November 2026, and phone numbers come from each hospice's own site.

HospiceOfficePhone
Amedisys Hospice CareHackensack201-342-7766
Atlantic Visiting Nurse Hospice (Atlantic Health)Morristown973-379-8400
Barnabas Health Home Care and Hospice (VNA Health Group)West Orange800-400-0981
Center for Hope Hospice and Palliative CareScotch Plains908-889-7780
Compassionate Care Hospice (Amedisys)Bloomfield973-916-1400
Grace Healthcare ServicesEdison732-225-4100
Hospice of New JerseyBloomfield973-893-0818
Life HospiceLivingston973-607-4930
Serenity Hospice CareHamilton609-227-2400
VITAS HealthcareLivingston973-994-4738

A few notes on the names. Barnabas Health Home Care and Hospice is the RWJBarnabas Health partnership with VNA Health Group, and the number above is VNA Health Group's hospice line. Compassionate Care Hospice and Amedisys Hospice Care are two separately certified hospices owned by the same company. Some offices have moved since Medicare's listing: Hospice of New Jersey's contact page now shows an office in Roseland, Life Hospice's site shows East Hanover, and VITAS lists a Roseland office. The phone numbers are the same.

Office location matters less than you might think. The team comes to your parent. What matters is how fast they answer, how often they visit and who shows up at 2 a.m.

The hospice comes to your parent. The office address is the least important thing on this list.

How do I check which hospices serve my parent's town?

Search Medicare's Care Compare for hospices using your parent's own ZIP code. It shows the hospices that reported serving that ZIP code, along with their family survey results and quality measures.

  1. Open Care Compare. Go to Medicare Care Compare for hospices and type the ZIP code where your parent lives, not yours.
  2. Look at the family survey. Hospices with enough completed family surveys get a star rating from 1 to 5. Read the details too, like whether families got help quickly and whether they would recommend the hospice.
  3. Compare two or three. Stars are one piece. A hospice with fewer surveys may have no stars at all, and that is not a bad sign by itself.
  4. Call. Ask how soon they can do a first visit in your parent's town, and how long a nurse takes to arrive at night.

Medicare updates its data regularly, and hospices add and drop service areas. Treat our table as a starting point and Care Compare as the current word. Our guide to hospice vs. palliative care has a full list of questions to ask on that first call.

Is there inpatient hospice in or near Essex County?

Yes. Hospice of New Jersey provides inpatient hospice care at Mountainside Medical Center in Montclair, and Atlantic Health offers it at three hospitals just outside the county. Center for Hope runs a residence in Scotch Plains.

Inpatient hospice is short-term care for pain or symptoms that can't be handled at home. It is different from moving in somewhere for the last months. Here is what we confirmed:

  • Mountainside Medical Center, Montclair. The hospital has partnered with Hospice of New Jersey to give general inpatient hospice care when symptoms can't be managed at home. Once symptoms are under control, the team plans the move back home or to a facility. The hospital's case management department is at 973-429-6136.
  • Atlantic Health hospitals. Atlantic Visiting Nurse Hospice offers general inpatient hospice at Morristown Medical Center, Overlook Medical Center in Summit and Chilton Medical Center in Pompton Plains.
  • Peggy's House, Scotch Plains. Center for Hope's residence offers a homelike setting next to the Ash Brook Reservation in Union County. For qualifications and cost, call 908-889-7780 and ask for a residential advisor.
  • Other hospices. VITAS and Life Hospice say they provide inpatient care when needed, in a hospital or nursing facility. Ask any hospice which local hospitals and nursing homes it uses for inpatient and respite stays.

Respite stays are a separate thing. Under Medicare, the hospice can arrange a short stay of up to five days at a time so a worn-out caregiver can rest. Ask where your hospice sends respite patients before you need it.

Which Essex hospitals have palliative care teams?

Several do. If your mom or dad is in the hospital with a serious illness, ask the doctor or nurse for a palliative care consult. That team can also help the family decide whether hospice is the right next step.

  • Cooperman Barnabas Medical Center, Livingston. Runs a Palliative and Supportive Care Program with doctors, advanced practice nurses, a social worker, pastoral care and a pharmacist. It earned The Joint Commission's advanced certification in palliative care in 2021. Hospital main number: 973-322-5000.
  • University Hospital, Newark. Its palliative care team works across the hospital, including intensive care, the emergency department and cancer care, and helps with advance care planning such as a POLST. Reach the team at 973-972-0147.
  • RWJBarnabas hospitals. RWJBarnabas Health lists Cooperman Barnabas, Clara Maass Medical Center in Belleville and Newark Beth Israel Medical Center among the hospitals where its hospice offers care.

If your parent has NJ FamilyCare (Medicaid), there is a newer option outside the hospital. Since April 1, 2026, NJ FamilyCare covers Community-Based Palliative Care for members with serious illness, at home and in other community settings, with no terminal diagnosis required. Members in a managed care plan should call the plan's member services and ask for the Community-Based Palliative Care team.

How do we start hospice from a hospital in Essex County?

Tell the hospital case manager or social worker that your family wants hospice, and name the hospice you want if you have one. The hospital sends the referral, and the hospice does an assessment to confirm your parent qualifies.

  1. Ask the attending doctor directly. "Would my mom qualify for hospice?" is a fair question. Medicare also covers a one-time consultation with a hospice doctor before your parent decides.
  2. Pick the hospice, or ask for a list. Federal law gives your parent the right to choose the hospice. A hospital may suggest the hospice it works with most. You can say yes, or name a different one.
  3. Decide where care will happen. Home, a relative's home, assisted living or a nursing home. If home, the hospice orders the hospital bed and other equipment, so ask when it will arrive.
  4. Sign the election form. Your parent, or the person legally making decisions for them, signs a hospice election statement.
  5. Know who to call. Before you leave the hospital, get the hospice's 24-hour number. Once hospice starts, call the hospice first, not 911, for problems with the terminal illness.

Hospital discharges move fast, so it helps to pick a hospice before the discharge day if you can. Our hospital discharge guide explains your rights when a discharge feels rushed.

If your parent is in a nursing home

Hospice can come into the nursing home or assisted living residence. The facility usually works with certain hospices, so ask which ones. Hospice covers hospice care there, but not the monthly room and board bill.

Where can Essex County families get help along the way?

Start with the county. The Essex County ADRC (Aging and Disability Resource Connection) at 973-395-8375 or 1-877-222-3737 takes applications for county caregiver programs and can point you to local help.

  • County respite program. Essex County's Respite Care Program gives family caregivers a break, with companion care, home health aides, medical adult day care and in-patient care. It has an income-based copay and is for Essex residents with a caregiver in place who are not on Medicaid. Apply through the ADRC. Our caregiver respite guide covers more options.
  • Home-delivered meals. The county's provider agencies deliver meals to people 60 and over who can't prepare their own. Chr-ill Care (973-744-8103), FOCUS in Newark (973-624-2528) and the Jewish Community Center of MetroWest (973-530-3414, kosher meals) serve the county.
  • Adult Protective Services. If you suspect an older adult is being neglected or exploited, call FOCUS at 1-866-903-6287.
  • Complaints about a hospice. Talk to the hospice's nurse manager first. The New Jersey Department of Health's 24-hour complaint hotline for health care facilities is 1-800-792-9770.

For senior centers, rides and lunch programs, see our Essex County senior centers guide and the Essex County page.

What support is there for the family afterward?

Every Medicare hospice must offer bereavement support to the family for up to a year after a death. Some hospices on our list, including Atlantic Visiting Nurse and Life Hospice, describe 13 months of follow-up, so ask what they offer.

Atlantic Visiting Nurse Hospice, for example, lists grief support groups, a men's group, individual counseling and Camp Clover, a free four-day bereavement day camp for children every August. Its bereavement coordinator is at 973-379-8442. Cooperman Barnabas lists a monthly support group run by VNA Health Group, at 732-491-7277. You do not have to have used a hospice to look for support. Our guide to grief support in New Jersey lists more groups.

When the time comes, the hospice nurse will help with the first calls, including the funeral home. Our guide to funeral homes and cemeteries in Essex County covers what happens next, and when a parent dies walks through the first weeks.

This page is general information, not medical or legal advice. For questions about a specific Medicare plan, the free SHIP counselors at 1-800-792-8820 can help.

Nearby counties: hospice in Bergen County, Morris County and Passaic County.

title: Palliative care in New Jersey: where to get it and who pays
dek: How to get a palliative care referral for a parent, the kinds of programs in New Jersey, NJ FamilyCare's new home palliative benefit, and what Medicare pays.
keyFacts: Palliative care is for any stage of a serious illness, and your parent can keep treatments aimed at a cure.
Medicare Part B covers palliative visits like other doctor visits: usually 20% after the $283 deductible in 2026.
NJ FamilyCare's Community-Based Palliative Care benefit started April 1, 2026, with no terminal diagnosis required.
To qualify for the NJ FamilyCare benefit, a member needs a serious disease plus functional decline, 2+ ER visits in 6 months, or a hospital stay in the past year.
Advance care planning costs $0 at a Medicare yearly wellness visit if the provider accepts assignment.
body:
Palliative care is medical care for the symptoms and stress of a serious illness, and in New Jersey the usual way in is a referral from your parent's doctor, a hospital team or a health plan. Your mom or dad does not have to be dying to get it, and they can keep every treatment they have now, from chemotherapy to dialysis.

Who pays depends on the setting. Medicare Part B covers visits from palliative care doctors and nurse practitioners much like other doctor visits, so your parent usually pays 20% after the yearly deductible. Since April 1, 2026, NJ FamilyCare (New Jersey's Medicaid program) also has a separate community-based palliative care benefit that brings a team to the home or a clinic. This guide covers how to ask for a referral, the kinds of programs you will find, and what each one costs. It is general information, not medical or legal advice.

If you are still sorting out how palliative care differs from hospice, start with our guide to hospice vs. palliative care, then come back here.

How do I get a palliative care referral for my mom or dad?

Ask your parent's main doctor or the specialist who treats the illness to make a referral to palliative care. In a hospital, ask the attending doctor or nurse for a palliative care consult. If your parent has NJ FamilyCare through a health plan, you can also call the plan's member services number.

Families often wait for a doctor to bring it up. You do not have to. A doctor may assume things are under control because the visits are short and your parent puts on a brave face. Say plainly what you see at home.

  1. Write down the hard parts. Note pain, breathlessness, nausea, poor sleep, falls, ER trips and anything your parent has stopped doing. Dates help.
  2. Ask the doctor directly. Try something like "Would a palliative care team help with Dad's symptoms? Can you refer him?" Ask who the referral goes to and how long the wait is.
  3. Check the insurance. Call the number on your parent's card and ask whether that palliative program is in network and whether a referral or prior approval is needed.
  4. Get the first visit on the calendar. Bring the medication list, recent test results and the name of the health care representative from your parent's advance directive.
  5. Follow up in a week. If nobody has called, call the doctor's office and the program yourself. Referrals do get lost.

If your parent is in the hospital now, this is a good moment to ask, before the discharge plan is set.

What kinds of palliative care programs are there in New Jersey?

There are three main kinds: a hospital consult team that sees patients during a stay, an outpatient clinic that your parent visits, and home-based programs that send clinicians to the house. Many health systems offer more than one.

TypeWhereBest for
Hospital consultDuring a hospital stayA hard admission or a big decision
Outpatient clinicClinic visits, often near cancer or heart centersPeople still getting out to appointments
Home-basedYour parent's homePeople who rarely leave the house
Facility visitsNursing home or assisted livingResidents of a care home

A hospital team usually includes a palliative care doctor or nurse practitioner, a social worker and often a chaplain. They help with symptoms and with family meetings about what comes next. Once your parent goes home, that team may not follow them, so ask, "Who takes over after discharge?"

The New Jersey Department of Health keeps a palliative and end-of-life resources page with links to palliative programs at many health systems, including Atlantic Health System, AtlantiCare, Hackensack Meridian Health, Hunterdon Healthcare, Inspira, Jefferson Health, Valley Health System and Virtua. The state says the list is for information only and is not an endorsement. Use it as a starting point, then ask your parent's doctors which program they work with most.

Can my parent get palliative care at home?

Yes, in many parts of New Jersey. Home-based palliative care is run by some hospices, home health agencies and physician practices. What it costs depends on the program and your parent's insurance.

A home program may include visits from a doctor or nurse practitioner, phone check-ins, help adjusting medicines and a social worker who can line up other services. It is usually not hands-on daily care. Bathing, meals and overnight help come from family, private aides or programs like Medicaid's long-term care benefit.

Two other kinds of home care are easy to confuse with home palliative care:

  • Medicare home health. Skilled nursing and therapy for people who are homebound, ordered by a doctor. It can help a lot with symptoms, but it is a separate benefit with its own rules. Our Medicare home health guide explains who qualifies.
  • Hospice at home. For people with a life expectancy of six months or less who have stopped treatment aimed at a cure. See hospice care in New Jersey.

When you call a home palliative program, ask exactly who visits, how often, and what is billed to Medicare, the health plan or your family.

What is NJ FamilyCare's community-based palliative care benefit?

It is a newer NJ FamilyCare benefit, live since April 1, 2026, that gives members with a serious illness a palliative care team at home or in a clinic. A terminal diagnosis is not required, and your parent can keep their current treatments.

The benefit was signed into law on December 21, 2023. It covers both managed care members and fee-for-service members. According to the state Division of Medical Assistance and Health Services (DMAHS), the team works with your parent and their doctor on a care plan. State guidance says the monthly bundle of services includes:

  • Care planning and care coordination
  • Advance care planning
  • Symptom management
  • Medication review, including stopping medicines that no longer help
  • Psychosocial, spiritual and caregiver support
  • Referrals to other Medicaid services
  • A phone line that answers 24 hours a day, 7 days a week

Who qualifies. The state's provider information sheet says a member needs a serious disease plus evidence of reduced quality of life, shown by functional decline, two or more emergency room visits in the past six months, or at least one hospital stay in the past year. A clinician confirms this with an in-person assessment. Your parent cannot be in hospice and this benefit at the same time.

People with Medicare and Medicaid. State guidance says people who have both can get the benefit unless they enter hospice. Medicare still pays first for other services.

How to ask for it

If your parent is in an NJ FamilyCare health plan, call the plan's member services number on the card and ask for the Community-Based Palliative Care team. Any health care provider can also refer your parent for an assessment. For general NJ FamilyCare questions, call 1-800-701-0710 (TTY 711).

For more on who qualifies for NJ FamilyCare as an older adult, see our guides to NJ FamilyCare for seniors and MLTSS long-term care.

What does Medicare pay for palliative care, and what will it cost?

Original Medicare has no separate palliative care benefit. Visits from palliative doctors, nurse practitioners, physician assistants and clinical social workers are covered under Part B like other medically necessary provider services, so your parent usually pays 20% of the Medicare-approved amount after the Part B deductible, which is $283 in 2026.

ItemWhat your parent pays
Part B deductible$283 in 2026
Palliative visitsUsually 20% after the deductible
Advance care planning at a wellness visit$0 if the provider accepts assignment
Advance care planning at other visitsDeductible and 20% apply

A few things change the bill.

  • Assignment. Ask whether the palliative clinicians accept Medicare assignment. If they do, they can charge only the deductible and coinsurance.
  • Medigap. A Medicare Supplement plan may pick up some or all of the 20%.
  • Medicare Advantage. Plans set their own copays and networks, and some require referrals. Call the plan before the first visit.
  • Hospital stays. Medicare Part B covers some doctor services your parent gets as a hospital inpatient, so a palliative consult can bring a Part B bill on top of the Part A hospital deductible.

The free State Health Insurance Assistance Program (SHIP) can walk you through a specific plan. Call 1-800-792-8820.

What should we ask the palliative care team?

Ask who is on the team, how to reach them after hours, how often they will see your parent, and how they share notes with the other doctors. Clear answers to those four questions tell you a lot.

  • Who will we see at visits, a doctor, a nurse practitioner, or both?
  • How often will you visit or check in, and can that change if things get worse?
  • What number do we call at night or on a weekend? Who answers?
  • Will you talk with Mom's cardiologist or oncologist, or do we carry messages?
  • Can you help with the medication list? Is anything there no longer helping?
  • Is there a social worker who can help us find aides, respite or Medicaid?
  • Do you see patients in nursing homes or assisted living if she moves?
  • When would you suggest hospice, and how would that conversation go?
  • What will we be billed for, and by whom?
The best palliative teams ask your parent what matters most before they talk about treatments.

Palliative care also looks after the family. If you are the one doing the driving, the night shifts and the pharmacy runs, tell the team. Ask about our state's respite and caregiver support programs too.

How do goals-of-care talks and POLST fit in?

A goals-of-care conversation is a sit-down with the medical team about what your parent values and what they want if their health gets worse. In New Jersey, the decisions from that talk can be written on a POLST, a medical order that EMS and hospitals must follow.

Palliative teams hold these conversations often, and they tend to do them well. A good one covers what your parent understands about the illness, what they hope for, what worries them, and which trade-offs they would accept. It is not a single meeting. Wishes can change as the illness changes.

  • Advance directive. Names a health care representative and records general wishes. Any adult can have one. Our estate planning guide covers the documents.
  • POLST. Practitioner Orders for Life-Sustaining Treatment. Signed by your parent and a physician, advanced practice nurse or physician assistant. Meant for serious, advancing illness. See our POLST guide.

Medicare Part B covers voluntary advance care planning. It costs nothing when it is part of the yearly wellness visit and the provider accepts assignment. When it happens during another visit, the deductible and 20% apply.

Say your dad has heart failure and has been in the hospital twice since spring. A palliative nurse practitioner could adjust his diuretic to ease the swelling, help him decide whether he wants another hospital stay if things get worse, and help fill out a POLST that records it. He keeps seeing his cardiologist the whole time.

The state's resources page also links to the New Jersey Health Care Quality Institute's Conversation of Your Life program, which offers guides for starting these talks at home.

For more help, the Aging and Disability Resource Connection can point you to local services at 1-877-222-3737. A geriatric care manager can also coordinate care if you live far away.

faq.q: How do I get palliative care for my mom in New Jersey?
faq.a: Ask her main doctor or the specialist treating her illness for a palliative care referral, or ask for a palliative consult if she is in the hospital. If she has an NJ FamilyCare health plan, you can also call the plan's member services number and ask for the Community-Based Palliative Care team.

faq.q: Does my dad have to stop treatment to get palliative care?
faq.a: No. Palliative care works alongside chemotherapy, dialysis and other treatments. Only hospice requires stopping treatment meant to cure the terminal illness.

faq.q: Does Medicare cover palliative care at home?
faq.a: Original Medicare has no separate palliative benefit, but visits from palliative doctors and nurse practitioners are covered under Part B like other doctor visits, usually with 20% coinsurance after the deductible. Whether a home program bills Medicare depends on the program, so ask exactly what is billed and to whom.

faq.q: What is NJ FamilyCare Community-Based Palliative Care?
faq.a: It is an NJ FamilyCare benefit that started April 1, 2026. Members with a serious illness and reduced quality of life can get a palliative care team at home or in a clinic, including care planning, symptom management, medication review, caregiver support and a 24/7 phone line. It cannot be used at the same time as hospice.

faq.q: Can someone with both Medicare and Medicaid get the NJ FamilyCare palliative benefit?
faq.a: Yes, according to state guidance, unless they enter hospice. Medicare still pays first for other covered services.

faq.q: Who can help us understand a palliative care bill?
faq.a: The free SHIP Medicare counselors at 1-800-792-8820 can explain Medicare and Medicare Advantage costs. For NJ FamilyCare questions, call 1-800-701-0710.

title: Adaptive equipment and assistive technology for seniors in NJ
dek: Walkers, shower chairs, magnifiers and more: what helps at home, what Medicare and NJ FamilyCare pay for, and where New Jersey families can try or borrow equipment.
keyFacts: Medicare Part B covers medically necessary equipment a doctor orders for home use: you pay 20% after the $283 deductible in 2026.
Medicare pays only if the supplier is enrolled in Medicare, even at a large chain store.
For wheelchairs and hospital beds, Medicare rents for 13 months of continuous use, then ownership passes to you.
New Jersey's assistive technology program (ATAC) lends devices to try before you buy: 1-800-922-7233.
NJ FamilyCare covers durable medical equipment and hearing aids.
body:
Adaptive equipment covers anything that makes daily life easier and safer when the body changes: a walker, a shower chair, a jar opener, a big-button phone, a video magnifier. For many older adults in New Jersey, the right few pieces are what make it possible to keep living at home.

Medicare Part B pays for some of it, mostly medical equipment like walkers, wheelchairs, commodes and hospital beds, when a doctor orders it for use at home and it comes from a Medicare-enrolled supplier. Your parent then pays 20% of the Medicare-approved amount after the deductible. Many everyday aids are not on Medicare's list, so New Jersey families also lean on NJ FamilyCare, the state's assistive technology program, county loan closets and the Commission for the Blind and Visually Impaired. This guide shows you where to go for each.

What kinds of adaptive equipment help most at home?

Start with whatever your mom or dad struggles with most each day. Bathing, getting up from a chair or toilet, walking, and dressing are the usual trouble spots. Small aids often solve more than people expect.

Getting around

  • Canes, including quad canes with a four-point base
  • Standard walkers and rollators with a seat and hand brakes
  • Transport chairs, manual wheelchairs and scooters
  • Stair rails on both sides and, for some homes, a stair lift

Bathroom

  • Grab bars anchored into studs, never a towel bar
  • Shower chair or tub transfer bench and a handheld shower head
  • Raised toilet seat, toilet safety frame or bedside commode

Dressing, eating and the kitchen

  • Reachers, long-handled shoehorns, sock aids and elastic laces
  • Built-up utensils, plate guards, nonslip mats and jar openers
  • Lever door handles and touch lamps

Bed and chair

  • Bed rails or a bed assist handle
  • A hospital bed, if getting in and out of a regular bed is no longer safe
  • Patient lifts for someone who cannot stand to transfer

Technology

  • Medical alert buttons and smart speakers that can call family
  • Amplified phones, captioned phones and TV listening devices
  • Magnifiers, large-print and talking devices, and screen readers

For room-by-room home changes and costs, see our aging in place guide. For the habits and fixes that lower fall risk, see preventing falls at home.

What does Medicare cover, and what will you pay?

Medicare Part B covers durable medical equipment (DME) that is medically necessary and ordered by your parent's doctor or other provider for use at home. After the Part B deductible ($283 in 2026), your parent pays 20% of the Medicare-approved amount if the supplier accepts assignment.

Medicare defines DME as equipment that can stand repeated use, is used for a medical reason, is generally useful only to someone sick or injured, is used in the home and is expected to last at least three years.

ItemMedicare Part B?
Canes, walkers, rollatorsYes, if medically necessary
Manual wheelchairsYes, if medically necessary
Power chairs, scootersYes, for use in the home, with an exam and written order
Commode chairsYes, if confined to bed or room
Hospital beds, patient liftsYes, if medically necessary
Hearing aidsNo
White canes for the blindNo

Medicare's official equipment reference list denies grab bars, bathtub seats and raised toilet seats as items that are not primarily medical. If you hope Medicare will pay for one, call 1-800-MEDICARE (1-800-633-4227) before you buy.

The supplier rules that matter

  • Use an enrolled supplier. Medicare pays only if the supplier is enrolled in Medicare and has a supplier number, even if it is a big chain store. Use Medicare's supplier directory.
  • Ask about assignment. A participating supplier must accept assignment, so it can charge only the deductible and 20%. A supplier that does not accept assignment can charge more.
  • Rentals. Medicare pays for most DME on a rental basis. For items like wheelchairs and hospital beds, Medicare rents for 13 months of continuous use, then the supplier must transfer ownership to your parent. Make sure the supplier accepts assignment for every rental month.
  • Repairs. If your parent rents, the supplier must keep the equipment working. If your parent owns it, Medicare pays 80% of the approved amount for repairs, up to the cost of replacing the item.
  • Power mobility. Medicare will not cover a power wheelchair or scooter needed only outside the home. Some power wheelchairs need prior authorization, which the supplier requests.

Medicare Advantage. Plans must cover the same categories of DME as Original Medicare, but they choose the suppliers and set the costs. Call the plan first. If it denies an item you think your parent needs, you can appeal. A Medigap policy may cover some of the 20%.

The free SHIP counselors at 1-800-792-8820 can help you sort out coverage or an appeal.

Does NJ FamilyCare pay for equipment?

Yes. Durable medical equipment and hearing aids are both on the list of services NJ FamilyCare covers, along with prosthetics, orthotics and occupational therapy. Coverage still depends on medical need and your parent's plan rules.

If your parent has both Medicare and NJ FamilyCare, Medicare usually pays first and NJ FamilyCare may help with what is left. Call the member services number on the NJ FamilyCare plan card before ordering and ask whether a prior approval is needed. For general questions, NJ FamilyCare's line is 1-800-701-0710 (TTY 711).

Our guides to NJ FamilyCare for seniors and MLTSS explain who qualifies. MLTSS members who need home changes or extra equipment should ask their care manager what the plan can add.

Where can you try or borrow equipment in New Jersey?

New Jersey's federally funded assistive technology program lets residents with disabilities try devices, borrow them for a short time, and find reused equipment for less. County loan closets lend walkers, wheelchairs and bath items, often for free.

New Jersey's assistive technology program

The Richard West Assistive Technology Advocacy Center (ATAC) of Disability Rights New Jersey runs the state's Assistive Technology Act program. It offers hands-on device demonstrations, a short-term loan library so you can try before you buy, and equipment reuse through a partnership with Goodwill Home Medical Equipment. Call 1-800-922-7233 (in New Jersey) or 609-292-9742, weekdays 9 a.m. to 5 p.m.

Trying first matters. A rollator that looks perfect online may be too heavy to lift into the car, and a tablet may be too fiddly for arthritic fingers. A short loan answers that before money is spent.

Used equipment. The state's basic needs site lists Used Home Medical Equipment from Goodwill, a warehouse at 300 Benigno Blvd. in Bellmawr in Camden County. It sells wheelchairs, scooters, walkers, lift chairs, hospital beds and bath items with no prescription. Call 609-812-2210 for hours and stock.

Loan closets. Many county offices on aging, senior centers, towns and faith groups lend equipment. For example, the Salem County Office on Aging and Disabilities lends wheelchairs, walkers, canes, commodes and shower benches at no cost to residents 60 and older and people with disabilities, first come, first served. Call 856-339-8622. In other counties, call the Aging and Disability Resource Connection at 1-877-222-3737 and ask what lends near your parent, or try your town's senior center.

  1. Name the problem. "Mom can't step over the tub" leads to better advice than "we need a shower chair."
  2. Ask the doctor or therapist. Get a written order for anything you want Medicare or NJ FamilyCare to pay for.
  3. Try or borrow first. Use ATAC or a loan closet for anything expensive or unfamiliar.
  4. Check the supplier. Confirm Medicare enrollment and assignment before anything is delivered.
  5. Set it up right. Have someone adjust walker height, install grab bars into studs and show your parent how to use each item.

What help is there for vision and hearing loss?

The New Jersey Commission for the Blind and Visually Impaired (CBVI) helps residents of any age with low vision learn daily living skills and get the right aids, with programs aimed at people 55 and older. For hearing, start with our hearing aid guide.

CBVI serves people whose vision loss affects daily life and who have best corrected vision of 20/70 or worse in the better eye, or a visual field of 40 degrees or less. Its independent living services include:

  • Rehabilitation teaching at home on cooking safely, writing guides, adaptive equipment and assistive technology
  • Orientation and mobility training for getting around the house and town
  • Low vision help to find visual aids that fit the degree of vision loss
  • Eye health nurses who teach about devices like talking glucometers and talking blood pressure monitors
  • LEAP classes at libraries for people 55 and older on speech and magnification technology

Call the CBVI regional office for your parent's county. Northern region (Bergen, Essex, Hudson, Morris, Passaic, Sussex, Warren): 973-648-2111. Central region (Hunterdon, Middlesex, Monmouth, Ocean, Somerset, Union): 732-308-4001. Southern region (Atlantic, Burlington, Camden, Cape May, Cumberland, Gloucester, Mercer, Salem): 856-482-3700.

Original Medicare does not cover hearing aids. Our hearing aids guide covers over-the-counter aids and New Jersey's help programs, and our guide to free eye exams and glasses covers vision care. For other disability questions, the NJ Division of Disability Services has trained staff on its information line at 1-888-285-3036.

How can an occupational therapist help?

An occupational therapist (OT) looks at how your parent bathes, dresses, cooks and moves through the house, then suggests equipment and safer ways to do each task. Medicare Part B helps pay for medically necessary outpatient OT when a doctor or other provider certifies the need.

After the deductible your parent pays 20%. Medicare sets no yearly dollar cap on medically necessary outpatient therapy, and therapy can aim to improve or simply maintain what your parent can do. If your parent is homebound, OT may also come through Medicare home health.

A good OT visit often turns up things families miss: a toilet that is too low, a bed that is too high, a bath mat that slides. Ask the doctor for an OT referral after a fall, a hospital stay or a new diagnosis like Parkinson's or a stroke. Our guide to staying active after surgery covers the weeks after rehab.

The best equipment is the piece your parent will actually use, set up the right way.

How do you avoid medical equipment scams?

Be wary of anyone who calls, knocks or advertises "free" braces, scooters or supplies paid for by Medicare. Medicare will never call to sell your parent anything or visit them at home.

Medicare itself warns that a few dishonest suppliers push expensive power wheelchairs and scooters on people who do not qualify.

  • Never give a Medicare number to a caller you did not contact.
  • Do not accept equipment your parent's doctor did not order. Refuse the delivery or return it.
  • Read every Medicare Summary Notice or plan statement for items your parent never got.
  • Report suspected fraud to 1-800-MEDICARE at 1-800-633-4227. New Jersey's Senior Medicare Patrol helps families check bills and report problems at 1-732-777-1940 ext. 1117.

Our guide to scams targeting New Jersey seniors covers the other calls to watch for.

faq.q: How do I get Medicare to pay for a walker for my mom?
faq.a: Her doctor or other provider must order it as medically necessary for use at home, and you must get it from a Medicare-enrolled supplier. If the supplier accepts assignment, she pays 20% of the Medicare-approved amount after the Part B deductible.

faq.q: Does Medicare pay for grab bars or a shower chair?
faq.a: No. Medicare's official equipment reference list denies grab bars, bathtub seats and raised toilet seats as items that are not primarily medical. A commode chair can be covered when your parent is confined to a bed or room. Call 1-800-MEDICARE before buying if you hope Medicare will pay.

faq.q: Where can I borrow a wheelchair for my dad in New Jersey?
faq.a: Many county offices on aging, senior centers and towns run free loan closets. Call the Aging and Disability Resource Connection at 1-877-222-3737 to find one near your dad. The state's assistive technology program, ATAC, also lends devices to try at 1-800-922-7233.

faq.q: Does Medicare cover a power wheelchair or scooter?
faq.a: Only when it is medically necessary for use inside the home. Your parent needs a face-to-face exam and a written order from a treating provider, and some power wheelchairs need prior authorization, which the supplier requests.

faq.q: Who helps older adults in New Jersey with low vision equipment?
faq.a: The New Jersey Commission for the Blind and Visually Impaired helps residents whose vision is 20/70 or worse in the better eye with correction, or whose visual field is 40 degrees or less. It offers in-home training, low vision aids and programs for people 55 and older.

faq.q: What should I do if a company sends my parent equipment nobody ordered?
faq.a: Do not accept or use it, check Medicare statements for charges, and report it to 1-800-MEDICARE (1-800-633-4227). New Jersey's Senior Medicare Patrol can help at 1-732-777-1940 ext. 1117.

title: Rehab after a hospital stay in NJ: Medicare's skilled care rules
dek: The 3-day rule, what you pay from day 21, what counts as skilled care, how to pick a rehab in New Jersey and how to appeal when the facility says Medicare will stop paying.
keyFacts: Original Medicare covers SNF rehab after an inpatient stay of at least 3 days in a row. Observation days do not count.
2026 costs per benefit period: $0 a day for days 1 to 20, $217 a day for days 21 to 100, all costs after day 100.
Coverage does not depend on improvement. Skilled care to maintain a condition or slow decline can be covered.
The SNF must give a Notice of Medicare Non-Coverage at least 2 days before coverage ends. Appeal by noon the day before.
NJ fast appeals: Commence Health, 1-866-815-5440. Ombudsman: 1-877-582-6995.
body:
Medicare Part A pays for short-term rehab in a skilled nursing facility after a hospital stay, but only when your parent was formally admitted as an inpatient for at least 3 days in a row and then needs skilled nursing or therapy every day. It covers up to 100 days in each benefit period. In 2026 your parent pays $0 a day for days 1 to 20 and $217 a day for days 21 to 100.

Most rehab stays end long before day 100. Coverage lasts only while your parent needs daily skilled care, and the facility decides when that stops. This guide explains what counts as skilled care, how to pick a rehab in New Jersey, and how to file a fast appeal when the notice says Medicare will stop paying. Our hospital discharge guide covers the hospital side, including observation status. This is general information, not legal advice.

Does Medicare pay for rehab after a hospital stay?

Yes, under Original Medicare, if your parent meets every condition on Medicare's list. Miss one and the rehab bill can land on the family.

According to Medicare.gov, your parent must:

  • Have Part A, with days left in the current benefit period.
  • Have a "qualifying inpatient hospital stay" of at least 3 days in a row. The day of admission counts. The day of discharge does not.
  • Enter a Medicare-certified skilled nursing facility (SNF) within a short time, generally 30 days, of leaving the hospital.
  • Need daily skilled nursing or therapy that a doctor or other provider has ordered.
  • Need that care for a condition treated during the hospital stay, or for a new condition that started while in the SNF for that condition.

Time spent in the emergency room or under observation before admission does not count toward the 3 days, even overnight. If your parent spent two nights "under observation" and one night as an inpatient, that is one inpatient day. Ask the hospital in plain words: is she admitted, or here under observation? Our discharge guide explains the MOON notice and how to appeal a change from inpatient to observation.

There are two exceptions. Some doctors belong to an Accountable Care Organization approved for a "Skilled Nursing Facility 3-Day Rule Waiver." Many Medicare Advantage plans also waive the 3-day stay. Ask the hospital case manager whether either applies.

Two nights under observation and one night admitted is one inpatient day, not three.

How long will Medicare pay for rehab, and what does it cost?

Up to 100 days per benefit period, with a daily charge starting on day 21. In practice, payment stops as soon as your parent no longer needs daily skilled care.

Days in the SNFYour parent pays (2026)
Days 1 to 20$0 a day
Days 21 to 100$217 a day
Day 101 onAll costs

The Part A deductible of $1,736 applies once per benefit period. Most people pay it for the hospital stay, so they do not pay it again for rehab. A benefit period starts the day your parent is admitted as an inpatient and ends after 60 days in a row with no inpatient hospital care or skilled care in a SNF. After that, a new hospital stay starts a new benefit period and a fresh set of 100 days.

Days 21 to 100 add up fast. At $217 a day, 30 days of coinsurance is $6,510. Medicare's SNF booklet says some Medigap policies pay all or part of that daily amount. Check the policy, or read our Medigap guide. If your parent has both Medicare and full NJ FamilyCare (Medicaid), most costs may be covered.

The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) usually announces the next year's Part A amounts in mid November. As of November 6, 2026, the 2027 figures had not been released. A stay that runs into January will use the 2027 rate for those days.

The 30-day rule works in your parent's favor after rehab, too. If your parent leaves the SNF and goes back to the same or another SNF within 30 days, Medicare's booklet says another 3-day hospital stay may not be needed.

What counts as skilled care?

Skilled care is nursing or therapy that only licensed professionals, or people they supervise, can safely do. Medicare pays for rehab only while your parent needs it every day.

Examples Medicare gives include intravenous fluids or medicines and physical therapy. For therapy alone, Medicare counts care as "daily" when it is needed and given 5 to 7 days a week.

Help with bathing, dressing, eating and getting to the bathroom is called custodial care. Medicare does not pay for a SNF stay when that is all your parent needs.

"She's plateaued" is not a reason to stop

Families often hear that therapy must end because a parent is no longer improving. Under the 2013 Jimmo v. Sebelius settlement, CMS clarified that coverage "does not turn on the presence or absence of a beneficiary's potential for improvement." Skilled care can be covered to maintain your parent's condition or to slow a decline, as long as the care truly needs a skilled professional. If the only reason given is "no progress," ask for the reason in writing and consider an appeal.

Is a rehab facility or an inpatient rehab hospital better?

It depends on how much therapy your parent can handle. An inpatient rehabilitation facility (IRF) gives intensive therapy under close physician supervision. A SNF gives a lighter daily schedule.

QuestionSNF rehabInpatient rehab (IRF)
Therapy levelDaily, lighterIntensive
3-day stay needed?Yes, in Original MedicareNo
Cost, 2026$0 days 1 to 20, then $217 a dayHospital rules: $0 days 1 to 60 after the deductible

For an IRF, a provider must certify that your parent needs intensive rehabilitation, continued medical supervision and coordinated care. CMS notes that in an IRF, therapy must be expected to improve your parent's function. If your parent moves straight from the hospital to an IRF, or within 60 days of discharge, Medicare.gov says there is no second deductible.

A third path is home. If your parent is homebound and needs part-time skilled care, Medicare home health costs $0 for covered visits and needs no hospital stay. It does not include round-the-clock help.

How do I choose a rehab facility in New Jersey?

Start with a shortlist from the hospital, check each one on Medicare Care Compare, then call or visit. You often have only a day or two, so split the work among family members.

  1. Get the list early. Ask the hospital case manager on day one or two which nearby SNFs have beds. Name your top choices in writing. Original Medicare lets your parent use any Medicare-certified SNF with a bed.
  2. Check Care Compare. On Medicare Care Compare, choose "Nursing homes including rehab services" and search by ZIP code. Open the separate ratings for inspections, staffing and quality. Our nursing home ratings guide explains how to read them.
  3. Call the ombudsman. New Jersey's Long-Term Care Ombudsman answers questions and takes complaints at 1-877-582-6995. Medicare suggests asking how many complaints a facility has had and whether they were resolved.
  4. Visit or send someone. Ask to see the latest inspection report. Facilities must show it on request.
  5. If your parent has Medicare Advantage, call the plan. Ask which SNFs are in network and whether the plan must approve the stay first.

Questions worth asking on the phone or at the front desk:

  • How many days a week, and how many minutes a day, will my mother get therapy?
  • Is there a separate rehab unit, or will she share a hall with long-term residents?
  • Who is the physician or nurse practitioner, and how often do they see rehab patients?
  • When is the first care plan meeting, and can family join by phone?
  • What happens if she gets sick at night? How often do rehab patients go back to the hospital?
  • Do you accept her Medicare Advantage plan or Medigap, and NJ FamilyCare if she needs long-term care later?

Distance matters too. A good facility close enough for daily family visits is often a better choice than a higher rated one an hour away.

What happens when rehab says Medicare will stop paying?

The SNF must give your parent a written "Notice of Medicare Non-Coverage" at least 2 days before covered services end. You can ask for a fast appeal by noon of the day before the end date on that notice.

The appeal goes to an independent reviewer called the Beneficiary and Family Centered Care Quality Improvement Organization (BFCC-QIO). For New Jersey, that is Commence Health, formerly Livanta, at 1-866-815-5440. The number should also be printed on the notice.

  1. Read the date. The notice gives the last covered day. Circle it and count back to noon the day before.
  2. Call Commence Health. A phone call starts the appeal. Your parent, or someone acting for her, can call.
  3. Say why it is too soon. For example: he still needs help from two people to stand, the wound is open, or no one is trained to manage his new medicines at home.
  4. Get the detailed notice. The SNF must then give a "Detailed Explanation of Non-Coverage" by the end of the day it hears from the QIO, stating the rule it relied on.
  5. Expect a quick answer. The QIO decides by close of business the day after it gets the information it needs.

If the QIO agrees services are ending too soon, Medicare keeps paying. If it agrees with the facility, your parent does not owe for care given before the end date on the notice, but may have to pay for days after it. If you miss the noon deadline, Medicare.gov describes other review options with different rules. For free, unbiased help, call New Jersey's State Health Insurance Assistance Program (SHIP) at 1-800-792-8820.

Key numbers for a rehab stay

Fast appeal (Commence Health, BFCC-QIO for NJ): 1-866-815-5440. NJ Long-Term Care Ombudsman: 1-877-582-6995. Free Medicare counseling (SHIP): 1-800-792-8820. 1-800-MEDICARE: 1-800-633-4227.

If your parent cannot go home

When Medicare days end and your parent still needs daily hands-on help, the family pays privately or applies for NJ FamilyCare. Our NJ FamilyCare and MLTSS guide and paying for long-term care guide explain the options. If your parent ends up in a nursing home for 60 days or more and qualifies for Medicaid, New Jersey's I Choose Home NJ program may help with a move back to the community.

How is rehab different with a Medicare Advantage plan?

The plan sets its own copays and network, may waive the 3-day stay, and often must approve the SNF stay before your parent arrives. The right to a fast appeal is the same.

  • Prior approval. Medicare's SNF booklet warns that your parent may have to pay for more, or all, of the stay if the plan was not told before admission. Make sure the hospital has sent the request.
  • Same coverage rules. Since a 2023 CMS rule, Advantage plans must follow Original Medicare's coverage rules and conditions when deciding what is medically necessary. They cannot hold your parent to a stricter standard for basic benefits.
  • Faster decisions. Starting in 2026, Advantage plans must answer urgent prior authorization requests within 72 hours and standard ones within 7 calendar days, and give a specific reason for any denial.
  • Copays from day 1. Medicare.gov says Advantage members may be charged copays during the first 20 days. Check the plan's Evidence of Coverage.

If the plan denies the stay, ask the plan for a fast appeal, and ask the doctor to support it. SHIP can walk you through it. If your parent is comparing plans, our Advantage vs. Medigap guide explains how rehab coverage differs.

Recovery often continues at home. Our guide to staying active after surgery has ideas for the weeks after rehab ends.

More guides that may help: appealing a Medicare decision and delirium after a hospital stay.

faq.q: How many days of rehab does Medicare pay for in New Jersey?
faq.a: Up to 100 days in a skilled nursing facility per benefit period, but only while your parent needs daily skilled nursing or therapy. In 2026 days 1 to 20 cost $0 and days 21 to 100 cost $217 a day. Many stays end well before day 100.

faq.q: How do I appeal for my mom when the rehab says Medicare coverage is ending?
faq.a: Look for the Notice of Medicare Non-Coverage, which must come at least 2 days before coverage ends. Call New Jersey's BFCC-QIO, Commence Health, at 1-866-815-5440 by noon the day before the end date on the notice. The reviewer decides by close of business the day after it gets the information it needs.

faq.q: Can rehab stop because my dad is not improving?
faq.a: Not for that reason alone. Under the Jimmo v. Sebelius settlement, Medicare coverage depends on the need for skilled care, not on potential for improvement. Skilled care to maintain his condition or slow a decline can be covered. Inpatient rehab hospitals are different, because there therapy must be expected to improve function.

faq.q: Does observation time count toward the 3-day rule?
faq.a: No. Only days as a formally admitted inpatient count, starting with the day of admission and not counting the day of discharge. Emergency room and observation time do not count, even overnight.

faq.q: How do I find a good rehab facility for my mother in NJ?
faq.a: Ask the hospital case manager for a list of SNFs with beds, then look each one up on Medicare Care Compare under nursing homes including rehab services. Read the separate inspection, staffing and quality ratings, call the NJ Long-Term Care Ombudsman at 1-877-582-6995, and visit if you can. If she has Medicare Advantage, confirm the facility is in network.

faq.q: Does Medigap pay the $217 daily rehab coinsurance?
faq.a: Some Medigap policies pay all or part of the SNF coinsurance for days 21 to 100. Check the policy or call the insurance company. Medicare Advantage plans set their own SNF copays, which can start on day 1.

title: Medicare Part D drug plans in NJ for 2027: costs and choices
dek: New Jersey has 11 stand-alone drug plans for 2027, a $2,400 out-of-pocket cap and lower prices on 15 drugs. Here is how to compare plans for a parent, and how PAAD, Senior Gold and Extra Help fit in.
keyFacts: 11 stand-alone Part D plans in New Jersey for 2027. Lowest premium: $5.30 a month (CMS).
2027 out-of-pocket cap: $2,400 on covered drugs. Highest allowed deductible: $700.
New negotiated Medicare prices on 15 drugs, including Ozempic and Trelegy Ellipta, start in 2027.
Open enrollment ends December 7, 2026. New coverage starts January 1, 2027.
PAAD and Senior Gold: 1-800-792-9745. Free plan comparisons from NJ SHIP: 1-800-792-8820.
body:
For 2027, people in New Jersey with Original Medicare can choose from 11 stand-alone Part D drug plans, according to the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS). The lowest premium is $5.30 a month. No plan may charge a deductible above $700, and once your out-of-pocket costs for covered drugs reach $2,400, you pay nothing more for the rest of 2027.

You have until December 7, 2026 to pick a plan for January. Several things change for 2027: a federal program that held down stand-alone premiums has ended, lower negotiated prices start for 15 widely used drugs, and the monthly payment option now renews on its own. This guide goes deeper on Part D than our open enrollment checklist, with a focus on what families should compare.

What does a Part D plan cost in New Jersey in 2027?

It depends on the plan and your parent's drugs. Each plan sets its own premium, may have a deductible, and then charges about 25% of drug costs until the $2,400 cap.

Part D figure20262027
Highest deductible$615$700
Out-of-pocket cap$2,100$2,400
Base premium (for penalty)$38.99$41.33

A Part D year has three stages. In the deductible stage, your parent pays the full cost of covered drugs until the deductible is met. Some plans have no deductible. In the initial coverage stage, your parent pays 25% coinsurance for generic and brand drugs. Once out-of-pocket spending reaches $2,400, catastrophic coverage starts and covered drugs cost $0 through December 31. Payments made on your parent's behalf, such as through Extra Help, count toward the cap.

Two costs sit outside these numbers. People with higher incomes pay an extra monthly amount called IRMAA, which in 2026 starts above $109,000 for single filers and $218,000 for joint filers. And insulin is capped at $35 for a one-month supply of each covered insulin, with no deductible.

Why could my parent's premium jump in 2027?

A temporary federal program that limited stand-alone premium increases ended at the close of 2026. Plans now price on their own, so some premiums will rise and others will fall.

CMS ran the Part D Premium Stabilization Demonstration in 2025 and 2026 to soften premium swings after the drug benefit was redesigned. In July 2026 CMS announced it would end the demonstration after 2026. In New Jersey, CMS reports that 100% of people in a stand-alone drug plan have access to a plan with a lower premium than they paid in 2026. Having access is not the same as being moved, though. If your parent does nothing, the current plan renews at its new 2027 price.

Look for the Annual Notice of Change your parent's plan mailed in September. It shows the 2027 premium, deductible and drug list. If it is lost, call the number on the plan card.

If your parent does nothing, the plan renews at its 2027 price. Check before December 7.

Which drugs get lower Medicare prices in 2027?

Medicare negotiated new prices for 15 Part D drugs that take effect in 2027. They include Ozempic, Rybelsus and Wegovy, Janumet, Tradjenta, Trelegy Ellipta, Breo Ellipta, Xtandi, Ibrance and Linzess.

CMS says the discounts range from 38% to 85% off the 2024 list price for a 30-day supply. The full list also includes Austedo, Calquence, Ofev, Otezla, Pomalyst, Vraylar and Xifaxan. CMS estimates people with Medicare drug plans will save $685 million out of pocket in 2027.

What your parent actually pays still depends on the plan's coinsurance, the deductible and the $2,400 cap. If your parent takes one of these drugs, enter it in Plan Finder and compare the yearly estimate across plans.

How does the Medicare Prescription Payment Plan work?

It spreads your parent's out-of-pocket drug costs into monthly bills across the calendar year. It does not lower what your parent owes in total.

Every Part D plan and every Medicare Advantage plan with drug coverage must offer it. There is no fee. Instead of paying at the pharmacy, your parent gets a monthly bill from the plan, separate from the premium. Medicare's own example: someone with $600 a month in drug costs who joins in January 2027 pays $200 the first month instead of $600, and never pays more than $2,400 for the year.

  • Best fit: high drug costs early in the year. Medicare suggests starting before September.
  • Poor fit: low or steady costs, or anyone who gets Extra Help, a Medicare Savings Program, or a state program such as PAAD or Senior Gold.
  • It renews on its own. The plan automatically renews your parent's participation each year unless they opt out. It ends if they switch plans, so sign up again with the new plan.
  • Missed bills. There is no interest or late fee. After a reminder, the plan can remove your parent from the payment option, but not from drug coverage. Always pay the premium first.

How do Extra Help, PAAD and Senior Gold work with Part D?

All three lower costs on top of a Part D plan. Extra Help is federal. PAAD and Senior Gold are New Jersey programs, and both require Medicare-eligible members to enroll in Part D.

Extra Help

For 2026, Medicare lists income limits of $23,940 for one person and $32,460 for a married couple, and resource limits of $18,090 and $36,100. In 2027, people with Extra Help pay a $0 premium on qualifying plans, a $0 deductible, and no more than $5.80 for a generic or $14.40 for a brand drug. They do not pay a Part D late penalty. People with Medicaid, a Medicare Savings Program or SSI get it automatically. Others apply through Social Security at 1-800-772-1213.

PAAD

PAAD is for New Jersey residents 65 and older, or on Social Security disability, with 2026 income under $54,943 single or $62,390 married. Your parent pays $5 for covered generics and $7 for brand drugs. PAAD pays the monthly premium for certain basic Part D plans priced at or below the regional benchmark, and for enhanced plans at or below the benchmark if the plan follows PAAD's billing rules. In Medicare Advantage, PAAD contributes up to the benchmark toward the drug part of the premium.

Senior Gold

Senior Gold covers 2026 income between $54,943 and $64,943 single, or $62,390 and $72,390 married. Your parent pays $15 plus 50% of the remaining cost of each covered drug, then a flat $15 once out-of-pocket costs pass $2,000 (single) or $3,000 (married). Senior Gold members pay their own Part D premium and any late penalty.

Before your parent switches plans

Call the PAAD and Senior Gold hotline at 1-800-792-9745 and ask whether the new plan works with the program. Neither program pays for diabetic test strips or lancets. Those go through Medicare Part B. For an unbiased plan comparison, call NJ SHIP at 1-800-792-8820.

How do I compare Part D plans for my mom in Plan Finder?

Use Medicare's Plan Finder with her exact drug list and pharmacy. It estimates her total yearly cost for each plan, which is the number that matters.

  1. Gather her bottles. Write down each drug name, dose and how often she takes it, including inhalers, injectables and insulin.
  2. Open Plan Finder. Go to Medicare.gov Plan Finder. You can log in with her Medicare.gov account or search by ZIP code.
  3. Add her pharmacies. Pick the one she uses plus a mail-order option. Preferred pharmacies can be cheaper.
  4. Sort by total cost. Compare estimated yearly drug costs plus premiums, not the premium alone.
  5. Check the fine print. For each drug, look for prior authorization, step therapy or quantity limits.
  6. Enroll by December 7. Enroll through Plan Finder, the plan, or 1-800-MEDICARE at 1-800-633-4227, open 24 hours a day. Keep the confirmation number.

If she has PAAD, Extra Help or a Medigap policy, tell the SHIP counselor so the comparison reflects it. Our prescription and bill help guide lists other ways to save. Be wary of callers who say they are "from Medicare" and want to switch her plan. Our scams guide explains what to do.

What if my parent misses December 7?

Most people must wait until next fall. There are a few exceptions, and going without drug coverage can bring a lifelong penalty.

  • Medicare Advantage members get one change from January 1 to March 31, including a return to Original Medicare with a stand-alone drug plan. People in Original Medicare cannot use that window to switch drug plans.
  • Extra Help or Medicaid. Medicare.gov says your parent may be able to change drug coverage once a month.
  • Moving, losing other coverage or entering a nursing home can open a Special Enrollment Period. SHIP can tell you whether one applies.

The Part D late enrollment penalty applies after 63 or more days in a row without Part D or other creditable drug coverage. It equals 1% of the national base premium for each full month without coverage, rounded to the nearest 10 cents, and is added to the premium for as long as your parent has Part D. With a 2027 base premium of $41.33, 14 months without coverage adds about $5.80 a month. If your parent is still choosing between Medigap and Advantage, see our Medigap guide.

More guides that may help: Extra Help and managing many medicines.

faq.q: How many Medicare Part D plans are there in New Jersey for 2027?
faq.a: CMS reports 11 stand-alone Part D plans for 2027, with a lowest premium of $5.30 a month. Medicare Advantage plans with drug coverage are separate, and New Jersey has 72 Advantage plans for 2027.

faq.q: What is the Part D out-of-pocket maximum for 2027?
faq.a: $2,400 for covered Part D drugs. After your out-of-pocket costs reach that amount, you pay $0 for covered drugs for the rest of 2027. Plans may charge a deductible of up to $700 before that.

faq.q: How do I pick a Part D plan for my dad?
faq.a: Enter every drug he takes, with the dose, and his pharmacy into Medicare's Plan Finder. Compare the estimated total yearly cost, not just the premium, and check for prior authorization or quantity limits. NJ SHIP at 1-800-792-8820 will run the comparison with you for free.

faq.q: Will PAAD pay my mom's Part D premium in 2027?
faq.a: PAAD pays the monthly premium for certain basic Part D plans priced at or below the regional benchmark, and for enhanced plans at or below the benchmark if the plan follows PAAD billing rules. Call 1-800-792-9745 before switching to confirm the plan works with PAAD.

faq.q: Should my parent sign up for the Medicare Prescription Payment Plan?
faq.a: It helps people with high drug costs early in the year by spreading them into monthly bills. It does not lower total costs. Medicare says it may not be a good fit for people with low or steady costs, or who get Extra Help or state help such as PAAD or Senior Gold.

faq.q: What happens if my mother does nothing during open enrollment?
faq.a: If her plan is still offered, it renews automatically at its 2027 premium and drug list. Read the Annual Notice of Change first, because premiums and covered drugs can change a lot from year to year.
