title: Vaccines after 65 in New Jersey: what Medicare covers
dek: Flu, COVID-19, RSV, shingles, pneumonia and Tdap: which shots the CDC recommends after 65, whether Part B or Part D pays, and where to get them in New Jersey.
keyFacts: Part B covers flu, COVID-19 and pneumococcal shots at $0 when the provider accepts assignment.
Part D covers shingles, RSV and Tdap with no copay or deductible.
CDC: one RSV dose at 75+, or at 50 to 74 with higher risk. Not a yearly shot.
CDC: two Shingrix doses, 2 to 6 months apart, for adults 50 and older.
NJ has 103 local health departments. Free Medicare help (SHIP): 1-800-792-8820.
body:
Medicare covers every vaccine routinely recommended for adults 65 and older, and for most of them your parent pays nothing. Part B covers flu, COVID-19 and pneumonia shots, plus hepatitis B for people who qualify. Part D drug plans cover shingles, RSV and Tdap with no copay and no deductible.

The catch is which card to show. A shingles or RSV shot is free only if your parent has Part D or a Medicare Advantage plan with drug coverage. This guide lists what the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) currently recommends after 65, which part of Medicare pays, and where to get vaccinated in New Jersey. Talk with your parent's doctor or pharmacist about which shots fit their health.

Which vaccines does Medicare cover, and under which part?

Flu, COVID-19, pneumococcal and hepatitis B shots are under Part B. Other vaccines recommended by the federal Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices (ACIP), including shingles, RSV and Tdap, are under Part D.

VaccineCovered byYour parent pays
FluPart B$0 *
COVID-19Part B$0 *
PneumococcalPart B$0 *
Hepatitis BPart B, if eligible$0 *
ShinglesPart D$0
RSVPart D$0
TdapPart D$0

* When the provider accepts Medicare assignment.

Medicare.gov says Part D plans cannot charge a copay or apply a deductible for vaccines ACIP recommends. Medicare Advantage plans that include drug coverage cover the Part D vaccines too. For hepatitis B, Part B pays if your parent never finished the series, does not know their history, or has a condition that raises risk, such as diabetes or end-stage kidney disease.

Free under Part D means your parent needs Part D. Without it, a shingles shot is billed at full price.

Which vaccines does the CDC recommend after 65?

The CDC's adult schedule currently in use is dated July 2, 2025. In September 2026 the CDC said its COVID-19 recommendations from that schedule remain in effect for the 2026 to 2027 season. Here is what it says for adults 65 and older.

VaccineHow often, 65+
FluEvery season
COVID-192 doses, about 6 months apart
RSVOnce (75+, or 50 to 74 at risk)
Shingles2 doses, 2 to 6 months apart
PneumococcalUsually 1 dose, by history
Td or TdapEvery 10 years

Flu, every fall

One dose each season. For 65 and older, the CDC prefers a high-dose, recombinant or adjuvanted flu vaccine. If none is available, any flu vaccine appropriate for age is better than skipping it. Medicare.gov notes this season's shots are trivalent, meaning they protect against three flu strains.

COVID-19

The schedule calls for 2 doses of the current vaccine for people 65 and older, about 6 months apart, with at least 2 months between them. People with a weakened immune system may get more. Medicare Part B covers the updated 2026 to 2027 Moderna, Pfizer-BioNTech and Novavax vaccines. The CDC also says each patient should talk through benefits and risks with a provider.

RSV, once

Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) can cause serious lung infections in older adults. The CDC recommends a single dose for everyone 75 and older, and for adults 50 to 74 at higher risk. Higher risk includes heart failure or coronary artery disease, lung disease such as COPD, diabetes with complications or insulin use, severe obesity, a weakened immune system, and living in a nursing home. People can tell the pharmacist about their own risk factor. It is not a yearly shot. The best time is late summer or early fall, ideally August through October, but it can be given any time.

Shingles

Two doses of the recombinant shingles vaccine (Shingrix), 2 to 6 months apart, for everyone 50 and older. This applies even if your parent already had shingles or got the older Zostavax shot years ago.

Pneumococcal

For adults 50 and older who never had a newer pneumococcal conjugate vaccine, the CDC recommends one dose of PCV20 or PCV21. Another option is PCV15 followed by PPSV23 at least a year later. If your parent had older pneumonia shots, the right next step depends on which ones and when, so bring any records to the pharmacist.

Tdap and Td

One dose of Tdap if your parent never had a Tdap shot at age 10 or older, then a Td or Tdap booster every 10 years. Tdap protects against tetanus, diphtheria and whooping cough.

Hepatitis B

Adults 60 and older with risk factors should get the series. Those without risk factors may get it, and should get it if they ask. For people 60 and older with diabetes, the CDC says to decide together with a provider.

Why does it matter whether a shot is Part B or Part D?

Because the pharmacy or office bills a different payer. Bring every card so they can bill the right one.

  • Bring the red, white and blue Medicare card for Part B shots, plus the Part D or Medicare Advantage card for shingles, RSV and Tdap.
  • Use a pharmacy in the drug plan's network. The pharmacy bills the plan directly. A doctor's office may not be set up to bill Part D, so ask before the shot.
  • No Part D? Your parent pays full price for the Part D vaccines. If your parent qualifies for PAAD or Senior Gold, those programs require a Part D plan anyway. Our Part D guide explains how to choose one, and open enrollment ends December 7, 2026.
  • Questions to ask the pharmacist: Which of these shots is my mother due for based on her record? Do you have the preferred flu vaccine for her age? Will you bill her Part D plan for the shingles or RSV shot? When should she come back for the second dose?
  • Charged by mistake? Call the plan or 1-800-MEDICARE at 1-800-633-4227. NJ SHIP gives free help at 1-800-792-8820.

Where can my parent get vaccinated in New Jersey?

At most pharmacies, at the doctor's office, and through local health departments. Medicare.gov lists the doctor's office and the local pharmacy as common places for flu and RSV shots.

  1. Call the pharmacy first. Ask which vaccines they have in stock, whether they take walk-ins, and whether they bill your parent's Part D plan.
  2. Ask the doctor's office. Many primary care offices give flu, COVID-19 and pneumococcal shots during a visit. A yearly Wellness visit is a good time to review what is due. Our staying well guide explains that visit.
  3. Try the local health department. New Jersey has 103 local health departments serving its 564 municipalities. Some hold flu clinics, so call and ask. Find yours on the NJ Department of Health local health directory. The department's adult vaccine brochure says people without insurance should ask their local health department about low-cost or free options.
  4. If your parent lives in a facility, ask the nursing home or assisted living residence about its vaccine clinic and how it bills Medicare.
  5. If your parent cannot leave home, ask the doctor's office or local health department whether anyone gives shots at home. Our guide to rides to medical appointments can help if a ride is the problem.
Questions about coverage?

New Jersey's State Health Insurance Assistance Program (SHIP) gives free, unbiased Medicare help at 1-800-792-8820. 1-800-MEDICARE (1-800-633-4227) is open 24 hours a day.

How do I find out which shots my mom already had?

Check New Jersey's vaccine registry, her pharmacy and her doctor's records. Then write the dates on her emergency info sheet.

The New Jersey Immunization Information System (NJIIS) is the state's free, confidential vaccine registry, run by the Department of Health. People born before 1998 are not enrolled automatically. To join, your parent signs an "NJIIS Consent to Participate" form at a provider's office. To get a copy of the record, ask a provider who uses NJIIS, or mail the "Request for Copy of NJIIS Immunization Record" form from njiis.nj.gov.

The Department of Health also points to the Docket app, which connects to NJIIS and shows records on a phone. Pharmacies keep their own records too, so ask each pharmacy your parent has used. If no record exists, the CDC schedule says to give recommended vaccines when history is incomplete or unknown.

  • Shingles: did she get both Shingrix doses, and when?
  • Pneumococcal: which type, and in what year?
  • RSV: has she had one dose? If so, she does not need another for now.
  • Tdap: when was her last tetanus shot?

What side effects should we expect?

Usually mild ones. The NJ Department of Health says some people get a slight fever or a sore arm, and severe reactions are rare.

If your parent has had a serious allergic reaction to a vaccine before, tell the pharmacist. Report any significant reaction to the federal Vaccine Adverse Event Reporting System (VAERS) at vaers.hhs.gov or 1-800-822-7967. Call 911 for trouble breathing, swelling of the face or throat, or a fast heartbeat soon after a shot.

If your parent is newly on Medicare, our Medicare 101 guide explains how Part B and Part D fit together.

faq.q: Does Medicare pay for the shingles vaccine?
faq.a: Yes, through Part D or a Medicare Advantage plan with drug coverage. Medicare.gov says you pay nothing for it if you have Part D. Original Medicare without a drug plan does not cover it.

faq.q: How do I get my mom an RSV shot in New Jersey?
faq.a: If she is 75 or older, or 50 to 74 with a condition such as heart or lung disease, call a pharmacy in her Part D plan's network and ask whether they have RSV vaccine. Bring her Medicare and drug plan cards. It is one dose, with $0 cost under Part D.

faq.q: Which flu shot is best for people over 65?
faq.a: The CDC prefers a high-dose, recombinant or adjuvanted flu vaccine for adults 65 and older. If none is available, any age-appropriate flu vaccine should be used. Part B covers it at $0 when the provider accepts assignment.

faq.q: How many COVID shots should my dad get this season?
faq.a: The CDC schedule calls for 2 doses of the current COVID-19 vaccine for people 65 and older, about 6 months apart, and says patients should discuss benefits and risks with a provider. Part B covers the updated 2026 to 2027 vaccines.

faq.q: How can I find my parent's vaccine records in NJ?
faq.a: Ask a provider who uses the New Jersey Immunization Information System (NJIIS), or mail the record request form from njiis.nj.gov. People born before 1998 must sign a consent form at a provider's office to be enrolled. Also ask each pharmacy your parent has used.

faq.q: Does Medicare cover a tetanus shot?
faq.a: Part D covers the Tdap vaccine with no copay or deductible. The CDC recommends one dose of Tdap for adults who never had it at age 10 or older, then a Td or Tdap booster every 10 years.

NJ Department of Health: Local public health, for the community
NJ Department of Health: Adult immunization brochure
NJ Department of Health: NJIIS information for adults
NJ Division of Aging Services: SHIP
VAERS: Vaccine Adverse Event Reporting System

title: Depression and loneliness in older adults: help in New Jersey
dek: How depression shows up in a parent, how loneliness fits in, what Medicare pays for, and the New Jersey lines to call.
keyFacts: Depression is not a normal part of aging, and most people improve with treatment (NIA).
Medicare covers one depression screening a year at $0 when the provider accepts assignment.
Therapy and medication visits cost 20% after the 2026 Part B deductible of $283.
NJ MentalHealthCares: 1-866-202-4357, 8 a.m. to 8 p.m. daily.
In a crisis, call or text 988, any time.
body:
Depression is common in older adults, but it is not a normal part of aging, and it usually gets better with treatment. In older people it often looks different than you might expect. Your mom or dad may not say they feel sad. They may seem flat, tired, cranky or uninterested, or they may complain of aches that have no clear cause. If several signs last more than two weeks, the National Institute on Aging (NIA) says it is time to talk with a doctor.

Medicare Part B covers a yearly depression screening at no cost when the provider accepts assignment, plus counseling, medication management and more intensive programs. In New Jersey, free phone help starts with NJ MentalHealthCares at 1-866-202-4357 for support and referrals, and 988 for anyone in crisis, any hour. This guide covers the signs, how loneliness fits in, what Medicare pays, where to call in New Jersey and how to bring it up with a parent.

If someone is in danger right now

Call or text 988, or chat at 988lifeline.org. It is free, confidential and open 24 hours a day, for the person who is struggling or for a worried family member. Press 1 for the Veterans Crisis Line or 2 for Spanish. If someone is in immediate medical danger, call 911.

How can I tell if my mom or dad is depressed?

Look for a cluster of changes that lasts two weeks or more. Sadness may not be the main sign. The NIA notes that older adults often show emotional numbness or a loss of interest instead, and may be less willing to talk about feelings than younger people.

Signs the NIA lists for older adults include:

  • A sad, anxious or "empty" mood that does not lift
  • Feeling hopeless, guilty, worthless or helpless
  • Irritability or restlessness
  • Losing interest in things they used to enjoy
  • Low energy, or moving and talking more slowly
  • Trouble concentrating, remembering or making decisions
  • Sleeping too much, too little, or waking very early
  • Eating more or less, with weight change they did not intend
  • Drinking more, or taking risks
  • Talk of death or suicide

In some families and cultures, depression shows up mostly as physical complaints, such as headaches, stomach trouble or pain. That is one reason it gets missed.

A few things can look like depression or make it worse. Medicines, alcohol and illnesses such as heart disease or stroke can all play a part. Depression is also common in people with dementia, and the two share symptoms. A doctor can sort this out with an exam, a medication review and lab tests. For memory concerns, our guide to free memory screening in New Jersey explains the next step.

Depression in an older parent often looks like "not interested" rather than "sad."

Is it loneliness or depression?

They are different, but they feed each other. Loneliness is the painful feeling of being alone or cut off. Social isolation is having few people to talk to. Depression is a medical condition that needs treatment.

The NIA says loneliness and isolation are linked to higher risk of depression, heart disease, high blood pressure, cognitive decline and dementia. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) also lists anxiety, suicidal thoughts and self-harm. A person can live alone and feel fine. A person can also feel lonely in a full house.

Common triggers in later life include a spouse's death, retirement, giving up the car, hearing loss and friends moving away. Hearing loss deserves its own mention. The NIA notes that older adults who cannot follow conversations may pull back from people out of frustration or embarrassment. A hearing check is worth booking. Our hearing aids guide covers New Jersey's help with the cost.

A simple test for families: if your parent perks up when someone visits or calls, loneliness may be the bigger issue, and more contact can help a lot. If nothing seems to reach them, even things they used to love, take it to the doctor. Our staying connected guide has ideas for building weekly contact, including telephone reassurance and friendly visitor programs.

What does Medicare cover for depression?

Original Medicare covers screening, outpatient therapy, medication management and hospital care for mental health. Medicare Advantage plans must cover the same services, though costs and networks vary by plan.

ServiceWhat you pay (2026)
Yearly depression screening$0 if the provider accepts assignment
Therapy and med visits20% after the $283 Part B deductible
Hospital clinic visitsA possible extra hospital copay
Inpatient stay$1,736 Part A deductible per benefit period
Psychiatric hospital190 lifetime days under Part A

Screening. The yearly screening must happen in a primary care setting, such as a doctor's office, that can provide follow-up treatment or referrals. The "Welcome to Medicare" visit and the yearly Wellness visit also cover a review of depression risk. Ask for the screening by name.

Who can provide therapy. Part B covers visits with psychiatrists and other doctors, clinical psychologists, clinical social workers, clinical nurse specialists, nurse practitioners, physician assistants, marriage and family therapists, and mental health counselors. Visits can happen in an office, a hospital outpatient department, a community mental health center or by telehealth.

More intensive help. Part B also covers partial hospitalization and intensive outpatient programs, psychiatric evaluation, family counseling when its main purpose is to help with treatment, and safety planning for someone at risk of suicide. After an emergency room visit for a behavioral health crisis, Medicare covers a follow-up phone call.

Antidepressants you take at home fall under Part D drug coverage. If your parent has trouble paying for prescriptions, see our guides to PAAD and prescription help in New Jersey.

The NIA says most people get better with treatment, usually talk therapy, medicine or both. Cognitive behavioral therapy and interpersonal therapy are common approaches. It is common to try more than one before finding what works, so tell the doctor if the first plan is not helping.

Where can older adults in New Jersey get help?

Start with your parent's primary care doctor. If you need help finding a therapist or a support group, New Jersey has several free phone lines run or funded through the state's Division of Mental Health and Addiction Services.

LineNumberHours
988 LifelineCall or text 98824/7
NJ MentalHealthCares1-866-202-43578 a.m. to 8 p.m. daily
NAMI NJ HelpLine1-866-626-46649 a.m. to 4 p.m. weekdays
Peer Recovery Warmline1-877-292-5588Weekdays 8 a.m. to 10 p.m., weekends 5 to 10 p.m.
Self-Help Clearinghouse1-800-367-6274Support group finder
Vet2Vet1-866-838-765424/7

NJ MentalHealthCares is a service of the Mental Health Association in New Jersey. A mental health professional answers live from 8 a.m. to 8 p.m., and they call back after hours. They offer emotional support, will speak in the language you prefer and keep a current list of New Jersey's public mental health services. They do not do crisis intervention, so use 988 or 911 in an emergency.

The NAMI NJ HelpLine is a peer support line for people with a mental health condition and for their family members. It is a good call if you are the adult child trying to figure out what to do.

The Peer Recovery Warmline is answered by trained people who have lived with a mental health condition themselves. Some older adults find that easier than talking to a clinician.

For loneliness, call the Aging and Disability Resource Connection (ADRC) at 1-877-222-3737. It connects you to your county office on aging. Ask about telephone reassurance, friendly visitors, senior center programs and rides. NJ 211 (dial 2-1-1) can also point you to local counseling and support groups. A weekly reason to leave the house matters. Our guide to volunteering after 60 is a good place to start.

How do I bring it up with my parent?

Gently, privately and more than once. Lead with what you have noticed and why you care, not with a diagnosis.

  1. Pick a calm moment. A drive or a walk often works better than a sit-down talk across a table.
  2. Name what you see. "You haven't been to cards in a month, and you seem tired a lot. I'm worried about you."
  3. Ask, then listen. "How have you really been feeling?" Let silence sit. Do not rush to fix.
  4. Use their words. Many older adults bristle at "depression." Try "run down," "not yourself" or "low."
  5. Make the doctor visit easy. Offer to book it, drive, and come in. Suggest they ask for the yearly depression screening Medicare covers.
  6. Write things down first. List the changes you have seen, when they started, and every medicine and supplement, so the doctor sees the full picture.
  7. Follow up. Check in after a week. Treatment takes time, and people often stop too soon.

The NIA suggests family and friends help by encouraging treatment, going to appointments, doing activities your parent enjoys together and suggesting walks, since physical activity can lift mood. You cannot treat depression yourself, and you should not have to. If you are the main caregiver and feeling worn down, read our caregiver burnout guide. Caregiver stress is itself a risk factor for depression.

What should I do if I'm worried about suicide?

Ask directly, and get help the same day. The NIA says asking whether someone is thinking about suicide does not make them more likely to act on it. It can open the door to help.

This is not a rare worry in later life. The CDC reports that people 80 and older had the highest suicide rate of any age group in 2024, and that across all ages the rate among men was nearly four times the rate among women. Warning signs include talk of being a burden, giving things away, putting affairs in order suddenly, and saying there is "no point anymore."

If you are worried:

  • Call or text 988 together, or call on your parent's behalf. The counselor will help you decide next steps.
  • In New Jersey, a 988 counselor can request a Mobile Crisis Outreach Response Team for adults 18 and older in a non-life-threatening crisis. The team comes to the person, and only 988 centers can send it.
  • New Jersey also has 24-hour psychiatric emergency screening services, which a person or a worried family member can contact directly.
  • Call 911 if there is immediate danger.
  • Remove or lock up firearms and stockpiled medicines while your parent gets help.

988 offers interpreters in more than 240 languages by phone, which matters in many New Jersey families.

What helps day to day?

Treatment comes first. Around it, small routines make a real difference. The NIA points to physical activity, a balanced diet, seven to nine hours of sleep, staying in touch with people and doing things you enjoy.

  • One fixed plan each week. A standing coffee, class or volunteer shift gives a reason to get dressed and go.
  • A regular call. Same day, same time. Put it on the calendar so it does not slide.
  • Move together. A short walk counts. Even ten minutes around the block helps.
  • Watch the alcohol. The NIA lists alcohol use disorder as a risk factor, and alcohol mixes badly with many medicines.
  • Fix the barriers. Hearing aids, updated glasses and a ride plan remove reasons to stay home.

Say your dad stopped going to his Thursday lunch after he gave up driving. A ride from the county, a friend who picks him up, or a standing phone call that same day can fill the gap while his doctor looks at whether something more is going on.

After a death in the family, grief and depression can look alike. Our grief support guide explains when grief needs more help.

faq.q: How do I get my mom checked for depression?
faq.a: Book a visit with her primary care doctor and ask for the yearly depression screening Medicare covers. It costs nothing if the doctor accepts assignment. Bring a list of the changes you have noticed and all her medicines.

faq.q: My dad is lonely but says he isn't depressed. What can I do?
faq.a: Help him build regular contact: a fixed weekly call, a class or senior center program, or a friendly visitor. Call the ADRC at 1-877-222-3737 to reach your county office on aging. If nothing seems to lift his mood after two weeks or more, talk to his doctor.

faq.q: Does Medicare pay for therapy?
faq.a: Yes. Part B covers individual, group and family therapy with psychiatrists, psychologists, clinical social workers, nurse practitioners, marriage and family therapists, mental health counselors and others. You pay 20% of the Medicare-approved amount after the Part B deductible, which is $283 in 2026. Telehealth visits are covered.

faq.q: Is NJ MentalHealthCares a crisis line?
faq.a: No. It offers free emotional support, information and referrals from 8 a.m. to 8 p.m. daily at 1-866-202-4357. For a crisis, call or text 988, or call 911 if someone is in immediate danger.

faq.q: Can I call 988 about my parent instead of for myself?
faq.a: Yes. 988 takes calls, texts and chats from people worried about someone else. In New Jersey, a 988 counselor can also send a mobile crisis team to an adult in a non-life-threatening crisis.

faq.q: Is depression just part of getting older?
faq.a: No. The National Institute on Aging says depression is common in older adults but not a normal part of aging, and most people get better with treatment.

sources: National Institute on Aging: Depression and Older Adults
National Institute on Aging: Loneliness and Social Isolation, Tips for Staying Connected
CDC: Health Effects of Social Isolation and Loneliness
NJ DMHAS: 988 and crisis services in New Jersey
Mental Health Association in New Jersey: NJ MentalHealthCares
seoDesc: Signs of depression and loneliness in older adults, what Medicare covers, NJ helplines like NJ MentalHealthCares and 988, and how to talk with a parent.

title: Sleep problems in older adults: causes and what helps in NJ
dek: Why sleep changes with age, how Medicare handles sleep tests and CPAP, which sleep aids to question, and what actually helps.
keyFacts: Older adults still need about 7 to 9 hours of sleep a night (NIA).
Insomnia is the most common sleep problem in adults 60 and older.
Medicare covers a 12-week CPAP trial for obstructive sleep apnea, then more if use is documented.
CPAP use must reach 4 hours a night on 70% of nights in 30 straight days within the first 3 months.
The AGS Beers Criteria flags Z-drugs, benzodiazepines and diphenhydramine sleep aids for older adults.
body:
Older adults need about the same sleep as younger adults, seven to nine hours a night, according to the National Institute on Aging (NIA). What changes is how they sleep. Sleep gets lighter and shorter, people wake more often, and they tend to go to bed and get up earlier. Feeling tired all day, or lying awake most nights, is not something your mom or dad has to accept as part of aging.

The most common causes are insomnia, sleep apnea, pain, medicines and conditions such as dementia. Medicare Part B covers sleep studies when there are signs of sleep apnea, and it covers CPAP machines if your parent uses one enough in the first three months. Many sleep pills carry real risks for older adults. This guide explains the causes, what Medicare pays for, which medicines to ask about, and when to see a doctor.

How much sleep do older adults need?

Seven to nine hours, the same as other adults. The NIA notes that older people spend less time in each stage of sleep and may wake up more during the night, so the same hours in bed can feel less restful.

Signs your parent is not sleeping well include waking up tired, being easily annoyed, and trouble falling or staying asleep. Poor sleep is more than an annoyance. The NIA links it to memory problems, low mood, strained relationships and a higher risk of falls and accidents. Over time, too little sleep can raise the risk of high blood pressure, heart disease and diabetes.

Falls are the big worry for many families. A parent who is groggy, gets up several times a night or takes a sleep aid is at higher risk on the way to the bathroom. Our fall prevention guide covers night lights, grab bars and other fixes.

Tired all day is a reason to see a doctor, not a normal part of getting older.

What causes poor sleep after 60?

Usually more than one thing at once. The NIA lists illness, medicines, mental health and pain as common culprits, along with sleep disorders that become more common with age.

ProblemWhat it looks like
InsomniaTrouble falling or staying asleep
Sleep apneaSnoring, pauses in breathing
Restless legsCrawling or tingling legs at night
Limb movementsLeg jerks every 20 to 40 seconds
REM behavior disorderActing out dreams

Insomnia is the most common sleep problem in adults 60 and older. It means trouble falling asleep or staying asleep at least three nights a week. Short bouts often follow stress or a change in routine. Chronic insomnia lasts more than three months.

Depression and worry often show up as early waking or sleeping too much. If your parent's sleep changed along with their mood, read our guide to depression and loneliness in older adults.

Habits matter too. Late-afternoon naps, caffeine late in the day, alcohol, a big dinner close to bedtime and a TV in the bedroom all work against sleep. The NIA advises avoiding alcohol, even small amounts.

REM sleep behavior disorder deserves a doctor visit because acting out dreams can cause injuries. Restless legs often improve with iron or medicine, so mention it.

Could it be sleep apnea, and does Medicare cover CPAP?

Loud snoring with pauses in breathing, gasping, or heavy daytime sleepiness can point to obstructive sleep apnea. Medicare covers testing and treatment, with rules families should know up front.

With sleep apnea, throat muscles relax during sleep and block the airway, so breathing stops for a few seconds again and again. The NIA warns that untreated sleep apnea can lead to serious problems, including heart attack. Not everyone who snores has it, which is why testing matters.

Sleep studies. Part B covers sleep tests, including some home tests, when your parent has clinical signs and symptoms of sleep apnea and a doctor orders the test. You pay 20% of the Medicare-approved amount after the Part B deductible, which is $283 in 2026. The most complete overnight test (Type I) is covered only in a sleep lab.

CPAP trial. A continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) machine blows air through a mask to keep the airway open. After a diagnosis, Medicare may cover a 12-week trial of CPAP, including the device and supplies.

The CPAP rule that trips people up

To keep coverage after the first three months, two things must happen. The doctor must see your parent in person between day 31 and day 91 of therapy and note that CPAP is helping. And the machine's data must show use of at least 4 hours a night on 70% of nights during any 30 days in a row in those first three months. Most machines record this automatically. If the doctor visit happens after day 91 but shows CPAP is helping, coverage picks up from that visit. If the usage target is missed, Medicare stops paying, and qualifying again takes another in-person doctor visit and a sleep test in a sleep lab.

Costs. Medicare pays the supplier to rent the machine for 13 months of continuous use, and then your parent owns it. You pay 20% of the approved amount for the rental and supplies such as masks and tubing, after the deductible. Use a supplier enrolled in Medicare that accepts assignment for all rental months. Otherwise you could be billed more, or have to pay up front.

Help your parent through the hard first weeks. Mask fit is the usual complaint. Ask the supplier about other mask styles before giving up. The NIA notes that a dental device, sleep position changes or surgery can help some people. Medicare Advantage plans have their own rules, so call the plan. For questions about Medicare coverage, New Jersey's free SHIP counselors are at 1-800-792-8820.

Which sleep medicines are risky for older adults?

Several common ones. The American Geriatrics Society (AGS) Beers Criteria, a list of medicines that are often best avoided by adults 65 and older, includes many sleep drugs and over-the-counter sleep aids. Never stop a prescribed medicine without talking to the doctor first.

The AGS lists these for insomnia as medicines to discuss with a doctor:

  • "Z-drugs" such as zolpidem (Ambien), zaleplon (Sonata) and eszopiclone (Lunesta)
  • Benzodiazepines such as lorazepam (Ativan), alprazolam (Xanax) and temazepam (Restoril)
  • Over-the-counter "PM" products and cough and cold remedies with diphenhydramine (Benadryl) or other first-generation antihistamines, such as Tylenol PM and Advil PM

In 2019 the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) added its strongest warning, a boxed warning, to eszopiclone, zaleplon and zolpidem. Rare but serious injuries and deaths have happened from sleepwalking, sleep driving and other activities done while not fully awake. If your parent does something like that and does not remember it, the FDA says to stop the medicine and call the doctor right away.

The NIA says sleep medicines may help short term but carry risks, can lead to dependence, can leave people groggy the next day and may stop working over time. Ask the pharmacist to review every medicine your parent takes, including supplements and anything bought off the shelf. The AGS suggests a review at least once a year and whenever a new drug is added. Our guide to staying well in New Jersey covers other checkups Medicare pays for.

What actually helps with insomnia?

Steady habits and a type of counseling called cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia (CBT-I). The AGS points to CBT-I as an alternative to sleep pills, and the NIA says counseling can help.

  1. Keep a sleep diary for two weeks. Write down bedtime, wake-ups during the night, final wake time, naps, caffeine, alcohol and exercise. Bring it to the doctor.
  2. Fix the schedule. Same bedtime and wake time every day, weekends and trips included.
  3. Build a wind-down routine. Reading, soft music or a warm bath. No screens in the bedroom.
  4. Move during the day. Regular exercise helps, but not within three hours of bedtime.
  5. Cut the late stuff. No caffeine late in the day (coffee, tea, chocolate, soda), no big meals two to three hours before bed, and fewer drinks of any kind in the evening.
  6. Skip late naps. A late-afternoon or evening nap steals from the night.
  7. Ask about CBT-I. A trained therapist can teach it, and there are guided phone apps and websites. Ask the doctor for a referral, and ask the therapist whether they take Medicare.

Make the bedroom safe for night trips, too. The NIA suggests a lamp within easy reach, a night light in the hall or bathroom, a phone with emergency numbers by the bed, smoke alarms on every floor, and no rugs or cords to trip on. Our adaptive equipment guide covers bed rails, motion lights and more.

How does dementia change sleep?

Dementia often scrambles the body clock. The NIA says people with Alzheimer's and related dementias may sleep too much or too little, wake often, and wander or call out at night. Poor sleep can make dementia symptoms worse, and it wears down the caregiver, too.

Daytime light, activity and a firm routine help. Late-day confusion and agitation, called sundowning, is so common that we cover it in its own guide to sundowning and evening routines. If nights are where things fall apart, ask the doctor to check for pain, infection, sleep apnea and medicine side effects before adding a sleep drug. New Jersey's resources after a diagnosis are in our dementia support guide.

If you are up every night with a parent, you need sleep too. Our guide to respite for New Jersey caregivers explains how to get a break.

When should my parent see a doctor about sleep?

When poor sleep lasts more than a few weeks, when daytime sleepiness gets in the way of life, or right away for certain warning signs.

Book a visit if your parent:

  • Snores loudly, gasps or stops breathing during sleep
  • Falls asleep while reading, watching TV or talking
  • Feels sleepy behind the wheel. Our guide to driving later in life covers safety checks.
  • Acts out dreams, kicks or falls out of bed
  • Has new confusion, mood changes or a fall
  • Uses sleep aids most nights, or wants to stop one

Bring the sleep diary, a full list of medicines and a note of what a bed partner or family member has seen at night. Questions worth asking: Could any of my medicines be keeping me up? Should I have a sleep study? Is CBT-I an option before pills? If I need CPAP, what does the supplier charge after Medicare?

Say your mom has been napping through the afternoon and your dad mentions she snores and seems to stop breathing. That is worth a call to her doctor this week. A home sleep test may be all it takes to find out.

faq.q: How do I get my dad tested for sleep apnea?
faq.a: Ask his doctor. Medicare Part B covers sleep tests, including some home tests, when he has signs of sleep apnea such as loud snoring, pauses in breathing or heavy daytime sleepiness. You pay 20% of the approved amount after the $283 Part B deductible in 2026.

faq.q: Why did Medicare stop paying for my mom's CPAP?
faq.a: Medicare covers a 12-week trial. To keep paying, the machine data must show use of at least 4 hours a night on 70% of nights during 30 days in a row in the first three months, and her doctor must see her in person between day 31 and day 91. If the visit is late but shows CPAP is helping, coverage picks up from that visit. If the usage target is missed, she needs a new in-person doctor visit and a sleep test in a lab to qualify again.

faq.q: Is it safe for my parent to take Tylenol PM or Benadryl to sleep?
faq.a: The American Geriatrics Society lists diphenhydramine and similar antihistamines, found in many PM products, as potentially inappropriate for adults 65 and older. Talk to the doctor or pharmacist about safer options such as CBT-I.

faq.q: Do older people need less sleep?
faq.a: No. The NIA says older adults need about the same seven to nine hours as other adults. Sleep tends to be lighter and more broken, so the quality often drops.

faq.q: Does my parent own the CPAP machine?
faq.a: Yes, eventually. Medicare pays the supplier to rent it for 13 months of continuous use. After that, your parent owns it.

faq.q: What can help my mom with dementia sleep at night?
faq.a: Daytime light and activity, a steady routine and a calm evening help. Ask her doctor to check for pain, infection, sleep apnea and medicine side effects before trying a sleep drug.

title: Stroke signs and what to do in New Jersey
dek: How to spot a stroke with B.E. F.A.S.T., why 911 beats driving, New Jersey's stroke center levels, and what Medicare pays for rehab.
keyFacts: B.E. F.A.S.T.: Balance, Eyes, Face, Arms, Speech, Time to call 911 (CDC).
Stroke risk about doubles every 10 years after age 55 (CDC).
New Jersey's July 2026 list names 65 state-designated stroke center hospitals.
Stroke risk within 90 days of a TIA may be as high as 17%, highest in the first week (CDC).
Medicare skilled nursing: $0 days 1 to 20, $217 a day days 21 to 100 in 2026.
body:
Use B.E. F.A.S.T. to spot a stroke: Balance loss, Eye or vision changes, Face drooping, Arm weakness, Speech trouble, Time to call 911. If you see any one of these signs come on suddenly, call 911 right away and note the time symptoms started. Do not drive your parent to the hospital yourself. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) says treatment starts in the ambulance, and the best treatments work only if a stroke is caught within hours.

In New Jersey, the Department of Health designates hospitals as stroke centers at different levels. Paramedics may take your parent to one. After the hospital, Medicare helps pay for rehab in a rehab hospital, a nursing facility, at home or as an outpatient. This guide covers the warning signs, what happens in the first hours, the state's stroke center list, rehab and Medicare costs, and how to lower the chance of another stroke.

Stroke signs? Call 911

Call 911 for any sudden face drooping, arm or leg weakness, trouble speaking, vision loss, loss of balance, confusion or a severe headache with no known cause. Note the time symptoms started. Do not wait to see if it passes.

What are the signs of a stroke?

Stroke signs come on suddenly. The CDC lists sudden numbness or weakness of the face, arm or leg (especially on one side), sudden confusion or trouble speaking or understanding, sudden trouble seeing, sudden trouble walking, dizziness or loss of balance, and a sudden severe headache with no known cause.

LetterCheck
B: BalanceDizzy or off balance?
E: EyesTrouble seeing?
F: FaceSmile. Does one side droop?
A: ArmsRaise both. Does one drift down?
S: SpeechRepeat a phrase. Slurred or strange?
T: TimeCall 911 and note the time

Older adults sometimes play it down. "I just feel a little off" or "my hand is asleep" can be the first sign. Strokes also happen overnight, so if your mom wakes up with new weakness or slurred speech, call 911 and tell them the last time she was known to be well.

Stroke risk rises with age. The CDC says the chance of stroke about doubles every 10 years after age 55. About 87% of strokes are ischemic, meaning a clot or blockage cuts off blood to the brain. The rest are hemorrhagic, caused by bleeding.

Write down the time. Doctors use it to decide which treatments are still possible.

Why call 911 instead of driving?

Because care starts on the way. The CDC says people who arrive by ambulance may be diagnosed and treated faster, since paramedics begin care in the ambulance, alert the hospital and may take the person to a specialized stroke center.

Time matters. For an ischemic stroke, a clot-busting drug called tPA (tissue plasminogen activator) works best when given soon after symptoms start. The CDC notes that people who reach the emergency room within three hours of their first symptoms often have less disability three months later than people whose care is delayed. Some patients also need a procedure to remove the clot, called a thrombectomy.

While you wait for the ambulance:

  • Note the time symptoms started, or when your parent was last seen well.
  • Grab their medicine list, especially any blood thinner, and their Medicare and insurance cards.
  • Unlock the door and turn on an outside light.

A filled-out emergency sheet saves precious minutes. Our free printable emergency info sheet has room for medicines, doctors and contacts. Medicare Part B covers emergency ground ambulance trips. You pay 20% of the Medicare-approved amount after the $283 Part B deductible in 2026.

What is a designated stroke center in New Jersey?

It is a hospital the New Jersey Department of Health has designated to meet set stroke care standards. Under the state's Stroke Center Act of 2004, updated by a 2020 law, hospitals must also hold national certification and have transfer agreements so complex cases can move quickly.

There are four levels:

  • Acute Stroke Ready Hospital. Can assess, stabilize and give clot-busting drugs, then usually transfers patients on.
  • Primary Stroke Center. Has an acute stroke team, 24/7 brain imaging, and transfer arrangements with a comprehensive center.
  • Thrombectomy-Capable Stroke Center. Meets primary standards and can remove clots with a catheter around the clock.
  • Comprehensive Stroke Center. Has neurosurgery and advanced procedures 24/7 and can take the most complex cases.

The state's July 2026 list names 65 hospitals across all 21 counties. These are the comprehensive and thrombectomy-capable centers on that list.

This is the state's designation list, not a ranking, and designations change. Check the current New Jersey list by county for primary centers near your parent. In an emergency, do not try to pick a hospital yourself. Call 911 and let paramedics decide.

What about a mini-stroke (TIA)?

Treat it as an emergency. A transient ischemic attack (TIA) causes stroke symptoms that go away within minutes. The CDC says many people ignore TIAs because they clear up, but a TIA signals a serious problem.

The CDC reports that the risk of stroke within 90 days of a TIA may be as high as 17%, with the greatest risk in the first week. If your dad had a few minutes of slurred speech or a numb arm that passed, he still needs medical care right away. Call 911 if symptoms are happening now. If they have already passed, call his doctor today, and go to the emergency room if you cannot reach the doctor quickly.

What happens after the hospital, and what does Medicare pay?

Rehab usually starts in the hospital within a day or two, according to the CDC. Before discharge, the team recommends where rehab should continue. You have a say, and you can ask questions.

SettingWhat you pay (2026)
Hospital stay$1,736 Part A deductible per benefit period
Rehab hospital (IRF)No new deductible if transferred from the hospital
Skilled nursing$0 days 1 to 20, $217 a day days 21 to 100
Home health$0 for covered visits
Outpatient therapy20% after the Part B deductible, no yearly cap

Inpatient rehabilitation facility (IRF). This is for people who need an intensive therapy program with doctor supervision. A provider must certify the need. Part A pays, and your parent does not pay a second deductible when moved straight from the hospital, or admitted within 60 days of leaving it, in the same benefit period.

Skilled nursing facility. Part A covers up to 100 days per benefit period after a qualifying inpatient stay of at least three days in a row. Time spent under observation does not count toward those three days. Our guide to rehab after a hospital stay explains the three-day rule and how to appeal an early discharge. Use nursing home ratings to compare facilities.

Home health. If your parent is homebound and needs part-time skilled care, Medicare pays for nursing and therapy visits at home. See our guide to Medicare home health care in New Jersey.

Outpatient therapy. Part B covers physical therapy, occupational therapy and speech therapy, including help with swallowing, when a provider certifies the need. Medicare sets no yearly limit on what it pays for medically necessary outpatient therapy.

Medicare Advantage plans have their own networks and often need approval in advance, so call the plan before discharge. Our hospital discharge guide lists questions to ask.

How can families support recovery at home?

Recovery can take weeks, months or years. The CDC says some people recover fully while others live with lasting problems, such as weakness on one side, trouble with speech, memory or judgment, swallowing problems, bladder issues and depression.

  1. Go to the discharge meeting. Get the medicine list, therapy orders and follow-up appointments in writing.
  2. Make the home safe. Clear paths, add grab bars and a shower chair, and set up a bedroom on the main floor if stairs are hard. Our adaptive equipment guide can help.
  3. Keep up with therapy. Practice the exercises between visits. Progress often comes from repetition.
  4. Watch mood. Depression is common after stroke, and therapy and medicine can help. Our guide to depression in older adults covers Medicare coverage and New Jersey helplines.
  5. Plan for driving. Vision, reaction time and judgment can change. Ask the doctor before your parent gets behind the wheel again.
  6. Get help for yourself. Call the ADRC at 1-877-222-3737 to reach your county office on aging about respite, home care programs and caregiver support.

The CDC also suggests stroke support groups. Ask the hospital or rehab team about one nearby. Family caregivers can look for their own group, too.

How do you lower the risk of another stroke?

By treating the causes. The CDC says one in four stroke survivors has another stroke within five years, so prevention after a first stroke matters a great deal.

The main medical causes are high blood pressure, high cholesterol, heart disease, atrial fibrillation (an irregular heartbeat) and diabetes. The CDC calls high blood pressure a leading cause of stroke, and it usually has no symptoms.

  • Check blood pressure often. At home, at the doctor or at a pharmacy.
  • Take medicines as prescribed. Never stop a blood thinner or blood pressure pill without talking to the doctor or pharmacist.
  • Do not smoke. Quitting lowers stroke risk.
  • Limit alcohol. The CDC advises no more than two drinks a day for men and one for women.
  • Move most days. The CDC recommends 150 minutes of moderate activity a week, such as brisk walking, as health allows.
  • Eat less salt. Fruits, vegetables and high-fiber foods help with blood pressure and cholesterol.

If cost is a barrier to blood pressure or cholesterol medicine, New Jersey's PAAD program can bring copays down to $5 or $7 for those who qualify. Bring a list of questions to every follow-up visit, and ask what your parent's own numbers should be.

More guides that may help: urgent care or the ER and heart failure.

faq.q: What should I do if I think my mom is having a stroke?
faq.a: Call 911 right away and note the time her symptoms started or when she was last seen well. Do not drive her yourself. Have her medicine list ready, especially any blood thinner.

faq.q: How do I find a stroke center near my parent in New Jersey?
faq.a: The New Jersey Department of Health posts a list of designated stroke centers by county on nj.gov. In an emergency, call 911 and let paramedics choose the hospital.

faq.q: My dad's symptoms went away after a few minutes. Does he still need care?
faq.a: Yes. That may have been a transient ischemic attack (TIA). The CDC says the risk of stroke within 90 days of a TIA may be as high as 17%, highest in the first week. Get medical care right away.

faq.q: Does Medicare pay for stroke rehab?
faq.a: Yes, when it is medically necessary. Part A covers inpatient rehab facilities and up to 100 days of skilled nursing per benefit period after a qualifying three-day inpatient stay. Home health visits cost $0 if your parent qualifies. Outpatient physical, occupational and speech therapy cost 20% after the Part B deductible, with no yearly limit.

faq.q: What does B.E. F.A.S.T. stand for?
faq.a: Balance loss, Eye (vision) changes, Face drooping, Arm weakness, Speech difficulty, and Time to call 911. The CDC uses it to help people recognize a stroke quickly.

faq.q: Can a stroke happen while someone is asleep?
faq.a: Yes. If your parent wakes up with new weakness, a drooping face or slurred speech, call 911 and tell them the last time your parent was known to be well.

sources: CDC: Signs and Symptoms of Stroke (May 2026)
CDC: Treatment and Intervention for Stroke
NJ Department of Health: Acute Stroke Services
NJ Department of Health: State Designated Stroke Center Hospitals by County (July 2026)

title: Hospice care in Bergen County, NJ: who serves your town
dek: The Medicare-certified hospices that serve Hackensack, Paramus, Fort Lee, Ridgewood and the rest of Bergen County, the residential hospice in Saddle River, and how to get started from a hospital bed.
keyFacts: Search Medicare Care Compare by your parent's ZIP code to see which hospices serve that town.
Your parent has the right to choose the hospice, even when a hospital suggests one.
Holy Name runs Villa Marie Claire, a 20-suite residential hospice in Saddle River: 551-248-4800.
Bergen County Division of Senior Services: 201-336-7400 or 1-877-222-3737.
NJ Department of Health complaint hotline: 1-800-792-9770.
body:
Families in Bergen County have more hospice choices than almost anywhere in the state. In Medicare's own data, at least a dozen Medicare-certified hospices that also name Bergen on their websites report serving towns from Hackensack and Paramus to Fort Lee and Ridgewood. Three of them are run by hospitals close to home: Holy Name in Teaneck, Valley in Paramus, and Visiting Health Services of New Jersey, a partnership of Hackensack Meridian Health and St. Joseph's Health.

Most hospice care happens at home, in assisted living or in a nursing home, with nurses and aides who come to your mom or dad. Bergen also has something many counties don't: Villa Marie Claire, a residential hospice in Saddle River. This page lists the hospices we confirmed, explains when a residence or a hospital stay makes sense, and shows how to get started. For how the Medicare benefit works and what it pays for, start with our statewide guide to hospice care in New Jersey.

Which hospices serve Bergen County?

The twelve hospices below reported serving Bergen ZIP codes to Medicare and name Bergen County, or every New Jersey county, on their own websites. Holy Name Hospice is the one exception to that wording: its hospice page does not list a service area, but it is based at Holy Name Medical Center in Teaneck and served all four of our sample ZIP codes in Medicare's data. We checked these listings in November 2026. This is not an endorsement or a ranking.

To build the list, we pulled Medicare's hospice ZIP code data for four sample ZIP codes: 07601 (Hackensack), 07652 (Paramus), 07024 (Fort Lee) and 07450 (Ridgewood). Every hospice here served at least three of the four. Hospice of New Jersey did not list 07024, VITAS did not list 07450, and Affinity did not list 07601. Phone numbers come from each hospice's own website.

HospiceOfficePhone
Affinity Care of New JerseyParsippany973-813-4999
Amedisys Hospice CareHackensack201-342-7766
Ascend HospiceClark908-931-9080
Compassionate Care Hospice (Amedisys)Bloomfield973-916-1400
Ennoble CareHackettstown973-567-3203
Grace Healthcare ServicesEdison732-225-4100
Holy Name HospiceTeaneck201-833-3188
Hospice of New JerseyBloomfield973-893-0818
Serenity Hospice CareHamilton609-227-2400
Valley Hospice (Valley Health)Paramus201-291-6131
Visiting Health Services of New JerseyWoodland Park844-777-0711
VITAS HealthcareRoseland973-994-4738

Some notes on the names and offices. Holy Name Hospice and Valley Hospice are hospital programs, and Visiting Health Services of New Jersey says it serves Passaic, Bergen and parts of Morris counties. Compassionate Care Hospice and Amedisys Hospice Care are separately certified hospices owned by the same company. Medicare lists Ascend's office in Cranford and Affinity's in Brick, while their own sites now show Clark and a North Jersey office in Parsippany. Life Hospice and Suncrest Hospice turned up in nearby data, but we left them off because Medicare's data or the hospice's own site did not match Bergen for our sample towns.

The office address matters less than you'd think. What matters is how fast the hospice answers the phone, how often the nurse visits and who comes at 2 a.m.

Ask every hospice the same question: if my mom is in pain at 2 a.m., how long until a nurse is at the door?

How do I check which hospices serve my parent's town?

Search Medicare Care Compare for hospices with your parent's own ZIP code. Service areas can differ from one ZIP code to the next, so our sample of four is only a starting point.

Care Compare shows each hospice's family survey results when enough families answered. A hospice with too few surveys may show no stars, which is not a bad sign on its own. Look at the details, such as whether families got help quickly and whether they would recommend the hospice. Then call two or three. Our guide to hospice vs. palliative care has a full list of questions for that first call.

A few questions matter more in Bergen, where traffic can slow a night visit:

  • Where is the nurse who covers our town based?
  • Do you have a nurse on call overnight, or a phone line that pages one?
  • Which nursing homes and assisted living residences near us do you already work in?
  • Do you have staff who speak the language my parent is most comfortable in?

Is there a residential or inpatient hospice in Bergen County?

Yes. Holy Name runs Villa Marie Claire, a residential hospice on 26 acres in Saddle River, reachable at 551-248-4800. For short hospital-level stays, ask any hospice which local hospitals it uses for inpatient care.

Holy Name describes Villa Marie Claire as having 20 patient suites, each with a private bathroom and a window on the gardens, plus bedrooms where family can stay overnight and a separate kitchen for families who keep kosher. The staff is made up of people who specialize in hospice care, with nurses, social workers, spiritual counselors and volunteers around the clock. Call to ask about admission, what Medicare covers there and what it does not, and to book a tour.

It helps to know the different kinds of care hospice can include:

  • Routine home care. The usual kind. Visits wherever your parent lives.
  • General inpatient care. Short-term care in a hospital or other facility when pain or symptoms can't be managed at home.
  • Respite care. Under Medicare, a short stay of up to five days at a time so a worn-out caregiver can rest.
  • Continuous home care. Extra nursing at home during a short crisis.

Room and board in a residence or nursing home is a separate question from the hospice benefit, so ask about it in writing.

What do the hospital-based hospices in Bergen offer?

Each of the three hospital-linked programs works closely with its own hospital, which can make a hospital-to-home move smoother. They are still hospices like the others, and your parent can choose any of them.

  • Holy Name Hospice, Teaneck. Part of Holy Name Medical Center's supportive care services. Its team lists physicians, visiting nurses, social workers, interfaith clergy, bereavement counselors, aides, volunteers and hospice doulas. Most patients get care at home. Call 201-833-3188.
  • Valley Hospice, Paramus. Part of Valley Health. It lists end-of-life doulas, therapy, dietary services, wound care, spiritual support and bereavement services, and says it works with area nursing homes, assisted living residences and The Valley Hospital. Call 201-291-6131.
  • Visiting Health Services of New Jersey, Woodland Park. A home health and hospice partnership of Hackensack Meridian Health and St. Joseph's Health. Its advisors answer 844-777-0711 around the clock.

If your parent is already in a Bergen hospital, ask the doctor for a palliative care consult. That team helps with symptoms and with the conversation about whether hospice is the right next step.

How do we start hospice from a Bergen hospital?

Tell the hospital case manager that your family wants hospice and which one you've picked. The hospital sends the referral, and the hospice comes to confirm your parent qualifies.

  1. Ask the doctor the direct question. "Would my dad qualify for hospice?" is fair to ask. Medicare also pays for a one-time visit with a hospice doctor to talk it through before your parent decides.
  2. Name the hospice you want. Tell the hospital case manager or social worker. Federal law gives your parent the right to choose. The hospital may suggest the hospice it uses most, and you can say no.
  3. Set up the place of care. Home, a relative's home, assisted living or a nursing home. For home, ask the hospice what day the hospital bed, oxygen and other equipment will arrive.
  4. Sign the election statement. Your parent signs it, or the person with legal authority to decide for them, such as a health care representative.
  5. Save the 24-hour number. Put it on the fridge and in every phone. Once hospice starts, call the hospice first, not 911, for symptoms of the terminal illness.

Discharge days move fast. If you can, choose the hospice a day or two ahead. Our hospital discharge guide explains your rights when a discharge feels rushed. If your parent's wishes are written down, bring a copy of the POLST form or advance directive.

Bergen County's helpline for families

The Bergen County Division of Senior Services, the county's Aging and Disability Resource Connection, answers at 201-336-7400 or 1-877-222-3737. Call about in-home services, meals and help for caregivers.

Where can Bergen families get help while a parent is on hospice?

Start with the county's Division of Senior Services at 201-336-7400. It is the lead agency for Bergen's Aging and Disability Resource Connection and can point you to in-home services, Meals on Wheels and caregiver programs.

  • Wellness Check Program. A free daily automated phone call to an older adult who lives alone. If nobody answers, the system calls a friend or relative you name. Ask the Division of Senior Services to enroll.
  • Dementia Friendly Bergen County. A county initiative listed by the Division of Senior Services for families living with dementia.
  • Adult Protective Services. If you suspect an older adult is being neglected or exploited, call the Bergen County Board of Social Services at 201-368-4300. After hours, call 1-800-624-0275.
  • Complaints about a hospice. Talk to the nurse manager first. The New Jersey Department of Health's 24-hour complaint hotline is 1-800-792-9770.
  • Respite for you. Our caregiver respite guide covers the state's programs.

If your parent has NJ FamilyCare (Medicaid), since April 1, 2026 it covers Community-Based Palliative Care for members with serious illness, at home, with no terminal diagnosis required. Members in a managed care plan should call member services and ask for it. For senior centers and lunch programs near you, see our Bergen County senior centers guide and the Bergen County page.

What support is there for the family afterward?

Every Medicare hospice must offer bereavement support to the family for up to a year after a death. Ask what that looks like: phone calls, mailings, groups or one-on-one counseling.

Several Bergen hospices list bereavement counselors on their teams, and Amedisys says it runs both virtual and in-person grief groups. You don't need to have used a hospice to find support. Our guide to grief support in New Jersey lists more options.

When the time comes, the hospice nurse will help with the first calls, including the funeral home. Our guide to funeral homes and cemeteries in Bergen County covers what happens next, and when a parent dies walks through the first weeks.

This page is general information, not medical or legal advice. For questions about a specific Medicare plan, the free SHIP counselors at 1-800-792-8820 can help.

faq.q: How do I find hospice for my mom in Bergen County?
faq.a: Search Medicare Care Compare for hospices using her ZIP code, then call two or three. If she is in the hospital, tell the case manager which hospice you want and they will send the referral.

faq.q: Which hospices serve Hackensack, NJ?
faq.a: In the Medicare ZIP code data we checked in November 2026, hospices serving 07601 included Amedisys, Ascend, Compassionate Care, Ennoble Care, Grace Healthcare Services, Holy Name, Hospice of New Jersey, Serenity, Valley Hospice, Visiting Health Services of New Jersey and VITAS. Check Care Compare for your exact ZIP code.

faq.q: Is there a hospice house in Bergen County?
faq.a: Yes. Villa Marie Claire in Saddle River is a residential hospice run by Holy Name, with 20 private suites and rooms for family. Call 551-248-4800 to ask about admission and costs.

faq.q: Can the hospital choose the hospice for my dad?
faq.a: No. Federal law gives your dad the right to choose his hospice. The hospital can suggest one, but you can name any Medicare-certified hospice that serves his town.

title: Hospice care in Morris County, NJ: who serves your town
dek: The Medicare-certified hospices that serve Morristown, Parsippany, Randolph, Denville and the rest of Morris County, where inpatient hospice is, and how to start care from a hospital bed.
keyFacts: Search Medicare Care Compare by your parent's ZIP code to see which hospices serve that town.
Your parent has the right to choose the hospice, even when a hospital suggests one.
Atlantic Health offers inpatient hospice at Morristown Medical Center and Chilton Medical Center.
Morris County aging and disability office: 973-285-6848, or the ADRC at 1-877-222-3737.
NJ Department of Health complaint hotline: 1-800-792-9770.
body:
Morris County families can choose from at least thirteen Medicare-certified hospices that serve towns from Morristown and Parsippany to Randolph and Denville and that show Morris County, or a Morristown office, on their own websites. Two are long-standing nonprofits based in Morristown: Atlantic Visiting Nurse, part of Atlantic Health, and the Visiting Nurse Association of Northern New Jersey, which dates to 1898.

Hospice care comes to your mom or dad, at home, in assisted living or in a nursing home. When symptoms get too hard to manage at home, Atlantic Health offers short inpatient hospice stays at Morristown Medical Center and at Chilton Medical Center in Pompton Plains. This page lists the hospices we confirmed, explains those inpatient options and walks through getting started. For how the Medicare benefit works, see our statewide guide to hospice care in New Jersey.

Which hospices serve Morris County?

The hospices below reported serving Morris ZIP codes to Medicare and name Morris County, or every New Jersey county, on their own websites. Atlantic Visiting Nurse is the one exception to that wording: its site does not list counties, but its office is in Morristown and it runs inpatient hospice at two Morris hospitals. We checked these listings in November 2026. This is not an endorsement or a ranking.

We pulled Medicare's hospice ZIP code data for four sample ZIP codes: 07960 (Morristown), 07054 (Parsippany), 07869 (Randolph) and 07834 (Denville). Every hospice below served all four, except Center for Hope, which did not list 07834, and Life Hospice, which did not list 07869. Phone numbers come from each hospice's own website.

HospiceOfficePhone
Affinity Care of New JerseyParsippany973-813-4999
Ascend HospiceClark908-931-9080
Atlantic Visiting Nurse Hospice (Atlantic Health)Morristown973-379-8400
Center for Hope Hospice and Palliative CareScotch Plains908-889-7780
Compassionate Care Hospice (Amedisys)Rockaway973-726-7510
Ennoble CareHackettstown973-567-3203
Grace Healthcare ServicesEdison732-225-4100
Hospice of New JerseyBloomfield973-893-0818
Life HospiceEast Hanover973-607-4930
Serenity Hospice CareHamilton609-227-2400
Suncrest HospiceParsippany862-701-2820

Visiting Nurse Association of Northern New JerseyMorristown1-800-938-4748

A few notes. Compassionate Care Hospice in Rockaway is an Amedisys company and is certified separately from the Compassionate Care office in Bloomfield; Medicare lists a different phone than the 24-hour number on its own page. Medicare lists Ascend's office in Cranford and Affinity's in Brick, while their sites now show Clark and a North Jersey office in Parsippany. Medicare lists Life Hospice in Livingston, and its site now shows East Hanover. The Visiting Nurse Association of Northern New Jersey uses the number 1-800-WE VISIT.

We left off a few hospices that showed up in Medicare's data for some Morris ZIP codes but whose own websites did not list Morris County, including Karen Ann Quinlan Hospice, which describes its area as Sussex and Warren counties and Pike County, Pennsylvania.

The two Morristown nonprofits are worth a closer look if you want a local agency. Atlantic Visiting Nurse Hospice says it is licensed by the New Jersey Department of Health, accredited by The Joint Commission and certified by Medicare. The Visiting Nurse Association of Northern New Jersey says it is licensed by the state, accredited by the Community Health Accreditation Partner (CHAP), and accepts Medicare, Medicaid, private insurance and private pay, with a foundation that helps residents facing financial hardship.

In Morris, the drive matters. Ask where the nurse who covers your parent's town is based.

How do I check which hospices serve my parent's town?

Search Medicare Care Compare for hospices using your parent's ZIP code, not yours. Western Morris towns near Sussex and Warren may have a different list than Morristown or Madison.

Look at the family survey results, then call two or three hospices. A hospice with too few surveys may show no stars, which is not a red flag on its own. Our guide to hospice vs. palliative care has a fuller list of first-call questions. In a county with long rural stretches, add these:

  • How long does it usually take a nurse to reach our town at night?
  • Can you start care tomorrow if we call today?
  • Which Morris nursing homes and assisted living residences do you visit now?
  • Where would my dad go for a short inpatient stay if his pain got out of control?

Where is inpatient hospice care near Morris County?

Atlantic Health offers general inpatient hospice at Morristown Medical Center and Chilton Medical Center in Pompton Plains, both in Morris County, and at Overlook Medical Center in Summit. Center for Hope runs Peggy's House, a hospice residence in Scotch Plains in Union County.

General inpatient care is short-term. It is for pain or symptoms that can't be handled at home. Once things are under control, your parent usually goes back home or to a facility. Here is what to know:

  • Atlantic Visiting Nurse Hospice. If your parent uses Atlantic's hospice, its team can arrange a general inpatient stay at Morristown, Chilton or Overlook. Main number: 973-379-8400.
  • Peggy's House, Scotch Plains. Center for Hope's homelike residence beside the Ash Brook Reservation. For qualifications and cost, call 908-889-7780 and ask for a residential advisor.
  • Other hospices. Life Hospice lists inpatient care in a hospital or nursing facility, plus respite and continuous care during a crisis. Ask any hospice which hospitals and nursing homes it uses.

Respite stays are different. Under Medicare, the hospice can arrange a short stay of up to five days at a time so the family caregiver can rest. Ask where your hospice sends respite patients before you need it.

What does hospice cost?

For someone on Original Medicare who qualifies, hospice care is covered under Part A. Your parent pays nothing for the hospice team's care, and at most a $5 copay for each prescription for pain and symptom relief, plus 5% of the Medicare-approved amount for inpatient respite care.

What Medicare does not cover is room and board, whether that is a nursing home, an assisted living residence or a hospice residence. It also does not cover treatment meant to cure the terminal illness while your parent is on hospice. Medicare Advantage members still get hospice through Original Medicare. NJ FamilyCare (Medicaid) and most private insurance also cover hospice. If money is tight, ask the hospice about its policy. Atlantic Visiting Nurse, for one, says no one is denied hospice because of an inability to pay.

How do we start hospice from a Morris hospital?

Tell the case manager or social worker that your family wants hospice and which one you've chosen. The hospital sends the referral, and the hospice confirms your parent qualifies.

  1. Ask the doctor the direct question. "Would my dad qualify for hospice?" is fair to ask. Medicare also pays for a one-time visit with a hospice doctor to talk it through before your parent decides.
  2. Name the hospice you want. Tell the hospital case manager or social worker. Federal law gives your parent the right to choose. The hospital may suggest the hospice it uses most, and you can say no.
  3. Set up the place of care. Home, a relative's home, assisted living or a nursing home. For home, ask the hospice what day the hospital bed, oxygen and other equipment will arrive.
  4. Sign the election statement. Your parent signs it, or the person with legal authority to decide for them, such as a health care representative.
  5. Save the 24-hour number. Put it on the fridge and in every phone. Once hospice starts, call the hospice first, not 911, for symptoms of the terminal illness.

Discharges can happen in a day. Our hospital discharge guide explains what to do if one feels rushed. If your parent has a POLST form, make sure the hospice gets a copy.

If your parent lives in a nursing home

Hospice can come into a Morris nursing home or assisted living residence. Ask the facility which hospices it already works with. The hospice benefit covers hospice care there, but not the monthly room and board bill.

Where can Morris families get help along the way?

Call the Morris County Division on Aging, Disabilities and Community Programming at 973-285-6848, or the statewide ADRC line at 1-877-222-3737. The office gives information, referrals and direct help to older adults, people with disabilities, veterans and caregivers.

  • Adult Protective Services. Morris County APS is run by the same county division, at 340 West Hanover Avenue in Morristown. Call 973-326-7282, day or night.
  • Rides. MAPS, the Morris Area Paratransit System, gives shared rides to residents 60 and older, veterans and people with disabilities. Call 973-829-8103.
  • Complaints about a hospice. Start with the nurse manager. The New Jersey Department of Health's 24-hour complaint hotline is 1-800-792-9770.
  • A break for you. Our caregiver respite guide lists state and county programs.

If your parent has NJ FamilyCare (Medicaid), it now covers Community-Based Palliative Care for members with serious illness, at home, since April 1, 2026. No terminal diagnosis is required. Ask the managed care plan's member services. For senior centers and lunch programs, see our Morris County senior centers guide and the Morris County page.

What grief support is there in Morris County?

Every Medicare hospice must offer bereavement support to the family for up to a year after a death. Atlantic Visiting Nurse and Life Hospice both describe 13 months of follow-up.

Atlantic Visiting Nurse Hospice lists a six-week Coping with Grief group each spring and fall, a monthly caregiver support group, a men's group, a ladies lunch group and a second-year group for women. It also runs Camp Clover, a free four-day bereavement day camp every August for children and teens who lost someone close. Its bereavement coordinator is at 973-379-8442.

You don't need to have used a hospice to join a group. Our guide to grief support in New Jersey lists more. When the time comes, the hospice nurse helps with first calls, including the funeral home. See funeral homes and cemeteries in Morris County and when a parent dies for the weeks that follow.

This page is general information, not medical or legal advice. For questions about a specific Medicare plan, the free SHIP counselors at 1-800-792-8820 can help.

title: Hospice care in Passaic County, NJ: who serves your town
dek: The Medicare-certified hospices that serve Paterson, Wayne, Clifton, West Milford and the rest of Passaic County, where to find inpatient care nearby, and how to start from a hospital bed.
keyFacts: Search Medicare Care Compare by your parent's ZIP code to see which hospices serve that town.
Your parent has the right to choose the hospice, even when a hospital suggests one.
Visiting Health Services of New Jersey, based in Woodland Park, answers 24 hours at 844-777-0711.
Passaic County Senior Services: 973-569-4060, or the ADRC at 1-877-222-3737.
NJ Department of Health complaint hotline: 1-800-792-9770.
body:
Passaic County runs from the city of Paterson up into the lakes and woods of West Milford, and hospice care reaches all of it. In Medicare's data, at least ten Medicare-certified hospices that also name Passaic on their own websites report serving Paterson, Wayne, Clifton and West Milford. One is based right in the county: Visiting Health Services of New Jersey in Woodland Park, a partnership of St. Joseph's Health and Hackensack Meridian Health.

Hospice nurses and aides come to your mom or dad, whether that is a house in Wayne, an apartment in Paterson or a nursing home in Clifton. This page lists the hospices we confirmed, explains where to look for inpatient care nearby, and shows how to start hospice from the hospital. For how the Medicare benefit works and what it pays for, see our statewide guide to hospice care in New Jersey.

Which hospices serve Passaic County?

The hospices below reported serving Passaic ZIP codes to Medicare and name Passaic County, or every New Jersey county, on their own websites. We checked these listings in November 2026. This is not an endorsement or a ranking.

We pulled Medicare's hospice ZIP code data for four sample ZIP codes: 07501 (Paterson), 07470 (Wayne), 07011 (Clifton) and 07480 (West Milford). Every hospice below served all four, except Ascend and Suncrest, which did not list 07501 in Paterson. Phone numbers come from each hospice's own website.
