A few notes. Visiting Health Services of New Jersey says it serves Passaic, Bergen and parts of Morris counties, and its advisors answer 24 hours a day. Compassionate Care Hospice and Amedisys Hospice Care are separately certified hospices owned by the same company. Medicare lists Ascend's office in Cranford and Affinity's in Brick, while their own sites now show Clark and a North Jersey office in Parsippany.

Some hospices served most or all of our sample ZIP codes in Medicare's data but did not list Passaic County on their own websites when we checked, including Valley Hospice, Ennoble Care and Atlantic Visiting Nurse. We left them off for that reason. If one of them serves your parent's town in Care Compare, call and ask.

If your parent is in a St. Joseph's Health or Hackensack Meridian Health hospital, ask the case manager whether the hospital works with Visiting Health Services of New Jersey, the two systems' joint home care and hospice partnership. That can make the handoff simple. You are still free to choose any hospice on this list, and it is fine to ask for two or three names.

A good hospice answers the phone at night. Call one at 9 p.m. before you choose, and see who picks up.

How do I check which hospices serve my parent's town?

Search Medicare Care Compare for hospices with your parent's own ZIP code. A hospice that covers Clifton may not cover Ringwood or West Milford, so check the exact town.

Read the family survey results, then call two or three. A hospice with too few surveys may show no stars, and that alone is not a warning sign. Our guide to hospice vs. palliative care has a full list of first-call questions. For Passaic families, add these:

  • Do you have nurses and aides who speak my parent's first language?
  • How long would a night visit take to reach West Milford or Ringwood?
  • Which nursing homes in Paterson, Wayne or Clifton do you visit now?
  • Where do your patients go for a short inpatient or respite stay?

Where is inpatient hospice care near Passaic County?

The closest dedicated options we confirmed are just over the county line: Atlantic Health's general inpatient hospice at Chilton Medical Center in Pompton Plains, and Holy Name's Villa Marie Claire residence in Saddle River. For a short inpatient stay, ask your hospice which hospitals and nursing homes it uses.

  • Chilton Medical Center, Pompton Plains. Atlantic Health offers general inpatient hospice there for patients of Atlantic Visiting Nurse Hospice whose pain or symptoms can't be managed at home. Call 973-379-8400.
  • Villa Marie Claire, Saddle River. A residential hospice run by Holy Name, with 20 private suites and rooms for family. Call 551-248-4800 to ask about admission and cost.
  • Your hospice's own arrangements. Most hospices on our list contract with local hospitals and nursing homes for inpatient and respite care. Ask which ones before you sign.

Here is how the levels of care differ. Routine home care is the usual visits. General inpatient care is short-term, hospital-level care for symptoms. Respite care, under Medicare, is a stay of up to five days at a time so a tired caregiver can rest. Continuous home care adds nursing at home during a short crisis.

What does hospice cost?

For someone on Original Medicare who qualifies, hospice care is covered under Part A. Your parent pays nothing for the hospice team's care, and at most a $5 copay for each prescription for pain and symptom relief, plus 5% of the Medicare-approved amount for inpatient respite care.

What Medicare does not cover is room and board, whether that is a nursing home, an assisted living residence or a hospice residence. It also does not cover treatment meant to cure the terminal illness while your parent is on hospice. Medicare Advantage members still get hospice through Original Medicare. NJ FamilyCare (Medicaid) and most private insurance also cover hospice. If money is tight, ask each hospice on your short list about its policy for families who can't pay.

How do we start hospice from a hospital?

Tell the hospital case manager or social worker that your family wants hospice and which one you've picked. The hospital sends the referral, and the hospice checks that your parent qualifies.

  1. Ask the doctor the direct question. "Would my dad qualify for hospice?" is fair to ask. Medicare also pays for a one-time visit with a hospice doctor to talk it through before your parent decides.
  2. Name the hospice you want. Tell the hospital case manager or social worker. Federal law gives your parent the right to choose. The hospital may suggest the hospice it uses most, and you can say no.
  3. Set up the place of care. Home, a relative's home, assisted living or a nursing home. For home, ask the hospice what day the hospital bed, oxygen and other equipment will arrive.
  4. Sign the election statement. Your parent signs it, or the person with legal authority to decide for them, such as a health care representative.
  5. Save the 24-hour number. Put it on the fridge and in every phone. Once hospice starts, call the hospice first, not 911, for symptoms of the terminal illness.

Discharges can come with little warning. Our hospital discharge guide explains your rights. If your parent has signed a POLST form, give the hospice a copy on day one.

Passaic County's help line

The Passaic County Department of Senior Services, Disability and Veterans' Affairs in Totowa answers at 973-569-4060. For the county's Aging and Disability Resource Connection, call 1-877-222-3737.

Where can Passaic families get help along the way?

Start with the county's Department of Senior Services. It is the county's Aging and Disability Resource Connection, and it does in-home evaluations, benefit screenings and care management.

  • Help at home. The department lists transportation, seasonal cleaning, housekeeping, certified home health aides, telephone reassurance, social adult day care and legal services for older residents.
  • Meals. It also runs congregate and home-delivered meals and nutrition counseling. Ask about home-delivered meals for a caregiver who can't leave the house.
  • Adult Protective Services. If you suspect an older adult is being neglected or exploited, call the Passaic County Board of Social Services at 973-592-1954. After hours, call 1-800-315-4561.
  • Complaints about a hospice. Talk with the nurse manager first. The New Jersey Department of Health's 24-hour complaint hotline is 1-800-792-9770.

If your parent has NJ FamilyCare (Medicaid), since April 1, 2026 it covers Community-Based Palliative Care for members with serious illness, at home, with no terminal diagnosis required. Call the plan's member services. Our caregiver respite guide, the Passaic County senior centers guide and the Passaic County page have more local help.

What support is there for the family afterward?

Every Medicare hospice must offer bereavement support to the family for up to a year after a death. Ask each hospice what it actually provides, since some offer groups and others mostly phone calls and mailings.

Affinity Care says its bereavement counseling runs for at least 13 months after a death, and Amedisys runs virtual and in-person grief groups. Our guide to grief support in New Jersey lists groups you can join even if your family did not use hospice.

When the time comes, the hospice nurse will help with the first calls, including the funeral home. See funeral homes and cemeteries in Passaic County and when a parent dies for what comes next.

This page is general information, not medical or legal advice. For questions about a specific Medicare plan, the free SHIP counselors at 1-800-792-8820 can help.

title: Hearing loss and dementia risk: what NJ families should know
dek: What the 2024 Lancet Commission and the ACHIEVE trial actually found about hearing loss and dementia, what Medicare covers, and how New Jersey helps pay for hearing aids.
keyFacts: 2024 Lancet Commission: hearing loss is tied to about 7% of dementia cases worldwide, tied for the largest changeable risk.
ACHIEVE trial (2023): hearing care slowed decline by 48% over 3 years in higher-risk older adults, with no difference across the whole group.
Original Medicare does not cover hearing aids. Part B covers diagnostic hearing exams.
NJ's HAAAD program repays up to $500 for one hearing aid or $1,000 for two.
HAAAD and PAAD: 1-800-792-9745.
body:
Untreated hearing loss is linked to a higher risk of dementia. In 2024 the Lancet Commission on dementia, a panel of 27 experts, estimated that hearing loss is tied to about 7% of dementia cases worldwide. That makes it one of the two largest risk factors people can change, alongside high LDL cholesterol in midlife. It does not mean hearing loss causes dementia in any one person, or that hearing aids will prevent it.

The best test so far, the ACHIEVE trial published in 2023, found that hearing aids did not slow the decline in thinking and memory across all 977 older adults in the study over three years. Among the participants at higher risk, though, hearing care slowed that decline by 48%. Getting your mom or dad's hearing checked and treated is worth doing, and New Jersey has programs that help pay. This page is general information, not medical advice.

What did the 2024 Lancet Commission find?

The Commission listed 14 risk factors that can be changed and estimated that nearly half of dementia cases, 45%, could be prevented or delayed if all of them were removed. Hearing loss and high LDL cholesterol were the largest, at 7% each.

The 14 factors are less education, hearing loss, high blood pressure, smoking, obesity, depression, physical inactivity, diabetes, excess alcohol, traumatic brain injury, air pollution, social isolation, high LDL cholesterol and untreated vision loss. The last two were added in 2024.

Risk factorShare of cases
Hearing loss7%
High LDL cholesterol (midlife)7%
Less education (early life)5%
Social isolation (later life)5%
Untreated vision loss2%
All 14 together45%

Among its recommendations, the Commission called for making hearing aids available to everyone with hearing loss and for reducing harmful noise.

Read these numbers with care. They are population estimates. The authors note that they assume the risk factors cause dementia, and that some links may be only partly causal. They also say lowering risk across a population does not guarantee that any one person will avoid dementia.

A risk factor is a nudge on the odds. It is not a diagnosis, and it is not a promise.

What did the ACHIEVE trial show about hearing aids?

ACHIEVE was the first large randomized trial to test whether treating hearing loss slows decline in thinking. Overall it did not. In a higher-risk group, hearing care cut the rate of decline by 48% over three years.

Researchers enrolled 977 adults aged 70 to 84 with untreated hearing loss and no substantial memory problems, at four sites in the United States. Half got hearing aids and counseling from an audiologist. The other half met with a health educator about healthy aging. Both groups had follow-up visits every six months. The results were published in The Lancet in July 2023.

Group3-year result
All 977 participantsNo difference in decline
238 from a heart health study (older, more risk factors)48% slower decline with hearing care
739 new community volunteersNo effect within 3 years

The study team says the higher-risk group was declining about three times faster, which made a benefit easier to see. They think the healthier group may benefit over a longer time, and they are still following everyone in the study. People who got hearing aids also reported much better communication, which matters on its own.

"Hearing loss is very treatable in later life, which makes it an important public health target to reduce risk of cognitive decline and dementia," said Dr. Frank Lin of Johns Hopkins University, who co-led the trial, in a National Institutes of Health summary. "Until we know more," he added, "we recommend for general health and well-being that older adults have their hearing checked regularly and any hearing issues properly addressed."

Why might hearing and memory be connected?

Researchers are still working this out. A 2025 review put the open question plainly, asking whether hearing loss is a cause, a catalyst or a consequence of dementia. The evidence is not settled.

Hearing loss is also very common, which is part of why it shows up so large in the Lancet math. The National Institute on Deafness and Other Communication Disorders says about one in three people ages 65 to 74 has hearing loss, and nearly half of those older than 75. It creeps in slowly, so family members often notice before your parent does. Common signs include asking people to repeat themselves, trouble following a conversation when two or more people talk, and a TV turned up louder than everyone else likes.

What is clearer is the daily effect. The National Institute on Aging says hearing loss can lead older adults to withdraw from others, feel lonely and become depressed. Social isolation and depression are themselves on the Lancet list. Say your dad stops going to his Thursday card game because he can't follow the table talk. He loses the conversation, the friends and the reason to get dressed and out the door.

Hearing can also make memory look worse than it is. If your mom never heard the doctor's instructions clearly, she cannot remember them later. That is one reason to have her wear her hearing aids, and bring her glasses, to any memory screening. Our guide to free memory screening in New Jersey explains what a screening can and cannot tell you.

Does Medicare pay for a hearing test or hearing aids?

Original Medicare pays for diagnostic hearing exams but not for hearing aids or the exams to fit them. Some Medicare Advantage plans add hearing benefits.

  • Diagnostic exams. Part B covers hearing and balance exams when a doctor or other provider orders them to see whether you need treatment. You can also see an audiologist once every 12 months without an order for gradual hearing loss and some other conditions.
  • Your share. After the Part B deductible, which is $283 in 2026, you pay 20% of the Medicare-approved amount, plus a copayment if the exam is in a hospital outpatient department.
  • Hearing aids. Original Medicare does not cover them. Medicare Advantage plans may, but benefits differ from plan to plan, so read the plan details during open enrollment.

Since October 17, 2022, adults 18 and older with perceived mild to moderate hearing loss can buy hearing aids over the counter, without an exam or prescription. See a doctor first if hearing changed suddenly, if one ear is much worse, or if there is pain, dizziness or drainage. Our guide to hearing aids for older adults in New Jersey covers OTC aids in more detail.

What help does New Jersey offer to pay for hearing aids?

New Jersey's HAAAD program repays up to $500 for one hearing aid or up to $1,000 for two in a calendar year. You must be enrolled in PAAD or Lifeline and meet the income limits.

ProgramWho it helps
HAAADAge 65+ (or 18 to 64 on Social Security Disability), 2026 income up to $54,943 single or $62,390 married, enrolled in PAAD or Lifeline
NJ Hearing Aid ProjectFree refurbished hearing aids, same age and income limits
NJ FamilyCareCovers hearing aids in all plans except Plan D
VAVeterans enrolled in VA health care
  1. Get into PAAD first. If your parent isn't enrolled, apply through NJSave, which also checks for Senior Gold and Lifeline. Call 1-800-792-9745. Our guide to PAAD and Senior Gold explains the rules.
  2. Buy after approval. The hearing aid receipt must be dated on or after the PAAD approval date.
  3. Keep the paperwork. HAAAD needs the receipt plus a doctor's statement that the aid is medically necessary or a copy of the prescription. For an OTC aid, call before you buy to ask if it will qualify.
  4. Apply. Mail the signed application to HAAAD, PO Box 715, Trenton, NJ 08625-0715. Checks usually arrive six to eight weeks after eligibility is approved.
Numbers to keep

HAAAD, PAAD and NJSave: 1-800-792-9745. NJ Division of the Deaf and Hard of Hearing: 1-800-792-8339. NJ FamilyCare: 1-800-701-0710. Alzheimer's New Jersey Helpline: 1-888-280-6055.

How do I bring up hearing with my mom or dad?

Talk about hearing, not memory. Most people will agree to a hearing test long before they will discuss dementia, and the hearing test is the useful step.

  • Pick a calm moment. Not right after a frustrating phone call or a loud family dinner.
  • Describe, don't diagnose. "I notice the TV is louder, and you skipped the book club" lands better than "You can't hear anything."
  • Make it routine. Suggest a hearing test the way you would an eye exam, and offer to go along.
  • Ask the doctor. At the yearly Wellness visit, mention the hearing changes. The doctor can order a diagnostic exam that Part B covers.
  • Keep them in the room. If your parent already wears hearing aids, help them wear them every day, keep batteries or chargers handy, and sit facing them when you talk.

Keeping your parent in conversation is good for them whatever the research ends up showing. For more ideas, see our guides to staying connected in New Jersey and healthy aging. If memory problems are already clear, after a dementia diagnosis lists where New Jersey families can turn.

More guides that may help: how dementia is diagnosed.

faq.q: Does hearing loss cause dementia?
faq.a: Not proven. Hearing loss is linked to a higher risk, and the 2024 Lancet Commission estimated it accounts for about 7% of dementia cases worldwide. The authors note some links may be only partly causal, and lowering risk does not guarantee any one person avoids dementia.

faq.q: Can hearing aids prevent dementia?
faq.a: No study has shown that. In the ACHIEVE trial, hearing aids did not slow decline across all 977 participants over three years, but slowed it by 48% in a higher-risk group. Researchers are still following participants.

faq.q: How do I get my mom to take a hearing test?
faq.a: Talk about hearing, not memory. Mention specific things you've noticed, suggest it like a routine eye exam, and offer to go with her. Her doctor can order a diagnostic hearing exam that Medicare Part B covers.

faq.q: Does Medicare pay for hearing aids in New Jersey?
faq.a: Original Medicare does not. Some Medicare Advantage plans add hearing benefits. New Jersey's HAAAD program repays up to $500 per hearing aid for people 65 and older enrolled in PAAD or Lifeline. Call 1-800-792-9745.

faq.q: Should my dad wear his hearing aids to a memory screening?
faq.a: Yes. If he can't hear the questions clearly, he may score worse than he should. Bring his glasses too.

faq.q: Where can I get free hearing aids for my parent in NJ?
faq.a: The NJ Hearing Aid Project gives free refurbished hearing aids to residents 65 and older (or on Social Security Disability) who meet the income limits. NJ FamilyCare covers hearing aids except in Plan D, and the VA provides them to enrolled veterans.

title: Incontinence help for older adults in NJ: care and supplies
dek: Bladder leaks are common and often treatable. What causes them, what Medicare and NJ FamilyCare pay for, and how to help your parent keep their dignity.
keyFacts: Original Medicare does not cover adult briefs or pads. You pay 100%.
Part B covers outpatient pelvic floor physical therapy: 20% after the $283 deductible in 2026.
NJ FamilyCare plans can cover medically necessary incontinence supplies with a prescription. Ask the plan.
Sudden new incontinence can signal a urinary tract infection. Call the doctor.
Medicare help: SHIP at 1-800-792-8820.
body:
Bladder or bowel leaks are common in later life, and they are often treatable. The National Institute on Aging (NIA) says incontinence can often be stopped or controlled, and that the simplest, safest treatments should come first. The first step for your mom or dad is a doctor's visit, not a bigger box of pads.

Money is the second surprise. Original Medicare does not pay for adult briefs, pads or other incontinence supplies, so families pay 100% of that cost. Medicare does help pay for the doctor visits, tests and pelvic floor physical therapy that can cut down on leaks. NJ FamilyCare, New Jersey's Medicaid program, can cover the supplies themselves with a prescription, though each health plan sets its own steps. This guide walks through causes, treatment, what is covered in New Jersey, skin care and how to bring it up kindly.

Why does incontinence happen in older adults?

Usually because muscles, nerves or mobility have changed, and sometimes because of something short term and fixable. A new leak problem deserves a checkup before anyone decides it is permanent.

The NIA lists short-term causes such as urinary tract infections, vaginal infection or irritation, constipation and some medicines. Longer-lasting incontinence can come from weak bladder or pelvic floor muscles, an overactive bladder, nerve damage from conditions such as diabetes or Parkinson's disease, pelvic organ prolapse, or arthritis that makes it hard to reach the bathroom in time. In men, most incontinence is tied to the prostate.

TypeWhat it looks like
StressLeaks with a cough, sneeze, laugh or lift
UrgeA sudden need to go, and not making it in time
OverflowSmall, steady leaks from a bladder that never fully empties
FunctionalNormal bladder, but trouble getting to the toilet quickly

Functional incontinence matters a lot for families. If your dad has normal bladder control but his walker, a dark hallway or a hard-to-open zipper slows him down, the fix may be a commode by the bed, night lights or easier clothing. Our guide to adaptive equipment covers raised toilet seats, toilet frames and bedside commodes.

Rushing to the bathroom is also a fall risk. The NIA notes that conditions that cause rushed trips to the bathroom, such as incontinence, can raise the chance of falling. See our fall prevention guide for a room-by-room checklist.

When should your parent see a doctor?

As soon as leaks start or change. Call promptly if incontinence comes on suddenly, or comes with fever, pain, burning, blood in the urine or new confusion, since an infection can be the cause.

The NIA also lists these signs worth raising with a doctor:

  • Needing to urinate more often or more suddenly
  • Cloudy urine, or blood in the urine
  • Pain while urinating
  • Urinating eight or more times a day
  • Passing only small amounts after a strong urge
  • Trouble starting, or a weak stream
  1. Keep a bladder diary for a few days. Write down drinks, bathroom trips and leaks, with times. The National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases (NIDDK) offers a free printable diary, and doctors use it to spot patterns.
  2. Bring every medicine and supplement. Some drugs cause or worsen leaks. Others used to treat bladder problems can cause constipation.
  3. Ask what type of incontinence this is. Treatment depends on the type.
  4. Ask about a referral. The primary care doctor may send your parent to a urologist, a urogynecologist or a physical therapist trained in pelvic floor therapy.
  5. Ask about any medication's effect on memory. The NIA says some overactive bladder medicines have been linked to a higher risk of cognitive decline in adults over 65. Your parent should not stop a prescribed drug without talking to the doctor, but it is a fair question to ask before starting one.
A new leak problem deserves a checkup before anyone decides it is permanent.

What treatments help, and does Medicare pay?

Many people improve with exercises and habit changes. Medicare Part B helps pay for the visits, tests and outpatient physical therapy involved.

Things your parent can start at home

  • Pelvic floor (Kegel) exercises. NIDDK says strong pelvic floor muscles hold urine better, and men can benefit too.
  • Timed voiding. Going on a schedule, then slowly stretching the time between trips.
  • Urge suppression. Holding still, slow breaths and quick pelvic floor squeezes can help a strong urge pass.
  • Fewer bladder irritants. NIDDK suggests limiting caffeine, carbonated drinks and alcohol.
  • Treating constipation. Constipation makes bladder problems worse.

Treatments a doctor may offer

NIDDK and the NIA describe medicines, vaginal estrogen cream, pessaries for women, bulking injections, electrical nerve stimulation, catheters for overflow incontinence and, as a last resort, surgery. Which one fits depends on the type and on your parent's overall health.

What Medicare covers

ItemOriginal Medicare
Doctor visits and testsPart B, 20% after deductible
Pelvic floor PTPart B, 20% after deductible
Catheters, ostomy suppliesPart B, 20% after deductible
Prescription drugsPart D plan
Briefs, pads, underpadsNot covered

The Part B deductible is $283 in 2026. Medicare covers medically necessary outpatient physical therapy when a doctor or other provider certifies the need, and there is no yearly dollar cap. Once a year's therapy costs pass $2,480 for physical and speech therapy combined, the therapist must confirm on the claim that more care is medically necessary. Urological supplies such as catheters are covered as prosthetic devices, and only from a supplier that participates in Medicare.

A Medigap policy usually picks up the 20% for covered services. If your parent has a Medicare Advantage plan, call the number on the card and ask about therapy copays, prior approval and whether the plan gives any allowance for incontinence products. Some plans offer extra benefits Original Medicare does not, but do not assume supplies are included. If this matters for next year, compare plans during open enrollment, which ends December 7. Free, unbiased help comes from SHIP Medicare counselors at 1-800-792-8820.

Who pays for adult briefs and pads in New Jersey?

For most families on Medicare alone, you do. The main exception is NJ FamilyCare, where health plans can cover medically necessary incontinence supplies with a prescription.

Medicare.gov is plain about it: Original Medicare does not cover incontinence supplies or adult diapers, and you pay 100% of the cost.

NJ FamilyCare

NJ FamilyCare members get most care through a health plan, and the plans follow the state's benefit rules for supplies. As one example, Horizon NJ Health's published policy (last reviewed August 2026) covers incontinence garments for members age 4 and older when they are medically necessary and prescribed. It allows up to 300 combined units a month, counting briefs, pads, liners, shields, guards and pull-ups, without prior approval when a participating provider orders them. Larger amounts need prior approval with medical records. The same policy also covers medically necessary wipes, including skin barrier wipes, with a prescription. Other plans set their own steps, so call member services on your parent's card and ask:

  • Which supplier do we order from, and will it deliver?
  • How many units a month are covered without prior approval?
  • Are underpads, wipes or skin barrier creams covered too?
  • What does the doctor need to write on the prescription?

If your parent has both Medicare and NJ FamilyCare, NJ FamilyCare may cover supplies Medicare does not, so ask the plan. If you think your parent might qualify, our NJ FamilyCare guide for seniors explains the income and asset rules, and the state line is 1-800-701-0710.

Taxes

The IRS says the cost of diapers counts as a medical expense only if they are needed to relieve the effects of a particular disease. Medical expenses are deductible only if your parent itemizes, and only the part above 7.5% of adjusted gross income. If you claim your parent as a dependent, different rules may apply to you. This is general information, not tax or legal advice, so check with a tax preparer.

Key numbers

Medicare questions: SHIP at 1-800-792-8820. NJ FamilyCare: 1-800-701-0710. Your county office on aging, through the Aging and Disability Resource Connection: 1-877-222-3737.

How do you protect your parent's skin?

Change wet or soiled products promptly, clean gently and use a barrier cream. Skin that stays damp breaks down fast, especially in someone who sits or lies down much of the day.

  • Use gentle cleansers made for this. NIDDK notes special skin cleaners and creams can keep skin from getting irritated, and creams can help block urine from the skin.
  • Pick the right product for the leak. A light pad for stress leaks, a brief for heavier or overnight leaks, washable absorbent underwear for some people. Men with steady leaks may ask the doctor about an external catheter.
  • Protect the bed and favorite chair. Large disposable or washable pads help, and they save mattresses.
  • Watch for redness, rash or open spots. Tell the doctor or home health nurse early.

Should your parent drink less water?

Usually not, unless a doctor says so. Cutting back too far can cause dehydration, constipation and more bladder irritation.

NIDDK says to ask the doctor whether to drink less during the day, but not to limit liquids to the point of dehydration. A 2023 research review on hydration in older adults, published through the National Library of Medicine, points out that people with urinary incontinence sometimes restrict fluids on their own, which raises their dehydration risk. Older adults also tend to feel less thirsty than younger people. A better plan is steady drinks through the day, fewer in the few hours before bed if the doctor agrees, and less caffeine and alcohol. Our guide to eating well after 70 has more on fluids.

How do you bring it up with your mom or dad?

Privately, calmly and as a health issue. Many older adults hide leaks out of embarrassment and stop going out because of them.

NIDDK notes that many people feel too embarrassed to talk about bladder problems, and that friends and family can make it easier. A few things that tend to help:

  • Lead with what they care about. "I noticed you skipped bridge again. Is getting to the bathroom part of it?"
  • Normalize it. Leaks are common, and doctors talk about them every day.
  • Use their words. Some people prefer "protective underwear" or "pads" to "diapers".
  • Offer to handle the logistics. Booking the appointment, ordering supplies, setting up a bathroom bag for outings.
  • Keep dignity in daily care. Knock, close doors, let your parent do what they can, and keep supplies out of sight of visitors.

If your parent has dementia, new incontinence can come with confusion and resistance. Regular bathroom reminders, clothing that is easy to remove and a clear path to the toilet help. Our sundowning guide covers late-day changes. If personal care is wearing you down, see caregiver burnout help in NJ, or look into a licensed home care agency if you want an aide to help with bathing and changing.

What to do this week

  1. Book a visit with the primary care doctor and start a three-day bladder diary before it.
  2. Make the path to the bathroom safe. Night lights, no throw rugs, a commode by the bed if needed.
  3. Check coverage. If your parent has NJ FamilyCare, call the plan about supplies. If not, ask the doctor about pelvic floor physical therapy under Part B.
  4. Set up skin care basics and a spare bag with a change of clothes for outings.
  5. Follow up in a month. If leaks are not better, ask about the next treatment step or a specialist.

For more on everyday health habits, see staying well in New Jersey.

faq.q: How do I get incontinence supplies covered for my mom in NJ?
faq.a: If she has NJ FamilyCare, ask her doctor for a prescription and call the member services number on her plan card to find out which supplier to use and how many units a month are covered. Original Medicare does not pay for briefs or pads. If she has a Medicare Advantage plan, call the plan and ask whether it offers any allowance.

faq.q: Does Medicare pay for adult diapers?
faq.a: No. Medicare.gov says Original Medicare does not cover incontinence supplies or adult diapers, and you pay 100% of the cost. Medicare Part B does cover doctor visits, tests, outpatient physical therapy and urological supplies such as catheters.

faq.q: Does Medicare cover pelvic floor physical therapy?
faq.a: Yes, when a doctor or other provider certifies it is medically necessary. After the Part B deductible ($283 in 2026), your parent pays 20% of the Medicare-approved amount. There is no yearly dollar cap, but above $2,480 in combined physical and speech therapy in 2026, the therapist must confirm the care is medically necessary.

faq.q: My dad suddenly started having accidents. What should I do?
faq.a: Call his doctor soon. A sudden change can come from a urinary tract infection, constipation or a new medicine, all of which can be treated. Call right away if it comes with fever, pain, blood in the urine or new confusion.

faq.q: Should my mother drink less so she leaks less?
faq.a: Only if her doctor says so. Health agencies warn against limiting liquids to the point of dehydration. Cutting caffeine and alcohol, and drinking less in the few hours before bed, are safer first steps.

faq.q: Are adult diapers tax deductible?
faq.a: Only in limited cases. The IRS says diapers count as a medical expense only if they are needed to relieve the effects of a particular disease, and medical expenses are deductible only above 7.5% of adjusted gross income for people who itemize. Ask a tax preparer about your family's situation.

title: Diabetes supplies and Medicare in New Jersey: what's covered
dek: Meters, strips, CGMs, insulin and shoes: what Medicare Part B and Part D pay for, where PAAD fits in, and the free diabetes services many older adults miss.
keyFacts: Part B covers meters, strips, lancets and eligible CGMs: 20% after the $283 deductible in 2026.
Insulin costs no more than $35 a month for each covered product, with no deductible.
Every 3 months: up to 300 strips if using insulin, 100 if not.
PAAD covers insulin and insulin supplies, but not test strips.
Medical nutrition therapy with a dietitian is free with a doctor's referral.
body:
Medicare Part B covers most of the equipment a person with diabetes uses at home: blood sugar meters, test strips, lancets, continuous glucose monitors (CGMs) when your parent qualifies, and traditional insulin pumps. Your mom or dad pays 20% of the Medicare-approved amount after the Part B deductible, which is $283 in 2026. Insulin costs no more than $35 for each month's supply of each covered product, whether it comes through Part B or a Part D drug plan.

The details are what trip families up. Syringes and pen needles fall under Part D, not Part B. Strips need a new prescription every year. And in New Jersey, PAAD helps with insulin and insulin supplies but not with test strips. This guide sorts out who pays for what, which free services your parent may be skipping, and how to avoid supply scams.

What diabetes supplies does Medicare Part B cover?

Part B treats meters, strips, lancets, CGMs and durable insulin pumps as durable medical equipment. Your parent needs a doctor's prescription and a supplier enrolled in Medicare.

ItemWho covers itYour parent pays
Meter, strips, lancetsPart B20% after deductible
CGM and sensorsPart B, if eligible20% after deductible
Durable insulin pumpPart B20% after deductible
Insulin in a Part B pumpPart BUp to $35 a month
Insulin in pens, vials, patch pumpsPart DUp to $35 a month
Syringes, pen needlesPart DPlan copay
Therapeutic shoesPart B, if eligible20% after deductible

How many test strips?

Medicare's July 2026 diabetes booklet says that every three months your parent may be able to get up to 300 test strips and 300 lancets if they use insulin, or 100 of each if they do not. More is possible when the doctor documents a medical need, and your parent may have to keep a log showing how often they actually test.

Who qualifies for a CGM?

Medicare may cover a CGM and its sensors when your parent has diabetes, takes insulin or has a history of problems with low blood sugar (hypoglycemia), and has had enough training, alone or with a caregiver, to use it. The doctor must evaluate your parent first. Once on a CGM, your parent needs routine in-person or Medicare-approved telehealth visits with the doctor.

What the prescription should say

Medicare lists what belongs on it: that your parent has diabetes, which meter and why (including any special meter for vision problems), whether they use insulin, how often to test, and how many strips and lancets they need a month. Your parent needs a new prescription for strips and lancets every 12 months, and must ask for each refill. Medicare will not pay for supplies that arrive without being requested.

Strips and lancets need a new prescription every 12 months, and every refill has to be requested.

How much does insulin cost on Medicare?

No more than $35 for a one-month supply of each covered insulin, with no deductible. A three-month supply generally costs no more than $105.

The cap applies under both Part B (insulin used in a traditional pump) and Part D (pens, vials, inhaled insulin and insulin used in patch pumps). Under Part D, it applies to everyone who takes insulin, including people who get Extra Help, who may pay less. If your parent has a Medigap policy that pays the Part B coinsurance, it should cover the Part B insulin cost.

Two catches. Part B does not cover syringes, needles, alcohol swabs or gauze, so those come through a Part D plan. And a patch pump covered by Part D may cost more than $35, since the cap is on the insulin, not the device. In 2026, once your parent's out-of-pocket Part D drug costs reach $2,100, they pay nothing more for covered drugs for the rest of the year. For next year's numbers and how to compare plans, see our guide to Part D plans for 2027. Open enrollment ends December 7.

How do PAAD and Senior Gold help with diabetes costs?

New Jersey's PAAD program covers insulin and insulin supplies at $5 for a generic and $7 for a brand name drug. It does not cover test strips or lancets, which the pharmacy bills to Part B instead.

For 2026, PAAD is open to New Jersey residents 65 or older, or 18 to 64 on Social Security disability, with income under $54,943 if single or $62,390 if married. PAAD works on top of a Part D plan, and it can pay the premium for some plans. Senior Gold helps people just above those limits, at $15 plus half of the remaining cost of each prescription. One application, NJSave, screens your parent for both, plus Extra Help and the Medicare Savings Programs. Our guides to PAAD and Senior Gold walk through the rules, and the state's line is 1-800-792-9745.

The Medicare Savings Programs can also pay the Part B premium and, at the lowest income level, the Part B deductible and 20% coinsurance on strips and CGM supplies. See Medicare Savings Programs in NJ.

Free help comparing plans

SHIP Medicare counselors in New Jersey can check which Part D plans cover your parent's diabetes drugs and how PAAD fits in. Call 1-800-792-8820. They do not sell insurance. For PAAD and Senior Gold, call 1-800-792-9745.

What diabetes services does Medicare cover that people skip?

Several, and some cost nothing. Training, nutrition counseling, eye and foot exams and special shoes are all in Part B.

  • Diabetes self-management training. Up to 10 hours in the first year (1 hour one-on-one and 9 hours in a group), then up to 2 hours of follow-up each year after. It needs a written order. A doctor can order all individual sessions for someone with low vision, hearing loss, a language barrier or cognitive limitations, or when no group class is available within 2 months. Your parent pays 20% after the deductible, but Medicare says there is no Part B deductible for this training at a Federally Qualified Health Center.
  • Medical nutrition therapy. Three hours with a registered dietitian in the first year and up to 2 hours a year after, with a doctor's referral. Your parent pays nothing.
  • Hemoglobin A1C tests. Covered when the doctor orders them, with nothing to pay for the lab test.
  • Eye exams for diabetic retinopathy. Once a year from an eye doctor, at 20% after the deductible. Glaucoma screening is also covered once every 12 months for people with diabetes. Routine exams for glasses are not. Our eye exams and glasses guide covers the rest.
  • Foot exams. Every six months for people with diabetic nerve damage and loss of protective feeling in the feet, at 20% after the deductible.
  • Therapeutic shoes. For severe diabetic foot disease, one pair of extra-depth shoes with three pairs of inserts each calendar year, or one pair of custom-molded shoes with two more pairs of inserts. The doctor treating the diabetes must certify the need, and a podiatrist or other qualified doctor must order them.
  • Vaccines. Part B covers flu, COVID-19, hepatitis B and pneumococcal shots. Part D covers other recommended adult vaccines, such as shingles and RSV, at no cost.

If your parent has prediabetes

The Medicare Diabetes Prevention Program is free for people who qualify. It runs 16 weekly sessions over six months, then six monthly follow-ups, with a trained coach. Your parent qualifies with an A1C of 5.7% to 6.4% (or certain other blood sugar results) within 12 months before the first session, a body mass index of 25 or more (23 or more for people who are Asian), and no prior diabetes or end-stage kidney disease diagnosis. Through December 31, 2029, sessions can be in person, live online or self-paced. Medicare.gov has a search tool to find programs near you.

Where should your parent get supplies, and how do you avoid scams?

From a pharmacy or supplier that participates in Medicare and accepts assignment. Otherwise your parent may pay the full charge up front.

A supplier that accepts assignment can charge only the deductible and 20% coinsurance, and must file the claim with Medicare. Before an order, ask two questions: "Do you participate in Medicare?" and "Do you accept assignment?" You can search for suppliers on Medicare.gov or call 1-800-MEDICARE (1-800-633-4227). If your parent lives in certain areas, Medicare may require a specific supplier for a durable insulin pump.

Diabetes supplies are a common target for fraud. Medicare will not pay for supplies your parent did not ask for, including meters, strips and lancets mailed automatically. Hang up on callers offering "free" meters or braces in exchange for a Medicare number. Check each Medicare Summary Notice for items your parent never got. New Jersey's Senior Medicare Patrol can help at 1-732-777-1940, ext. 1117. Our guides to Medicare scams and scams in New Jersey explain how to report it.

How can you help a parent with diabetes from day to day?

Keep supplies stocked, keep appointments on the calendar and keep the doctor in the loop about lows.

  1. Make a supply list. Meter model, strip brand, lancets, CGM sensors, insulin, pen needles, with the pharmacy or supplier for each and the date the prescription runs out.
  2. Set refill reminders. Strips and sensors do not refill on their own under Medicare's rules.
  3. Book the yearly eye exam and twice-yearly foot checks if your parent qualifies.
  4. Ask for a dietitian referral. Medical nutrition therapy is free with a referral. Our guide to eating well after 70 covers appetite and meal help.
  5. Plan for lows. Keep fast sugar by the bed and in the car. Tell the doctor about any low that needed help, since a history of lows can make your parent eligible for a CGM.
  6. Review drug coverage each fall. Compare plans with SHIP before December 7.

This is general information about Medicare and New Jersey programs, not medical or legal advice. Your parent's doctor and plan have the final word on what is needed and covered.

faq.q: How do I get my dad's diabetes test strips covered by Medicare?
faq.a: His doctor writes a prescription that says he has diabetes, whether he uses insulin, how often to test and how many strips and lancets he needs a month. Fill it at a pharmacy or supplier that participates in Medicare and accepts assignment. He needs a new prescription every 12 months and must request each refill.

faq.q: Does Medicare cover a continuous glucose monitor?
faq.a: Yes, under Part B, if your parent has diabetes, takes insulin or has a history of problems with low blood sugar, and has been trained to use it. The doctor must evaluate your parent first. Your parent pays 20% of the Medicare-approved amount after the deductible.

faq.q: How much does insulin cost with Medicare in 2026?
faq.a: No more than $35 for a one-month supply of each covered insulin, with no deductible, whether it comes through Part D or is used in a pump covered by Part B. A three-month supply generally costs no more than $105.

faq.q: Does PAAD pay for diabetic test strips?
faq.a: No. PAAD covers prescription drugs, insulin and insulin supplies, but not testing supplies such as strips and lancets. If your parent has Medicare Part B, the pharmacy bills Part B for those.

faq.q: How can I get my mom free diabetes classes or a dietitian?
faq.a: Ask her doctor for a referral to medical nutrition therapy, which Medicare covers at no cost for people with diabetes or kidney disease, and a written order for diabetes self-management training. Many Federally Qualified Health Centers offer both.

faq.q: Someone called offering my mother a free glucose meter. Is it real?
faq.a: Treat it as a likely scam. Medicare will not pay for supplies your parent did not request. Do not give out her Medicare number. Report the call to 1-800-MEDICARE or New Jersey's Senior Medicare Patrol at 1-732-777-1940, ext. 1117.

title: Eating well after 70: nutrition help in New Jersey
dek: What older adults need more of, why appetite fades, when Medicare pays for a dietitian, and the meals and food benefits New Jersey offers adults 60 and older.
keyFacts: After 70, aim for at least 800 IU of vitamin D and 1,200 mg of calcium a day (NIA).
Medicare covers free dietitian visits for diabetes or kidney disease, with a referral.
Senior farmers market benefits: age 60+, income up to $29,526 for one person.
Food packages (CSFP): age 60+, income up to $23,940 for one person in 2026.
County meal programs: call the ADRC at 1-877-222-3737.
body:
After 70, many people need fewer calories but just as many nutrients, and some need more of a few, such as vitamin D and calcium. Appetite often shrinks, taste and smell fade, and chewing or shopping gets harder. The result can be a quiet slide toward eating too little, especially for someone who lives alone.

New Jersey has real help. Medicare pays for free sessions with a registered dietitian for people with diabetes or kidney disease. County offices on aging run group meals and home-delivered meals. Income-eligible adults 60 and older can get farmers market benefits and a USDA food package, on top of SNAP. This guide covers what your mom or dad needs to eat, the warning signs to watch for, and where to get help.

What do older adults need more of?

Protein, fluids, and a few vitamins and minerals stand out. The National Institute on Aging (NIA) suggests getting protein through the day to help keep muscle, and drinking water throughout the day.

NutrientDaily target after 70
Vitamin DAt least 800 IU (20 mcg)
Calcium1,200 mg
Vitamin B122.4 mcg
SodiumNo more than 2,300 mg

Those targets come from the NIA's guide to vitamins and minerals for older adults. A few notes on each:

  • Protein. The NIA suggests adding seafood, dairy or fortified soy, plus beans, peas and lentils, to meals. Eggs, nut butters, yogurt and cottage cheese are easy for small appetites.
  • Vitamin D and calcium. Both protect bones. Food sources include fortified milk, yogurt, canned salmon or sardines with bones, and leafy greens. The NIA says not to go above 4,000 IU of vitamin D or 2,000 mg of calcium a day.
  • Vitamin B12. Some people over 50 have trouble absorbing the B12 in food. The NIA suggests fortified cereals or asking the doctor about a supplement.
  • Sodium. Most of it comes from processed and restaurant food, not the salt shaker. Herbs, lemon and vinegar add flavor without salt.

The NIA says most older adults can get what they need from food, and that supplements can interact with medicines. Vitamin K, for example, can weaken the blood thinner warfarin. Have your parent check with the doctor or pharmacist before adding any supplement.

How much should your parent drink?

Enough, steadily, through the day. Older adults often feel less thirsty even when they need fluids, so waiting for thirst does not work well.

A 2023 review of research on hydration in older adults, available through the National Library of Medicine, found that thirst often fades with age and the kidneys hold onto water less well. It describes a 2022 European geriatric nutrition guideline that suggests at least 1.6 liters a day from drinks for women and 2 liters for men, roughly 7 and 8.5 cups. That is a starting point only. People with heart failure or kidney disease may be told to limit fluids, so follow the doctor's advice.

  • Keep a full water bottle or pitcher in sight, and refill it at set times.
  • Count soup, milk, tea, coffee and watery fruits like melon.
  • Offer a drink with every medicine and every meal.
  • Watch hot days closely. Our guide to cooling centers lists where to go in a heat wave.

If your parent drinks less because of bladder leaks, that is worth a doctor's visit. See our guide to incontinence help.

Why do older adults stop eating well?

Usually for a reason that can be fixed: dentures, medicines, mood, loneliness or trouble shopping and cooking. Unplanned weight loss is the sign to act on.

The NIA lists the common roadblocks and what helps:

  • Feeling full fast. Smaller meals more often, with nutrient-dense snacks such as nuts, cheese and dried fruit.
  • Food tastes bland. Taste and smell change with age, dental problems and medicine. Herbs, spices and lemon help.
  • Medicines. Some dull appetite or dry the mouth. Ask the doctor or pharmacist whether another drug would work.
  • Chewing or swallowing trouble. See the dentist about tooth pain or loose dentures. Tell the doctor if food feels stuck. Medicare Part B covers medically necessary speech-language therapy, which treats swallowing problems. Our dental care guide covers low-cost options.
  • Arthritis, stroke or Parkinson's. An occupational therapist can suggest easier utensils or a kitchen setup. See adaptive equipment.
  • Eating alone, or feeling down. The NIA says sadness can cause loss of appetite. If low mood lasts more than a few weeks, talk with the doctor. Our guide to depression and loneliness lists help in New Jersey.
Unplanned weight loss is the sign to act on.

The NIA warns that sudden, unintended weight loss can be a sign of a serious medical problem, and that being underweight raises the risk of osteoporosis and makes it harder to recover from illness. If your parent's clothes are loose or the scale has dropped without trying, book a visit. Medicare's yearly Wellness visit includes a weight check and a written prevention plan at no cost when the provider accepts assignment.

Does Medicare pay for a dietitian?

Yes, for people with diabetes or kidney disease, or who had a kidney transplant in the last 36 months. Medical nutrition therapy is free with a doctor's referral.

Medicare Part B covers 3 hours with a registered dietitian (or another qualified nutrition professional) in the first calendar year, and up to 2 hours of follow-up each year after. Hours do not carry over. If a change in your parent's health calls for a new diet, the doctor can refer for more. The sessions include an assessment, counseling on what to eat and follow-up visits. Many Federally Qualified Health Centers offer this service.

For people with diabetes, Medicare also covers diabetes self-management training, which includes nutrition. See our guide to diabetes supplies and Medicare. Original Medicare does not cover a dietitian for weight or general healthy eating without one of those conditions, though some Medicare Advantage plans add nutrition benefits. Call the plan to ask.

Where can your parent get meals in New Jersey?

Through the county office on aging, which runs group meals at senior centers and other sites, and home-delivered meals for people who are homebound.

  • Group (congregate) meals. Hot meals for adults 60 and older and their spouses at senior centers, churches and community sites. There is no set price. Federal rules bar charging a fee for meals funded by the Older Americans Act, and sites may ask for a voluntary contribution. The company matters as much as the food for someone who eats alone.
  • Home-delivered meals. For adults 60 and older who are homebound because of illness, disability or isolation, after a needs assessment. Our Meals on Wheels guide has the phone number for every county.

Call the Aging and Disability Resource Connection at 1-877-222-3737 to reach your parent's county office. Ask about medically tailored or diabetic meals, weekend meals and waiting lists. Our first visit to a senior center guide can ease a reluctant parent into group meals.

What food benefits can older adults get?

SNAP, the Senior Farmers Market Nutrition Program and the Commodity Supplemental Food Program all serve income-eligible older adults in New Jersey. Your parent may qualify for more than one.

ProgramAgeIncome, 1 person
Farmers market (SFMNP)60+Up to $29,526 a year
Food package (CSFP)60+Up to $23,940 a year
SNAPAnyNet income test

Senior Farmers' Market Nutrition Program

Run by the NJ Department of Health through county agencies, usually the county office on aging, it gives adults 60 and older money for fresh, locally grown fruits, vegetables and herbs at approved farmers markets and farm stands. Gross income must be at or below 185% of the federal poverty guidelines: $29,526 a year for one person or $40,034 for two. Amounts can vary by county. Gloucester County, for example, gave eligible residents $40 in 2026 through a printed QR code, first come, first served, and its 2026 benefits are already fully given out. Call your county office in the spring to ask when 2027 sign-ups open.

Commodity Supplemental Food Program

This USDA program gives adults 60 and older a package of USDA foods through local food banks. In New Jersey, the Department of Health sets the 2026 income limit at 150% of the federal poverty guidelines: $23,940 a year for one person or $32,460 for two. Your parent may also qualify through other federal programs. Dial 2-1-1 or check the state's CSFP page to find the food bank that serves your county.

SNAP

Households with someone 60 or older skip SNAP's gross income test, and out-of-pocket medical costs above $35 a month can be deducted. Our SNAP guide for seniors explains the rules, and food and utility help covers food pantries and heating aid.

One call to start

Your county office on aging handles group meals, home-delivered meals and, in most counties, farmers market benefits. Reach it through the Aging and Disability Resource Connection at 1-877-222-3737, or dial 2-1-1 for food banks and pantries.

How can you help from a distance?

Look in the fridge, set up deliveries and make meals social. Small, regular checks catch problems early.

  1. Check the kitchen on your next visit. Expired food, an empty fridge or many uneaten meals are signals.
  2. Ask about weight at the next doctor's visit, and whether a dietitian referral makes sense.
  3. Stock easy protein. Yogurt, eggs, canned fish, beans, nut butter, cheese and shelf-stable milk.
  4. Put water in reach and pair drinks with daily routines.
  5. Apply for benefits. Call the county office about meals and next season's farmers market benefits, and check SNAP.
  6. Make meals social. A weekly lunch at a senior center, a standing video call at dinner, or a cooking class.

This is general information, not medical advice. Your parent's doctor or a registered dietitian can set targets that fit their health and medicines.

faq.q: My mom is losing weight and barely eating. What should I do?
faq.a: Book a doctor's visit. The National Institute on Aging warns that sudden, unintended weight loss can signal a serious medical problem. Bring her medicine list, since some drugs dull appetite, and ask about dental problems, mood and a dietitian referral. Meanwhile, offer small, frequent meals with protein.

faq.q: Does Medicare pay for a nutritionist?
faq.a: Medicare Part B pays for medical nutrition therapy with a registered dietitian at no cost for people with diabetes or kidney disease, or who had a kidney transplant in the last 36 months, with a doctor's referral. It covers 3 hours in the first year and up to 2 hours a year after. Some Medicare Advantage plans add more nutrition benefits.

faq.q: How do I get meals delivered to my dad in New Jersey?
faq.a: Call his county office on aging, which runs home-delivered meals for adults 60 and older who are homebound. Someone will do a needs assessment first. You can reach the county through the Aging and Disability Resource Connection at 1-877-222-3737. There is no set charge for meals funded under the federal Older Americans Act, though a voluntary contribution may be suggested.

faq.q: Who qualifies for senior farmers market vouchers in NJ?
faq.a: Adults 60 and older with gross income at or below 185% of the federal poverty guidelines, which is $29,526 a year for one person or $40,034 for two. Benefits come through county agencies, usually the office on aging, and in some counties they run out on a first come, first served basis.

faq.q: How much water should an older adult drink?
faq.a: There is no single number. A 2022 European geriatric nutrition guideline suggests at least 1.6 liters a day from drinks for women and 2 liters for men. People with heart failure or kidney disease may need less, so follow the doctor's advice. Drinking steadily through the day matters, since thirst often fades with age.

faq.q: Should my parent take vitamin supplements?
faq.a: Only after checking with the doctor or pharmacist. The National Institute on Aging says most older adults can get what they need from food, and some supplements interact with medicines.

title: Advance directives in New Jersey: forms, witnesses and storage
dek: New Jersey's free advance directive forms let your parent name a health care representative and spell out treatment wishes. Here is what each section asks, how to sign it, where to keep it and how to change it.
keyFacts: New Jersey has two advance directives: a proxy directive (health care representative) and an instruction directive (living will).
Sign before two adult witnesses, or a notary, attorney or other person allowed to give oaths. No lawyer is needed.
The named representative or alternate cannot be a witness, and you can name only one primary representative.
The Department of Health does not list a state registry. The directive takes effect once it reaches the doctor or facility and your parent lacks capacity.
Medicare Part B covers advance care planning at the yearly Wellness visit at no cost if the doctor accepts assignment.
body:
New Jersey's advance directive form comes in two parts. The proxy directive names a health care representative to make medical decisions if your mom or dad cannot. The instruction directive, often called a living will, says what treatment they would or would not want. The state publishes free blank versions of both, written by the New Jersey Commission on Legal and Ethical Problems in the Delivery of Health Care. You can use one, the other, or both.

No lawyer and no notary are required. The form must be signed and dated in front of two adult witnesses, or before a notary, attorney or other person allowed to give oaths. New Jersey has no state registry to file it with, so the copies you hand out are what doctors will actually see.

General information, not legal or medical advice

The forms are straightforward, but the choices are personal. Talk them over with your parent's doctor. An elder law attorney can review them alongside a will and power of attorney.

What advance directive forms does New Jersey use?

The New Jersey Department of Health posts two forms: a two-page proxy directive and a five-page instruction directive. Both are free to download and print from the Department of Health's advance directive page.

You do not have to use these exact forms. The state's Long Term Care Ombudsman says an advance directive can be as simple as a letter stating your wishes or naming the person you trust, as long as it is written, signed and properly witnessed. Hospitals and health plans often hand out their own versions too.

Either document takes effect only after the doctor in charge of your parent's care decides they cannot understand their diagnosis, their treatment options or the likely benefits and harms. If your parent recovers that ability, the doctor must go back to asking your parent.

The Department of Health also says no insurer, doctor, hospital or nursing home can require you to have one. Having one does not affect life insurance, health insurance or government benefits. And New Jersey recognizes an advance directive that is valid in another state.

What does the proxy directive ask your parent to decide?

Who speaks for them, who backs that person up, and whether that person may stop a feeding tube or IV nutrition. Everything else is optional.

  • One health care representative. The state's FAQ says you cannot name two people as co-primary. Pick one.
  • Alternates in order. You can name one or more alternates who step in if the first choice is unable, unwilling or unavailable. If the first choice becomes available again, they take back over.
  • Feeding tubes. Section C asks your parent to initial one line. Either the representative may direct that artificially provided fluids and nutrition be withheld or withdrawn, or the representative does not have that power.
  • Extra instructions. Your parent can require the representative to consult certain family members, or limit what the representative may decide.

There are limits on who can serve. Your parent's attending physician cannot be the representative. Neither can the operator, administrator or an employee of a hospital or nursing home where your parent is a patient or resident, unless they are related.

The representative can see medical records and talk with doctors. They cannot be made to pay for the care they approve. A spouse, adult child, friend or neighbor can all serve. What matters is that the person will follow your parent's wishes even when they personally disagree.

Have the conversation before the signing. The signature section of the state form says your parent has discussed the terms with the representative and that the person has willingly agreed to take on the job. Ask your parent to talk through a few real situations, such as a stroke, a long ICU stay or advanced dementia. Write down anything that does not fit the checkboxes in the space for additional instructions.

Choose the person who will say what Mom wants, even when it is hard to hear.

What does the New Jersey instruction directive cover?

It lets your parent describe when they would want life-sustaining treatment stopped or never started. It also covers CPR, feeding tubes, brain death and organ donation.

Part One starts with a choice. Your parent initials either "all medically appropriate measures" to sustain life, or a statement that there are circumstances when they would not want life prolonged. If they pick the second, they initial the situations that apply:

  • A terminal condition, confirmed by the attending doctor and at least one other doctor. Your parent writes in what terminal means to them, such as a few days, a few weeks, or a life expectancy of six months or a year.
  • Permanent unconsciousness, confirmed by two doctors.
  • A serious, irreversible illness that may not be terminal, when the burdens of treatment become greater than the benefits. There is space to describe which losses of ability your parent would find unacceptable.

Section C asks specifically about artificially provided fluids and nutrition, and about CPR, in the situations your parent initialed. Section D is open space for anything else, such as a wish to be cared for at home or in a certain hospital. A woman can add instructions about what should happen if she is pregnant.

Two sections people often miss:

  • Brain death (Section E). New Jersey uses whole brain death as a legal standard for declaring death. A person whose religious beliefs reject that standard can initial a statement asking that death be declared only when heartbeat and breathing stop.
  • Anatomical gifts (Section F). Your parent can choose to donate any needed organs, only certain ones, or the whole body for study, or say they do not wish to donate. Our guide to body and organ donation in New Jersey explains how to register and what families do at the time of death.

State law also allows an advance directive to be supplemented by a video or audio recording, which some families find useful for explaining values in a parent's own voice.

How do you sign an advance directive in New Jersey so it counts?

Sign and date it in front of two adult witnesses who also sign, or acknowledge it before a notary public, an attorney or another person authorized to give oaths. The health care representative and any alternate cannot be witnesses.

Our guide to planning when you are aging alone walks through signing in more detail. One practical tip: bring two neighbors or friends who are not named anywhere in the document, so no one has to be swapped out at the last minute.

Where should you keep an advance directive in New Jersey?

With the people who will need it. Under N.J.S.A. 26:2H-59, an advance directive becomes operative when it is given to the attending physician or the health care facility and your parent is found to lack capacity. A copy no one has seen does not help.

The Department of Health's advance directive pages do not mention any state registry for these documents. That makes handing out copies your job.

  1. Make several copies. Keep the signed original somewhere easy to reach at home, not in a safe deposit box.
  2. Give copies out. The state suggests the representative, the alternates, family members and every doctor. Section D of the proxy form and Section G of the instruction form have lines to record who got one.
  3. Bring it to every admission. The state says to hand over a copy when your parent is admitted to a hospital or nursing home. Ask that it be scanned into the chart.
  4. Put it on the fridge list. Our printable emergency info sheet has a line for where the advance directive is kept.
  5. Keep a photo on your phone. If you are the representative, a picture of the signed pages can save time in an emergency room.
  6. Add it to the papers file. Our important papers checklist keeps it with the will and power of attorney.

Medicare Part B covers a conversation about advance care planning as part of the Welcome to Medicare visit and the yearly Wellness visit. Your parent pays nothing for it there if the doctor accepts assignment. That is a natural time to bring the forms and ask questions.

How do you change or cancel it?

To change it, fill out and sign a new one with the same witnessing rules, then replace every old copy. To cancel it, your parent can tell a doctor, nurse, social worker, family member, the representative or another reliable witness, out loud or in a letter.

Good times to review it are after a new diagnosis, a death or divorce, a move, or when the named representative's own health or situation changes. Write the review date on the copy, and collect the old versions so two different forms are not floating around.

Does my parent also need a POLST?

Only if they are seriously ill or frail. An advance directive speaks for your parent later. A POLST is a doctor's order that emergency crews follow right away, and it works alongside the advance directive.

The advance directive covers medical decisions only. Money and property need a separate durable power of attorney. Our estate planning guide shows how the pieces fit together.

faq.q: Where do I get a New Jersey advance directive form for my mom?
faq.a: The New Jersey Department of Health posts free proxy directive and instruction directive forms on its advance directive page. Print them, fill them in with your mom, and have her sign before two adult witnesses or a notary. Many hospitals also hand out forms.

faq.q: Does an advance directive have to be notarized in New Jersey?
faq.a: No. It can be signed and dated in front of two adult witnesses who also sign. A notary, attorney or other person allowed to give oaths can be used instead of witnesses. The health care representative cannot be a witness.

faq.q: Is there a registry for advance directives in New Jersey?
faq.a: The Department of Health's advance directive pages do not mention one, so plan on sharing copies yourself. Give copies to the health care representative, alternates, family and doctors, and bring a copy to every hospital or nursing home admission.

faq.q: Can my brother and I both be Dad's health care representative?
faq.a: Not as co-primaries. The state's FAQ says you can name only one primary representative. Your dad can name one of you first and the other as an alternate, and he can require the representative to consult the other before deciding.

faq.q: Is an advance directive from Florida valid in New Jersey?
faq.a: The New Jersey Department of Health says New Jersey recognizes an advance directive that is valid in another state. If your parent now lives mostly in New Jersey, it can still be worth signing a New Jersey form so local doctors know it well.

faq.q: How do I cancel or change my parent's advance directive?
faq.a: To cancel it, your parent tells a doctor, nurse, social worker, family member, the representative or another reliable witness, out loud or in writing. To change it, your parent signs a new one with the same witnessing rules. Collect and replace the old copies.

sources: NJ Department of Health: Advance Directive Forms and FAQs
