title: Snowbirds: Medicare and NJ benefits if you winter in Florida
dek: Original Medicare follows you south. Most Advantage networks, PAAD and New Jersey's property tax programs have rules that do not. Here is what to check before your parent leaves for the winter.
keyFacts: Original Medicare works with any provider that takes Medicare in all 50 states
Advantage plans must drop members away over 6 months unless they offer a visitor or traveler benefit
PAAD does not cover drugs bought outside New Jersey
ANCHOR and Senior Freeze never pay on a vacation or second home
Free NJ SHIP Medicare counseling: 1-800-792-8820
body:
If your mom or dad spends winters in Florida, Medicare for snowbirds comes down to one question: which kind of Medicare do they have? Original Medicare works with any doctor or hospital that takes Medicare, anywhere in the United States. A Medicare Advantage plan usually covers only emergencies and urgent care outside its service area, and federal rules say the plan must drop a member who is away more than 6 months unless it offers a special visitor or traveler benefit.

New Jersey's own programs have rules too. PAAD does not pay for drugs bought outside New Jersey. Senior Freeze and ANCHOR pay only on your main home, never a vacation or second home. This guide covers what to check before the car is packed, and what to do while your parent is away. It is general information, not legal or tax advice.

Does Medicare work in Florida if I live in New Jersey?

Original Medicare does. Medicare Advantage often does not, except for emergencies and urgent care.

Medicare.gov says that with Original Medicare (Part A and Part B) you can use "any doctor or hospital that takes Medicare, anywhere in the U.S." A Medigap supplement policy follows the same rules, so a parent with Original Medicare and Medigap can see a doctor in Naples or Boca Raton the same way they would in Morristown. You may pay more if the doctor does not accept assignment, so ask before the visit.

Medicare Advantage plans work differently. With an HMO, Medicare.gov says you generally must use the plan's network, except for emergency care, out-of-area urgent care and temporary out-of-area dialysis. Care outside the network may cost the full price. PPO plans pay something for out-of-network care, at a higher cost, and you are always covered for emergency and urgent care. Our guide to choosing between Advantage and Medigap covers the bigger trade-off.

CoverageRoutine care in Florida
Original MedicareYes, any provider that takes Medicare
MedigapFollows Original Medicare
Advantage HMOEmergency and urgent care only, as a rule
Advantage PPOOut of network, at a higher cost
Part D drug planDepends on the plan's pharmacy network

Telehealth can help too. Medicare.gov says that through December 31, 2027, Medicare covers telehealth services you get from anywhere in the U.S., including your home. Ask the New Jersey doctor's office whether it can see your parent by video while they are out of state.

Original Medicare travels. Most Advantage networks stay home.

Will my Medicare Advantage plan drop me if I spend the winter away?

It can, if your parent is gone more than 6 months in a row. Federal rules require the plan to disenroll a member who leaves the service area for more than 6 months, unless the plan offers a visitor or traveler benefit.

The rule is in federal regulations at 42 CFR 422.74. Some plans offer a visitor or traveler option for members who are away longer than 6 months but less than 12. A plan may limit that option to certain areas. People who use it are disenrolled on the first day of the 13th month after they left. If your parent's plan has no such benefit, a long winter can end their coverage.

Two smaller details catch people off guard:

  • Returned mail counts. The same rule says a member can be treated as temporarily absent when required plan mail comes back to the plan as undeliverable with no forwarding address. Keep mail flowing.
  • A permanent move is different. Moving to Florida for good opens a short Special Enrollment Period to pick a new plan. Our guide to leaving New Jersey in retirement explains that window and the rest of a full move.

Call the plan's member services line before your parent leaves and ask:

  • Does my plan have a visitor or traveler benefit? Does it cover Florida, and which county?
  • Which doctors or urgent care centers near my winter address count as in network?
  • Do I need prior approval for anything I get while I am away?
  • How many months can I be gone before you disenroll me?

Write down the name of the person you spoke with and the date. Ask for anything important in writing.

How do I fill prescriptions while I'm away?

Use a pharmacy in your drug plan's network, plan refills before you go, and do not count on PAAD out of state.

Medicare drug plans and Advantage plans with drug coverage use pharmacy networks. Network pharmacies usually cost less. Federal rules (42 CFR 423.124) require plans to allow out-of-network fills when you cannot reasonably use a network pharmacy and you do not do it routinely. A plan can charge you the difference in price, and it sets limits. So a lost bottle on vacation may be covered. Filling every month at an out-of-network pharmacy is not.

Stand-alone drug plans have their own absence rule. Under 42 CFR 423.44, a drug plan must disenroll someone who has been out of its service area for more than 12 months in a row. A typical Florida winter is well short of that, but returned mail can again be treated as a sign you are away.

PAAD does not travel

The New Jersey Division of Aging Services says plainly that drugs purchased outside the State of New Jersey are not covered by PAAD. If your parent has Senior Gold instead, call the hotline at 1-800-792-9745 before the trip and ask how out-of-state fills are handled. Your parent's Part D plan may still pay its share at a Florida network pharmacy, but the state help that brings a brand drug down to $7 will not apply to that fill.

Say your mom lives in Toms River, has PAAD, and spends January through March near Sarasota. Before she leaves, she can ask her doctor for prescriptions that cover the trip, ask her plan whether it allows an early refill before travel, and ask about mail order. She should fill in New Jersey whenever she can. When PAAD is the main payer, the state limits a first prescription to a 34-day supply, and refills to a 34-day supply or 100 unit doses, whichever is greater. Read our PAAD guide and Senior Gold guide for more on both programs.

Can I keep PAAD, Senior Freeze and Stay NJ if I winter in Florida?

Usually yes, as long as New Jersey stays your parent's true home. These programs are for New Jersey residents and their main home, and they do not cover a second home.

  • PAAD and Senior Gold. You must be a New Jersey resident. See our PAAD guide for income limits.
  • ANCHOR. The New Jersey Division of Taxation says the address you claim must have been your main home on October 1 of the benefit year. A vacation or second home does not qualify.
  • Senior Freeze. You must have owned and lived in your New Jersey home since the base date the state sets, and the program does not pay on a vacation or second home.
  • Stay NJ. For the 2025 benefit, the state says you must have owned and lived in a home for the full 12 months of 2025. If your parent was away for months, call the Property Tax Relief hotline at 1-888-238-1233 and ask how the state treats that time.

Watch for a conflict with Florida. The Florida Department of Revenue says its homestead exemption is for a home that is your permanent residence, and the application asks whether you lived there on January 1 and whether you claim residency in another state. Claiming Florida as your permanent residence while also telling New Jersey that your house here is your main home sends two different messages. That is a question for a tax professional before anyone files.

State income tax follows the same idea. New Jersey's Division of Taxation says that if New Jersey is not your domicile, you are a resident only if you keep a permanent home here and spend more than 183 days here. Changing domicile is a bigger step than wintering away. Our guides to leaving New Jersey and how New Jersey taxes retirement income explain it.

What about NJ FamilyCare and other state health help?

NJ FamilyCare (Medicaid) pays for out-of-state care only in limited situations, such as emergencies. Call before the trip.

Federal rules (42 CFR 431.52) require a state Medicaid program to pay for care in another state for its residents in a few cases. These include a medical emergency, when the person's health would be put at risk by traveling home, and when the state decides on medical advice that the care is more available in the other state. Routine visits are another matter. Most NJ FamilyCare members are in a managed care plan with its own network, so call the plan and NJ FamilyCare at 1-800-701-0710 before your parent leaves and ask what is covered in Florida.

If your parent gets home care through MLTSS or another New Jersey program, the services are arranged around their New Jersey home. Talk with the care manager well before any long trip. Our guide to NJ FamilyCare for seniors covers who qualifies.

How do I keep mail, renewals and records from slipping?

Make sure every renewal and plan notice reaches your parent within days, and keep copies of key papers in both homes.

Many New Jersey benefits arrive by mail. The PAAD renewal form, for example, comes about four months before the card expires, and the state says to call 1-800-792-9745 if it has not arrived at least two months before. A missed renewal can end coverage just as a missed bill can.

  1. Set up mail forwarding. Arrange temporary forwarding with the Postal Service, or have a trusted neighbor or family member open and send on anything official.
  2. Call each plan. Tell the Advantage or drug plan the dates and the winter address, and ask the questions above.
  3. Refill and stock up. Fill prescriptions in New Jersey before leaving, and ask about early refills and mail order.
  4. Find care near the winter home. Note an in-network urgent care center and the nearest hospital. With Original Medicare, confirm the doctor takes Medicare.
  5. Pack the paperwork. Bring the Medicare card, plan cards, PAAD card, a medication list and our free emergency info sheet.
  6. Mark the calendar. Medicare Open Enrollment runs October 15 to December 7, which is when many snowbirds are packing. Review the plan before you go.

Leaving the country? Medicare generally does not cover care outside the U.S. Medicare.gov says Part B may pay for some care on a cruise ship that is in a U.S. port or no more than 6 hours away from one, and that drug plans do not cover drugs bought outside the U.S. Some Medigap policies cover emergency care abroad. Check the policy before the trip.

Free help before the trip

New Jersey's State Health Insurance Assistance Program (SHIP) gives free, unbiased Medicare counseling. Call 1-800-792-8820. While in Florida, that state's SHINE program answers Medicare questions at 1-800-963-5337. You can also call Medicare at 1-800-633-4227.

If you help from a distance, our guide to long-distance caregiving has more ideas for keeping track of a parent's paperwork. Comparing drug plans for next year? See Part D plans in New Jersey for 2027.

faq.q: Can I use Medicare in Florida if I live in New Jersey?
faq.a: Yes, with Original Medicare. Medicare.gov says you can use any doctor or hospital that takes Medicare anywhere in the U.S. Medicare Advantage plans generally cover only emergency and urgent care outside their service area, unless the plan has out-of-network or traveler benefits.

faq.q: How long can I be away before my Medicare Advantage plan drops me?
faq.a: Federal rules say an Advantage plan must disenroll a member who is out of the service area for more than 6 months, unless the plan offers a visitor or traveler benefit. That option can allow up to 12 months. Call your plan to ask what it offers.

faq.q: Will PAAD pay for my prescriptions in Florida?
faq.a: No. The NJ Division of Aging Services says drugs purchased outside New Jersey are not covered by PAAD. Fill prescriptions in New Jersey before you leave, and ask your Part D plan about early refills and mail order.

faq.q: How do I make sure my mom keeps her Medicare plan while she winters in Florida?
faq.a: Call her plan with her winter dates and address. Ask whether it has a visitor or traveler benefit, which providers near her are covered, and how long she can be gone. Set up mail forwarding so plan notices are never returned as undeliverable.

faq.q: Can my dad keep Senior Freeze and ANCHOR if he spends winters away?
faq.a: These programs pay only on a New Jersey main home, not a vacation or second home. If New Jersey stays his true home, he can usually keep applying. Call the Property Tax Relief hotline at 1-888-238-1233 with questions about time spent away.

faq.q: Who can help me compare Medicare options before a winter move?
faq.a: New Jersey SHIP counselors give free, unbiased help at 1-800-792-8820. In Florida, the SHINE program answers Medicare questions at 1-800-963-5337.

title: Medicare if you are still working past 65 in New Jersey
dek: Working past 65 can mean waiting on Part B with no penalty, or it can mean a costly gap. Here is how employer size, HSAs, COBRA and the 8-month window work, and how to sign up when you retire.
keyFacts: Job plan with 20+ employees usually pays first, so Part B can wait
Under 20 employees, Medicare usually pays first
8-month Part B window starts when the job or coverage ends; COBRA does not extend it
Stop HSA contributions 6 months before applying for Medicare or Social Security
Retiring? File CMS-40B and CMS-L564 with Social Security
body:
If you are still working past 65 and have health insurance from that job, you may not need Medicare Part B yet. The deciding factor is usually the size of the employer. When the job, or your spouse's job, has 20 or more employees, the group plan generally pays first and you can wait on Part B with no penalty. Under 20 employees, Medicare usually pays first, and skipping Part B can leave big bills unpaid.

This guide goes past the basics in our Medicare 101 guide for turning 65. It covers the Part A and health savings account trap, how the 8-month window really works, the forms Social Security wants when you retire, and the rules for New Jersey public employees. It is general information, not legal or tax advice.

Do I have to sign up for Medicare at 65 if I am still working?

Not always. If you have group coverage from your current job, or your spouse's current job, at an employer with 20 or more employees, you can usually delay Part B without a penalty.

Medicare.gov's "who pays first" rules set the order. With 20 or more employees (or a multi-employer plan where at least one company has 20 or more), the group plan pays first and Medicare pays second. With fewer than 20, Medicare pays first. Medicare.gov warns that in that case your job coverage might not pay if you do not have both Part A and Part B.

Your coveragePays firstPart B at 65?
Current job, 20+ workersJob planCan usually wait
Spouse's job, 20+ workersJob planCan usually wait
Current job, under 20MedicareUsually sign up
COBRA or retiree planMedicareSign up
Marketplace or individualNot job basedSign up

A few setups look like job coverage but are not. Medicare.gov says that if you are self-employed, or your plan is not available to everyone at the company, you should ask the insurer whether it counts as employer group health plan coverage as defined by the IRS. If it does not, sign up at 65. If your employer gives you a stipend to buy your own policy, Medicare pays first once you sign up. Ask your insurer before you skip anything.

Even at a large employer, ask HR one question in writing: "Does our plan require me to enroll in Medicare at 65?" Some plans have their own rules. Keep the answer.

Count the employees before you skip Part B. Twenty is the line.

Should I take Part A at 65 if I keep my job plan?

Often yes, because most people pay no premium for Part A. The big exception is anyone putting money into a health savings account (HSA).

Medicare.gov says that if you do not have to pay a Part A premium, you can sign up when you turn 65 or any time later. Part A can act as backup coverage for hospital stays. But Part A is hard to undo. Medicare.gov says you can generally drop Part A only if you pay a premium for it. And if you start Social Security retirement benefits, you are usually enrolled in Part A automatically.

The HSA rule

The IRS says that beginning with the first month you are enrolled in Medicare, your HSA contribution limit is zero. That includes retroactive coverage. When you sign up for premium-free Part A after 65, Medicare.gov says coverage starts 6 months back from when you sign up or apply for Social Security, but never before the month you turned 65.

So Medicare.gov tells workers with an HSA that they and their employer should stop contributing 6 months before they retire or apply for Social Security. Contributions made during a backdated Medicare month count as excess contributions, which can mean a tax penalty.

Say you live in Montclair, work for a large company with an HSA plan, and plan to retire at 67 at the end of June. You apply for Medicare in May, a month before the job plan ends. Part A can then reach back 6 months, to November, so your last HSA contribution should be for October. The money already in the account is still yours. The IRS says you can use it tax free for qualified expenses, and after 65 that includes Medicare premiums, though not Medigap premiums.

How does the 8-month Special Enrollment Period work?

It gives you 8 months to sign up for Part B with no penalty, starting when the job ends or the job coverage ends, whichever happens first. COBRA does not stretch it.

Medicare.gov is direct about COBRA. Your 8-month Special Enrollment Period starts when you stop working "even if you choose COBRA or other coverage that's not Medicare." Retiree coverage ending does not give you a new window either. If you miss the 8 months, you wait for the General Enrollment Period (January 1 to March 31) and may owe a lifelong Part B penalty of 10% for each full 12 months you could have had Part B. Our turning 65 guide shows what that penalty costs.

When does Part B start?

  • Coverage generally starts the month after you sign up.
  • If you sign up while you or your spouse are still working, or within the first full month after job coverage ends, Medicare.gov says you can ask to delay the start by up to 3 months.
  • To avoid a gap, Medicare.gov suggests signing up about a month before your job coverage ends.

Why the start date matters for Medigap

Your one-time Medigap Open Enrollment Period starts the first month you are both 65 and enrolled in Part B, and lasts 6 months. During it, insurers in New Jersey must sell you a policy whatever your health. Delaying Part B while you work also delays that window, which protects it. Starting Part B early and then keeping your job plan can waste it. Our Medigap guide explains the plans.

Drug coverage

Your job plan should send a yearly notice saying whether its drug coverage is "creditable," meaning as good as Medicare's. Keep every one. You avoid the Part D penalty as long as you do not go 63 days or more without creditable coverage. When job coverage ends, Medicare.gov says you have 2 full months after the month it ends to join a drug plan or Advantage plan. See Part D plans in New Jersey for 2027 when you are ready to compare.

How do I sign up for Part B when I retire?

Apply through Social Security with two forms: the CMS-40B application and the CMS-L564, where your employer confirms your coverage.

  1. Get your end date. Ask HR the exact date your group health coverage ends. For a spouse's plan, ask about their date.
  2. Get the employer form. Ask HR to complete Section B of the CMS-L564, Request for Employment Information.
  3. If the employer cannot help. A company that closed or a hard to reach HR office does not have to sink you. Social Security says to fill in Section B yourself as best you can, without the employer's signature, and send other proof, such as W-2s showing pre-tax medical contributions, pay stubs with health premium deductions, insurance cards with an effective date, or explanations of benefits from the plan.
  4. Apply. Use Social Security's online option for Part B during a Special Enrollment Period and upload your proof, or fax or mail the forms to your local office. On the application, give the month you want Part B to start.
  5. Pick the rest of your coverage. Once Part B is set, choose a Medigap policy and drug plan, or a Medicare Advantage plan. Our guide to Advantage or Medigap walks through the choice.
  6. Keep copies. Save the forms, the HR letter and your creditable coverage notices in one folder.

Social Security's number is 1-800-772-1213. Our guide to Social Security offices in New Jersey lists local offices.

What if I work for the State of New Jersey, a school or a town?

While you are actively working, the State Health Benefits Program (SHBP) and School Employees' Health Benefits Program (SEHBP) generally do not require Medicare. At retirement, they do.

The October 2026 SHBP and SEHBP program guidebook says that, in general, a Medicare-eligible employee or covered family member does not need Medicare while the employee keeps working. The exception is end-stage renal disease after a 30-month coordination period.

Retirement is different. The New Jersey Division of Pensions and Benefits says that if you or your dependent are 65, or have been on Social Security disability for 24 months or more, you must enroll in Parts A and B to keep SHBP or SEHBP retiree coverage. It suggests applying to Social Security 90 days before your retiree health benefits start. Coverage can be terminated if you do not enroll. Retired members on Medicare are automatically enrolled in the program's OptumRx Medicare Part D plan. Questions go to the Division at 609-292-7524. Our guide to PERS, TPAF and PFRS retirement covers the pension side.

Which mistakes cost working New Jerseyans the most?

Most problems come from assuming a plan counts when it does not, or from missing the 8-month clock.

  • Small employer, no Part B. Under 20 workers, Medicare pays first. Skipping Part B can leave you paying what Medicare would have covered.
  • Counting on COBRA. It does not extend your window. Sign up for Part B within 8 months of leaving the job.
  • Going out of network. Medicare.gov warns that if your employer HMO or PPO pays first and you go outside its network, it is possible neither the plan nor Medicare will pay.
  • Joining Part D on your own. Medicare.gov warns that if you have employer coverage and get Medicare drug coverage, you may lose your employer health and drug coverage for you and your dependents. Call the benefits administrator first.
  • Forgetting the HSA. Stop contributions 6 months before you apply for Medicare or Social Security.
  • Ignoring your income. Higher earners pay more for Part B and Part D. If your income drops when you retire, Social Security can use a newer year. Our turning 65 guide explains the SSA-44 form.

If your employer or health plan gave you wrong information and you missed your chance, Medicare.gov describes an exceptional conditions Special Enrollment Period for that situation. It lasts 6 months from the day you tell Social Security, and you use form CMS-10797.

Get a free second opinion

New Jersey's State Health Insurance Assistance Program (SHIP) gives free, unbiased Medicare counseling at 1-800-792-8820. For questions about which coverage pays first, Medicare's Benefits Coordination and Recovery Center is at 1-855-798-2627.

Planning the work side too? Our guide to working after 60 in New Jersey covers the Social Security earnings test and age discrimination rights, and our retirement planning checklist helps you line up the rest.

faq.q: Do I need Medicare Part B if I am still working at 65?
faq.a: Not if you have group coverage from your current job, or your spouse's current job, at an employer with 20 or more employees. That plan usually pays first, so you can delay Part B without a penalty. At a smaller employer, Medicare usually pays first and you should generally sign up.

faq.q: Does COBRA count as coverage for delaying Part B?
faq.a: No. Medicare.gov says your 8-month Special Enrollment Period starts when you stop working, even if you choose COBRA. Sign up for Part B within those 8 months to avoid a penalty and a gap.

faq.q: Can I keep contributing to my HSA after 65?
faq.a: Only until you enroll in any part of Medicare. The IRS says your limit is zero starting the first month of Medicare, including backdated months. Premium-free Part A can be backdated up to 6 months, so Medicare.gov says to stop contributions 6 months before you apply.

faq.q: My dad is retiring at 68. How do I help him sign up for Part B?
faq.a: Have him apply through Social Security about a month before his job coverage ends. He needs form CMS-40B and form CMS-L564, which his employer completes. He can apply online and upload proof, or fax or mail the forms. Call 1-800-772-1213 with questions.

faq.q: What if my mom's employer can't fill out the CMS-L564?
faq.a: Social Security accepts other proof of job-based coverage, such as W-2s showing pre-tax medical contributions, pay stubs with health premium deductions, insurance cards with an effective date, or explanations of benefits from the plan.

faq.q: Do New Jersey state and school retirees have to take Medicare?
faq.a: Yes. The NJ Division of Pensions and Benefits says SHBP and SEHBP retirees and dependents who are eligible must enroll in Medicare Parts A and B to keep retiree coverage. It suggests applying to Social Security 90 days before retiree health benefits start.

title: How to appeal a Medicare denial in New Jersey
dek: A denied claim, service or prescription is not the last word. Here are the deadlines, forms and five levels of appeal for Original Medicare, Advantage plans and Part D, and where New Jersey families get free help.
keyFacts: Original Medicare: appeal within 120 days of receiving the Medicare Summary Notice
Advantage and Part D plans: appeal within 65 days of the denial letter
Fast appeals: 72 hours for plans; 24 hours for a fast drug coverage decision
ALJ hearing needs $200 in dispute in 2026 and 2027
Free help from NJ SHIP: 1-800-792-8820
body:
To appeal a Medicare denial, start with the notice that told you about it. If your parent has Original Medicare, that is the Medicare Summary Notice, and the first appeal generally must be filed within 120 days of receiving it. If they have a Medicare Advantage or Part D drug plan, the plan's denial letter starts the clock, and the appeal is due within 65 days of the date on that letter.

Every path has five levels, and each decision letter explains how to go to the next one. Most disputes are settled at the first or second level, often with a better letter from the doctor. This guide covers bills, services and drugs. For a hospital discharge or a rehab stay that is ending, there is a faster process, covered in our rehab guide and hospital discharge guide. This is general information, not legal advice.

Which appeal process applies to my parent?

It depends on whether the denial came from Original Medicare, a Medicare Advantage plan or a Part D drug plan. Look at the top of the notice.

CoverageFirst appealDeadline
Original MedicareRedetermination120 days from the notice
Advantage planPlan reconsideration65 days from the denial
Part D drug planPlan redetermination65 days from the denial

Missed a deadline? You can still ask. Federal rules let the reviewer accept a late appeal for "good cause," such as a serious illness, a death in the family, records lost in a fire, or wrong information from Medicare. Explain the reason in writing.

Circle the date. Every Medicare appeal runs on a clock.

How do I appeal a denied claim in Original Medicare?

Ask the Medicare Administrative Contractor for a redetermination, using the form or the instructions on the Medicare Summary Notice. A decision generally comes within 60 days.

The Medicare Summary Notice (MSN) lists each service, what Medicare paid and what it denied. The deadline is printed on it. Under federal rules, you have 120 days from the day you receive it, and Medicare assumes you received it 5 days after the date on the notice.

You can file in two ways:

  • Fill out the Redetermination Request Form (CMS-20027) and send it to the contractor address on the MSN.
  • Or circle the denied items on a copy of the MSN, write why you disagree, add your parent's name, phone and Medicare Number, and mail it to the address on the last page.

Include anything that helps, such as a letter from the doctor explaining why the care was needed. If Medicare agrees, the payment shows up on the next MSN. If not, you get a Medicare Redetermination Notice.

Level 2: an independent reviewer

If the answer is still no, you have 180 days to ask a Qualified Independent Contractor (QIC) for a reconsideration. Use the Medicare Reconsideration Request Form (CMS-20033) and send a copy of the redetermination notice. The QIC generally decides within 60 days.

Say your dad in Paramus gets an MSN showing that Medicare denied a scan. Call the doctor's billing office first. Sometimes a code was entered wrong and the office can fix and resubmit the claim. If the code was right, ask the doctor for a short letter saying why the scan was medically necessary, and file the redetermination with that letter attached.

How do I appeal a Medicare Advantage denial?

Ask the plan for a reconsideration within 65 days of the denial notice. If the plan says no again, it must send your case to an independent reviewer automatically.

Advantage plans call a coverage decision an "organization determination." Your parent, a representative or the doctor can ask for one before getting care. Under federal rules, a plan must answer a standard request for an item or service within 14 days, or within 7 days for items that need prior authorization (starting in 2026). A request for a Part B drug must be answered within 72 hours. If a plan misses its deadline, that counts as a denial you can appeal.

For the appeal itself, Medicare.gov gives the plan these deadlines:

  • Care not yet received: 30 days
  • Payment for care already received: 60 days
  • Part B drug: 7 days
  • Fast appeal, when waiting could seriously harm health: 72 hours

The plan can take up to 14 more days in some cases and must tell you in writing why. If the doctor asks for a reconsideration of care not yet received, the doctor must let your parent know. When the plan upholds its denial, the case goes on to an Independent Review Entity (IRE) without you having to file anything.

Many Advantage denials involve prior authorization for scans, surgery, rehab or home care. The doctor's office often handles those requests. Ask the office whether they have appealed, and ask for a copy of the denial letter so you can track the deadline yourself.

What if my parent's drug plan won't cover a prescription?

Ask the plan for a coverage determination or an exception. Standard requests must be answered within 72 hours, and fast requests within 24 hours.

Part D plans must give network pharmacies a notice explaining how to ask the plan for a coverage decision. If the pharmacist says a drug is not covered, ask for that notice and the reason. Then your parent or the prescriber can call the plan, write a letter or send the Model Coverage Determination Request form.

  • Exceptions. To cover a drug that is off the formulary, or to lower its cost tier, the prescriber must send a statement with the medical reason. The 72-hour clock starts when the plan gets that statement.
  • Repayment. If your parent already paid for the drug, the request must be in writing, and the plan has 14 days to decide.
  • Appeal. If the plan says no, ask for a redetermination within 65 days. The plan must decide within 7 days, 14 for payment, or 72 hours for a fast appeal.
  • Level 2. If the plan upholds the denial, you have 60 days to ask the Part D Independent Review Entity to look at it.

If your parent has PAAD, a drug that is off the Part D plan's list will not be filled by PAAD either. The state says the person must switch to a covered drug or the doctor must request an exception from the plan. Our PAAD guide and Part D guide for 2027 explain how the two fit together.

What happens if level 2 says no?

You can ask for a hearing before an administrative law judge, then a review by the Medicare Appeals Council, then federal court. Each step has a 60-day deadline, and the last two need a minimum dollar amount.

LevelWho decidesMinimum amount
3Administrative law judge (OMHA)$200 in 2026 and 2027
4Medicare Appeals CouncilNo minimum
5Federal district court$1,960 in 2026, $2,000 in 2027

To ask for a hearing, follow the directions in the level 2 decision. You can use the form OMHA-100, write a letter, or file online with the Office of Medicare Hearings and Appeals. Hearings are usually held by phone or video. You can also ask for a decision based on the written record alone. Claims can sometimes be combined to reach the court minimum.

By level 3, the paperwork gets heavier. This is a good time to ask for free help from the groups listed below, or from a lawyer. Our guide to free legal help for seniors lists options in New Jersey.

How do I file a Medicare appeal for my mom or dad?

Your parent can name you as their representative on form CMS-1696, Appointment of Representative. Send a copy with each appeal.

Medicare.gov asks for a copy of the Appointment of Representative form, or another written document with the required details, whenever a representative files. A doctor can also ask for a fast appeal or a coverage decision on a patient's behalf. If your parent can no longer sign, a durable power of attorney or guardianship may give you the authority. Our guide to power of attorney in New Jersey explains how that works.

  1. Find the notice. Locate the MSN or the plan's denial letter. Note the date and the deadline.
  2. Call the provider. Ask whether the claim was coded correctly and whether the office will help with the appeal.
  3. Get a doctor's letter. One page on why the care or drug is medically necessary often does more than anything else.
  4. Use the right form. CMS-20027 for an Original Medicare redetermination, the plan's instructions for Advantage or Part D, and CMS-1696 if you are filing for your parent.
  5. Keep copies and proof. Copy everything you send. Mail with tracking, or note the date and name of anyone you speak with.
  6. Watch for the answer. If the decision does not come on time, call. A missed deadline by an Advantage or drug plan counts as a denial you can take to the next level.
Free help with a Medicare appeal

New Jersey's State Health Insurance Assistance Program (SHIP) helps with claims and denials for free at 1-800-792-8820. For fast appeals when a hospital or rehab says Medicare will stop paying, call Commence Health, New Jersey's Medicare quality improvement organization, at 1-866-815-5440. Medicare itself is at 1-800-633-4227.

If an MSN shows a service your parent never got, that is not an appeal. It may be fraud. Our guide to Medicare scams in New Jersey explains how to report it to the Senior Medicare Patrol at 1-732-777-1940, ext. 1117. If home health visits were denied, our home health guide explains what Medicare covers.

faq.q: How long do I have to appeal a Medicare denial?
faq.a: For Original Medicare, you generally have 120 days from receiving the Medicare Summary Notice. For a Medicare Advantage or Part D plan, you have 65 days from the date on the plan's denial notice. Later levels usually allow 60 days, except 180 days to request an Original Medicare reconsideration.

faq.q: How do I appeal a Medicare denial for my mom?
faq.a: Have her sign form CMS-1696, Appointment of Representative, naming you. Then file the appeal using the instructions on her Medicare Summary Notice or plan denial letter, and include a copy of the form. Her doctor can also request some appeals for her.

faq.q: How fast does a Medicare Advantage plan have to decide an appeal?
faq.a: Medicare.gov says 30 days for care you have not received, 60 days for payment, 7 days for a Part B drug, and 72 hours for a fast appeal. The plan can extend by up to 14 days in some cases and must tell you why in writing.

faq.q: What if my dad's drug plan refuses to cover his prescription?
faq.a: He or his prescriber can ask the plan for a coverage determination or an exception. The plan must decide within 72 hours, or 24 hours for an expedited request. An exception needs a statement from the prescriber with the medical reason.

faq.q: Is there a minimum dollar amount to appeal?
faq.a: Not for the first two levels. An administrative law judge hearing requires $200 in dispute in 2026 and 2027. Federal court review requires $1,960 in 2026 and $2,000 in 2027. Claims can sometimes be combined.

faq.q: Who helps with Medicare appeals in New Jersey for free?
faq.a: SHIP counselors help with claims and denials at 1-800-792-8820. For fast appeals when a hospital or rehab says coverage is ending, call Commence Health at 1-866-815-5440.

title: Medical alert systems in NJ: costs and when NJ FamilyCare pays
dek: Original Medicare will not pay for a medical alert button. MLTSS, JACC and some Advantage plans can. Here is how the systems work, what to compare and which sales pitches to hang up on.
keyFacts: Original Medicare does not cover medical alert systems
MLTSS and JACC can pay for one in a care plan
JACC caps all services at $1,156 a month in 2026
FTC Cooling-Off Rule: 3 business days to cancel most in-home sales of $25+
ADRC for JACC and Medicaid help: 1-877-222-3737
body:
A medical alert system, also called a personal emergency response system (PERS), is a button your parent wears that calls a monitoring center when pressed. Original Medicare does not pay for one. In New Jersey, NJ FamilyCare's long-term care benefit (MLTSS) and the state's JACC program can pay for a medical alert system for people who qualify, and some Medicare Advantage plans include one as an extra benefit.

Everyone else pays the company directly, usually a monthly monitoring fee and sometimes equipment or activation fees on top. This guide explains how these systems work, who pays in New Jersey, how to compare costs and contracts without getting stuck, and the sales tactics to hang up on. For whether a parent is safe living alone in the first place, start with our guide to that question.

How does a medical alert system work?

Your parent presses a button on a pendant or wristband. The device connects to a response center, and a trained operator talks with your parent and calls the people or services on the list.

New Jersey's MLTSS rules describe the service the same way. There is a one-time setup, then a monthly fee for monitoring by staff at the response center. The state pays for several kinds of units, which is a useful map of what is on the market:

  • Landline units. A base station plugs into the home phone line. The button works within range of the base.
  • Cellular units. The base uses a cell signal, so no landline is needed.
  • Mobile units. A device that works away from home, often with location tracking.
  • Fall detection. An add-on, for landline or cellular units, that tries to sense a fall and call even if the button is not pressed.

Depending on what your parent tells the operator, the center may call a family member, a neighbor or 911. Ask each company exactly how its operators decide.

Does Medicare pay for a medical alert system?

Original Medicare does not. Medicare's equipment list denies "telephone alert systems" because they are emergency communication devices, not medical treatment.

Medicare Advantage plans can choose to offer a personal emergency response system as an extra benefit. Federal rules list it among the supplemental benefit categories plans may include. Not every plan does, and the details vary by plan. Check the plan's Evidence of Coverage or call member services. Medigap policies do not add benefits like this. Our guide to Advantage or Medigap explains the difference, and free NJ SHIP counselors at 1-800-792-8820 can look at your parent's plan.

When does NJ FamilyCare or JACC pay for a medical alert?

Both programs can pay for a PERS as part of a care plan for someone who needs nursing home level care and wants to stay home.

ProgramWho qualifiesWhat to know
MLTSSNJ FamilyCare members who need nursing home level careFor people who live alone or are alone for long stretches
JACC60+, nursing home level care, not on MedicaidCounts toward the $1,156 monthly cap
Medicare AdvantageMembers of plans that offer itVaries by plan
Original MedicareNobodyNot covered

MLTSS. The state's service rules say the PERS is for a member who lives alone or is alone for significant amounts of time, as written in the plan of care, and the company must be approved by the member's managed care plan. Ask the care manager. Our MLTSS guide covers who qualifies.

JACC. Jersey Assistance for Community Caregiving lists a PERS among its services. In 2026 your parent must be 60 or older, need help with at least three daily activities such as bathing or dressing, and have income no higher than $4,855 a month ($6,582 for a couple) and countable assets of $40,000 or less ($60,000 for a couple). All services together are capped at $1,156 a month plus care management, and a sliding-scale copay may apply. See our JACC guide.

One call starts both

The Aging and Disability Resource Connection (ADRC) at 1-877-222-3737 reaches your parent's county office on aging, which screens for JACC and helps with Medicaid. County offices also coordinate telephone reassurance, a regular check-in call that some families use alongside a button.

What does a medical alert system cost?

Prices change often and vary by company and features, so the only number that matters is the full cost in writing for your parent's setup. Ask for it as a yearly total.

The charges to ask about, line by line:

  • The monthly monitoring fee, and whether it can go up during the contract
  • Equipment, either a purchase price or a monthly lease
  • Activation, setup or installation fees
  • An extra monthly fee for fall detection, a second button, a mobile unit or a lockbox for a spare key
  • Shipping, both to your parent and for returning equipment
  • Replacement cost if the button is lost or broken
  • Any charge to cancel, and how much notice the company wants

Ask too whether a yearly prepayment is refundable if your parent moves to assisted living, goes into the hospital for a long stay, or dies. Families get caught here more than anywhere else.

Get the full yearly cost, the cancellation terms and the refund policy in writing before your parent signs.

How do I choose a medical alert system for my dad?

Start with how he actually lives. A man who never leaves the house needs something different from one who still walks to the diner every morning.

Questions about the device

  • Is it waterproof enough to wear in the shower? Bathrooms are a common place for falls.
  • How far from the base does the button work? Test it in the basement, the garage and the yard.
  • Does the base work if the power goes out, and for how long on its backup battery?
  • For cellular units, how strong is the signal inside his home?
  • How does the device tell you it needs charging, and will he remember to charge it?
  • If it has fall detection, what happens if it misses a fall or calls by mistake?

Questions about the company

  • Who answers, the company's own center or another firm? Is it staffed around the clock?
  • Can operators speak your parent's first language, and can they serve someone who is hard of hearing?
  • Who is on the call list, in what order, and how do you change it?
  • Will family get a text or call each time the button is pressed?
  • How often should you test it, and does testing cost anything?
  1. Check coverage first. Call the ADRC about JACC or MLTSS and check any Medicare Advantage plan before paying privately.
  2. Compare two or three companies using the questions above and the line-by-line costs.
  3. Read the contract. Look for the length, automatic renewal, cancellation and refund terms.
  4. Set up the call list together. Include a neighbor who has a key and can get there fast.
  5. Practice. Have your parent press the button once with you in the room so a real call is not the first one.
  6. Test it monthly and post the company's number on the fridge with our emergency info sheet.

A button only works when it is worn. Many older adults take it off at night or leave it on the dresser. If your parent will not wear one, a cell phone kept in a pocket, a smartwatch with fall alerts or a daily check-in call may be a better fit. Our fall prevention guide covers what lowers the risk of falling in the first place, and aging alone in NJ has check-in ideas for people with no family nearby.

What are the red flags with medical alert sales?

Hang up on any robocall that offers a "free" medical alert system. The Federal Trade Commission has sued operations that sent huge numbers of these calls to older people.

In a 2015 complaint against Lifewatch Inc., filed with the Florida Attorney General, the FTC said Lifewatch and its partners made at least a billion unsolicited robocalls, mostly to older consumers, pitching supposedly free medical alert systems. A 2019 court order permanently banned Lifewatch and two people named with it from telemarketing. Warning signs include:

  • A recorded call saying a relative or doctor already ordered a device for your parent
  • A request for a Medicare number, Social Security number or bank details to "ship the free device"
  • Pressure to sign today, or a contract much longer than a year
  • A salesperson at the door who will not leave paperwork to read

If your parent bought a system in their home for $25 or more, the FTC's Cooling-Off Rule usually gives three business days to cancel for a full refund. The seller must give two copies of a cancellation form. Mail one, by certified mail, before midnight of the third business day. Saturdays count as business days. The rule does not cover sales made entirely by phone, mail or online, so read those contracts for their own cancellation terms. This is general information, not legal advice.

Report problems to the NJ Division of Consumer Affairs at 1-800-242-5846 or at ReportFraud.ftc.gov. If someone asked for a Medicare number, call the Senior Medicare Patrol at 1-732-777-1940 ext. 1117. Our guides to scams targeting NJ seniors and Medicare scams cover more.

faq.q: How do I get a free medical alert system for my mom in New Jersey?
faq.a: Call the ADRC at 1-877-222-3737. If your mom needs nursing home level care, MLTSS (if she has NJ FamilyCare) or JACC (if she does not) can include a medical alert system in her care plan. Also check whether her Medicare Advantage plan offers one. Ignore robocalls offering free devices.

faq.q: Does Medicare cover medical alert systems?
faq.a: Original Medicare does not. Its equipment list denies telephone alert systems. Some Medicare Advantage plans offer a personal emergency response system as an extra benefit, so check the plan's Evidence of Coverage.

faq.q: Is fall detection worth it?
faq.a: It can help someone who might not be able to press a button after a fall, but ask each company what happens when the device misses a fall or calls by mistake, and what the extra monthly fee is. A button only helps if your parent wears it, including in the shower.

faq.q: My dad signed a medical alert contract with a salesman at his house. Can he cancel?
faq.a: Usually, if the sale was $25 or more. The FTC's Cooling-Off Rule gives three business days to cancel many sales made at home. Mail the cancellation form, ideally by certified mail, before midnight of the third business day. Then report any problems to NJ Consumer Affairs at 1-800-242-5846.

faq.q: Does a medical alert work during a power outage?
faq.a: It depends on the unit. Ask how long the base station runs on its backup battery and whether a landline unit still works if the phone line is down. Cellular and mobile units depend on a charged battery and a signal.

NJ Division of Aging Services: Jersey Assistance for Community Caregiving (JACC)
NJ Division of Aging Services: 2026 Program Guide
CMS: National Coverage Determination 280.1, Durable Medical Equipment Reference List
CMS: 2025 Part C Technical Specifications (supplemental benefit categories)
FTC: Buyer's remorse, the FTC's Cooling-Off Rule may help

title: Extra Help for Medicare drug costs: who qualifies in NJ
dek: Extra Help can cut a parent's Part D costs to a few dollars a prescription. Here are the 2026 limits, the 2027 copays, and how to apply from New Jersey.
keyFacts: 2027 Extra Help copays: up to $5.80 generic, $14.40 brand, $0 deductible.
2026 limits: income $23,940 single, $32,460 couple; resources $18,090 and $36,100.
New Jersey 2027 premium cap: Extra Help pays a plan's basic premium up to $36.28 a month.
Automatic with full Medicaid, a Medicare Savings Program or SSI.
Apply through Social Security at 1-800-772-1213 or NJSave at 1-800-792-9745.
body:
Extra Help is the federal program that lowers Medicare drug costs for people with limited income and savings. In 2027, someone with Extra Help pays no deductible, no more than $5.80 for a covered generic and no more than $14.40 for a covered brand drug, and usually no premium. For 2026, a single person qualifies with income up to $23,940 and resources up to $18,090, according to Medicare.gov.

Your mom or dad gets Extra Help automatically if they have full Medicaid, a Medicare Savings Program or Supplemental Security Income (SSI). Everyone else applies through Social Security, online or at 1-800-772-1213. In New Jersey, the state's NJSave application screens for it too. Our Part D guide for 2027 gives a short summary. This page covers the rules, the paperwork and what happens after approval.

What does Extra Help pay for in 2027?

It covers the Part D deductible, most or all of the monthly premium, and caps each prescription at a few dollars. It also removes the Part D late enrollment penalty while your parent has it.

CostWith Extra Help, 2027
Deductible$0
Generic drugUp to $5.80
Brand drugUp to $14.40
After $2,400$0 per drug
Medicaid and QMBUp to $4.90
Late penaltyNone

Medicare lists the premium as $0, and for many plans it is. The fine print matters in New Jersey. Extra Help pays a plan's basic premium up to a regional cap that CMS sets each year. For 2027, the New Jersey amount is $36.28 a month. If your parent picks a plan with a higher basic premium, or an enhanced plan with extra benefits, they may owe the part above that amount.

The $2,400 out-of-pocket cap counts payments made on your parent's behalf, including Extra Help. Once total covered drug costs reach it, prescriptions cost nothing for the rest of the year. People with both full Medicaid and the Qualified Medicare Beneficiary (QMB) program pay no more than $4.90 a drug.

For 2026, CMS also set $0 cost sharing for people with full Medicaid who live in a nursing home or get Medicaid home and community-based services. Ask the county board of social services if that applies to your parent.

Who qualifies for Extra Help?

People with Medicare whose income and resources are under the yearly limits. For 2026 those are $23,940 in income and $18,090 in resources for one person, and $32,460 and $36,100 for a married couple.

2026 limitSingleCouple
Income$23,940$32,460
Resources$18,090$36,100

The resource figures include $1,500 per person that Social Security sets aside for burial expenses when an applicant says they expect to use some savings that way. Without that, CMS lists the limits as $16,590 for one person and $33,100 for a couple. The 2027 income limits are tied to the federal poverty guidelines, which come out early in the year, so expect updated numbers in early 2027.

What counts and what doesn't

  • Income that counts. Social Security, pensions, wages, self-employment earnings, annuities, veterans benefits, Railroad Retirement, rental income, alimony and workers' compensation.
  • Income that doesn't. SNAP, housing assistance, home energy assistance, disaster aid, help from others with household bills, the earned income tax credit and payments for medical treatment and drugs.
  • Resources that count. Cash, checking, savings and retirement accounts, stocks, bonds and mutual funds, and real estate other than the home.
  • Resources that don't. The home, one car, furniture and personal items, a burial plot, and up to $1,500 set aside for burial.

A few rules catch families off guard. If your parents are married and live together, both incomes and both sets of savings count, even if only one applies. If they live apart, only the applicant's count. And Medicare says someone a bit over the income limit may still qualify if they support other family members who live with them.

The house, the car and the burial plot don't count. Many parents rule themselves out because they forget that.

Who gets Extra Help automatically?

Anyone with full Medicaid, a Medicare Savings Program, or SSI. They do not need to apply. Medicare mails a purple notice confirming it.

That makes the Medicare Savings Programs a useful door in New Jersey. QMB, SLMB and QI pay the Part B premium, and enrollment in any of them brings Extra Help with it. Our guide to QMB, SLMB and QI in New Jersey has the state's income and asset limits. If your parent is close to those limits, an NJSave application can open both doors at once.

The reverse also works. Medicare says that when someone applies for Extra Help, Social Security sends the information to the state to start a Medicare Savings Program application, unless the applicant says no on the form.

If your parent qualifies automatically and has no drug plan, Medicare enrolls them in one and sends a yellow or green notice naming it. Check that the plan covers their drugs and pharmacy. They can switch.

How do I apply for Extra Help for my mom or dad?

Apply through Social Security online at ssa.gov/extrahelp, or call 1-800-772-1213 to set up an appointment. You can apply any time of year, before or after joining a drug plan.

  1. Gather the numbers. Your parent's Medicare card, Social Security number, and recent statements for every bank, retirement and investment account. Have a list of every income source with monthly amounts.
  2. Pick a way to file. Fill in the online application together, or call Social Security. The phone line runs 8 a.m. to 7 p.m., Monday to Friday. TTY users can call 1-800-325-0778.
  3. Or use NJSave. New Jersey's single application screens for Extra Help along with PAAD, Senior Gold, the Medicare Savings Programs and Lifeline. Call 1-800-792-9745 for help or a paper copy.
  4. Mention burial savings. If your parent has money set aside for a funeral, say so. It raises the resource limit by $1,500.
  5. Watch the mail. Social Security sends a decision. If approved, keep the Notice of Award with your parent's medical papers.

Married couples who live together and both want Extra Help can use one application. If you want a person to walk you through it, call the State Health Insurance Assistance Program (SHIP) at 1-800-792-8820. SHIP counselors are free and do not sell insurance. Our page on Social Security offices in New Jersey explains in-person options.

What happens after my parent is approved?

Extra Help lasts through December 31 of that year, even if income changes mid-year. Your parent can also switch Medicare drug plans once a calendar month instead of waiting for open enrollment.

  • A plan is assigned if needed. If your parent has no drug plan, Medicare enrolls them in one and mails a notice with the start date.
  • Monthly plan changes. A switch takes effect on the first day of the next month. That helps if the assigned plan leaves out a drug your parent takes. The monthly switch is into a stand-alone drug plan. Someone in a Medicare Advantage plan can use it to return to Original Medicare with a drug plan, but not to pick a different Advantage plan. It is not open to anyone the plan has flagged as at risk under its drug management program for opioids.
  • Yearly review. Eligibility is checked each year. No letter means Extra Help and the same plan continue. A gray notice means your parent no longer qualifies automatically and should apply. A blue notice means Medicare moved them to a new plan, because the old plan's premium rose above the New Jersey cap or the plan is leaving Medicare.
  • A death in the family. If a spouse dies, the change in Extra Help may be delayed for a year. Report marriage, divorce, separation or a spouse's death at 1-800-772-1213.

If the pharmacy charges the wrong amount

Call the drug plan first. The plan must accept proof such as the purple, yellow or green Medicare notice, the Social Security Notice of Award, an SSI award letter or a Medicaid card. Tell the plan how many days of medicine are left. You can also call Medicare at 1-800-633-4227 to confirm the Extra Help level.

If your parent qualified but had no drug plan and paid full price, Medicare's Limited Income Newly Eligible Transition (LI NET) program may repay part of it. Keep the receipts and call LI NET at 1-800-783-1307.

What if Social Security turns my parent down?

Your parent can appeal within 60 days, using form SSA-1021. They can also reapply any time their income or savings drop.

The 60 days start the day after the denial letter arrives, and Social Security assumes it arrived five days after its date unless you show otherwise. Social Security holds the appeal as a phone hearing unless your parent asks for a case review. Someone who was not part of the first decision decides. A family member, friend or lawyer can help.

Before appealing, check the math. Was retirement money counted twice? Was the burial exclusion applied? Did the application count income from a spouse who lives elsewhere? Those are fair questions to raise. A SHIP counselor can help you look. For Medicare plan denials, which are a different process, see our guide to appealing a Medicare denial.

How does Extra Help fit with PAAD and Senior Gold?

They stack. Extra Help is federal and works inside the Part D plan. PAAD and Senior Gold are New Jersey programs with much higher income limits. NJSave checks for all of them at once.

A parent under the Extra Help income limit is also under PAAD's limit, so apply for both. (PAAD is not open to people who get Medicaid.) A parent above the Extra Help limit may still get PAAD, which brings copays to $5 for generics and $7 for brand drugs. Our guide to prescription and bill help shows how the pieces fit.

One caution from Medicare. If your parent has drug coverage from a former employer or union, joining a Medicare drug plan can end that coverage, even with Extra Help. Call the benefits office before enrolling. The Medicare Prescription Payment Plan, which spreads drug costs into monthly bills, is usually a poor fit for anyone with Extra Help.

Numbers to keep handy

Social Security (apply for Extra Help): 1-800-772-1213. NJSave and PAAD hotline: 1-800-792-9745. NJ SHIP free Medicare counseling: 1-800-792-8820. Medicare: 1-800-633-4227. LI NET: 1-800-783-1307.

This is general information, not legal or financial advice. Limits change every January. Check the official pages linked below before you decide your parent does not qualify.

faq.q: How do I apply for Extra Help for my mom?
faq.a: Sit with her and fill in the online application at ssa.gov/extrahelp, or call Social Security together at 1-800-772-1213 to set up an appointment. New Jersey's NJSave application (1-800-792-9745) also screens for Extra Help, PAAD and the Medicare Savings Programs in one form.

faq.q: Does my dad's house count against the Extra Help limit?
faq.a: No. The home he lives in, one car, furniture, personal items, a burial plot and up to $1,500 set aside for burial do not count. Bank accounts, retirement accounts, stocks, bonds and other real estate do.

faq.q: Is Extra Help really a $0 premium?
faq.a: For many plans, yes. Extra Help pays a plan's basic premium up to a regional cap, $36.28 a month in New Jersey for 2027. A plan with a higher basic premium, or an enhanced plan, can leave your parent owing the difference.

faq.q: What are the Extra Help income limits for 2027?
faq.a: They are set from the federal poverty guidelines released early each year, so 2027 limits were not yet published as of November 2026. The 2026 limits are $23,940 for one person and $32,460 for a married couple.

faq.q: Can my parent get Extra Help and PAAD at the same time?
faq.a: Yes. Extra Help is federal and PAAD is a New Jersey program. They work together, and the NJSave application checks for both.

faq.q: What if my parent was denied Extra Help?
faq.a: Appeal within 60 days with Social Security form SSA-1021, or reapply if income or savings have dropped. A free SHIP counselor at 1-800-792-8820 can help check whether something was counted wrong.

title: Managing many medications: help for older adults in NJ
dek: A pharmacist review through the Medicare drug plan, a list that works, the right pill box, and where to drop old medicines in New Jersey.
keyFacts: Every Medicare Part D plan must run a Medication Therapy Management (MTM) program.
MTM drug cost threshold: $1,276 a year in 2026 and $1,340 in 2027 (CMS).
Plans may require no more than 3 chronic conditions and 8 Part D drugs for MTM.
Project Medicine Drop boxes sit in participating NJ police headquarters, open all year.
NJ SHIP free Medicare help: 1-800-792-8820.
body:
Medication management for older adults starts with one complete list of every pill, patch, drop and supplement. Then a pharmacist or doctor needs to review that list at least once a year. In New Jersey, most families can get that review through the Medicare drug plan. Every Part D plan must run a Medication Therapy Management program, and people who meet the plan's criteria, which combine several chronic conditions, several drugs and higher yearly drug costs, are enrolled automatically.

The rest is daily routine and safe cleanup. A weekly pill box, reminders tied to meals, one pharmacy for everything, and a trip to a police station drop box for old bottles go a long way. This guide covers each step for your mom or dad, with the Medicare rules for 2026 and 2027.

What is Medicare's medication review, and does my parent qualify?

It is called Medication Therapy Management (MTM). Every Medicare drug plan must offer it to members who meet the plan's targeting rules, and those members are enrolled unless they opt out.

Federal rules set the outer limits. A plan can require no more than three chronic conditions and no more than eight Part D drugs. Your parent must also be likely to have yearly covered drug costs at or above a threshold CMS sets.

MTM ruleLimit
Chronic conditionsPlan may require up to 3
Part D drugsPlan may require up to 8
Drug cost, 2026$1,276 a year
Drug cost, 2027$1,340 a year
EnrollmentAutomatic, opt out

Plans must count ten conditions toward the chronic disease rule: Alzheimer's disease, arthritis and osteoporosis, heart failure, diabetes, high cholesterol, end-stage kidney disease, HIV/AIDS, high blood pressure, mental health conditions such as depression, and lung disease such as COPD or asthma. Members in a plan's drug management program for opioids and similar drugs also qualify.

What the program includes

  • A yearly comprehensive review. A pharmacist or other qualified provider goes through every medicine with your parent, in person or by live telehealth. Your parent gets a written summary and may get an action plan.
  • Quarterly check-ins. The plan reviews your parent's prescriptions at least every three months and follows up with your parent or the doctor when something looks off.
  • Help when memory is a problem. If your parent can't take part because of cognitive impairment, the pharmacist can do the review with a caregiver or other authorized person.
  • Disposal information. Plans must tell members how to get rid of leftover controlled substances safely.

To check, call the member services number on your parent's plan card. Ask, "Is my mother enrolled in your Medication Therapy Management program, and when is her next comprehensive medication review?" If she is not eligible, ask whether the plan offers any other pharmacist review.

If your parent takes eight or more medicines for several chronic conditions, ask the drug plan whether they qualify for a free pharmacist review.

What other medicine reviews does Medicare cover?

The yearly Wellness visit includes a review of current prescriptions. Chronic care management, a monthly Part B service for people with two or more serious chronic conditions, includes one too.

Bring every bottle to the Wellness visit so the review is complete. Chronic care management is less known. A doctor's office builds a care plan listing your parent's health problems, other providers and medications, offers round-the-clock access for urgent needs, and helps when your parent moves between settings, such as hospital to home. After the Part B deductible, your parent pays 20% of the Medicare-approved amount. Ask the primary care office if it offers the service.

Transitions are where many medication mistakes start. After a hospital or rehab stay, ask for a written list of what to stop, start and change before your parent leaves. Our hospital discharge guide has a checklist.

How do we keep a medication list that actually works?

Write down every prescription, over-the-counter drug, vitamin and supplement, with the dose, the time, the prescriber and the reason. Keep one copy at home and one in your parent's wallet.

The National Institute on Aging (NIA) suggests showing the list to every provider, including dentists and physical therapists. Bring the actual bottles to the yearly review. Old prescriptions and duplicates turn up that way.

  • Use one pharmacy. NIA says keeping all prescriptions at one pharmacy helps the pharmacist catch a new drug that could clash with an old one. If that's not possible, share the full list at each pharmacy.
  • Know each pill by sight. Your parent should be able to tell medicines apart by size, shape, color or the number on the pill.
  • Ask for easier labels and caps. Pharmacists can print larger labels and use bottles that are easier to open. If those caps are not childproof, store the bottles out of reach of visiting grandchildren.
  • Lock up pain medicine. NIA advises keeping opioids such as morphine or codeine in a locked cabinet or drawer.

Put the list where an EMT will find it. Our free printable emergency info sheet has space for it.

Pill organizers, blister packs or something more?

Start simple. A weekly pill box filled at the same time each week works for many people. If your parent misses doses even with a box, ask the pharmacy about other packaging or bring in more help.

  1. Match the box to the schedule. Pick a box with as many slots a day as your parent has dose times. A morning and evening box is easier than four slots if the doctor can simplify the schedule.
  2. Fill it from the bottles, not memory. Do it at a table with good light, with the current list in front of you.
  3. Tie doses to daily habits. NIA suggests linking doses to meals or bedtime, and using charts, timers or reminder apps.
  4. Ask the pharmacy what it offers. Some pharmacies sort pills into sealed packets or cards by date and time, or line up refills so everything is ready on one day. Ask whether there is a fee and whether your parent's plan pays.
  5. Check in. Count what's left in the box at the end of the week. A pattern of missed evening doses tells you something.

If an aide helps at home, know the limits. In New Jersey, a certified home health aide may give medicines only under a nurse's delegation. Our home health aide guide explains the rule. A visiting nurse through Medicare home health care is another option when your parent qualifies.

Which medicines deserve a second look?

Ask the doctor or pharmacist whether every drug is still needed. The American Geriatrics Society's Beers Criteria lists medicines that are often best avoided or used with caution after 65.

NIA calls taking many medicines "polypharmacy" and notes that people 65 and older take more medicines than any other age group. Researchers study "deprescribing," safely reducing or stopping drugs that may no longer help. Bring it up directly: "Are there any of these we could reduce or stop?" Never stop a prescription without talking to the prescriber first.

Mixing can be the problem. NIA's own examples are aspirin with the blood thinner warfarin, and a sleep aid with an allergy pill, which together can slow reactions and make driving dangerous. Many over-the-counter sleep aids appear on the Beers list. Our guide to sleep problems in older adults covers them. Dizziness from medicine is also a common cause of falls. See preventing falls at home.

Questions to ask the pharmacist

  • Is it safe to drive on this medicine?
  • With food or without? Anything to avoid eating or drinking?
  • Does "four times a day" mean every six hours, or four times while awake?
  • What should my parent do after a missed dose?
  • Can this tablet be split or crushed if swallowing is hard?

How do we get rid of old medicines in New Jersey?

Use a Project Medicine Drop box. The NJ Division of Consumer Affairs places secure boxes inside participating police department headquarters, where anyone can drop off unused or expired medicines anonymously, seven days a week, all year.

The Division posts the list of drop box locations by county. Call the police department before you go to confirm the box is in service and what it accepts. Consumer Affairs can be reached at 1-800-242-5846 (toll free in New Jersey) or 973-504-6200.

Other options, according to the FDA:

  • DEA Take Back Days. The U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration runs National Prescription Drug Take Back Day events. Police often host them locally.
  • Pharmacy kiosks and envelopes. Some pharmacies have drop-off kiosks or give out prepaid mail-back envelopes, sometimes free.
  • At home, as a last resort. If no take-back option is handy, mix pills or liquids (don't crush them) with coffee grounds, dirt or cat litter, seal it in a bag or can, and put it in the trash.
  • The flush list. A few dangerous drugs, such as fentanyl patches, should be flushed if no take-back is available. Only flush medicines on the FDA's flush list.
  • Inhalers. Don't put them in the trash or a fire. Ask your local trash and recycling office.

Scratch personal information off every label before the bottle goes out. For needles and syringes, follow the FDA's separate guidance or ask the pharmacist.

Where to call

Your parent's drug plan: the number on the plan card, for a Medication Therapy Management review. NJ SHIP free Medicare counseling: 1-800-792-8820. PAAD and NJSave: 1-800-792-9745. NJ Consumer Affairs (Project Medicine Drop): 1-800-242-5846.

If cost is why your parent skips doses, fix that first. PAAD brings copays to $5 and $7, and Extra Help caps 2027 Part D copays at $5.80 and $14.40. Once covered drug costs reach $2,400 in 2027, Part D copays stop for the year.

faq.q: How do I get a pharmacist to review all of my mom's medicines?
faq.a: Call the number on her Medicare drug plan card and ask if she is enrolled in the plan's Medication Therapy Management program. If she takes several drugs for several chronic conditions, she may already be eligible for a yearly comprehensive review with a pharmacist, in person or by live telehealth.

faq.q: Can I do the medication review for my dad if he has dementia?
faq.a: Yes. Federal rules let the pharmacist do the comprehensive medication review with a caregiver or other authorized person when the member can't take part because of cognitive impairment.

faq.q: Who qualifies for Medicare Medication Therapy Management?
faq.a: Each plan sets its rules within federal limits. A plan can require up to three chronic conditions and up to eight Part D drugs, plus likely yearly drug costs of at least $1,276 in 2026 or $1,340 in 2027. People in a plan's drug management program also qualify.

faq.q: Where can I drop off old medicines in New Jersey?
faq.a: At a Project Medicine Drop box inside a participating police department headquarters. The NJ Division of Consumer Affairs lists locations by county. Some pharmacies also have kiosks or mail-back envelopes.

faq.q: What is the Beers list?
faq.a: The American Geriatrics Society Beers Criteria is a list of medicines that are often best avoided or used with caution by adults 65 and older. Ask the doctor or pharmacist whether any of your parent's medicines are on it, and never stop a drug without the prescriber's advice.

faq.q: Can a home health aide give my parent's pills?
faq.a: In New Jersey, a certified home health aide may give medications only under a registered nurse's delegation. Otherwise aides can remind, not administer. Ask the agency how it handles medications before the first shift.
