title: Finding a geriatrician or primary care doctor in NJ
dek: How to find a geriatrician in New Jersey, when your parent needs one, what Medicare pays, and how doctor home visits work.
keyFacts: Geriatricians are internists or family doctors with extra training in older adult care.
Fewer than 7,000 geriatricians practice in the U.S. (American Geriatrics Society).
Part B covers doctor visits at 20% after the $283 deductible in 2026.
Medicare covers medically necessary doctor home visits; homebound status is not required.
NJ SHIP free Medicare counseling: 1-800-792-8820.
body:
To find a geriatrician in New Jersey, search Medicare's Care Compare tool for doctors listing geriatric medicine near your parent's ZIP code, then call to ask who is taking new Medicare patients. The American Geriatrics Society runs a second directory of its members. Large hospital systems often have geriatric practices too, so call the one your parent already uses.

Expect a search. There are fewer than 7,000 geriatricians in the whole country, according to the American Geriatrics Society. Many families end up with a geriatrician for a one-time assessment and a good primary care doctor, nurse practitioner or physician assistant for everyday care. This guide covers both paths, what Medicare pays and when a doctor can come to the house.

What does a geriatrician do?

A geriatrician is a medical doctor board-certified in internal medicine or family medicine with extra training in caring for older adults. They focus on people juggling several conditions, memory changes, falls and many medications at once.

The American Geriatrics Society sums up the work as "the 5Ms." They are multicomplexity (several health problems at once), mind (memory, thinking and mood), mobility (moving safely and preventing falls), medications, and what matters most to the patient. In practice, a geriatrician may spend a visit asking what your dad wants to be able to do, then trim medicines and order therapy toward that goal.

Geriatricians often work with a team: geriatric nurse practitioners, physician assistants, social workers, consultant pharmacists, dietitians and physical, occupational and speech therapists. They see patients in offices, hospitals, rehab centers, nursing homes, assisted living and, sometimes, at home.

Does my parent need a geriatrician or a regular primary care doctor?

Most older adults do well with a general internist or family doctor. The American Geriatrics Society suggests a geriatrician when health problems are causing frailty or disability, or when the family is stretched thin.

Signs it may be time, from the society's guidance:

  • Memory or thinking changes, depression or incontinence.
  • Trouble moving around or with self-care, such as bathing and dressing.
  • So many specialists that no one is steering the whole plan.
  • A treatment plan your parent can't follow.
  • Family caregivers feeling real stress and strain.

The society notes these patients tend to be over 75 and living with several conditions. A geriatrician can also consult. Your mom keeps her own doctor, sees the geriatrician for a full assessment, and the recommendations go back to her regular doctor.

An example

Say your mom in Paramus is 82. She sees a cardiologist, a kidney doctor and her primary care doctor, takes eleven medicines and has fallen twice this year. Each doctor handles one piece, and nobody looks at the whole picture. That is the kind of case geriatricians train for. A consult could mean one long visit that goes through every medicine, looks at how she walks and gets up from a chair, checks memory and mood, and asks what she most wants to keep doing. The result is a written plan her own doctor can carry out.

If memory is the main worry, read our guide to getting a dementia diagnosis.

You don't always need a geriatrician for life. Sometimes one good assessment changes the whole plan.

Why is it so hard to find a geriatrician?

There are not enough of them. The American Geriatrics Society counts fewer than 7,000 in the United States, and it cites a federal projection of a shortage of 1,740 geriatricians by 2036.

That shapes the search. Practices may have waiting lists or take only patients over a certain age. Widen the net. Ask about geriatric nurse practitioners, who can examine, diagnose, treat and prescribe. Ask whether a geriatrics practice takes consult referrals even if it is not taking new primary care patients. And if your parent loves their current doctor, a good internist who listens may serve better than a long wait.

While you look, ask the current doctor two things. Can the office send a referral to a geriatrics practice for a one-time assessment? And can it schedule a longer visit to go over every medicine and every specialist's plan? One longer, focused visit with the doctor your parent already has can do much of the work. Write down the questions ahead of time and send them through the patient portal so the doctor sees them before you arrive.

How do I find a geriatrician in New Jersey?

Use two free directories, then call. Medicare's Care Compare lists doctors who take Medicare. The American Geriatrics Society's HealthinAging site lists members.

  1. Search Care Compare. On Medicare Care Compare, choose Doctors and clinicians, enter your parent's ZIP code and search for geriatric medicine. Note practices within a drive your parent can manage.
  2. Check the society's directory. The HealthinAging directory lists American Geriatrics Society members. It is not an endorsement. Search by state first for the most results. You can also call 800-563-4916 to have a list mailed.
  3. Call the hospital system. Ask the main line of the hospital your parent uses whether it has a geriatrics practice or senior care center, and how referrals work.
  4. Check the plan. If your parent has Medicare Advantage, confirm the doctor is in network before booking. Advantage plans can change their networks each year, so check again every fall.
  5. Check the license. New Jersey's Health Care Profile, linked from the State Board of Medical Examiners, has information on doctors licensed in the state. The Division of Consumer Affairs also runs a free online license verification.

When you call, ask "Are you taking new Medicare patients?" Medicare notes that a practice may treat someone as new if they haven't been seen there in three years, so even a former patient should ask.

What does Medicare pay for a geriatrician?

Part B covers medically necessary doctor visits the same way for geriatricians and other doctors. After the Part B deductible, $283 in 2026, your parent usually pays 20% of the Medicare-approved amount.

How much more depends on how the doctor works with Medicare.

Doctor's statusWhat it means
Accepts assignmentCharges only the deductible and coinsurance
Non-participatingCan charge up to 15% more in most cases
Opted outMedicare pays nothing except emergencies

Most doctors accept assignment, but ask. Some practices charge a yearly membership fee on top of visits. Ask what the fee covers and whether the doctor still bills Medicare. If a doctor has opted out, your parent would sign a private contract and pay the full cost. Medicare suggests calling your State Health Insurance Assistance Program first. In New Jersey that is SHIP at 1-800-792-8820.

A Medigap plan or Medicaid may cover the 20%. Two Medicare services are worth asking a new practice about. The yearly Wellness visit includes a cognitive check and a review of medicines, explained in Medicare 101. Chronic care management, for people with two or more serious chronic conditions, pays a practice to keep a care plan and coordinate with other providers. Our guide to managing many medications has more.

Can a doctor come to my parent's home?

Yes, when it is medically necessary. Medicare Part B pays for home visits by doctors and qualified nurse practitioners and physician assistants, and your parent does not have to be homebound.

The rules come from Medicare's billing guidance. The visit must be medically reasonable and necessary, and the doctor must be there in person. It counts as a doctor visit, so the usual Part B cost sharing applies. It is different from Medicare home health care, which sends nurses and therapists and does require homebound status. Home visits can also happen in assisted living.

House-call practices are often run by doctors, nurse practitioners or physician assistants focused on people who can't easily get to an office. Ask the primary care office, the hospital's geriatrics program or the Medicare Advantage plan who makes home visits in your parent's town. Ask the same questions you would of any practice: Medicare assignment, after-hours coverage and which hospital they use. If getting to appointments is the problem, our guide to rides to medical appointments lists county options.

What should we ask and bring to the first visit?

Bring every pill bottle, a short list of your top three worries, and a family member who can take notes. Ask how the practice handles calls, refills and hospital stays.

  • Who covers nights and weekends, and can family call with questions?
  • How fast can a sick visit be booked?
  • Does the doctor see patients in the hospital, rehab or at home?
  • Is there a social worker or nurse care manager on the team?
  • Will you talk with my parent about goals and future care wishes?

Before the visit, ask the office for the form that lets the doctor share information with you. Bring copies of any advance directive or power of attorney. Our emergency info sheet doubles as a one-page summary for a new doctor. If your parent needs someone to coordinate care between visits, a geriatric care manager plays a different role from the doctor.

Free help with Medicare questions

NJ SHIP counselors can explain assignment, Advantage networks and private contracts at 1-800-792-8820. Medicare: 1-800-633-4227. American Geriatrics Society directory by mail: 800-563-4916.

faq.q: How do I find a geriatrician for my mom in New Jersey?
faq.a: Search Medicare Care Compare for doctors listing geriatric medicine near her ZIP code, check the American Geriatrics Society's HealthinAging directory, and call the hospital system she uses to ask about its geriatrics practice. Then ask each office if it takes new Medicare patients.

faq.q: Does Medicare cover a geriatrician?
faq.a: Yes. Part B covers medically necessary visits with a geriatrician like any other doctor. After the deductible ($283 in 2026), your parent usually pays 20% of the Medicare-approved amount if the doctor accepts assignment.

faq.q: At what age should someone see a geriatrician?
faq.a: There is no set age. The American Geriatrics Society suggests one when health problems cause frailty or disability, when memory or mood changes appear, when many specialists are involved, or when caregivers are under strain. These patients tend to be over 75.

faq.q: Will Medicare pay for a doctor to visit my dad at home?
faq.a: Yes, when the visit is medically necessary. Part B pays for home visits by doctors and qualified nurse practitioners and physician assistants. Your dad does not have to be homebound, and regular Part B cost sharing applies.

faq.q: What if no geriatrician near us is taking new patients?
faq.a: Ask whether the practice does one-time consults while your parent keeps a regular doctor, ask about geriatric nurse practitioners, and consider a primary care doctor with a strong record caring for older adults.

faq.q: How do I check a New Jersey doctor's license?
faq.a: Use the New Jersey Health Care Profile linked from the State Board of Medical Examiners, or the state's free online license verification. Both are run by the NJ Division of Consumer Affairs.

title: Leqembi and Kisunla in NJ: new Alzheimer's drugs and Medicare
dek: Who qualifies for the new anti-amyloid Alzheimer's drugs, what Medicare's registry rule means for your parent, the ARIA risk and MRI schedule, list prices, and the questions to ask a New Jersey memory specialist.
keyFacts: Leqembi and Kisunla are for mild cognitive impairment or mild dementia due to Alzheimer's, with amyloid confirmed by a test.
Medicare Part B covers them when the doctor reports to a CMS-approved registry. You pay 20% after the $283 deductible (2026).
Both carry a boxed warning for ARIA, brain swelling or small bleeds, so regular brain MRIs are required.
Since July 2026, Leqembi can be started with a weekly shot at home after at least two supervised doses.
Alzheimer's Association 24/7 Helpline: 1-800-272-3900.
body:
Leqembi (lecanemab) and Kisunla (donanemab) are the two drugs the FDA has approved that go after the disease process in early Alzheimer's, not only the symptoms. Both are antibodies that clear amyloid, a sticky protein that builds up in the brain. They are meant for people with mild cognitive impairment or mild dementia due to Alzheimer's, and a test has to confirm amyloid first. Neither one cures the disease or brings back lost memory. In the main trials, decline on a standard rating scale was 27% slower with Leqembi and 29% slower with Kisunla than with a placebo over about 18 months.

Medicare Part B covers both drugs for people who qualify, as long as the prescribing doctor reports on the treatment to a registry approved by the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS). After the Part B deductible ($283 in 2026), your parent pays 20% of the Medicare-approved amount. The harder parts are a side effect called ARIA, the brain MRIs needed to watch for it, and finding a specialist team that offers the drugs. This guide is general information, not medical advice. Only your parent's doctors can say whether a drug fits.

What are Leqembi and Kisunla?

They are lab-made antibodies, given by infusion or injection, that bind to amyloid and help the body clear it. The FDA labels say treatment should start only in the mild cognitive impairment or mild dementia stage, the group studied in the trials.

The older Alzheimer's pills, such as donepezil, help manage some symptoms, according to the National Institute on Aging (NIA). People in the Leqembi trials could keep taking them.

LeqembiKisunla
MakerEisai, with BiogenEli Lilly
First approved20232024
How it is givenIV about 1 hour, or a shot at homeIV about 30 minutes
How oftenIV every 2 weeks, or a shot every weekEvery 4 weeks
After 18 monthsCan move to IV every 4 weeks or a smaller weekly shotDoctor may stop sooner, once a PET scan shows amyloid is very low
MRI checksBefore starting, then after 1, 2, 3 and 6 monthsBefore starting, then before infusions 2, 3, 4 and 7

Two recent changes matter. In July 2026 the FDA approved the Leqembi Iqlik autoinjector as a starting dose, so a person can begin treatment with weekly shots at home instead of infusions every two weeks. The label says a health care provider must guide at least the first two shots and then decide whether your parent or a caregiver can give them. And in July 2025, Kisunla's label switched to a slower dose build-up over the first three infusions because it led to less ARIA.

Kisunla has a planned stopping point. In its main trial, 47% of people had amyloid low enough to stop by week 52 and 69% by week 76.

Who can get these drugs?

A person qualifies only if a doctor diagnoses mild cognitive impairment or mild dementia due to Alzheimer's and a test confirms amyloid in the brain. People in moderate or later stages were not studied and are not candidates.

Amyloid can be confirmed in three ways. A PET scan shows it directly. A spinal tap measures it in spinal fluid. And in May 2025 the FDA cleared the first blood test for this, the Lumipulse G pTau217/Beta-Amyloid 1-42 Plasma Ratio, for adults 55 and older with symptoms who are seen in a specialty setting. The FDA says it is not a stand-alone test. Results must be read alongside other clinical information.

The doctor will also bring up a gene test for ApoE4. Both labels say ApoE4 testing should be done before treatment, after a conversation about what the results mean. About 15% of people with Alzheimer's carry two copies of the gene, and they have a higher rate of ARIA, including serious ARIA. In the Leqembi trial, people with two copies did not show a benefit on the main rating scale, although some other measures favored the drug. A person can still be treated without the test, but then nobody knows whether they are in the higher-risk group.

Some people face extra risk. The Leqembi label urges caution for people who need blood thinners. In its trial, 2.5% of people taking Leqembi with an anticoagulant had a bleed in the brain, compared with none on placebo. MRI signs of earlier tiny bleeds also raise the risk of ARIA. Make sure the specialist has your parent's full medication list, including aspirin.

What is ARIA, and how risky is it?

ARIA stands for amyloid-related imaging abnormalities. It means swelling (ARIA-E) or small bleeds (ARIA-H) in the brain that show up on an MRI. It usually causes no symptoms and fades, but it can be serious and, rarely, fatal, which is why both drugs carry a boxed warning.

In the trialsLeqembiKisunla
Any ARIA on MRI21% (placebo 9%)29%*
ARIA with symptoms3%3% swelling with symptoms*
Brain bleed over 1 cm0.7% (placebo 0.1%)1%*

*Kisunla figures come from the label's study of the current, slower dosing schedule, through 12 months. Under the original dosing in its main trial, ARIA showed up in 36% of people, compared with 14% on placebo.

The labels list headache, confusion, vision changes, dizziness, nausea and trouble walking as possible ARIA symptoms. Seizures can happen.

Tell the ER about the drug

ARIA swelling can look like a stroke. The labels warn doctors to think about ARIA before giving a clot-busting drug. If your parent is on Leqembi or Kisunla and has sudden symptoms, call 911 and tell the ER team the drug's name right away. Keep the name, dose and the specialist's phone number on a card in your parent's wallet. For the warning signs of stroke, see our stroke signs guide.

Does Medicare cover Leqembi and Kisunla?

Yes, under Part B, for people with Medicare who meet the medical criteria and whose doctor takes part in a CMS-approved registry or study. Your parent pays 20% of the Medicare-approved amount after the Part B deductible.

The registry rule comes from CMS's national coverage decision for this group of drugs. In practice it falls on the doctor, not the family. Under the CMS National Patient Registry, the prescribing clinician or staff submit information when treatment starts and then every six months for up to 24 months. CMS also lists other approved studies, including the Alzheimer's Association's ALZ-NET registry. When you call a practice, ask plainly, "Do you submit to the CMS registry for these drugs?" If the answer is no, Medicare will not pay there.

Plan on other costs too. Medicare.gov notes that the scans and tests before and during treatment can add to the bill. CT, MRI and PET scans fall under Part B at 20% after the deductible, and a hospital outpatient department may charge a separate copayment. For amyloid PET, CMS ended its national one-scan-per-lifetime limit in October 2023 and left coverage to the regional Medicare contractors, so ask before the scan whether it will be covered.

Other coverage changes the math:

  • Medigap. A Medigap plan or other secondary insurance can pick up some or all of the 20% Part B share, depending on the plan. Our guide to Medigap plans in New Jersey explains which plans cover what.
  • Medicare Advantage. Call the plan for cost details. Ask about prior approval, which infusion sites and MRI centers are in network, and the copay for each.
  • The at-home shot. Eisai says Leqembi Iqlik counts toward the Part D yearly out-of-pocket cap, which is $2,100 in 2026 and $2,400 in 2027. Medicare.gov also says that if someone does not meet the Part B criteria, a Part D plan might cover the drug. Check your parent's drug plan list during open enrollment. Our Part D 2027 guide covers the cap.

For free plan help, call New Jersey SHIP at 1-800-792-8820.

What do Leqembi and Kisunla cost?

At list price, treatment runs roughly $20,000 to $40,000 a year depending on the drug and dose. What your parent actually pays depends on Medicare, supplemental coverage and help programs.

Drug and doseList price
Leqembi IV, every 2 weeks$28,270 a year for a 165 lb person
Leqembi Iqlik start, weekly$770 a week ($60,060 over 18 months)
Leqembi Iqlik upkeep, weekly$385 a week ($20,020 a year)
Kisunla, every 4 weeks$731.49 per vial; a full 1,400 mg dose uses 4 vials

Leqembi prices are Eisai's list prices as of July 2026. IV Leqembi is dosed by weight, so the yearly cost changes with your parent's weight. The Kisunla price is Lilly's list price per 350 mg vial, as of October 1, 2026, which works out to about $2,926 for each full-dose infusion. List prices leave out infusion fees, MRIs and other tests.

Both companies run support programs. Eisai's Leqembi Companion program (1-833-453-7362) helps with insurance questions, and Eisai has a patient assistance program for eligible uninsured patients. Lilly Support Services is at 1-800-545-5979, and the Lilly Cares Foundation (1-800-545-6962) helps qualified people get Lilly medicines at no cost. Eisai's copay card is not valid for people on Medicare. If your parent has trouble with drug plan costs, New Jersey's PAAD program may help those under its income limits.

How does a New Jersey family get started?

Start with a firm diagnosis and a referral to a memory specialist, usually a neurologist or a hospital memory center, that already gives these drugs. Your parent's primary care doctor can make the referral.

  1. Get the diagnosis pinned down. Treatment requires mild cognitive impairment or mild dementia due to Alzheimer's. Our guide to getting a dementia diagnosis in New Jersey walks through the tests.
  2. Ask for a memory specialist who offers anti-amyloid treatment. Not every neurologist does. The Alzheimer's Association 24/7 Helpline at 1-800-272-3900 and Alzheimer's New Jersey at 1-888-280-6055 can talk through options and local resources.
  3. Expect screening visits. These include an amyloid test, a baseline MRI, a talk about ApoE4 testing and a review of medicines.
  4. Map the logistics. Find out where the infusions or first shots happen, where the MRIs are done and how far that is from home.
  5. Check costs before the first dose. Call the Medicare plan or Medigap insurer, and ask the practice's billing office what your parent will owe for each infusion and scan.

Questions worth asking the specialist:

  • Do you submit to the CMS registry or another CMS-approved study?
  • Which drug would you suggest for my mom, and why?
  • Where are infusions given, and could she use the at-home shot instead?
  • Who do we call at night or on weekends if she has a headache or new confusion?
  • Are there clinical trials she could join instead or as well?

For trials, Alzheimer's New Jersey runs a Clinical Trial Connections program, and the NIA's ADEAR Center (1-800-438-4380) can help families find studies.

How do we decide whether it is worth it?

It is a personal call that weighs a modest slowing of decline against real risk, frequent visits and cost. Yes and no can both be reasonable.

IV Leqembi means a trip every two weeks for 18 months, plus at least five MRIs in the first six months, counting the baseline scan. Kisunla means a monthly trip, and it may stop sooner. The at-home Leqembi shot cuts travel but needs someone steady enough to give a weekly injection and spot an allergic reaction. If your parent no longer drives, line up rides early. Our guide to rides to medical appointments lists options by county.

Whatever you choose, the steps that matter for every diagnosis still apply. Get legal papers signed while your parent can take part (see estate planning basics), and lean on the support listed in our guide to life after a dementia diagnosis.

The drug decision belongs to your parent and the doctor. Your job is to make sure the right questions get asked.

faq.q: Does Medicare pay for Leqembi or Kisunla for my mom?
faq.a: Yes, if she has mild cognitive impairment or mild dementia due to Alzheimer's, a test confirms amyloid, and her doctor takes part in a CMS-approved registry or study. Part B pays the rest after she meets the deductible ($283 in 2026) and pays 20% of the Medicare-approved amount. MRIs and other tests are billed separately.

faq.q: What is the Medicare registry for Alzheimer's drugs?
faq.a: It is a data collection program that CMS requires for coverage. The prescribing clinician or staff submit information when treatment starts and every six months for up to 24 months. Families do not fill anything out, but the doctor must participate, so ask before you book.

faq.q: Can Leqembi be given at home?
faq.a: Yes. In July 2026 the FDA approved Leqembi Iqlik, a weekly autoinjector, as a starting dose. A health care provider must guide at least the first two shots, then decides whether the patient or a caregiver can give them at home. MRI checks are still required.

faq.q: How do I know if my dad is a candidate for the new Alzheimer's drugs?
faq.a: He needs a diagnosis of mild cognitive impairment or mild dementia due to Alzheimer's and a confirmed amyloid test, such as a PET scan, spinal fluid test or an FDA-cleared blood test. A memory specialist also weighs his MRI, his medicines (especially blood thinners) and ApoE4 status. Ask his primary care doctor for a referral.

faq.q: What are the warning signs of ARIA?
faq.a: The labels list headache, confusion, vision changes, dizziness, nausea and trouble walking. Seizures can occur. Most ARIA causes no symptoms and is found on scheduled MRIs. Call the specialist about any new symptom, and call 911 for sudden stroke-like symptoms, telling the ER which drug your parent takes.

faq.q: Do Leqembi and Kisunla cure Alzheimer's?
faq.a: No. They clear amyloid and, in trials, slowed decline on a rating scale by 27% (Leqembi) and 29% (Kisunla) compared with placebo over about 18 months. They do not stop the disease or restore memory.

title: Getting a dementia diagnosis in New Jersey: the steps
dek: How a dementia evaluation works, from the first doctor visit to brain scans and specialists, what Original Medicare pays for each test, the closest research centers to New Jersey, and how to prepare your mom or dad.
keyFacts: Most dementia evaluations start with the primary care doctor and include a history, memory tests, lab work and often a brain scan.
Original Medicare: covered lab tests usually $0; CT, MRI and PET scans 20% after the $283 Part B deductible (2026).
New Jersey has no NIA-funded Alzheimer's Disease Research Center. The closest are three in New York City and one in Philadelphia.
The NIA estimates 10% to 20% of people 65 and older with mild cognitive impairment develop dementia over a year.
NIA ADEAR Center for questions and referrals: 1-800-438-4380.
body:
Getting a dementia diagnosis in New Jersey usually starts with your parent's primary care doctor and, for many families, continues with a neurologist, geriatrician or memory center. The National Institute on Aging (NIA) says doctors ask the person and a family member about health and daily life, test memory and thinking, order blood and urine tests, check for depression and may order brain scans. It often takes more than one visit. Several causes of memory trouble can be treated, so the first goal is to rule those out.

Original Medicare covers the main steps. Medically necessary lab tests usually cost nothing, and CT, MRI and PET scans cost 20% of the Medicare-approved amount after the Part B deductible ($283 in 2026). New Jersey has no NIA-funded Alzheimer's Disease Research Center, but four are within reach in New York City and Philadelphia. This guide covers the evaluation itself. If your parent has not had a memory screening yet, start with our guide to free memory screening in NJ. This is general information, not medical advice.

Where do we start for a dementia diagnosis?

With your parent's own primary care doctor. That doctor knows the medical history and medicines, can order the first round of tests and can refer to a specialist.

Book a visit that is only about memory and thinking. A rushed appointment about blood pressure leaves no time. When you call, say what you have noticed and ask for a longer slot if the office offers one. If your parent has not had a Medicare cognitive assessment, ask about it. Our memory screening guide explains what Medicare covers for that visit.

You can share your worries with the office before the visit. A short letter or portal message listing what you have seen gives the doctor a head start, especially if your parent tends to say everything is fine. To hear back, though, you need your parent's permission. Medicare's fact sheet for family caregivers says the doctor must get the patient's permission to talk with you, and the office can tell you how to set that up. Separately, your parent can name you on the Medicare "Authorization to Disclose Personal Health Information" form (CMS-10106) so 1-800-MEDICARE can talk with you about claims.

If your parent refuses to go, our memory screening guide has ideas drawn from Alzheimer's New Jersey's advice, and how to start the conversation about care helps with the bigger talk.

What tests are part of a dementia evaluation?

A full evaluation pairs a careful history with memory tests, lab work and often a brain scan. Doctors use the results to rule out other causes and to tell which type of dementia, if any, is present.

StepWhat it showsOriginal Medicare cost
History and examMedicine side effects, other illness, how daily life has changedOffice visit; 20% after deductible
Memory and thinking testsWhich skills are affected and how muchPart of the visit
Blood and urine testsThyroid, vitamin, kidney or liver problems, infectionUsually $0
Mood checkDepression or anxiety that can cloud thinkingPart of the visit
CT or MRIStroke, tumor, fluid buildup, shrinkage20% after deductible
PET scanBrain activity or amyloid20% after deductible; check coverage first
Spinal fluid or blood biomarkersAmyloid and tau proteins linked to Alzheimer'sAsk before the test

A few notes on the newer tests. In May 2025 the FDA cleared the first blood test to help diagnose Alzheimer's, the Lumipulse G pTau217/Beta-Amyloid 1-42 Plasma Ratio. It is for adults 55 and older with symptoms who are seen in a specialty setting, and the FDA says it is not a stand-alone test. The NIA says blood test results alone should not be used to diagnose dementia. For amyloid PET, CMS dropped its national one-scan limit in October 2023 and now leaves coverage to regional Medicare contractors, so ask the office to confirm coverage first.

Gene tests come up less often. The NIA says a few rare forms of dementia are caused by specific genes, and it recommends talking with a genetic counselor before and after testing. Risk-gene tests such as ApoE4 cannot diagnose dementia.

The NIA also notes that some tests may not be covered by every insurer. If your parent has a Medicare Advantage plan, call the plan before each scan. For hospital outpatient scans, Medicare.gov says your parent may owe the hospital a copayment, and that advanced imaging done outside a hospital must come from an accredited provider.

Which kind of specialist should my parent see?

A neurologist is the most common choice. Geriatricians, geriatric psychiatrists and neuropsychologists also diagnose dementia, and memory centers bring several of them together.

  • Neurologist. A doctor for the brain and nervous system who can conduct and review brain scans.
  • Geriatrician. A doctor for older adults who knows how the body changes with age and whether symptoms point to a serious problem.
  • Geriatric psychiatrist. Specializes in the mental and emotional problems of older adults and can assess memory and thinking.
  • Neuropsychologist. Gives detailed tests of memory and thinking, which can be repeated later to track change.
  • Memory clinic or center. A team at a hospital or medical school, usually with scanning on site.

With Original Medicare, your parent can see any specialist who accepts Medicare. Medicare Advantage plans often require in-network doctors and sometimes a referral, so check first. If you cannot find a specialist nearby, the NIA suggests calling the neurology department at the nearest medical school.

The NIA also funds Alzheimer's Disease Research Centers, which can help with diagnosis and care. None is in New Jersey. These are the closest, from the NIA directory:

CenterCityPhone
Columbia UniversityNew York212-305-2447
Icahn School of Medicine at Mount SinaiNew York212-241-8329
NYU LangoneNew York212-263-8088
University of PennsylvaniaPhiladelphia215-349-8226

These centers focus on research, so ask what clinical services they offer and whether they take your parent's insurance. If your parent might want to try the new Alzheimer's drugs, ask any specialist whether they offer them. See our guide to Leqembi and Kisunla.

How long does a dementia diagnosis take?

There is no set timeline. It usually takes more than one visit, since lab results, a scan and a specialist appointment each take time, and some answers only come from watching how things change.

The NIA says doctors may repeat tests to see how memory and thinking change over time, and that people with memory problems should return every six to 12 months. Specialist waits can be long, so get your parent's name on a list as soon as there is a referral. Ask to be called if an earlier slot opens, and ask whether the practice offers telehealth for follow-up talks.

While you wait, keep notes. Write down dates and examples: a missed bill, a pot left on the stove, getting lost on the way to ShopRite. Notes beat memory at the appointment, and they help the doctor see a pattern.

Call the doctor promptly, without waiting for the specialist, if confusion comes on suddenly over hours or days. The NIA lists delirium, infections and medication side effects among the causes of dementia-like symptoms, and these need quick care.

How do I prepare my mom for the appointment?

Bring a written timeline of changes, every medicine she takes and someone who knows her well. Make sure she can see and hear clearly so the tests measure her thinking and not her eyesight.

  1. Write one page of changes. When they started, what they look like, and whether they are getting worse. The NIA says doctors ask about daily activities, behavior and personality, so include those.
  2. Gather every medicine. Bring the bottles or a full list, including over-the-counter sleep aids, allergy pills and supplements. Some can affect memory.
  3. Bring glasses and hearing aids. Hearing loss can make memory tests look worse. See our guide on hearing loss and dementia risk.
  4. Collect past records. Earlier scans, hospital discharge papers and a list of other doctors save repeat testing.
  5. Sort out permission. Ask the office how your mom can give the doctor permission to talk with you, and do it before the visit.
  6. Plan the day. Pick a time when she is usually at her best, arrange the ride and plan something pleasant afterward.

Questions to bring:

  • Is this mild cognitive impairment, dementia or something else?
  • What type do you think it is, and how sure are you?
  • What else could be causing it, and have we ruled those out?
  • What tests come next, and what will they cost?
  • Should she see a specialist, and whom do you recommend?
  • Is it still safe for her to drive, cook and handle money?
  • Are there treatments or clinical trials that might fit?
  • When should we come back, and what should make us call sooner?

What do the results mean?

The answer may be mild cognitive impairment, a specific type of dementia, or another cause that can be treated. Each one leads to different next steps.

Mild cognitive impairment (MCI) means more memory or thinking trouble than is usual for someone's age, while the person can still handle daily life. The NIA estimates that 10% to 20% of people 65 and older with MCI develop dementia over a year. Many do not, and some stay the same or improve. The NIA advises a check every six to 12 months.

Dementia means thinking problems that get in the way of daily life. The NIA lists several types: Alzheimer's disease (the most common), vascular dementia, Lewy body dementia, frontotemporal dementia and mixed dementia. The type matters because it shapes treatment and what to expect. Some doctors describe Alzheimer's as "possible" or "probable" because no single test is perfect.

A treatable cause may turn up instead. The NIA names medication side effects, vitamin shortfalls, thyroid, kidney or liver problems, depression and normal pressure hydrocephalus, which often improves with treatment.

If the diagnosis is dementia, ask the doctor about Medicare's cognitive assessment and care plan visit, and whether the practice takes part in CMS's GUIDE Model. GUIDE, which began in July 2024, offers care navigation, a 24/7 support line, caregiver training and up to $2,500 a year in respite for eligible people with Original Medicare. Then turn to our guide on where New Jersey families can turn after a diagnosis. Get legal papers in place while your parent can still take part. Our guides to power of attorney and estate planning explain the documents. A geriatric care manager can help coordinate the appointments if you live far away.

A clear diagnosis gives your family a map for the next stretch of the road.

faq.q: How do I get my mom evaluated for dementia in New Jersey?
faq.a: Book a visit with her primary care doctor that is only about memory, and bring a written list of changes and all her medicines. The doctor can order blood tests and a brain scan and refer her to a neurologist, geriatrician or memory center. Ask how she can give the doctor permission to talk with you.

faq.q: What kind of doctor diagnoses dementia?
faq.a: Primary care doctors often start the process. Neurologists are the most common specialists, and geriatricians, geriatric psychiatrists and neuropsychologists also diagnose dementia. Memory clinics at hospitals and medical schools bring these specialists together.

faq.q: Does Medicare pay for dementia testing?
faq.a: Yes, when the tests are medically necessary. Medicare-covered lab tests usually cost nothing. CT, MRI and PET scans cost 20% of the Medicare-approved amount after the Part B deductible, and hospital outpatient scans may add a copayment. Ask before newer tests such as amyloid PET or blood biomarkers.

faq.q: Is there an Alzheimer's Disease Research Center in New Jersey?
faq.a: No. The closest NIA-funded centers are at Columbia University, Mount Sinai and NYU Langone in New York City, and the University of Pennsylvania in Philadelphia. Ask each about clinical services and insurance.

faq.q: Can a blood test diagnose dementia?
faq.a: Not by itself. The FDA cleared the first blood test to help detect Alzheimer's-related amyloid in May 2025, for adults 55 and older with symptoms seen in specialty care. The NIA says blood test results alone should not be used to diagnose dementia.

faq.q: What should I do if my dad suddenly becomes confused?
faq.a: Call his doctor right away, or 911 if it is severe or comes with other stroke signs. Sudden confusion over hours or days can come from delirium, an infection or a medication problem, which need quick care and are different from the slow changes of dementia.

title: Parkinson's disease resources in New Jersey
dek: The New Jersey APDA center, the Parkinson's Foundation Helpline and nearby Centers of Excellence, what Medicare covers for therapy and deep brain stimulation, help for veterans, and safety steps for families.
keyFacts: APDA NJ Information and Referral Center, Rutgers Robert Wood Johnson Medical School, New Brunswick: 732-235-5012.
Parkinson's Foundation Helpline: 1-800-473-4636, weekdays 9 a.m. to 7 p.m. ET, English and Spanish.
Medicare covers outpatient physical, occupational and speech therapy with no yearly limit when medically necessary.
Medicare covers deep brain stimulation for advanced, levodopa-responsive Parkinson's that meets set criteria.
The VA treats Parkinson's as a presumptive condition for Agent Orange exposure.
body:
New Jersey families dealing with Parkinson's disease have two main places to start. The American Parkinson Disease Association (APDA) runs an Information and Referral Center for New Jersey at Rutgers Robert Wood Johnson Medical School in New Brunswick, at 732-235-5012. The Parkinson's Foundation Helpline, 1-800-473-4636 (1-800-4PD-INFO), answers questions and gives referrals to specialists, support groups and exercise programs in English and Spanish. Both are free.

Medicare Part B covers physical, occupational and speech therapy with no yearly dollar limit when it is medically necessary, including therapy to maintain function or slow decline. It also covers deep brain stimulation surgery for people who meet set criteria. The Parkinson's Foundation chapter that covers New Jersey lists two Centers of Excellence, both in Philadelphia. Veterans exposed to Agent Orange may qualify for VA benefits, because the VA treats Parkinson's as a presumptive condition. This guide is general information, not medical advice.

Who can help a New Jersey family with Parkinson's?

Start with the APDA center in New Brunswick for New Jersey referrals, and the Parkinson's Foundation Helpline for questions about treatment and daily life. Both can point you to support groups near you.

WhoWhat they offerPhone
APDA NJ Information and Referral CenterLocal referrals, support groups, education732-235-5012
APDA national officeInformation and programs1-800-223-2732
Parkinson's Foundation HelplineAnswers, specialist and group referrals; weekdays 9 a.m. to 7 p.m. ET1-800-473-4636
VA Philadelphia PADRECCSpecialty care for enrolled veterans215-823-5934
NJ ADRCYour county office on aging1-877-222-3737

The APDA center sits at 125 Paterson Street in New Brunswick, inside Rutgers Robert Wood Johnson Medical School. APDA says its services include education, support groups, exercise and wellness classes, information and referrals, and financial support programs. The center also houses APDA's Center for Advanced Parkinson Disease Research. Call or email apda@rwjms.rutgers.edu and ask what is running near your parent's town.

The Parkinson's Foundation Helpline is staffed by information specialists from several health professions. They can search the foundation's database for doctors trained in Parkinson's, support groups and Parkinson's-focused exercise programs nearby, and mail or email information packets. Press 3 for Spanish. The foundation does not give financial aid, but its specialists can refer you to groups that help with medicine, rides and respite.

For a wider list of caregiver groups, including ones for spouses, see our guide to caregiver support groups in New Jersey.

What kind of doctor should treat Parkinson's?

A neurologist, ideally a movement disorders specialist, a neurologist with extra training in Parkinson's and similar conditions. Many families keep the primary care doctor for everything else and see the specialist a few times a year.

Getting the diagnosis right matters. The National Institute on Aging (NIA) says there is no blood or lab test for most Parkinson's. Doctors diagnose it from the history and a neurological exam, and improvement on medicine is another clue. Conditions such as multiple system atrophy and dementia with Lewy bodies can look like Parkinson's at first but need different care. If the diagnosis feels uncertain or the medicine is not helping, a second opinion from a movement disorders specialist is reasonable.

The Parkinson's Foundation designates Centers of Excellence, typically at academic medical centers, where a movement disorders neurologist leads a team. Its New Jersey and Pennsylvania chapter lists two: the University of Pennsylvania Movement Disorders Center and Jefferson Health's Comprehensive Parkinson's Disease and Movement Disorder Center, both in Philadelphia. For North Jersey families, or to find a specialist closer to home, use the foundation's Find Care search or ask the Helpline.

Questions to ask a new specialist:

  • How sure are you that this is Parkinson's and not a related condition?
  • Do you work with physical, occupational and speech therapists who know Parkinson's?
  • Who do we call between visits if a medicine stops working or causes side effects?
  • Should we watch for memory, mood or sleep changes, and who treats those?
  • When would deep brain stimulation or other advanced treatments make sense?
  • Are there clinical trials my dad could join?

What does Medicare cover for Parkinson's?

Original Medicare covers specialist visits, outpatient therapy and home health care for people who qualify, and Part D drug plans cover prescriptions. For therapy and doctor visits, your parent pays 20% of the Medicare-approved amount after the Part B deductible ($283 in 2026).

  • Physical therapy. Medicare.gov says therapy can restore movement or "improve or maintain your current function, or slow your rate of decline." That wording matters for a disease that changes over years. A doctor, nurse practitioner, clinical nurse specialist or physician assistant must certify the need.
  • Occupational therapy. Help with dressing, bathing, cooking and setting up the home.
  • Speech-language therapy. Medicare covers therapy for speech, swallowing and thinking skills. The NIA lists speaking too softly and trouble swallowing among the symptoms of Parkinson's.
  • No yearly cap. Medicare.gov says there is no limit on how much Medicare pays for medically necessary outpatient therapy in a calendar year.
  • Home health. If your parent is homebound, Medicare may cover therapy and nursing at home. See Medicare home health care in NJ.
  • Medicines. Parkinson's drugs go through Part D. The yearly out-of-pocket cap on covered drugs is $2,100 in 2026 and $2,400 in 2027. New Jersey's PAAD program can lower copays for people under its income limits.

If your parent has a Medicare Advantage plan, check its network and approval rules for therapy. For free help with a plan question or a denied claim, call New Jersey SHIP at 1-800-792-8820.

Never stop levodopa suddenly

The NIA warns that people with Parkinson's should never stop taking levodopa without telling their doctor. Stopping suddenly can cause serious problems, such as being unable to move or trouble breathing. Before any hospital stay or surgery, make sure the team knows the exact medicine schedule. The Parkinson's Foundation Helpline at 1-800-473-4636 can send its free Hospital Safety Guide.

Does Medicare cover deep brain stimulation?

Yes, for people who meet the criteria in Medicare's national coverage decision. Deep brain stimulation, or DBS, places thin wires in the brain connected to a device in the chest, and the NIA says it can ease tremor, slowness and stiffness for people who no longer respond well to medicine alone.

For the most common Parkinson's DBS targets, Medicare's policy requires all of the following:

  • A Parkinson's diagnosis based on at least two main features: tremor, rigidity or slowness.
  • Advanced Parkinson's, measured on standard rating scales.
  • A clear response to levodopa, with well-defined "on" periods.
  • Disabling symptoms or drug side effects, such as unwanted movements or "off" periods, despite the best medical treatment.
  • Willingness and ability to cooperate during surgery and with follow-up adjustments.

Medicare does not cover DBS for "Parkinson's plus" syndromes, or when dementia, depression or other thinking problems would get worse from the surgery or keep the person from benefiting. Current psychosis or substance abuse also rules it out. The policy requires experienced neurosurgeons, and a movement disorders specialist must take part in choosing patients and in care after surgery. Ask the hospital to explain your parent's share of the cost, and if your parent has an Advantage plan, call the plan before scheduling.

What should veterans with Parkinson's know?

The VA lists Parkinson's disease and parkinsonism as presumptive conditions for Agent Orange exposure. A veteran who served in a qualifying place and time does not have to prove the disease came from service.

Qualifying service includes Vietnam, including its inland waterways and nearby offshore waters, from January 9, 1962, to May 7, 1975. The PACT Act added places such as U.S. or Royal Thai bases in Thailand through June 30, 1976, and Laos from December 1, 1965, to September 30, 1969. Service in or near the Korean DMZ from September 1, 1967, to August 31, 1971 also counts. A veteran files a disability claim with medical records showing the diagnosis and discharge papers such as a DD214. The VA added parkinsonism to the list in 2021, and it says that if it denied a parkinsonism claim in the past, it will review the case again on its own.

For care, the VA runs Parkinson's Disease Research, Education and Clinical Centers, called PADRECCs. The Philadelphia PADRECC (215-823-5934) is the closest to most of New Jersey. A veteran must be enrolled in VA health care, and a VA primary care doctor or neurologist sends the referral. Our veterans benefits guide explains how to enroll and where to get free help with a claim.

How can we keep a parent with Parkinson's safe at home?

Focus on falls, medicine timing and the changes Parkinson's brings beyond movement. Small steps at home and a clear plan for hospital visits prevent many emergencies.

  1. Prevent falls. The NIA lists impaired balance among the four main symptoms. Ask for a physical therapy balance evaluation, and see our fall prevention guide for home changes.
  2. Keep a medicine schedule. Write down every dose and time, and keep a copy in your parent's wallet and on the fridge. Bring it to every hospital and ER visit.
  3. Watch mood, sleep and memory. The NIA says depression, sleep problems and memory difficulties can come with Parkinson's. Tell the doctor about changes, and see our guide to getting a dementia diagnosis if memory slips.
  4. Review driving. Ask the doctor whether Parkinson's symptoms or medicines affect driving. See driving later in life.
  5. Line up help before you need it. As needs grow, aides can help with bathing and dressing. Our guide to home health aides in NJ explains costs and vetting.

Here is a hypothetical. Say your mother in Edison was diagnosed two years ago and has started freezing in doorways. A sensible next round might be a call to the APDA center for local groups, a visit with a movement disorders specialist to adjust medicine, and a Medicare-covered physical therapy evaluation focused on balance and walking. That is three calls, each with a clear purpose.

Parkinson's usually moves slowly, which gives families time to plan. Use that time to put a power of attorney and health care wishes on paper, and to take breaks of your own.

Save two numbers today: 732-235-5012 for New Jersey help and 1-800-473-4636 for answers.

faq.q: Where can I find Parkinson's help for my dad in New Jersey?
faq.a: Call the APDA New Jersey Information and Referral Center at Rutgers Robert Wood Johnson Medical School in New Brunswick at 732-235-5012 for local referrals and support groups. The Parkinson's Foundation Helpline at 1-800-473-4636 answers treatment questions and refers families to specialists, weekdays 9 a.m. to 7 p.m. Eastern.

faq.q: Are there Parkinson's Foundation Centers of Excellence near New Jersey?
faq.a: The Parkinson's Foundation New Jersey and Pennsylvania Chapter lists two Centers of Excellence, the University of Pennsylvania Movement Disorders Center and Jefferson Health's Comprehensive Parkinson's Disease and Movement Disorder Center, both in Philadelphia. The foundation's Helpline can help you find a specialist closer to home.

faq.q: Does Medicare cover physical therapy for Parkinson's?
faq.a: Yes. Part B covers medically necessary outpatient physical, occupational and speech therapy, including therapy to maintain function or slow decline, with no yearly limit. A doctor or other qualified provider must certify the need, and your parent pays 20% of the Medicare-approved amount after the deductible.

faq.q: Does Medicare pay for deep brain stimulation?
faq.a: Yes, for people who meet Medicare's criteria, including advanced Parkinson's that responds to levodopa and disabling symptoms or side effects despite the best medical treatment. It is not covered for Parkinson's plus syndromes or when dementia or depression would interfere with the benefit.

faq.q: How do I get VA benefits for my father's Parkinson's from Agent Orange?
faq.a: The VA treats Parkinson's disease and parkinsonism as presumptive conditions for Agent Orange exposure. If he served in a qualifying place and time, such as Vietnam between January 9, 1962, and May 7, 1975, he can file a disability claim with his diagnosis and discharge papers without proving the disease came from service.

faq.q: Is there a test for Parkinson's disease?
faq.a: For most people, no. The National Institute on Aging says there are no blood or lab tests to diagnose non-genetic Parkinson's. Doctors use the medical history and a neurological exam, and improvement on medicine is another sign.

title: Living with COPD in New Jersey: oxygen, rehab and help
dek: What Medicare pays for pulmonary rehab and home oxygen, where to get free help quitting, how to follow NJ air quality alerts, and support for families.
keyFacts: Medicare Part B covers pulmonary rehab for moderate to very severe COPD. You pay 20% after the $283 deductible (2026).
Rehab: up to 36 sessions, plus 36 more if Medicare's contractor approves.
Home oxygen is rented for 36 months, and the supplier must keep serving your parent for up to 5 years.
NJ Quitline: 1-866-657-8677, free for NJ residents 18 and older.
American Lung Association Lung HelpLine: 1-800-586-4872, press 2.
body:
COPD (chronic obstructive pulmonary disease) has no cure, but living with COPD in New Jersey gets easier with the right help. That means a pulmonary rehab program, oxygen if blood levels run low, free coaching to quit smoking, and a plan for bad air days. Medicare Part B covers pulmonary rehab for moderate to very severe COPD and covers home oxygen when tests show your parent needs it.

This guide is for older adults with COPD and the family members who help them. It explains what Medicare pays for, how the oxygen rental rules work, where New Jersey residents get free help to quit, how to follow the state's air quality forecasts, and when to call the doctor. It is general information. Your mom or dad's lung doctor sets the treatment plan.

What is COPD, and how is it treated?

COPD is a group of lung diseases, mainly emphysema and chronic bronchitis, that block airflow and make breathing hard. Treatment cannot undo the damage, but it can ease symptoms, keep your parent more active and slow the disease.

The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) says nearly 16 million U.S. adults have COPD, and many more don't know they have it. Adults 65 and older are among the groups most likely to have it. Smoking is the main cause, but people who never smoked can get COPD too. Common signs are frequent coughing, wheezing, extra mucus and getting winded during everyday tasks. A breathing test called spirometry measures how much air your parent can breathe in and push out.

The National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute (NHLBI) says treatment depends on how severe the COPD is. Mild COPD may need only a short-acting inhaler, which lasts about 4 to 6 hours. Moderate or severe COPD often calls for daily long-acting inhalers, which last 12 hours or more, sometimes combined with an inhaled steroid. Antibiotics may treat flare-ups caused by infection.

Inhalers are easy to use wrong. NHLBI suggests bringing the inhaler to every visit so the provider can check technique. If your dad has several inhalers and other pills, our guide to managing many medications can help keep them straight.

Vaccines matter more with COPD, because infections can set off flare-ups. NHLBI lists flu, COVID-19 and pneumonia shots, and recommends the RSV vaccine for people 60 and older with COPD. Our guide to vaccines after 65 explains what Medicare covers.

  1. Get the details. Ask how severe the COPD is and for a copy of the spirometry results.
  2. Ask for a rehab referral. Medicare needs a referral from the doctor treating the lung disease.
  3. Get a flare-up plan in writing. Ask which medicines to use, and when to call or go to the emergency room.
  4. Check the inhaler. Have the doctor or pharmacist watch your parent use it.
  5. Catch up on vaccines. Flu, COVID-19, pneumonia and RSV.
  6. Call the NJ Quitline if anyone in the home smokes: 1-866-657-8677.
  7. Sign up for air quality alerts through EnviroFlash.

Does Medicare cover pulmonary rehab for COPD?

Yes. Medicare Part B covers pulmonary rehab for moderate to very severe COPD, which federal rules define as GOLD stages II, III and IV, when the doctor treating the lung disease refers your parent.

Pulmonary rehab is a supervised program of exercise, breathing training and education. Under the federal rule (42 CFR 410.47), every session must include exercise prescribed by a physician. It must also teach breathing management and track progress. A doctor must sign the treatment plan and review it every 30 days.

Medicare covers up to two one-hour sessions a day, for up to 36 sessions over up to 36 weeks. Your parent can get 36 more sessions if Medicare's regional contractor approves them. Medicare also covers pulmonary rehab for people with confirmed or suspected COVID-19 whose breathing symptoms last at least four weeks.

In a doctor's office, your parent pays 20% of the Medicare-approved amount after the Part B deductible, which is $283 in 2026. In a hospital outpatient department, there is also a hospital copayment for each session. A Medigap policy can pick up much of that share. See our Medigap guide. If your parent has a Medicare Advantage plan, call the plan to ask about copays, network programs and any approval it requires first.

To find a program, ask the lung doctor or call the cardiopulmonary rehab department at a nearby hospital. The American Association of Cardiovascular and Pulmonary Rehabilitation keeps an online program directory. Our guide to rides to medical appointments lists county and volunteer options.

Medicare benefitWhat to know
Pulmonary rehab20% after the Part B deductible
Rehab sessionsUp to 36, plus 36 if approved
Home oxygenRented, 20% after the deductible
Oxygen rental36 months, service up to 5 years
Quit-smoking counselingUp to 8 in 12 months, $0
Lung cancer CT scanYearly if eligible, $0

How does Medicare pay for home oxygen?

Part B covers home oxygen when your parent's provider says they aren't getting enough oxygen, oxygen therapy may help, and a blood gas test falls in a set range. Your parent rents the equipment from a supplier enrolled in Medicare and pays 20% of the approved amount after the deductible.

Per Medicare.gov, your parent rents the oxygen equipment for 36 months. The monthly rental covers the equipment, refills of tanks or cylinders, tubing and other supplies, and the servicing needed to keep it working. After 36 months the rental payments stop, but the supplier must keep providing oxygen and equipment for as long as your parent needs it, up to five years from the start.

After the 36 months, if your parent uses a concentrator or a home fill system, there may be a coinsurance charge every six months for maintenance. The supplier can only charge it if they come to the home to inspect and service the equipment. After five years, your parent gets new equipment and a new 36-month cycle begins. It can be the same supplier or a different one.

A few protections are worth knowing. The supplier must give your parent equipment that fits their mobility needs inside and outside the home. The supplier can't switch the type of equipment unless the doctor orders a change. The supplier must also deliver enough oxygen each month. If your mom is running low on refills, call the supplier right away. Before signing up, ask whether the supplier accepts assignment, so your parent isn't billed above Medicare's approved amount.

Oxygen and fire

NHLBI warns that oxygen is a fire risk. No one should smoke, and no flammable materials should be used, near oxygen. Concentrators also need electricity, so plan ahead for storms and outages. See our guide to hurricane and power outage prep for utility medical lists and backup plans.

Where can my parent get free help to quit smoking in NJ?

The NJ Quitline at 1-866-657-8677 (1-866-NJSTOPS) offers free coaching by phone and online to New Jersey residents 18 and older. Medicare also covers up to eight quit-smoking counseling sessions in 12 months, at no cost if the provider accepts assignment.

The CDC says that for smokers with COPD, quitting is the most important part of treatment.

According to the New Jersey Department of Health, people who register with the Quitline get a welcome kit with a quit guide, an online portal to track progress, one-on-one coaching calls, email tips and live chat with a quit coach. The two-call program is meant for people ready to quit within 30 days, and it can be used three times in 12 months. People who qualify and enroll in it can get two free weeks of nicotine patches. The state lists phone hours of Monday to Friday from 8 a.m. to 9 p.m., Saturday from 8 a.m. to 7 p.m. and Sunday from 9 a.m. to 5 p.m., and callers can leave a message at other times. The Quitline's own site says live coaches are available 24/7. You can also enroll at njquitline.org.

The state lists lines in other languages, including Spanish at 1-855-335-3569, Mandarin and Cantonese at 1-800-838-8917, Korean at 1-800-556-5564 and Vietnamese at 1-800-778-8440.

If your parent smoked heavily, ask about lung cancer screening. Medicare covers a yearly low-dose CT scan for people 50 to 77 with no symptoms who smoke now or quit within the last 15 years and have at least a 20 pack-year history. A visit to talk over the risks and benefits comes first. Our cancer support guide covers screening and what Medicare pays for cancer treatment.

How do I keep track of air quality for my dad in New Jersey?

Check the New Jersey Department of Environmental Protection (NJDEP) daily forecast, or sign up for free EnviroFlash alerts by email or text. When the Air Quality Index (AQI) climbs above 100, the air is unhealthy for sensitive groups, which includes people with lung disease.

NJDEP says forecasts usually come out in the afternoon for the next day, covering ozone and fine particle pollution. You can see the forecast on the NJDEP AQI page or at AirNow.gov, which also has a free phone app.

AQI colorWhat it means
Green, 0 to 50Good
Yellow, 51 to 100Moderate
Orange, 101 to 150Unhealthy for sensitive groups
Red, 151 to 200Unhealthy

On poor air days, NHLBI suggests staying indoors with the windows closed and using an air filter, especially during wildfire smoke. It also warns against cold air, chemical fumes, dust, smoke from cooking and heating fuels, and secondhand smoke. For heat waves, see our guide to cooling centers. The American Lung Association also offers free virtual home assessments to help people with COPD improve indoor air.

What help is there for families and caregivers?

The American Lung Association's free Lung HelpLine at 1-800-586-4872 (press 2) is staffed by registered nurses, respiratory therapists and tobacco treatment specialists. It can help with oxygen resources, insurance questions, finding a specialist and support groups.

The association also offers free Lung Health Navigators and Better Breathers Clubs, support groups for people with lung disease and their families, in person or on Zoom. Find a club on the Better Breathers Club page, and call the facilitator before going, since the association asks members to confirm meeting times. NHLBI also publishes a free COPD Caregiver's Toolkit.

NHLBI suggests keeping things your parent uses often in one easy spot. It also suggests a rolling cart, long-handled grabbers, loose clothes and fewer trips up the stairs. If eating leaves your mom winded, smaller meals more often and resting before meals may help. See our guide to adaptive equipment.

COPD can bring fear, anxiety and depression, NHLBI notes, and treatment helps. If your parent is homebound and needs skilled nursing or therapy, Medicare home health may come to the house. Our guide to Medicare home health care explains the rules. For advanced COPD, palliative care can help with breathlessness and planning, alongside regular treatment.

Questions to bring to the lung doctor:

  • How severe is my COPD, and what do my test numbers mean?
  • Would pulmonary rehab help me, and can you refer me?
  • Am I using my inhalers correctly?
  • Should my oxygen levels be tested, at rest and while walking?
  • What should I do at the first sign of a flare-up?
  • Which vaccines am I missing?

When should we call the doctor or 911?

Call the doctor when symptoms get worse or there are signs of infection, such as a fever. NHLBI says to seek emergency care for a severe flare-up.

Keep the phone numbers for the doctor, the hospital and a person who can drive, plus directions and a current medicine list, where everyone can find them. Our free emergency info sheet has room for all of it.

Watch the heart, too. NHLBI says heart and lung problems often go together, and heart attacks and strokes are more likely during a COPD flare-up and in the weeks and months after. If your parent also has heart failure, see our guide to heart failure care and Medicare.

faq.q: How do I get my mom into pulmonary rehab in NJ?
faq.a: Ask the doctor who treats her COPD for a referral. Medicare Part B covers pulmonary rehab for moderate to very severe COPD (GOLD stages II to IV) when that doctor refers her. Then call the cardiopulmonary rehab department at a nearby hospital, or search the AACVPR program directory, and ask whether the program takes her Medicare plan.

faq.q: How much does pulmonary rehab cost with Medicare?
faq.a: In a doctor's office, your parent pays 20% of the Medicare-approved amount after the Part B deductible ($283 in 2026). In a hospital outpatient department there is also a copayment each session. Medigap can cover much of that share. Medicare Advantage plans set their own copays.

faq.q: Does Medicare pay for home oxygen forever?
faq.a: Medicare pays rent on oxygen equipment for 36 months. After that, the supplier must keep providing oxygen and equipment for as long as it is needed, up to five years from the start. After five years your parent gets new equipment and a new 36-month rental period begins.

faq.q: My dad's oxygen supplier keeps running late on refills. What can I do?
faq.a: Medicare.gov says the supplier must give him the amount of oxygen he needs each month. Call the supplier right away when he runs low. If problems continue, call 1-800-MEDICARE, or get free counseling from NJ SHIP at 1-800-792-8820.

faq.q: Is there free help to quit smoking in New Jersey?
faq.a: Yes. The NJ Quitline at 1-866-657-8677 offers free coaching to residents 18 and older, and people who qualify in its two-call program can get two free weeks of nicotine patches. Medicare also covers up to eight quit-smoking counseling sessions a year at no cost.

faq.q: How do I get air quality alerts for my parent's town?
faq.a: Sign up for EnviroFlash, a free email or text alert service from the EPA and NJDEP, linked from NJDEP's AQI page. You can also check AirNow.gov or its free app. When the AQI is above 100, people with lung disease should limit time outdoors.
