title: Heart failure in older adults: care and Medicare in NJ
dek: The warning signs families should watch, salt and fluid limits, Medicare's cardiac rehab rules, help at home after a hospital stay, and when palliative care fits.
keyFacts: MedlinePlus: call the doctor for a gain of more than 2 to 3 pounds in a day or 5 pounds in a week, unless the doctor sets a different number.
Medicare covers cardiac rehab for stable heart failure with an ejection fraction of 35% or less.
Cardiac rehab: up to 36 sessions, plus 36 if approved. You pay 20% after the $283 Part B deductible (2026).
Medicare home health costs $0 for covered services if your parent is homebound and needs skilled care.
Free Medicare counseling in NJ: SHIP at 1-800-792-8820.
body:
Heart failure means the heart can't pump enough blood and oxygen to meet the body's needs. It does not mean the heart has stopped. For older adults, good heart failure care comes down to daily habits: taking medicines as prescribed, weighing in every morning, cutting salt, and calling the doctor quickly when symptoms change.

In New Jersey, Medicare helps pay for much of that care. Part B covers cardiac rehab for stable chronic heart failure with an ejection fraction of 35% or less. Medicare home health can send a nurse after a hospital stay if your parent is homebound. Palliative care can ease symptoms at any stage. This guide covers the warning signs, salt and fluid, cardiac rehab, help at home and the questions to ask. It is general information, and your parent's cardiologist sets the plan.

What is heart failure in older adults?

Heart failure is a long-term condition in which a weakened or stiff heart can't keep up. The CDC says nearly 6.7 million U.S. adults have it. There is no cure, but treatment can help people live longer, more active lives with fewer symptoms.

The CDC lists coronary artery disease and heart attacks, high blood pressure, diabetes, obesity and heart valve disease among the conditions that raise the risk. Common symptoms are shortness of breath during daily activities, trouble breathing when lying down, tiredness, and weight gain with swelling in the feet, legs, ankles or belly.

Families should know one thing that is easy to miss. NHLBI says older adults who aren't very active may never feel short of breath. Instead, they may seem tired and confused. The American Heart Association (AHA) adds that a caregiver or relative may notice memory problems or confusion before the patient does.

Treatment usually includes several medicines. NHLBI lists water pills (diuretics) and aldosterone antagonists to remove extra fluid, ACE inhibitors and ARBs to relax blood vessels, beta blockers to slow the heart rate, and newer drug groups such as SGLT-2 inhibitors. Each has side effects, so your parent should report anything new rather than quietly skipping doses. Our guide to managing many medications can help keep a long list organized.

Which heart failure symptoms mean we should call the doctor?

Call the doctor for a weight gain of more than 2 to 3 pounds in a day or 5 pounds in a week, new swelling, more shortness of breath, or needing to sit up or use more pillows to breathe at night. Those can mean fluid is building up.

MedlinePlus, from the National Library of Medicine, says to weigh every morning on the same scale, after using the bathroom and before eating, in similar clothes. Write the number down every day. The AHA says to ask the doctor how much gain counts as a problem for your parent, since the number can differ from person to person.

SignWhat to do
Over 2 to 3 lbs in a dayCall the doctor
Over 5 lbs in a weekCall the doctor
New or worse swellingCall the doctor
Short of breath lying downCall the doctor
Possible heart attackCall 911

MedlinePlus also lists these reasons to call: feeling very tired, weak, dizzy or lightheaded; waking up short of breath an hour or two after falling asleep; wheezing; a cough that won't go away or brings up pink, foamy spit; peeing a lot at night; belly pain; side effects from medicines; and a pulse that is very slow, very fast or not steady.

When to call 911

NHLBI says to call 911 any time someone might be having a heart attack, even if you aren't sure. Signs include chest pain, pressure or discomfort, pain in the arms, back, neck or jaw, shortness of breath, sweating a lot for no reason, nausea and sudden dizziness. Don't drive your parent to the hospital. An ambulance crew can start treatment on the way.

The AHA has a free printable symptom tracker. Keep it on the fridge next to the scale. Unsure whether a symptom needs the ER? See our guide to urgent care or the ER.

How much salt and fluid are OK with heart failure?

MedlinePlus says a provider may ask someone with heart failure to keep sodium between 1,500 and 2,300 mg a day. As heart failure gets worse, some are asked to limit fluids to 6 to 9 cups (1.5 to 2 liters) a day. Follow your parent's own doctor, because the right limits vary.

Salt makes the body hold on to fluid, and it makes people thirsty. MedlinePlus warns that much of it hides in foods that don't taste salty, such as soups and canned, frozen and prepared foods. Reading labels together on a grocery trip is a good start. Ask the doctor whether a dietitian visit makes sense.

Some common habits can make heart failure worse. MedlinePlus says pain relievers called NSAIDs, such as ibuprofen and naproxen, can cause the body to hold sodium. Ask the doctor or pharmacist before your parent takes any over-the-counter pain pill. MedlinePlus also advises against alcohol, and suggests asking the pharmacist whether grapefruit juice affects any of your parent's medicines.

Water pills work best at the same time every day. MedlinePlus suggests not taking them right before bed, so your parent isn't up all night. Blood tests check potassium and kidney function.

Does Medicare cover cardiac rehab for heart failure?

Yes, if your parent has stable chronic heart failure with a left ventricular ejection fraction of 35% or less and moderate or worse symptoms (NYHA class II to IV) despite at least six weeks of the best heart failure treatment. Your parent pays 20% after the Part B deductible.

The ejection fraction is the share of blood the heart pumps out with each beat. Ask the cardiologist for your parent's number. Under the federal rule (42 CFR 410.49), heart failure with a higher ejection fraction does not meet the heart failure test on its own. Your parent may still qualify through another condition, such as a heart attack in the last 12 months, bypass surgery, stable angina, a valve repair or replacement, a stent or angioplasty, or a heart transplant.

Cardiac rehab combines exercise prescribed by a doctor, education and counseling on heart risks, and a check on emotional health. A doctor must sign and review the plan every 30 days. Regular cardiac rehab is limited to two one-hour sessions a day, up to 36 sessions over up to 36 weeks, with 36 more if Medicare's contractor approves. Intensive cardiac rehab, offered only by approved programs, allows up to 72 one-hour sessions over up to 18 weeks.

In a doctor's office, your parent pays 20% of the Medicare-approved amount after the $283 Part B deductible (2026). In a hospital outpatient department, there is also a hospital copayment. Medicare Advantage plans set their own copays and networks, so call the plan first. To find a program, ask the cardiologist or the hospital, or use the AACVPR program directory. Several sessions a week means a lot of driving, so see our guide to rides to medical appointments.

What help is there at home after a heart failure hospital stay?

If your parent is homebound and needs skilled care, Medicare home health can send a nurse and therapists to the house at no cost for covered services. A home health nurse can teach daily weights, medicines and warning signs.

Ask the hospital team about home health before discharge. Our guide to Medicare home health care explains who counts as homebound and how to choose an agency. If your parent needs a short stay in rehab first, see rehab after a hospital stay.

  1. Fill every prescription before going home. MedlinePlus recommends it, and compare the new list to the old one.
  2. Set up the scale. Same scale, every morning, numbers on a chart.
  3. Book follow-up visits. Ask when labs for sodium, potassium and kidney function are due.
  4. Clear the kitchen. Swap salty soups and frozen meals for lower-sodium choices.
  5. Ask about cardiac rehab. Ask if your parent qualifies, and get a referral.
  6. Write down who to call. The cardiologist's after-hours number, and what counts as a 911 call.

MedlinePlus says energy returns slowly after a hospital stay, and feeling sad or depressed is common. Your parent may need help with daily tasks at first. Our hospital discharge guide covers the paperwork and what to ask before leaving.

Other conditions affect heart failure too. NHLBI says sleep apnea is common in people with heart failure, and treating it may help symptoms. See our guide to sleep problems in older adults. MedlinePlus recommends flu and COVID-19 shots and asking about a pneumonia shot.

When does palliative care make sense for heart failure?

Palliative care can start at any stage of a serious illness, alongside regular treatment. NHLBI says that when heart failure is very serious, palliative or hospice care can improve quality of life, ease symptoms, avoid unneeded tests and support the family.

Heart failure often follows a pattern of ups and downs, with more hospital stays over time. That is a good moment to talk about goals. Our guides to palliative care in NJ and hospice vs. palliative care explain what Medicare covers. To put your parent's wishes in writing, see advance directives and POLST.

Living with heart failure can bring fear, anxiety and depression. NHLBI says treatment for depression can improve quality of life, and support groups help many people. The AHA runs a free online Support Network for patients and caregivers.

Questions to ask the cardiologist:

  • What type of heart failure does my parent have, and what is the ejection fraction?
  • How much weight gain should make us call, and who do we call after hours?
  • What are the daily limits for sodium and fluids?
  • Does my parent qualify for cardiac rehab?
  • Which over-the-counter medicines should we avoid?
  • Would palliative care help now?

For free help with Medicare costs or plan questions, call NJ SHIP at 1-800-792-8820.

faq.q: How do I help my dad manage heart failure at home?
faq.a: Help him weigh himself every morning on the same scale and write it down, keep his medicines on schedule, and cut back on salty soups and canned or frozen foods. Learn the warning signs, such as a gain of more than 2 to 3 pounds in a day or 5 pounds in a week, and keep the cardiologist's after-hours number handy.

faq.q: Does Medicare pay for cardiac rehab for heart failure?
faq.a: Yes, for stable chronic heart failure with an ejection fraction of 35% or less and NYHA class II to IV symptoms despite at least six weeks of optimal treatment. After the Part B deductible ($283 in 2026), your parent pays 20%, plus a hospital copay in hospital outpatient programs.

faq.q: My mom has heart failure but her ejection fraction is normal. Can she get cardiac rehab?
faq.a: Not under Medicare's heart failure rule alone, which requires an ejection fraction of 35% or less. She may qualify through another condition, such as a heart attack in the past 12 months, bypass surgery, stable angina, a valve repair or replacement, or a stent. Ask her cardiologist.

faq.q: How much salt can someone with heart failure have?
faq.a: MedlinePlus says a provider may set a limit of 1,500 to 2,300 mg of sodium a day. Your parent's own doctor may set a different number, and may also limit fluids.

faq.q: Can someone with heart failure take ibuprofen?
faq.a: Ask the doctor first. MedlinePlus says NSAIDs such as ibuprofen and naproxen can make the body hold on to sodium and worsen heart failure.

faq.q: When should my mother with heart failure go to the ER?
faq.a: Call 911 for chest pain, pressure or other signs of a possible heart attack, or for a severe, sudden change in breathing. Don't drive her yourself. For gradual changes such as weight gain or swelling, call her doctor the same day.

title: Cancer support for older adults in New Jersey
dek: Free screening through NJCEED, what Medicare pays for treatment, finding a cancer center, free rides from the American Cancer Society, and help for caregivers.
keyFacts: NJCEED offers free screening if income is at or below 250% of the federal poverty level and you're uninsured or underinsured: 1-800-328-3838, press 3.
American Cancer Society helpline, 24/7: 1-800-227-2345. It also books free Road To Recovery rides.
Rutgers Cancer Institute in New Brunswick is the only NCI-designated Comprehensive Cancer Center based in NJ.
Part D caps covered drug costs at $2,100 in 2026 and $2,400 in 2027.
NCI Cancer Information Service: 1-800-422-6237, weekdays 9 a.m. to 9 p.m. ET.
body:
Cancer support for older adults in New Jersey comes from a handful of dependable places. Medicare pays for most screening tests and for chemotherapy and radiation. The state's NJCEED program offers free screening to people who are uninsured or underinsured. The American Cancer Society runs a 24-hour helpline and free rides to treatment, and Rutgers Cancer Institute in New Brunswick is the only Comprehensive Cancer Center designated by the National Cancer Institute (NCI) that is based in New Jersey.

This guide is for older adults facing cancer and the family members helping them. It covers free screening, what Medicare pays for treatment, how to choose a doctor and a center, getting to appointments, support for caregivers, and when palliative care fits. It is general information, not medical or legal advice.

Where can my parent get free cancer screening in NJ?

If your parent has Medicare, most screening tests cost nothing when the provider accepts assignment. If your parent is uninsured or underinsured with income at or below 250% of the federal poverty level, the New Jersey Cancer Education and Early Detection program (NJCEED) offers free screening. Call 1-800-328-3838 and press 3.

Medicare testRule and cost
Screening mammogramWomen 40+, yearly, $0
Screening colonoscopyEvery 10 years, or 2 if high risk, $0
PSA blood testMen over 50, yearly, $0
Low-dose lung CTAges 50 to 77 who qualify, yearly, $0

A few details from Medicare.gov matter. If a doctor removes a polyp during a screening colonoscopy, your parent pays 15% of the approved amount, plus a 15% facility coinsurance in a hospital outpatient department or surgery center. The lung CT is for people with no symptoms who smoke now or quit within the past 15 years and have at least a 20 pack-year history, and a counseling visit comes first. Ask the doctor whether a given screening still makes sense at your parent's age and health.

NJCEED, run by the New Jersey Department of Health, covers breast, cervical, colorectal and prostate cancer. Beyond screening, it offers education, case management, follow-up and help getting into treatment. Services run through 21 contracted lead agencies, and every county has at least one. NJCEED is most useful for someone not yet on Medicare. Say your mom is 62, retired early and lost her job's health coverage. She may qualify. The NJCEED page lists screening locations. Ask the local agency about age rules for each test.

What does Medicare cover for cancer treatment?

Part A covers chemotherapy and radiation during a hospital stay. Part B covers them as an outpatient or in a doctor's office or clinic, and your parent usually pays 20% after the deductible. Part D covers most cancer pills, and in 2026 it caps out-of-pocket costs for covered drugs at $2,100 for the year. The cap rises to $2,400 in 2027.

TreatmentWho pays
Hospital stayPart A, $1,736 deductible (2026)
Outpatient chemoPart B, usually 20%
Outpatient radiationPart B, 20% after deductible
Most cancer pillsPart D, $2,100 yearly cap (2026)
Clinical trialsSome costs, like visits and tests

The Part B deductible is $283 in 2026. Medicare.gov says that for chemo in a hospital outpatient setting, the copayment won't be more than the Part A inpatient deductible. Part B also covers some cancer drugs taken by mouth, if the same drug comes in an injectable form, and anti-nausea pills taken before, during or within 48 hours of chemo.

The 20% adds up fast with months of treatment. Original Medicare has no yearly limit on it, which is why many people buy Medigap. See our Medigap guide. If money is tight, check the Medicare Savings Programs and, for prescriptions, PAAD and Extra Help. Our guide to Part D for 2027 explains how to spread drug costs over the year.

With a Medicare Advantage plan, call the plan before treatment starts. Ask whether the oncologist and cancer center are in network, what the copays are, and which treatments need prior approval.

How do we find the right cancer doctor and cancer center?

Start with a referral from your parent's primary doctor, and check that the doctor and center take your parent's Medicare plan. NCI says a second opinion is very common, most doctors welcome it, and it suggests getting one before treatment begins.

NCI's Find a Cancer Center page lists its designated centers by state. In New Jersey, it lists Rutgers Cancer Institute of New Jersey in New Brunswick as a Comprehensive Cancer Center. NCI says Rutgers earned NCI designation in 1997 and comprehensive status in 2002, with Princeton University as its consortium partner. NCI also says Georgetown Lombardi Comprehensive Cancer Center in Washington, D.C., is an NCI-recognized research consortium with John Theurer Cancer Center at Hackensack University Medical Center in Bergen County. Families near New York City or Philadelphia can check the same NCI list for centers across the river.

Many older adults get their care at hospitals closer to home. NCI notes that a cancer team includes more than one kind of doctor. Medical oncologists, radiation oncologists, surgeons and hematologists may all be involved. NCI suggests asking a center whether it has experience treating your parent's kind of cancer and whether it has been rated by state or other groups.

For a second opinion, the new doctor will need the records, including pathology reports, scans and test results. Your parent's doctor can send them. NCI's Cancer Information Service at 1-800-422-6237 (1-800-4-CANCER) can help find a specialist. It is open Monday to Friday, 9 a.m. to 9 p.m. Eastern, in English and Spanish.

  1. Get the diagnosis in writing. The type of cancer, the stage and the pathology report.
  2. Ask who is in charge. Find out who coordinates care and who to call with problems after hours.
  3. Check the plan. Confirm the doctors and center are in network, and ask about prior approval.
  4. Consider a second opinion before treatment starts.
  5. Line up rides. Treatment can mean several visits a week.
  6. Call the American Cancer Society at 1-800-227-2345 for rides, lodging and other help.
  7. Name a health care representative so someone can speak for your parent if needed.

How can my mom get free rides to cancer treatment?

The American Cancer Society's Road To Recovery program gives free rides to cancer-related appointments with trained volunteer drivers. Call 1-800-227-2345 several business days ahead, because rides take time to arrange.

The society says other rules may apply. For example, a caregiver may need to ride along if the patient can't walk without help. Volunteer drivers aren't available everywhere, so ask what serves your parent's town. If treatment is far from home, the society may also help with lodging.

If your parent has NJ FamilyCare, Medicaid covers rides to medical appointments. Counties also run senior and disability transportation. Our guide to rides to medical appointments lists the options.

What support is there for my parent and for us?

The American Cancer Society's helpline at 1-800-227-2345 answers 24 hours a day, seven days a week, with help in more than 200 languages. NCI's Cancer Information Service answers weekdays. Both are free.

The society's cancer information specialists can answer questions about treatment, side effects, pain control, clinical trials and coping. They can also point families to support groups, medical equipment, wigs, financial programs and transportation. Its ACS CARES program offers one-on-one support for patients and caregivers.

Caregivers need help too. NCI says many cancer caregivers look back and wish they had asked for help sooner. Its advice is to take an honest look at what you can and can't do, hand off tasks like meals, errands and rides, and take at least 15 to 30 minutes a day for yourself. Support groups meet in person, by phone and online. Our guides to respite and family leave in NJ and caregiver support groups cover New Jersey options.

If your parent smokes, quitting still helps, even after a diagnosis. NCI's quitline is 1-877-448-7848, and the NJ Quitline is 1-866-657-8677.

When do palliative care and hospice fit in cancer care?

Palliative care can begin at any stage of cancer, alongside chemo, radiation or surgery. It focuses on pain, nausea, fatigue and other symptoms, and on helping the family make choices. Hospice is for when the goal shifts to comfort.

Many families wait too long to ask about palliative care because they think it means giving up. It doesn't. Ask the oncologist whether the cancer center has a palliative care team. Our guides to palliative care in New Jersey and hospice vs. palliative care explain who provides it and what Medicare pays.

Planning ahead takes pressure off later. An advance directive names who speaks for your parent and records their wishes. A POLST form turns those wishes into medical orders for someone who is seriously ill.

Questions to ask the oncologist:

  • Is the goal of this treatment to cure the cancer, control it or ease symptoms?
  • What side effects should we expect, and which ones need a call right away?
  • How many visits a week, and for how long?
  • Is there a nurse navigator or social worker we can call?
  • Are there clinical trials my parent could join?
  • Can we meet the palliative care team now?

faq.q: How do I get my mom free rides to chemo in NJ?
faq.a: Call the American Cancer Society at 1-800-227-2345 and ask about Road To Recovery, which uses volunteer drivers. Call several business days before the appointment. If she has NJ FamilyCare, Medicaid also covers rides to medical appointments, and many counties run senior transportation.

faq.q: Does Medicare pay for chemotherapy?
faq.a: Yes. Part A covers chemo during a hospital stay. Part B covers it in a doctor's office, clinic or hospital outpatient department, where your parent usually pays 20% after the $283 deductible (2026). Part D covers most cancer pills, with a $2,100 out-of-pocket cap on covered drugs in 2026.

faq.q: Who qualifies for free cancer screening through NJCEED?
faq.a: New Jersey residents with income at or below 250% of the federal poverty level who are uninsured or underinsured. It covers breast, cervical, colorectal and prostate cancer screening. Call 1-800-328-3838 and press 3, or find a lead agency in your county on the NJ Department of Health site.

faq.q: Should my dad get a second opinion on his cancer diagnosis?
faq.a: It is his choice, and NCI says second opinions are very common and most doctors welcome them. NCI suggests getting it before treatment starts. His doctor can send the records, and NCI's Cancer Information Service at 1-800-422-6237 can help find a specialist. If he has Medicare Advantage, check the plan's rules first.

faq.q: Is Rutgers Cancer Institute the only NCI-designated cancer center in New Jersey?
faq.a: It is the only one based in the state. NCI lists Rutgers Cancer Institute of New Jersey in New Brunswick as a Comprehensive Cancer Center, a status it has held since 2002. NCI also says John Theurer Cancer Center at Hackensack University Medical Center is part of an NCI-recognized research consortium with Georgetown Lombardi Comprehensive Cancer Center in Washington, D.C. Many people also get cancer care at hospitals closer to home.

faq.q: How can I take care of myself while caring for a parent with cancer?
faq.a: NCI suggests asking for help early, handing off tasks like meals and rides, joining a support group and taking at least 15 to 30 minutes a day for yourself. The American Cancer Society helpline at 1-800-227-2345 can connect caregivers to support, and NJ has respite and family leave programs.

title: Urgent care or the ER? A guide for older adults in NJ
dek: Which symptoms mean 911, what urgent care can safely handle, and what Medicare charges in each place in 2026. A plain guide for older adults and the families who drive them.
keyFacts: Sudden confusion, chest pain, trouble breathing or one-sided weakness means the ER or 911
Medicare Part B covers urgent care at 20% after the $283 deductible (2026)
No ER copays if admitted to the same hospital for a related problem within 3 days
Medicare Advantage plans must cover emergency and urgent care even out of network
NJ Poison Control: 1-800-222-1222, 24 hours a day
body:
Go to the emergency room, or call 911, when a problem could kill or permanently disable your mom or dad. That means chest pain or pressure, trouble breathing, sudden weakness on one side, sudden confusion, a head injury, heavy bleeding or a possible broken bone. Urgent care is for problems that need attention today but are not life threatening, like a sore throat, a sprain, a minor cut or a mild fever. When you are not sure, call 911 or the doctor's after-hours line rather than guessing.

The choice matters for older adults in two ways. Waiting at an urgent care center with a heart attack or stroke costs time that cannot be won back. Going to the ER for a sinus infection costs money and hours. This guide covers the warning signs that call for 911, what urgent care can handle, what Medicare pays in each place in 2026, what to bring, and the quieter problems in older adults that are easy to underrate. It is general information, not medical advice.

When should an older adult go to the ER instead of urgent care?

Go to the ER for anything that might be life threatening or disabling. MedlinePlus, the National Library of Medicine's health site, puts it simply. If a person could die or be permanently disabled, it is an emergency.

MedlinePlus lists these as reasons to go to an emergency department or call 911:

  • Trouble breathing, fainting or passing out
  • Pain in the arm or jaw
  • An unusual or bad headache, especially one that starts suddenly
  • Dizziness or weakness that does not go away
  • Sudden confusion
  • Heavy bleeding, a deep wound or a serious burn
  • A possible broken bone or loss of movement
  • Coughing up or throwing up blood
  • Severe pain anywhere in the body
  • A severe allergic reaction with trouble breathing, swelling or hives
  • Vomiting or diarrhea that does not stop
  • Poisoning or an overdose of a medicine or alcohol
  • A seizure

Heart attacks do not always look like the movies. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) says symptoms include chest discomfort that lasts more than a few minutes or comes and goes, feeling weak or faint, a cold sweat, pain in the jaw, neck, back, arms or shoulders, and shortness of breath. Women are more likely to also have unusual tiredness and nausea or vomiting. If you see these signs in your mom, do not let her talk you into "waiting to see."

Sudden confusion in an older adult is an ER problem, even when the person seems calm.

When should you call 911 instead of driving?

Call 911 when your parent cannot safely wait or travel. MedlinePlus says to call so the emergency team comes to you for choking, stopped breathing, a head injury with fainting or confusion, a neck or spine injury, a severe burn, severe chest pain or pressure, severe shortness of breath, a seizure lasting more than a minute, or suddenly being unable to speak, see, walk or move.

For a possible stroke, call 911 every time. Our stroke signs guide explains the B.E. F.A.S.T. signs and why paramedics, not a family car, should make the trip.

Medicare Part B covers ground ambulance rides when traveling in any other vehicle could endanger your parent's health. You pay 20% of the Medicare-approved amount after the Part B deductible. Medicare covers the trip only to the nearest appropriate facility that can give the care needed. If a non-emergency ride might not be covered, the ambulance company must give a written notice called an Advance Beneficiary Notice before the trip.

For a poisoning or a medicine mix-up where your parent is awake and breathing normally, call the New Jersey Poison Control Center at 1-800-222-1222. It answers 24 hours a day, and you can also text 973-339-0702. If your parent is hard to wake, having a seizure or struggling to breathe, call 911 first.

What can urgent care handle?

Urgent care centers treat common, mild illnesses and minor injuries when your parent cannot get in to see their own doctor soon enough. MedlinePlus lists colds, flu, earaches, sore throats, migraines, low fevers and limited rashes, plus sprains, back pain, minor cuts and burns, minor broken bones and minor eye injuries.

A few cautions for older adults:

  • Know what is on site. Centers differ in whether they have X-rays, lab work or someone who can stitch a wound. Call ahead and ask.
  • Bring the full medicine list. An urgent care doctor does not know your dad's history. A common antibiotic or cough medicine can interact with blood thinners or heart drugs.
  • Expect to be sent on. If the staff think the problem is more serious, they will send your parent to the ER. That is the system working.
  • Tell the regular doctor. Ask for a visit summary and send it to the primary care office so the record stays in one place.

Two other options sit between urgent care and doing nothing. Many doctors' offices have an after-hours line answered by a nurse or doctor on call, and many health plans run a free nurse advice line. Medicare also covers telehealth visits from anywhere in the U.S., including home, through December 31, 2027. You pay the same 20% coinsurance as for an in-person visit. Save these numbers in your parent's phone now, along with the closest ER and urgent care center.

What does Medicare pay for urgent care and the ER?

Both are covered by Medicare Part B, but the ER usually costs your parent more. In 2026 the Part B deductible is $283 a year.

WhereWhat Original Medicare patients pay
Urgent care20% of the approved amount after the Part B deductible. A hospital-run center can add a copay.
ER visitA copay for the visit, a copay for each hospital service, and 20% of the doctor's bill after the deductible.
Admitted within 3 daysNo ER copays if admitted to the same hospital for a related problem. Medicare counts the visit as part of the inpatient stay.
Ambulance20% of the approved amount after the deductible.
Telehealth20% after the deductible, same as in person.

MedlinePlus notes that care in an emergency department can cost two to three times or more than the same care in a doctor's office. A Medigap policy or retiree plan may pick up some of these costs. Our guide to Medicare Advantage vs. Medigap explains how each works.

Medicare Advantage plans

If your parent has a Medicare Advantage plan, the plan sets its own copays for urgent care and the ER, often as flat dollar amounts. Check the plan's Evidence of Coverage or call the number on the card. Medicare.gov says your parent can always get emergency care and urgent care when needed, even from a doctor or hospital outside the plan's network. Bring the plan card, not the red, white and blue Medicare card.

Every ER must see your parent

A federal law, the Emergency Medical Treatment and Labor Act, requires hospitals that take part in Medicare and offer emergency services to give a medical screening exam to anyone who asks for emergency care, regardless of ability to pay. If an emergency condition is found, the hospital must stabilize the patient or arrange an appropriate transfer.

One more word to know. If your parent stays the night, ask whether they are an inpatient or "under observation." It changes the bill and whether Medicare will later pay for rehab. Our hospital discharge guide explains observation status.

What should you bring to the ER or urgent care?

A few minutes of gathering saves hours of questions. Keep a bag or folder ready.

  1. The medicine list. Every prescription, over-the-counter drug, vitamin and supplement, with the dose and how often. Our free emergency info sheet has a space for this.
  2. Insurance cards. With Original Medicare, bring the Medicare card plus any Medigap or retiree card. With Medicare Advantage, bring the plan card instead. If the card is lost, a Medicare.gov account lets you print a copy.
  3. Advance directive and POLST. Bring copies of any advance directive or POLST form your parent has.
  4. Glasses, hearing aids and dentures. Older adults understand and answer questions better when they can see and hear.
  5. Doctor names and numbers. The primary care doctor and any specialists, like a cardiologist.
  6. A phone charger and a short list of family contacts. ER waits can be long.
  7. Your notes. When symptoms started, what changed and what your parent has eaten or taken today.
Numbers to save in your parent's phone

Emergency: 911. NJ Poison Control: 1-800-222-1222 (text 973-339-0702). Suicide and Crisis Lifeline: call or text 988. Medicare: 1-800-633-4227. Add the doctor's after-hours line, the plan's nurse line, the nearest ER and the nearest urgent care center.

What if your parent falls, seems confused or reacts badly to a medicine?

These three are the situations families most often underrate.

A fall

The CDC counts about 4.5 million emergency department visits a year from falls by older adults. It says an older person who falls and hits their head should see a doctor right away to make sure there is no brain injury, and that head injuries can be especially serious for people who take blood thinners. If your dad takes a blood thinner and bumps his head, get him checked that day even if he says he feels fine. Call 911 if he cannot get up, may have broken a bone, or is confused or drowsy. Our fall prevention guide covers what helps afterward.

Sudden confusion

MedlinePlus lists sudden confusion as a reason to go to the ER. In older adults it can come from an infection, dehydration, a new medicine or a stroke. It can also be delirium, a sudden change in attention and thinking that is a medical problem in its own right. Read our guide to delirium after surgery or a hospital stay to learn the signs.

A bad reaction or a double dose

If your mom took too much of a pill or the wrong one and seems okay, call Poison Control for advice. If she has trouble breathing, swelling of the face or throat, or is hard to wake, call 911. Bring the pill bottles with you.

If your parent talks about hurting themselves, call or text 988, or call 911. Do not leave them alone.

What happens after the visit?

Follow up matters as much as the visit itself.

  • Get the paperwork. Ask for the discharge instructions and the list of any new prescriptions. Read them before you leave.
  • Fill new prescriptions at the usual pharmacy so the pharmacist can check them against everything else your parent takes.
  • Call the primary care doctor within a day or two. Ask whether they want to see your parent and whether any old medicine should stop.
  • Watch the first night. Older adults can be more confused after a long ER visit. If your parent is worse rather than better, call the doctor or go back.
  • Check the bills. Compare the Medicare Summary Notice or plan statement with what actually happened. If Medicare denies something your parent needed, you can appeal. See our guide to Medicare appeals in New Jersey.

Frequent ER trips are a signal too. If your parent has been to the ER several times this year, ask the doctor about a fuller look at medicines, falls and memory. A primary care doctor who knows older adults well can head off many of those visits. Our guide to finding a geriatrician in New Jersey explains where to start.

faq.q: How do I know if my mom should go to urgent care or the ER?
faq.a: Go to the ER or call 911 for anything that could be life threatening: chest pain or pressure, trouble breathing, sudden confusion, sudden weakness on one side, a head injury, heavy bleeding or a possible broken bone. Urgent care is for colds, flu, sore throats, sprains, minor cuts and burns and similar problems. If you are unsure, call her doctor's after-hours line or 911.

faq.q: My dad fell and hit his head but says he is fine. Does he need to be seen?
faq.a: Yes. The CDC says an older person who falls and hits their head should see a doctor right away to check for a brain injury, and that head injuries are especially serious for people on blood thinners. Call 911 if he is confused, drowsy, vomiting or cannot get up.

faq.q: Does Medicare cover urgent care?
faq.a: Yes. Medicare Part B covers urgently needed care. With Original Medicare your parent pays 20% of the Medicare-approved amount after the Part B deductible, which is $283 in 2026. A hospital outpatient setting can add a copayment. Medicare Advantage plans set their own copays.

faq.q: Does Medicare Advantage cover the ER outside the network?
faq.a: Yes. Medicare.gov says people in Medicare Advantage plans can always get emergency care and urgent care when needed, even if the doctor or hospital is not in the plan's network. Copays depend on the plan.

faq.q: Can an ER turn my parent away for not having money or insurance?
faq.a: No. Under the federal Emergency Medical Treatment and Labor Act, hospitals that take part in Medicare and offer emergency services must give a medical screening exam to anyone who asks for emergency care, and must stabilize an emergency condition or arrange an appropriate transfer, regardless of ability to pay.

faq.q: Who do I call if my parent took the wrong pills?
faq.a: If your parent is awake and breathing normally, call the New Jersey Poison Control Center at 1-800-222-1222, 24 hours a day, or text 973-339-0702. If they are hard to wake, having a seizure or struggling to breathe, call 911.

title: Delirium after surgery or a hospital stay: signs for NJ families
dek: Sudden confusion after surgery is common in older adults, often missed, and partly preventable. The signs to watch for, how it differs from dementia, and what to ask the hospital team.
keyFacts: Delirium affects 25% or more of hospitalized adults 65+ after major surgery or illness (NIA)
The quiet, sleepy form makes up as much as 75% of cases and is easy to miss (AGS)
The Hospital Elder Life Program cut new delirium by 40% in a trial of 852 patients 70+ (NEJM, 1999)
NJ law lets inpatients name a caregiver who must be told of discharge and taught after-care tasks
Recovery often takes a week or more and can take months in people 85+ or with dementia
body:
Delirium is a sudden change in attention, awareness and thinking. In older adults it often starts within a few days of surgery or a serious illness, and it can come and go within the same day. Your dad may be sharp in the morning and confused, agitated or unusually sleepy by evening. It is a medical problem that needs prompt attention, and families are often the first to notice it because they know what normal looks like.

Delirium is common, often missed and partly preventable. The National Institute on Aging (NIA) says it affects 25% or more of hospitalized adults 65 and older after major surgery or acute illness. Simple steps that families can help with, like glasses, hearing aids, sleep and getting out of bed, are part of the programs shown to lower the risk. This guide explains the signs, how delirium differs from dementia, what to do and ask in the hospital, and what recovery looks like at home. It is general information, not medical advice.

What is delirium, and how common is it after surgery?

Delirium is a sudden state of confusion caused by a physical illness, a medicine or the stress of surgery. The American Geriatrics Society (AGS) describes it as a problem with attention, awareness and thinking that comes on quickly and changes often. Other names you may hear are "acute confusional state" and "acute brain syndrome."

GroupHow often delirium occurs
Age 65+ after major surgery or illness25% or more (NIA)
Age 70+ in the hospitalAbout one in three (AGS)
High-risk surgery, like a broken hipUp to half (AGS)
Older adults in intensive careMore than 80% (NIA)
Older adults arriving at the ERUp to 15% (AGS)

The NIA lists these risk factors for delirium after surgery: memory or thinking problems before surgery, certain medicines, poorly controlled pain, constipation, fever, infection, depression, alcohol use, lack of sleep, low oxygen and being unable to move. Long operations such as heart surgery and hip fracture repair add risk. The NIA says that without other risk factors, current evidence suggests anesthesia alone is unlikely to cause delirium.

The AGS also uses a memory aid for reversible causes, spelling DELIRIUM: drugs, electrolyte and fluid problems, lack of drugs (such as stopping sleeping pills or alcohol too suddenly, or too little pain medicine), infection, reduced vision or hearing, problems inside the skull such as a stroke or head injury, urinary and bowel problems, and heart and lung disease. Often there is more than one cause.

How is delirium different from dementia?

Delirium comes on over hours to days and swings up and down. Dementia develops gradually and steadily affects memory and reasoning. A person can have both, and people with dementia are more likely to develop delirium.

DeliriumDementia
StartSudden, hours to daysGradual
Main problemAttention and alertnessMemory and reasoning
Day to dayComes and goesFairly steady
CauseIllness, medicine, surgeryBrain disease
OutlookOften improves when the cause is treatedUsually progressive

The difference matters. Staff who do not know your mom may assume her confusion is "just her dementia" or "just her age." If you know she was managing her own checkbook last week, say so clearly. The NIA notes that delirium in people with dementia can worsen their decline, and that delirium in people without memory problems may signal a higher risk of later cognitive impairment. Either way, it deserves a workup.

You are the only person in the room who knows what your parent was like last Tuesday.

What are the signs families should watch for?

Look for a change from your parent's normal self, especially one that comes and goes. The AGS gives four key signs:

  1. Trouble concentrating or following a conversation
  2. Changes in behavior, personality, mood or attention
  3. Changes in awareness, being either very alert or very drowsy
  4. Any change in function, such as sleeping more or eating less

Other signs include talking that does not make sense, not knowing the time or place, seeing things that are not there, restlessness, new incontinence, and being more alert in the morning and worse at night.

The quiet kind is the one that gets missed

Delirium comes in three forms. In hyperactive delirium a person is restless, agitated or very alert. In hypoactive delirium they are sleepy, move less and seem unaware of what is going on. Mixed delirium switches between the two, sometimes within a single day.

The AGS says the hypoactive, or quiet, form happens in up to 75% of people with delirium, and health care providers may assume it is depression. It also says health care professionals do not recognize delirium in up to half of the people who have it. If your mom is usually chatty and now barely responds, or dozes through a visit from her grandchildren, tell the nurse that it is new.

After you get home

Delirium can start or continue after discharge. If your parent becomes suddenly confused at home, call the doctor that day. If they are very drowsy, cannot stay awake, have a fever or trouble breathing, or you suspect a fall, call 911. Our guide to urgent care or the ER lists the signs that need an emergency room.

What can families do to help prevent delirium in the hospital?

Quite a lot. The NIA describes two programs proven to prevent delirium. One, the Hospital Elder Life Program (HELP), lowered new cases of delirium by 40% in its first controlled trial, which followed 852 hospital patients 70 and older and was published in the New England Journal of Medicine in 1999. Both rely on having a familiar person present, making sure the patient has glasses and hearing aids, allowing uninterrupted sleep, and getting the patient moving as soon as possible. The AGS adds fluids, a normal day and night routine, and avoiding risky medicines where non-drug options will do.

  1. Pack the senses. Bring glasses, hearing aids with fresh batteries and dentures, and make sure they are actually in use.
  2. Help with orientation. Mention the day, date and place in normal conversation. A large calendar, a clock and a few family photos help. Written signs help people with memory problems.
  3. Protect sleep. Ask whether overnight vital signs or medicines can be timed to avoid waking your parent. Ask about cutting night noise. Open the blinds for bright morning light.
  4. Get moving. Ask when your parent can sit in a chair and walk with help. The AGS suggests moving about three times a day when possible.
  5. Encourage fluids and meals. Help with the tray and offer drinks unless the team has limited them.
  6. Bring the full medicine list, including sleep aids, allergy pills and anything bought over the counter.
  7. Be there, in shifts. The AGS notes many hospitals let family stay overnight with a person who has delirium or is at high risk. Ask about the hospital's policy and split nights among siblings or trusted friends.

Medicines are a big piece. The AGS says drugs that lower the brain chemical acetylcholine, including some medicines for anxiety, sleep, pain, depression and allergies, are more likely to cause delirium. The NIA lists antihistamines, sleep aids, antipsychotics, muscle relaxants and bladder drugs among medicines that can affect thinking in older adults. Do not stop a prescribed medicine on your own. Ask the team to review every one. Our guide to managing many medications has more on this.

Planning surgery? Ask whether the team will check your parent's thinking beforehand. An NIA report notes that not enough hospitals check thinking before elective surgery in patients 65 and older, though it helps spot who is at risk.

What should you ask the hospital team?

Be specific and keep a notebook. Useful questions include:

  • "Is my mother being screened for delirium? How often?"
  • "Does this hospital have a delirium prevention program, such as HELP, or a geriatrics team we can ask for?"
  • "What could be causing this? Has she been checked for infection, dehydration, constipation and trouble urinating?"
  • "Which of her medicines could be adding to the confusion? Can any be stopped or lowered?"
  • "How is her pain being managed?" Untreated pain is a risk factor too.
  • "Can she get out of bed today, and who will help her?"
  • "Can a family member stay overnight?"
  • "Will you avoid restraints?" The AGS says physical or drug restraints should not be used in most cases because they can harm the person, with narrow exceptions in intensive care.

The AGS says medicines are generally not effective for delirium and can cause severe side effects. They are used only rarely, for severe symptoms. Treatment means finding and fixing the causes and creating a safe, familiar, calm setting.

Name yourself as the caregiver

New Jersey's caregiver law, P.L. 2014, c. 68, requires hospitals to give each patient the chance to name a caregiver. If your parent names you and signs consent to share medical information, the hospital must notify you of a discharge or transfer, no later than when the discharge order is written. Before a discharge home, it must also consult with you on a discharge plan and show you how to do any after-care tasks, with a live or recorded demonstration and time for your questions. A parent with delirium may not remember the instructions, so this matters.

Being named caregiver under that law is not the same as being your parent's health care representative, and it does not oblige you to do the after-care tasks. If your parent cannot decide, the person named as health care representative in an advance directive speaks for them. If nothing is in place, read our guide to advance directives in New Jersey once things settle.

How long does recovery take, and what happens at home?

Many people recover within days to weeks, but some take months. MedlinePlus says delirium often lasts about a week and it may take several weeks for thinking to return to normal. The NIA says the swings usually fade within a week or two. The AGS says delirium may last weeks to months in older adults, and recovery is slowest when it is severe, when the person has dementia, or when they are 85 or older.

Delirium can also have effects that last. The NIA links it to readmission within 30 days, ER visits, falls and discharge to a long-term care facility, and says people who have had delirium show a steeper decline in thinking over later years on average. That is a reason to take it seriously. It is not a prediction for your parent.

Planning the trip home

  • Do not rush to judge. A parent who is confused at discharge may improve a great deal over the next few weeks. Make short-term plans before permanent ones.
  • Arrange supervision. The AGS says a person returning home with delirium needs monitoring so everyone stays safe. That may mean family staying over, a short rehab stay or home health care. Our guides to hospital discharge, rehab after a hospital stay and Medicare home health care explain the options and the Medicare rules.
  • Keep the routine steady. Same meals, same chair, lights on in the day and dim at night, glasses and hearing aids in.
  • Watch falls. Delirium is a leading risk factor for falls. See our fall prevention guide.
  • Book a follow-up visit within a week or two. Ask the doctor to recheck medicines and thinking. If memory problems remain after recovery, Medicare's yearly Wellness visit includes a cognitive assessment, and Medicare covers a separate, more detailed visit to check for dementia, depression, anxiety or delirium when there is a concern. Our memory screening guide explains next steps.
When to call right away

Call your parent's doctor the same day for any new or worse confusion after a hospital stay. Call 911 if they are hard to wake, have trouble breathing, have chest pain, or may have fallen and hit their head. For general questions about dementia and memory, the NIA's ADEAR Center answers at 1-800-438-4380.

Delirium is hard on families, too. Watching a parent not recognize you, even for an afternoon, is frightening. Take turns, sleep when you can, and ask the county office on aging about respite if recovery stretches on.

faq.q: My mom has been confused since her hip surgery. Is that dementia?
faq.a: Not necessarily. Confusion that starts suddenly after surgery and comes and goes is a classic sign of delirium, which is common after hip fracture repair. Tell the care team that the change is new and ask them to look for causes such as infection, dehydration, pain, constipation or medicines. People with dementia can also get delirium on top of it.

faq.q: How can I help prevent delirium for my dad in the hospital?
faq.a: Make sure he has his glasses, hearing aids and dentures. Mention the date and place, bring a calendar and photos, help him eat and drink, ask the team to protect his sleep and get him up and walking as soon as it is safe, and give them a full medicine list. Ask whether family can stay overnight.

faq.q: How long does delirium last in older adults?
faq.a: MedlinePlus says it often lasts about a week and thinking may take several weeks to return to normal. The American Geriatrics Society says it can last weeks to months in older adults, with slower recovery when it is severe, when the person has dementia or is 85 or older.

faq.q: What is hypoactive delirium?
faq.a: It is the quiet form of delirium. The person is sleepy, slow and withdrawn instead of agitated. The American Geriatrics Society says it accounts for up to 75% of cases and may be mistaken for depression.

faq.q: Are there medicines for delirium?
faq.a: The American Geriatrics Society says medicines are generally not effective for delirium and can cause severe side effects. They are used rarely, for severe symptoms. Treatment focuses on finding and fixing the causes and keeping the person safe, calm and oriented.

faq.q: Will the hospital tell me when my parent is being discharged?
faq.a: Under New Jersey's caregiver law, hospitals must give inpatients the chance to name a caregiver. If your parent names you and consents to sharing information, the hospital must notify you of the discharge, and before a discharge home it must consult you on the discharge plan and show you how to do after-care tasks.

sources: Researchers test new approaches to prevent delirium in older adults, National Institute on Aging
A multicomponent intervention to prevent delirium in hospitalized older patients, Inouye et al., New England Journal of Medicine, 1999
Preventing delirium in older adults: Hospital Elder Life Program, Commonwealth Fund
Delirium: Basic facts, American Geriatrics Society, HealthInAging.org (updated May 2023)
What is dementia? Symptoms, types, and diagnosis, National Institute on Aging
Cognitive health and older adults, National Institute on Aging (reviewed June 11, 2024)
N.J.S.A. 26:2H-5.28, hospital to consult with designated caregiver
seoDesc: Delirium after surgery or a hospital stay is common in older adults and often missed. Signs, how it differs from dementia, and how NJ families can help.

title: Free printable medication list for older adults in NJ
dek: A one-page medication record for your mom or dad: every medicine, dose, reason, prescriber and start date, plus supplements and allergies. How to fill it in, when to update it, and how to get rid of old pills in New Jersey.
keyFacts: NIA says a medicine list should include each medicine or supplement, the amount, the times taken, the prescribing doctor and the reason.
NIA says to show the list to every provider, including physical therapists and dentists.
Medicare's yearly wellness visit includes a review of current prescriptions, at no cost if the provider accepts assignment.
Medicare drug plans must offer a free medication review, with a written summary and medication list, to members who qualify.
NJ Project Medicine Drop boxes are inside participating police headquarters, available seven days a week, 365 days a year, and anonymous.
body:
A printable medication list is one page that records every medicine your mom or dad takes: the name and dose, when they take it, what it is for, who prescribed it and when they started. It also covers over-the-counter pills, vitamins, supplements, allergies and the pharmacy. Fill in our free sheet below, keep it current, and bring it to every doctor visit and every hospital trip.

This is the full record. Our emergency info sheet is the short summary on the fridge for paramedics, and its medicines line can simply say "see medication list." Keep this longer sheet in the grab folder, in your parent's wallet or purse, and as a photo on your phone.

Why keep a written medication list for a parent?

Because nobody else has the whole picture. Each doctor, the pharmacy and the hospital may see only part of what your parent takes. The list is the one place it all comes together.

The National Institute on Aging (NIA) says people 65 and older tend to take more medicines than any other age group. Many see a primary doctor and two or three specialists, and each one prescribes from their own records. The cardiologist may not know about the sleep aid from the drugstore shelf. The dentist may not know about the blood thinner.

A written list earns its keep at a few specific moments.

  • At a new doctor. Intake forms ask for every medicine and dose. Handing over a page is faster and more accurate than remembering.
  • In the ER. Staff need to know about blood thinners, insulin, heart medicines and allergies right away.
  • After a hospital stay. Medicines are often stopped, started or changed. The old list shows exactly what changed.
  • When someone else steps in. The sibling filling the pill box this week and the aide on Thursday work from the same page.
  • When something feels off. If Dad is suddenly dizzy or foggy, the start dates show what is new.
The start date column is the easiest one to skip, and often the best clue to a new side effect.

What should go on a medication list?

Every medicine, in every form, with enough detail that a stranger could refill it. NIA recommends writing the name of each medicine or supplement, the amount, the times it is taken, the prescribing doctor and the reason for it.

ColumnWhat to write
Medicine, doseName and strength from the label
WhenTimes of day, with food or not
What forPlain words, like blood pressure or sleep
PrescriberThe doctor who ordered it
StartedMonth and year

Then add the things people forget.

  • Over-the-counter medicines. Pain relievers, antacids, allergy pills, sleep aids and laxatives. NIA says to mention everything, even ones used only now and then.
  • Vitamins and supplements. Fish oil, calcium, vitamin D, herbal products. Ask the pharmacist whether any of them interact with the prescriptions.
  • Anything that isn't a pill. Eye drops, inhalers, creams, patches, injections and nasal sprays.
  • "As needed" medicines. Write how often your parent actually uses them.
  • Allergies and bad reactions. The drug and what happened, such as a rash, swelling or trouble breathing. If there are none, write "none known" so nobody wonders whether the line was skipped.
  • The pharmacy. Name and phone. NIA suggests filling all prescriptions at one pharmacy so the records are in one place.

Copy names and strengths exactly as the label prints them, including "mg" or "mcg." If the bottle shows a generic name and your mom calls it by the brand, write both. Leave Medicare and insurance ID numbers off. The plan name is enough.

How do we fill it in the first time?

Do it once, carefully, at the kitchen table with your parent and every bottle in the house. It takes about an hour. After that, updates take a minute.

  1. Gather everything. Bring every bottle, box, tube and inhaler to one table. Check the bathroom, the bedside drawer, the purse and the car.
  2. Fill in the sheet from the labels. Ask your parent what each one is for and when they really take it. The answer may not match the label, and the doctor needs to know that.
  3. Check it with the pharmacist. Ask the pharmacy for a printout of current prescriptions and compare. Ask about anything that looks doubled up or out of date.
  4. Make copies. NIA suggests keeping one at home and one in a wallet or purse. Add a photo on your phone and a copy for the sibling or aide who helps most.
  5. Set two review dates a year. Pick dates that are easy to remember, like a birthday and the fall clock change.

How often should we update the list?

Every time anything changes, and twice a year even if nothing did. Write the date at the bottom so anyone can tell how current it is.

Changes come more often than families expect. A new prescription, a dose change at a checkup, a medicine stopped in the hospital, a supplement a friend swore by. When a medicine stops, cross it out and move it to the "stopped" lines with the date and the reason. That history helps when a doctor later asks whether a drug was tried before.

If a side effect shows up, write it down too. NIA advises against stopping a medicine because of uncomfortable side effects before talking with a health care provider. Bring the note to the next visit, or call the office sooner if it is serious.

Should we bring the list to every doctor visit and to the hospital?

Yes. NIA says to show the list to all of your health care providers, including physical therapists and dentists. Bring the paper or the photo even when you think the office already has it.

At each visit, ask the doctor to look at the whole list, including medicines other doctors prescribed. A few questions worth asking:

  • Is there anything on this list my mom no longer needs?
  • Could any of these cause dizziness, confusion or falls?
  • Do any of them interact with each other or with her supplements?
  • Is there a lower cost version of any of these?
  • What should we do if she misses a dose?

Medicare's yearly wellness visit includes a review of current prescriptions, and your parent pays nothing for it if the provider accepts assignment. That is a good day to bring the bottles as well as the list.

For a hospital stay, put the list in the bag first. Our hospital stay checklist covers what else to pack. At discharge, ask for the updated list and redo this sheet that day. Our guide to when a parent leaves the hospital explains why medicine mix-ups after discharge are so common. If your parent struggles to keep track day to day, our guide to managing many medications covers pill organizers, blister packs and pharmacist reviews.

Can Medicare pay for a pharmacist to review the list?

Often, yes. Every Medicare drug plan must offer a medication therapy management program, and members who qualify get a free review with a written summary and a medication list. Call the number on the drug plan card to ask whether your parent qualifies. For free help with drug plan questions, call New Jersey's State Health Insurance Assistance Program (SHIP) at 1-800-792-8820. If the cost of the medicines is the problem, see our guide to PAAD, New Jersey's prescription help program.

How do we get rid of old medicines in New Jersey?

Take them to a Project Medicine Drop box inside a participating police headquarters. The NJ Division of Consumer Affairs runs the program and says the boxes are anonymous and available seven days a week, 365 days a year.

Call the station first to ask what its box accepts. Pharmacy kiosks, take back days and the FDA's rules for the trash and the flush list are in our medication management guide.

Wrong pill or a double dose?

Call New Jersey Poison Control at 1-800-222-1222, 24 hours a day. Have the medication list and the bottle in hand when you call. If your parent is unconscious or having trouble breathing, call 911.

faq.q: How do I make a medication list for my mom?
faq.a: Gather every bottle, box, inhaler and tube in the house, including vitamins and over-the-counter pills. For each one write the name and strength, when she takes it, what it is for, who prescribed it and when she started. Add allergies and her pharmacy, check it against a pharmacy printout, and date it.

faq.q: What is the difference between a medication list and an emergency info sheet?
faq.a: The emergency info sheet is a one-page summary on the fridge for paramedics, with doctors, conditions, allergies and contacts. The medication list is the full record of every medicine with dose, timing, reason, prescriber and start date. The fridge sheet can say "see medication list."

faq.q: Should vitamins and supplements go on my dad's medication list?
faq.a: Yes. The National Institute on Aging says to list all medicines, including over-the-counter drugs, and to mention everything to the doctor, even ones used only now and then. Some supplements interact with prescriptions, so ask the pharmacist.

faq.q: How often should a medication list be updated?
faq.a: Every time a medicine starts, stops or changes dose, after every hospital stay, and at least twice a year. Write the date at the bottom each time.

faq.q: Does Medicare pay for a medication review?
faq.a: Part D plans must offer a free medication therapy management program to members who meet certain requirements. It includes a review of their medicines, a written summary and a medication list. Call the drug plan to ask whether your parent qualifies. The yearly wellness visit also includes a review of current prescriptions.

faq.q: Where can I drop off old medicines in New Jersey?
faq.a: At a Project Medicine Drop box inside a participating police headquarters, run by the NJ Division of Consumer Affairs. The boxes are anonymous and available seven days a week, 365 days a year. Call the station first to ask what its box accepts. Pharmacy kiosks and take back events are other options.
